The total is 8,580, and the chapter closes, twice over, with the seal on every chapter so far: as the LORD commanded. Four chapters have ordered a nation counted, a camp arranged, a tribe substituted, a workforce assigned, and not one arrangement was somebody’s good idea.

Each one with his task of serving or carrying. That is not a bad summary of a life, and the difference between drudgery and worship is not in the weight of the load but in who assigned it.

And there is a shadow over the whole arrangement. All this careful holiness exists because God had come to live among a people who could not survive him. Every layer of goatskin says: he is here, and you cannot come. Then a man walked into the middle of the camp with no covering over him, touched lepers and they were made clean, and took the distance away: for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father (Eph. 2:18). The Kohathites carried the presence of God without daring to look at it. We are invited to look, and it has a human face.

4.theology:
The Peril and Glory of Holiness. God’s holiness is a consuming reality; his nearness is both Israel’s glory and her peril. The coverings are mercy, allowing sinful men to serve and live.

Mediation Before Approach. There is no access to the glory of God except through appointed mediation, fulfilled in Christ, who alone handled the glory and clothes us to draw near.

Every Servant Assigned. Each clan, each man, each peg is named and counted. In the body of Christ every member is gifted, placed and precious.
4.examples:
Then: The holy things were wrapped in blue and borne on poles, untouched and unseen; every Levite knew his task, from the ark to the tent pegs.

Now: What the Kohathite could not touch, you behold in the face of Christ and live. Approach the holy God with reverence, clothed in his righteousness, and take up your appointed burden in his house by the Spirit who gifted you for it, for no faithful service is overlooked by the God who counts every servant by name.

5.title: Laws on Uncleanness and Unfaithfulness
5.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel that they put out of the camp everyone who is leprous or has a discharge and everyone who is unclean through contact with the dead.<sup>3</sup>You shall put out both male and female, putting them outside the camp, that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell."<sup>4</sup>And the people of Israel did so, and put them outside the camp; as the LORD said to Moses, so the people of Israel did.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>6</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, When a man or woman commits any of the sins that people commit by breaking faith with the LORD, and that person realizes his guilt,<sup>7</sup>he shall confess his sin that he has committed. And he shall make full restitution for his wrong, adding a fifth to it and giving it to him to whom he did the wrong.<sup>8</sup>But if the man has no next of kin to whom restitution may be made for the wrong, the restitution for wrong shall go to the LORD for the priest, in addition to the ram of atonement with which atonement is made for him.<sup>9</sup>And every contribution, all the holy donations of the people of Israel, which they bring to the priest, shall be his.<sup>10</sup>Each one shall keep his holy donations: whatever anyone gives to the priest shall be his."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>12</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, If any man's wife goes astray and breaks faith with him,<sup>13</sup>if a man lies with her sexually, and it is hidden from the eyes of her husband, and she is undetected though she has defiled herself, and there is no witness against her, since she was not taken in the act,<sup>14</sup>and if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife who has defiled herself, or if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife, though she has not defiled herself,<sup>15</sup>then the man shall bring his wife to the priest and bring the offering required of her, a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. He shall pour no oil on it and put no frankincense on it, for it is a grain offering of jealousy, a grain offering of remembrance, bringing iniquity to remembrance.<sup>16</sup>"And the priest shall bring her near and set her before the LORD.<sup>17</sup>And the priest shall take holy water in an earthenware vessel and take some of the dust that is on the floor of the tabernacle and put it into the water.<sup>18</sup>And the priest shall set the woman before the LORD and unbind the hair of the woman's head and place in her hands the grain offering of remembrance, which is the grain offering of jealousy. And in his hand the priest shall have the water of bitterness that brings the curse.<sup>19</sup>Then the priest shall make her take an oath, saying, 'If no man has lain with you, and if you have not turned aside to uncleanness while you were under your husband's authority, be free from this water of bitterness that brings the curse.<sup>20</sup>But if you have gone astray, though you are under your husband's authority, and if you have defiled yourself, and some man other than your husband has lain with you,<sup>21</sup>then' (let the priest make the woman take the oath of the curse, and say to the woman) 'the LORD make you a curse and an oath among your people, when the LORD makes your thigh fall away and your body swell.<sup>22</sup>May this water that brings the curse pass into your bowels and make your womb swell and your thigh fall away.' And the woman shall say, 'Amen, Amen.'<sup>23</sup>"Then the priest shall write these curses in a book and wash them off into the water of bitterness.<sup>24</sup>And he shall make the woman drink the water of bitterness that brings the curse, and the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain.<sup>25</sup>And the priest shall take the grain offering of jealousy out of the woman's hand and shall wave the grain offering before the LORD and bring it to the altar.<sup>26</sup>And the priest shall take a handful of the grain offering, as its memorial portion, and burn it on the altar, and afterward shall make the woman drink the water.<sup>27</sup>And when he has made her drink the water, then, if she has defiled herself and has broken faith with her husband, the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain, and her womb shall swell, and her thigh shall fall away, and the woman shall become a curse among her people.<sup>28</sup>But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, then she shall be free and shall conceive children.<sup>29</sup>"This is the law in cases of jealousy, when a wife, though under her husband's authority, goes astray and defiles herself,<sup>30</sup>or when the spirit of jealousy comes over a man and he is jealous of his wife. Then he shall set the woman before the LORD, and the priest shall carry out for her all this law.<sup>31</sup>The man shall be free from iniquity, but the woman shall bear her iniquity."
5.overview:
With the camp ordered, chapter 5 turns to its purity. The unclean are put outside, wrongs are confessed and restored, and suspected unfaithfulness in marriage is brought before God in a solemn ordeal. The governing reason is stated plainly: “in the midst of which I dwell.” Holiness is not fussiness but the response to the nearness of a holy God.

The ordeal of bitter water is one of Scripture’s strangest passages, yet it reveals a God who defends the wronged and brings hidden things to light. And the chapter points to Christ, who suffered outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12), drank the cup of God’s wrath in our place (Mark 14:36), and brings the defiled back into the dwelling of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Putting the Unclean Outside the Camp
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who are ceremonially unclean must be put outside the camp because God dwells in its midst.
verseByVerse.theology: The presence of God demands the purity of his dwelling place; holiness flows from his nearness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the unclean put outside the camp. Now: Christ bore our uncleanness outside the camp to bring us in.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel that they put out of the camp everyone who is leprous or has a discharge and everyone who is unclean through contact with the dead. You shall put out both male and female, putting them outside the camp, that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell." And the people of Israel did so, and put them outside the camp; as the LORD said to Moses, so the people of Israel did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three conditions put a man outside the camp, and the reason is given without softening: that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell.

Skin disease, bodily discharge and contact with a corpse are all forms of the body coming apart: decay, leakage, death. They are not sins; none is anybody’s fault. They are the visible marks of a world under the curse, and where the Author of life dwells, the evidences of death are put at a distance.

It was a hard command, and Israel obeyed it: families put out their own relatives. These laws were temporary, reversible and had cleansing built in; but a man carrying his sick brother’s bedding to the edge of the camp was not consoled by that on the day.

Under this law uncleanness spreads and holiness does not. Then a leper knelt before Jesus, and Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him (Mark 1:41), and the contamination did not travel up his arm; the cleansing travelled down it. In him holiness proved the more contagious of the two. The camp had to put its unclean outside. He went outside and brought them in.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprous” covers several skin diseases (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When a person wrongs another and so breaks faith with the LORD, they must confess, make full restitution, and add a fifth.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin against a neighbor is sin against God; true repentance includes confession and concrete restitution.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: full restitution with a fifth added. Now: gospel repentance bears the fruit of confession and restored relationships.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, When a man or woman commits any of the sins that people commit by breaking faith with the LORD, and that person realizes his guilt, he shall confess his sin that he has committed. And he shall make full restitution for his wrong, adding a fifth to it and giving it to him to whom he did the wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law turns to wrongs between people. The offence is theft or fraud against a neighbour, and God calls it breaking faith with the LORD.

If I cheat a man in business, what has God got to do with it? Everything. There is no purely horizontal sin, because every person you deal with belongs to God and every dealing happens in his presence. David said it of a sin that had ruined two other lives: Against you, you only, have I sinned (Ps. 51:4).

Then the shape of real repentance, in three steps. He realizes his guilt: a sin, not a mistake or a difficult season. He shall confess it, named specifically, not deplored in general. And he shall make full restitution, adding a fifth: the money goes back, and more than went missing. All of it happens inside the covenant, before the God who has already made a way back for the guilty.

Zacchaeus went further still. When Christ came into his house he offered four times over (Luke 19:8), the penalty for a stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1), and Jesus did not tell him to sit down. Notice the order: Jesus came to him first, and the restitution followed. Grace has never made restitution unnecessary. It is what finally makes it possible, and the Spirit of Christ still gives the will to make things right.

verseByVerse.quote: But if the man has no next of kin to whom restitution may be made for the wrong, the restitution for wrong shall go to the LORD for the priest, in addition to the ram of atonement with which atonement is made for him. And every contribution, all the holy donations of the people of Israel, which they bring to the priest, shall be his. Each one shall keep his holy donations: whatever anyone gives to the priest shall be his."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a case that closes the last door: if the wronged man has no next of kin, the restitution for wrong shall go to the LORD for the priest. In every human system a debt with no claimant evaporates. God’s law says the money is still owed, and he receives it himself.

There is no such thing as a wrong that has outlived its victim. Time does not discharge a debt and neither does a funeral.

Read alone, that is very bad news, because most of us have wronged people we can no longer find. Read in the light of the whole Bible, it is the reason the cross was necessary and the reason it is enough. Every debt is owed ultimately to God, which is precisely why it had to be settled with God, and was.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–31 — The Ordeal of Bitter Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A husband suspecting his wife of unfaithfulness brings her to the priest for a solemn ordeal that exposes guilt or vindicates innocence.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who sees in secret defends the wronged and brings hidden sin to light, refusing to let unfaithfulness corrode his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: bitter water to test hidden unfaithfulness. Now: every hidden thing will be brought to light before the One who judges righteously.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, If any man's wife goes astray and breaks faith with him, if a man lies with her sexually, and it is hidden from the eyes of her husband, and she is undetected though she has defiled herself, and there is no witness against her, since she was not taken in the act, and if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife who has defiled herself, or if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife, though she has not defiled herself, then the man shall bring his wife to the priest and bring the offering required of her, a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. He shall pour no oil on it and put no frankincense on it, for it is a grain offering of jealousy, a grain offering of remembrance, bringing iniquity to remembrance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the section that troubles modern readers most: a husband suspects his wife of adultery and cannot prove it. There is no evidence and no witness. And twice over the law describes the man: the spirit of jealousy comes over him whether she has defiled herself or though she has not defiled herself.

That double clause is the key to the passage. The law explicitly contemplates that the woman may be entirely innocent and the man simply consumed.

Without this statute, a jealous husband in the ancient world had no procedure and no restraint: she could be divorced, disgraced, put out or worse, at his discretion. This law takes the matter out of his hands. He may not act. He must bring it to the priest, in public, and let God decide. The grain offering of jealousy has no oil and no frankincense, none of the marks of a joyful offering. Nobody is meant to enjoy this.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the priest shall bring her near and set her before the LORD. And the priest shall take holy water in an earthenware vessel and take some of the dust that is on the floor of the tabernacle and put it into the water. And the priest shall set the woman before the LORD and unbind the hair of the woman's head and place in her hands the grain offering of remembrance, which is the grain offering of jealousy. And in his hand the priest shall have the water of bitterness that brings the curse. Then the priest shall make her take an oath, saying, 'If no man has lain with you, and if you have not turned aside to uncleanness while you were under your husband's authority, be free from this water of bitterness that brings the curse. But if you have gone astray, though you are under your husband's authority, and if you have defiled yourself, and some man other than your husband has lain with you, then' (let the priest make the woman take the oath of the curse, and say to the woman) 'the LORD make you a curse and an oath among your people, when the LORD makes your thigh fall away and your body swell. May this water that brings the curse pass into your bowels and make your womb swell and your thigh fall away.' And the woman shall say, 'Amen, Amen.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ceremony is deliberately strange: holy water, dust from the tabernacle floor, and the written curse washed off the scroll into the cup.

There is nothing in that cup that could harm anybody, and that is the design. Other ancient Near Eastern ordeals worked differently: the accused was thrown into a river, and the river did the damage. Israel’s ordeal has no mechanism at all. If anything happens to this woman, God did it. The verdict is removed from the water, the priest and above all the husband, and placed with the only one who knows.

Nor is she a passive victim. The priest states the oath in both directions, be free from this water if innocent, and she answers for herself: Amen, Amen. An innocent woman had every reason to say it loudly, because the only power in the cup was the God who knew she had done nothing.

Why only wives? Adultery by either partner was a capital crime under the law (Lev 20:10). This rite dealt with suspicion without evidence, and it protected the wife from a jealous husband’s violence by putting the verdict in God’s hands. It was part of Israel’s ceremonial law and does not apply today. The NIV’s “miscarry” in verse 21 is an interpretation; the curse is on the woman’s ability to bear children, and the text does not describe an abortion.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the priest shall write these curses in a book and wash them off into the water of bitterness. And he shall make the woman drink the water of bitterness that brings the curse, and the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain. And the priest shall take the grain offering of jealousy out of the woman's hand and shall wave the grain offering before the LORD and bring it to the altar. And the priest shall take a handful of the grain offering, as its memorial portion, and burn it on the altar, and afterward shall make the woman drink the water. And when he has made her drink the water, then, if she has defiled herself and has broken faith with her husband, the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain, and her womb shall swell, and her thigh shall fall away, and the woman shall become a curse among her people. But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, then she shall be free and shall conceive children. "This is the law in cases of jealousy, when a wife, though under her husband's authority, goes astray and defiles herself, or when the spirit of jealousy comes over a man and he is jealous of his wife. Then he shall set the woman before the LORD, and the priest shall carry out for her all this law. The man shall be free from iniquity, but the woman shall bear her iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second outcome is the one usually forgotten: if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, then she shall be free and shall conceive children. She is not merely acquitted but publicly blessed, with vindication before the community and children in her arms. The gossip ends the day she walks out cleared by God himself, and no husband can reopen it.

She is not merely acquitted. She is blessed, publicly, with the very thing a woman under this suspicion most needed — vindication in front of the whole community and children in her arms. The gossip in that camp ends the day she walks out of the tabernacle cleared by God himself. No husband can reopen it. No neighbour can whisper about it. A jealous man had one route available to him and it was a route that could exonerate his wife beyond any possibility of appeal.

The law is a hard one and belongs to a world not ours. But its direction is clear. It removes a woman from the power of a man who cannot prove anything; forbids him to act on his own suspicion; costs him an offering; stages the matter before God rather than in the household; and gives the innocent a public verdict she could get no other way. In its own world, this statute protects. Nothing in it licenses a jealous or controlling husband today: suspicion is not proof, a spouse who threatens or harms is sinning gravely, and anyone in that danger should seek safety at once and tell the church’s elders.

Verse 31 says the husband shall be free from iniquity: he does not sin by bringing a genuine suspicion to God rather than acting on it himself. A man eaten by a jealousy he cannot resolve has somewhere to take it. A suspicion, about a marriage or anything else, wants to fester or explode. Scripture offers a third way: casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet. 5:7). Let him be the judge, because he is, and you are not.

5.theology:
Holiness Because God Dwells. Every purity command flows from the presence of the holy God. Where God lives, the marks of sin and death cannot remain.

Repentance That Restores. Sin against a neighbor is breaking faith with the LORD; true repentance confesses the specific sin and makes full restitution.

The God Who Sees in Secret. The ordeal reveals a God who exposes hidden sin, defends the innocent, and brings every secret thing to light before the righteous Judge.
5.examples:
Then: The unclean were put outside, wrongs were restored with a fifth added, and hidden unfaithfulness was brought before God, because the holy God dwelt in Israel’s midst.

Now: Christ went outside the camp bearing your uncleanness, drank the cup you deserved, and was the faithful one in your place, so that your standing rests on his record, not yours. Walk in the light by his Spirit, confess your sins, make things right with those you have wronged, and when you fail, come back to the One who knows every secret and yet declares you clean.

6.title: The Nazirite Vow and the Priestly Blessing
6.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When either a man or a woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD,<sup>3</sup>he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink. He shall drink no vinegar made from wine or strong drink and shall not drink any juice of grapes or eat grapes, fresh or dried.<sup>4</sup>All the days of his separation he shall eat nothing that is produced by the grapevine, not even the seeds or the skins.<sup>5</sup>"All the days of his vow of separation, no razor shall touch his head. Until the time is completed for which he separates himself to the LORD, he shall be holy. He shall let the locks of hair of his head grow long.<sup>6</sup>"All the days that he separates himself to the LORD he shall not go near a dead body.<sup>7</sup>Not even for his father or for his mother, for brother or sister, if they die, shall he make himself unclean, because his separation to God is on his head.<sup>8</sup>All the days of his separation he is holy to the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"And if any man dies very suddenly beside him and he defiles his consecrated head, then he shall shave his head on the day of his cleansing; on the seventh day he shall shave it.<sup>10</sup>On the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two pigeons to the priest to the entrance of the tent of meeting,<sup>11</sup>and the priest shall offer one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, and make atonement for him, because he sinned by reason of the dead body. And he shall consecrate his head that same day<sup>12</sup>and separate himself to the LORD for the days of his separation and bring a male lamb a year old for a guilt offering. But the previous period shall be void, because his separation was defiled.<sup>13</sup>"And this is the law for the Nazirite, when the time of his separation has been completed: he shall be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting,<sup>14</sup>and he shall bring his gift to the LORD, one male lamb a year old without blemish for a burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish as a sin offering, and one ram without blemish as a peace offering,<sup>15</sup>and a basket of unleavened bread, loaves of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil, and their grain offering and their drink offerings.<sup>16</sup>And the priest shall bring them before the LORD and offer his sin offering and his burnt offering,<sup>17</sup>and he shall offer the ram as a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD, with the basket of unleavened bread. The priest shall offer also its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>18</sup>And the Nazirite shall shave his consecrated head at the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall take the hair from his consecrated head and put it on the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace offering.<sup>19</sup>And the priest shall take the shoulder of the ram, when it is boiled, and one unleavened loaf out of the basket and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the Nazirite, after he has shaved the hair of his consecration,<sup>20</sup>and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. They are a holy portion for the priest, together with the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed. And after that the Nazirite may drink wine.<sup>21</sup>"This is the law of the Nazirite. But if he vows an offering to the LORD above his Nazirite vow, as he can afford, in exact accordance with the vow that he takes, then he shall do in addition to the law of the Nazirite."<sup>22</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>23</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, Thus you shall bless the people of Israel: you shall say to them,<sup>24</sup>The LORD bless you and keep you;<sup>25</sup>the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you;<sup>26</sup>the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.<sup>27</sup>"So shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them."
6.overview:
Chapter 6 gives two of the most beautiful provisions in the Law: the Nazirite vow of consecration, and the priestly benediction by which God puts his name upon his people. Together they answer chapter 5’s question, how a sinful people can dwell with a holy God: by consecration and by blessing.

Both find their fulfillment in Christ. He was not a Nazirite (he drank wine), yet he is the perfectly consecrated One the vow pictured, who set himself apart for his people (John 17:19) and was never defiled by sin; and he is the great High Priest who, lifting his hands at Bethany (Luke 24:50–51), blessed his people and ascended, the face of God shining upon us forever in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Nazirite Vow of Consecration
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Any Israelite may take a vow of special consecration, abstaining from the vine, leaving the hair uncut, and avoiding all contact with the dead.
verseByVerse.theology: Total devotion to the LORD is open to all his people, not priests alone; consecration touches every part of life.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Nazirite set apart by visible signs. Now: every believer called to wholehearted consecration to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When either a man or a woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD, he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink. He shall drink no vinegar made from wine or strong drink and shall not drink any juice of grapes or eat grapes, fresh or dried. All the days of his separation he shall eat nothing that is produced by the grapevine, not even the seeds or the skins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things are remarkable before the vow is even described. The first is the word: Nazirite means “one separated, or one consecrated”, from the same root as the holy crown on the high priest’s turban. This is a person made, for a season, into something like a consecrated object.

The second is either a man or a woman. Everything else in Numbers so far has been determined by birth: priest, Levite, soldier. This is the first arrangement anybody may enter, and the only qualification is wanting to. A woman or a shepherd from the smallest clan could take on a consecration close to a priest’s. Holiness is not rationed to the professionals.

The first sign is abstinence from the vine, to almost comic lengths: not even the seeds or the skins. Nothing is said against wine itself; Scripture calls it a gift that gladdens the heart of man (Ps. 104:15). That is why it is chosen. The Nazirite lays down for a season a legitimate joy, not a sin, so completely that even a raisin is out.

Is the Nazirite vow for today? Samson, Samuel and John the Baptist were Nazirites for life, and Paul cut his hair because of a vow (Acts 18:18), perhaps a Nazirite one, and later joined four men completing theirs (Acts 21:23–26). The vow belonged to the ceremonial law, fulfilled in Christ, and no Christian is bound to it. Jesus was a “Nazarene”, from Nazareth (Matt 2:23), not a Nazirite; he drank wine (Luke 7:34). What remains is the call to belong wholly to God (Rom 12:1).
verseByVerse.note: “Nazirite” means “one separated” or “one consecrated” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "All the days of his vow of separation, no razor shall touch his head. Until the time is completed for which he separates himself to the LORD, he shall be holy. He shall let the locks of hair of his head grow long. "All the days that he separates himself to the LORD he shall not go near a dead body. Not even for his father or for his mother, for brother or sister, if they die, shall he make himself unclean, because his separation to God is on his head. All the days of his separation he is holy to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second sign is public: uncut hair. Everyone could see a Nazirite coming; he carried his vow on his head, where neither he nor anybody else could forget it.

The third sign is the hardest thing in the chapter: no contact with the dead, not even for his father or for his mother. Word comes that his mother has died, and he may not touch the body or stand at the grave. Ordinary priests could bury their parents (Lev. 21:2–3); only the high priest was held to this. For the length of his vow, an ordinary Israelite is bound tighter than a priest.

The reason is not squeamishness: his separation to God is on his head. Death is what has gone wrong with the world, and this man has put himself, for a season, on the side of life. And one greater than any Nazirite would walk up to a coffin, touch it, and say Young man, I say to you, arise (Luke 7:14). He did not have to keep away from death. Death had to keep away from him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if any man dies very suddenly beside him and he defiles his consecrated head, then he shall shave his head on the day of his cleansing; on the seventh day he shall shave it. On the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two pigeons to the priest to the entrance of the tent of meeting, and the priest shall offer one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, and make atonement for him, because he sinned by reason of the dead body. And he shall consecrate his head that same day and separate himself to the LORD for the days of his separation and bring a male lamb a year old for a guilt offering. But the previous period shall be void, because his separation was defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the case nobody can plan for: a man dies suddenly beside him. He did nothing wrong and could not have prevented it, and is defiled. He must shave his head, bring a sin offering, a burnt offering and a lamb for a guilt offering, and begin again from day one: The previous period shall be void. Eleven months of a twelve-month vow, wiped.

Two things must be said, and both are needed. First, defilement is objective, not measured by intention: a man can be entirely innocent and entirely unclean at once. That is uncomfortable to modern ears, and it is the plain teaching of the passage.

Second, there is a way back, provided in the same breath. God does not say the man is disqualified. He says: here is the sacrifice, start again. Anybody who has had a long, good work ruined by something they did not do knows the sick feeling of verse 12. God’s answer is not to pretend the damage did not happen. It is a lamb, and a new first day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Completion of the Vow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the days of separation are fulfilled, the Nazirite brings offerings, shaves his head, and burns the hair on the altar.
verseByVerse.theology: Consecration culminates in joyful sacrifice and offering; the dedicated life is given back to God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the completed vow sealed with sacrifice. Now: the consecrated life offered to God as a living sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the law for the Nazirite, when the time of his separation has been completed: he shall be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting, and he shall bring his gift to the LORD, one male lamb a year old without blemish for a burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish as a sin offering, and one ram without blemish as a peace offering, and a basket of unleavened bread, loaves of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil, and their grain offering and their drink offerings. And the priest shall bring them before the LORD and offer his sin offering and his burnt offering, and he shall offer the ram as a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD, with the basket of unleavened bread. The priest shall offer also its grain offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the days are complete, the Nazirite does not simply walk away. He comes to the door of the tent with a whole procession of offerings, each with its meaning.

Among them is a sin offering. A man at the summit of his devotion, who has gone without wine for a year and stayed away from his own family’s funerals, cannot conclude the thing without an animal to atone for his sin.

That guards against the trap that waits for the serious. The more a man gives up for God, the more he begins to think it counts for something. Israel’s law shut that door at the moment it was most likely to open: the ceremony celebrating a completed consecration required him to confess he was still a sinner who needed blood. The vow had not made him acceptable. He kept it because he was already the Lord’s, and the one whose consecration was flawless offered it for us.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Nazirite shall shave his consecrated head at the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall take the hair from his consecrated head and put it on the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace offering. And the priest shall take the shoulder of the ram, when it is boiled, and one unleavened loaf out of the basket and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the Nazirite, after he has shaved the hair of his consecration, and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. They are a holy portion for the priest, together with the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed. And after that the Nazirite may drink wine. "This is the law of the Nazirite. But if he vows an offering to the LORD above his Nazirite vow, as he can afford, in exact accordance with the vow that he takes, then he shall do in addition to the law of the Nazirite."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the strangest moment: he shaves his consecrated head at the entrance and puts the hair on the fire under the peace offering. The hair is the vow, the sign everybody recognised him by, and he burns it.

He does not keep it. There is no relic, no memento, nothing to show anybody afterwards. The entire outward evidence of his devotion goes up in smoke on the altar, and he walks home with a shaved head looking like everybody else. That is where genuine consecration ends — not in a trophy but in an offering, and not in the man being visibly holier but in God being given the whole thing back.

Then the Nazirite may drink wine. There is no suggestion that the abstaining life was superior. The season of separation was real and it was a season. Most of the Christian life is lived after the hair is burned, in the ordinary run of things, and it is no less consecrated for that.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives Aaron and his sons the words by which they are to bless Israel, putting the divine name upon the people.
verseByVerse.theology: God himself is the source of all blessing; the priest is only the channel of the name and favor of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priest pronouncing God’s name over Israel. Now: the face of God shines upon us forever in Christ, our great High Priest.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, Thus you shall bless the people of Israel: you shall say to them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the chapter turns. God has spent five chapters ordering this camp; now he gathers it up and gives his people a blessing, and he does not leave the wording to the priest. He dictates it.

Aaron does not compose a benediction out of his own goodwill; he is handed a script. What the people hear at the end of every service is not their priest’s hope for them but God’s declaration over them, in God’s own words, through a man’s mouth. That is why a benediction is not a closing prayer and should never be spoken as one. It is not the minister asking God to be kind; it is God telling the congregation what he is.

And these particular words have outlived everything around them. A silver amulet inscribed with this blessing, dug up in a tomb outside Jerusalem, is older than the Dead Sea Scrolls by centuries (see the note on v. 24). Israel wore these lines round her neck into the grave.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD bless you and keep you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing comes in three lines, each beginning with the covenant name, so that the name falls on the congregation three times. Each line is longer than the last: in Hebrew three words, then five, then seven. The blessing swells as it goes.

To bless is to give good: the harvest, the child, the rain. To keep is the watchman’s word, to guard what has been given. Blessing without keeping is worth little: good things are given and then lost, the health, the marriage, the years. So the first thing God says over his people is that he gives and then stands over what he has given.

Jesus made the word his own on the last night: I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost (John 17:12). In Numbers 6 the keeping was a blessing over a camp in a desert. In his mouth it is a report.
verseByVerse.note: The Aaronic (priestly) blessing. A version of it, on two tiny silver scrolls found in Jerusalem and dated to about 600 BC, is the oldest known copy of any biblical text.

verseByVerse.quote: the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second line rises from what God gives to what God is toward his people. A shining face lights up when it sees you, as a father’s does when a child comes into the room, and because it is involuntary we trust it more than words.

Its opposite is the terror of the Old Testament: How long will you hide your face from me? (Ps. 13:1); Hide not your face from me (Ps. 27:9). A hidden face is worse than anger: the absence of regard, the sense that God has turned away to something else. And here God commands his priests to tell his people, week after week, that his face is turned toward them and lit up.

Run the test on yourself. Not what you believe about God’s existence, or his power, or even his forgiveness — but this: when God looks at you, what is his face doing? Most people who have any belief at all imagine something between disappointment and patience. This verse says otherwise, and the New Testament says where the light comes from: God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor. 4:6). If you want to know what the face of God looks like when it is turned toward sinners, there is a face, and it looked at Peter across a courtyard after he had denied it three times (Luke 22:61).

verseByVerse.quote: the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third line is the summit. To lift up his countenance is to raise the eyes and hold the look: not a glance, attention.

The last word is shalom, which English flattens into the absence of trouble. Shalom is wholeness: everything in its place, nothing broken, nothing missing. It is what a room is like when the quarrel is over, what a body feels when the illness has gone, and what a life is when its accounts with God are settled.

Gifts, then a face, then peace. And Paul gives the word an address: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 5:1). Aaron asked shalom for a people who would be in open rebellion within five chapters, not knowing how it would be paid for. It cost the life of the one who is himself our peace (Eph. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: "So shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then God explains what has happened: So shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them.

Read the benediction again and count: the LORD, the LORD, the LORD. Three times the name is spoken, and God says that is the transaction. The priest is not describing a blessing; he is placing the name of God on a people, as a brand on a possession or a signature on a deed. Israel walks away carrying the name of the God who owns them.

And it is God, not the priest, who blesses. Aaron supplies the mouth. That is a relief to anybody who has sat under a preacher he did not admire, and a warning to anybody in the pulpit. The words carry because of whose they are.

The New Testament blesses the same way, and it is no accident that the church’s benedictions are built on this pattern. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all (2 Cor. 13:14) — three lines, and the name three times over, and the name is now known to be Father, Son and Spirit. What Aaron placed on Israel in a wilderness, the church places on her people every Sunday. And Christ himself, at the very end, closed, after his last words to them, with a blessing: lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven (Luke 24:50–51). He went up with his hands in the air over his people, and nothing has happened since to make him put them down.

6.theology:
Consecration for All. The Nazirite vow opened priestly devotion to any Israelite, man or woman. Holiness is not the preserve of a clerical caste; every believer may relinquish good things to declare that God is better.

God Is the Source of Blessing. The priest only pronounces; God himself blesses. The threefold benediction puts the divine name upon his people, guaranteed by his pledge, “I will bless them.”

Christ the Consecrated High Priest. Jesus is the wholly consecrated One the vow pictured, who touched our death and conquered it, and the High Priest in whose face the light of God shines upon us forever.
6.examples:
Then: Israelites took the Nazirite vow to be wholly the LORD’s, and Aaron put God’s name upon the people.

Now: You live under a greater benediction: the face of God shines upon you in Christ, who has put the Father’s name upon you and given you peace. Out of that, and by his Spirit, hold even good things loosely for the joy of nearness to God.

7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the longest chapter in Numbers, and at first glance the most tedious: twelve tribal chiefs bring identical offerings for the dedication of the altar, recorded twelve separate times, day by day. Yet the repetition is the sermon. Every gift is the same, so none is greater or lesser before God; each is recorded separately, so none is overlooked. We are equal before God, yet known individually.

The chapter closes with God speaking to Moses from above the mercy seat. The dedication of the altar leads to communion, and it all points to Christ, in whom every offering finds its meaning and through whom God speaks to us still.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Wagons and Oxen for the Levites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the tabernacle’s dedication, the chiefs bring wagons and oxen, distributed to the Gershonites and Merarites for transport.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides means for the service he commands; the gifts of the people equip the work of his house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: wagons given for carrying the tabernacle. Now: God supplies what his church needs to bear his glory forward.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day when Moses had finished setting up the tabernacle and had anointed and consecrated it with all its furnishings and had anointed and consecrated the altar with all its utensils, the chiefs of Israel, heads of their fathers' houses, who were the chiefs of the tribes, who were over those who were listed, approached and brought their offerings before the LORD, six wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon for every two of the chiefs, and for each one an ox. They brought them before the tabernacle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This chapter is a flashback. The tent was raised on the first day of the first month of the second year (Exod. 40:17), a month before Numbers 1 opens; the episode is told here because it belongs with the ordering of the camp.

The first thing that happens after the dwelling place of God is finished is that the leaders bring him a present. Nobody asked them to; no command requires it.

And what they brought was six wagons and twelve oxen. Not gold or incense, nothing that would be seen inside the tent. Transport. Somebody had worked out that a tabernacle which has to be dismantled, carried across a wilderness and reassembled needs carts.

It is the least glamorous gift in the chapter and the first recorded. There is a kind of giving that looks hard at the actual work and asks what would make it possible, and it rarely produces anything anybody admires. God took the wagons.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Accept these from them, that they may be used in the service of the tent of meeting, and give them to the Levites, to each man according to his service." So Moses took the wagons and the oxen and gave them to the Levites. Two wagons and four oxen he gave to the sons of Gershon, according to their service. And four wagons and eight oxen he gave to the sons of Merari, according to their service, under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest. But to the sons of Kohath he gave none, because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God accepts, and distributes them to each man according to his service. Gershon, carrying curtains and coverings, gets two wagons; Merari, carrying frames, bars and bases, dead weight in timber and metal, gets four. The provision is matched to the burden.

But Kohath gets none, because the holy things went on the shoulder. Kohath had the highest privilege in the camp and no help at all. The most sacred load in Israel was walked on human shoulders for forty years. There is no shortcut for the holiest work, and the men given the greatest honour had the sorest backs.

Centuries later a king forgot this verse. David brought the ark up to Jerusalem on a new cart (2 Sam. 6:3) — new, expensive, respectful, and expressly forbidden here. The oxen stumbled, Uzzah reached out, and a man died on a happy afternoon. It was not irreverence that killed him. It was a good idea substituted for an explicit instruction. God had said shoulders.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–88 — The Twelve Days of Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For twelve days, one chief each day brings an identical offering for the dedication of the altar; each is recorded separately.
verseByVerse.theology: God receives each worshiper individually; the repetition declares that no offering is lost in the crowd, and all are equal before him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: twelve identical gifts, each named and recorded. Now: every act of worship seen, valued, and received by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the chiefs offered offerings for the dedication of the altar on the day it was anointed; and the chiefs offered their offering before the altar. And the LORD said to Moses, "They shall offer their offerings, one chief each day, for the dedication of the altar."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the theological centre of the chapter: one chief each day. Twelve days.

The gifts were identical, and the whole thing could have been done in one magnificent morning, twelve men stepping forward together. It would have been more impressive and vastly more efficient. God spread it over nearly a fortnight so that every man got a day of his own. Elizur of Reuben had the fourth day to himself, with the whole camp watching him and nobody else.

That is not administrative eccentricity. It is a decision about how God receives what people bring him, and the next seventy verses make it unmistakable.

verseByVerse.quote: He who offered his offering the first day was Nahshon the son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah. And his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Nahshon the son of Amminadab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah goes first, as at the muster and on the march, and Nahshon brings the gift that all twelve will bring.

See it once, because the reader will meet it eleven more times. Silver plate and basin full of fine flour and oil: the grain offering, the produce of a life. A golden dish of incense: prayer. A bull, a ram and a lamb for a burnt offering, given wholly to God. A goat for a sin offering, because even at a dedication sin has to be answered. And the peace offering, the meal shared with God and each other.

Everything a person can bring to God is in that list: the food off his table, his prayers, his whole self, his guilt, and his company. Nothing is missing, and nothing in the twelve days will be added to it.
