This was the offering of Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai. On the eleventh day Pagiel the son of Ochran, the chief of the people of Asher: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Pagiel the son of Ochran. On the twelfth day Ahira the son of Enan, the chief of the people of Naphtali: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Ahira the son of Enan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now sixty-six verses in which nothing new is said: day two, Issachar, the same; day three, Zebulun, the same. Twelve times in full, in the longest chapter of the five books of Moses.

Any editor would cut it: say it once, add “the remaining eleven brought the same”, and save four pages. God evidently thought something would be lost. Summarised, eleven of these men would have become “the others.” Instead every one has his name, tribe, father, day and inventory written into the word of God. Nobody is a footnote to the man who went first.

The arrangement rules out a second thing. Because every gift was identical, nobody could outgive anybody. There was no largest offering and no smallest, no chief who could be admired for his generosity and none who could be quietly ashamed on his day. Twelve men, twelve equal gifts, twelve equal days. God designed a ceremony in which competition was structurally impossible, which anybody who has ever watched a collection plate go round will recognise as a mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: This was the dedication offering for the altar on the day when it was anointed, from the chiefs of Israel: twelve silver plates, twelve silver basins, twelve golden dishes, each silver plate weighing 130 shekels and each basin 70, all the silver of the vessels 2,400 shekels according to the shekel of the sanctuary, the twelve golden dishes, full of incense, weighing 10 shekels apiece according to the shekel of the sanctuary, all the gold of the dishes being 120 shekels; all the cattle for the burnt offering twelve bulls, twelve rams, twelve male lambs a year old, with their grain offering; and twelve male goats for a sin offering; and all the cattle for the sacrifice of peace offerings twenty-four bulls, the rams sixty, the male goats sixty, the male lambs a year old sixty. This was the dedication offering for the altar after it was anointed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the totals, and one number stands out. Burnt offerings and sin offerings run to twelve of each kind; the peace offerings run to sixty rams, sixty goats and sixty lambs, with twenty-four bulls.

The peace offering is far and away the largest item — more than four times the rest put together. And the peace offering is the one that gets eaten. The burnt offering went up in smoke entirely; the sin offering dealt with guilt; the peace offering was cooked, shared out, and consumed by the worshippers and the priests together, in God’s presence, as a meal.

So the largest element in the dedication of Israel’s altar was dinner. The place where sin was dealt with was inaugurated with a shared feast, which is the direction the whole Bible runs, from a lamb eaten in Egypt, to a table in an upper room, to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9). God settles the sin so that he can sit down and eat with people.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 89 — God Speaks from the Mercy Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Moses entered the tent to speak with God, he heard the voice from above the mercy seat, between the cherubim.
verseByVerse.theology: The dedication of the altar opens the way to communion; the gifts of the people lead to the voice of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God’s voice from between the cherubim. Now: God speaks to us in his Son, from the throne of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Moses went into the tent of meeting to speak with the LORD, he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat that was on the ark of the testimony, from between the two cherubim; and it spoke to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, after twelve days of giving, one verse of receiving, the verse the chapter has been waiting for: God speaks from above the mercy seat.

The geography is the theology. Inside the ark were the tablets of the law Israel had already broken, silently condemning everybody in the camp. Over the box was a slab of gold called the kapporet, the mercy seat: a lid, where once a year the high priest sprinkled blood. And at either end, two cherubim, the creatures who had guarded the way back into Eden (Gen. 3:24).

God does not speak from inside the box. He speaks from the lid — from above the broken law, out of the space where the blood goes, between the two guardians who had once been posted to keep men out. If the voice had come from the tablets it would have had nothing to say to Israel but the sentence. It comes from the covering.

The Greek Old Testament translated kapporet with the word Paul uses of Christ: whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith (Rom. 3:25). God still does not speak to sinners over the law they have broken; he speaks from the place where the blood was applied, and that place is a person.

The chiefs gave for twelve days, and at the end of it the tent was not silent. That is what the whole apparatus was for — not so that Israel could give God things, but so that God could talk to Israel. He had come down to live in the middle of the camp, and he wanted to speak.

7.theology:
God Receives Each One Individually. No worshiper is lost in the crowd; God knows and welcomes each by name, giving each his own day at the altar.

Equal Yet Known. The identical offerings teach that all come to God on the same terms, by the same blood; the separate records, that each is known with perfect particularity.

The Voice from the Mercy Seat. Communion with God comes only over the blood-covered mercy seat, fulfilled in Christ, the true propitiation, through whom God now speaks to us.
7.examples:
Then: Twelve chiefs each brought identical gifts on his own day, and the dedication opened the way to the voice of God.

Now: You are never a statistic to God. You come to him on the same ground as every other believer, the blood of Christ, and he receives your worship individually and speaks to you in his Son. Give freely as the chiefs did, not to be noticed, and draw near to hear the voice from the mercy seat.

8.title: The Levites Consecrated: Cleansed and Given to God
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to Aaron and say to him, When you set up the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light in front of the lampstand."<sup>3</sup>And Aaron did so: he set up its lamps in front of the lampstand, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>4</sup>And this was the workmanship of the lampstand, hammered work of gold. From its base to its flowers, it was hammered work; according to the pattern that the LORD had shown Moses, so he made the lampstand.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>6</sup>"Take the Levites from among the people of Israel and cleanse them.<sup>7</sup>Thus you shall do to them to cleanse them: sprinkle the water of purification upon them, and let them go with a razor over all their body, and wash their clothes and cleanse themselves.<sup>8</sup>Then let them take a bull from the herd and its grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, and you shall take another bull from the herd for a sin offering.<sup>9</sup>And you shall bring the Levites before the tent of meeting and assemble the whole congregation of the people of Israel.<sup>10</sup>When you bring the Levites before the LORD, the people of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites,<sup>11</sup>and Aaron shall offer the Levites before the LORD as a wave offering from the people of Israel, that they may do the service of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Then the Levites shall lay their hands on the heads of the bulls, and you shall offer the one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering to the LORD to make atonement for the Levites.<sup>13</sup>And you shall set the Levites before Aaron and his sons, and shall offer them as a wave offering to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>"Thus you shall separate the Levites from among the people of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine.<sup>15</sup>And after that the Levites shall go in to serve at the tent of meeting, when you have cleansed them and offered them as a wave offering.<sup>16</sup>For they are wholly given to me from among the people of Israel. Instead of all who open the womb, the firstborn of all the people of Israel, I have taken them for myself.<sup>17</sup>For all the firstborn among the people of Israel are mine, both of man and of beast. On the day that I struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt I consecrated them for myself,<sup>18</sup>and I have taken the Levites instead of all the firstborn among the people of Israel.<sup>19</sup>And I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the people of Israel, to do the service for the people of Israel at the tent of meeting and to make atonement for the people of Israel, that there may be no plague among the people of Israel when the people of Israel come near the sanctuary."<sup>20</sup>Thus did Moses and Aaron and all the congregation of the people of Israel to the Levites. According to all that the LORD commanded Moses concerning the Levites, the people of Israel did to them.<sup>21</sup>And the Levites purified themselves from sin and washed their clothes, and Aaron offered them as a wave offering before the LORD, and Aaron made atonement for them to cleanse them.<sup>22</sup>And after that the Levites went in to do their service in the tent of meeting before Aaron and his sons; as the LORD had commanded Moses concerning the Levites, so they did to them.<sup>23</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>24</sup>"This applies to the Levites: from twenty-five years old and upward they shall come to do duty in the service of the tent of meeting.<sup>25</sup>And from the age of fifty years they shall withdraw from the duty of the service and serve no more.<sup>26</sup>They minister to their brothers in the tent of meeting by keeping guard, but they shall do no service. Thus shall you do to the Levites in assigning their duties."
8.overview:
Chapter 8 opens with the lighting of the lampstand and turns to the consecration of the Levites. Chosen as substitutes for the firstborn (ch 3), they are now cleansed, presented to God as a “wave offering,” and given back to Aaron for the service of the tent.

They do not merely perform duties; they are themselves the gift, “wholly given.” The chapter anticipates the call of Romans 12 to present ourselves as living sacrifices, and Christ, the truly consecrated Servant, given by the Father and giving himself wholly for us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Lampstand Lit Before the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Aaron is to set up the seven lamps so they give light in front of the lampstand, made of hammered gold as God showed Moses.
verseByVerse.theology: The light of the sanctuary shines before God; his servants are called to be light-bearers in his house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: seven lamps burning before the LORD. Now: the church shines as light in a dark world, in Christ the true Light.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and say to him, When you set up the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light in front of the lampstand." And Aaron did so: he set up its lamps in front of the lampstand, as the LORD commanded Moses. And this was the workmanship of the lampstand, hammered work of gold. From its base to its flowers, it was hammered work; according to the pattern that the LORD had shown Moses, so he made the lampstand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the Levites are consecrated, the lamps are lit.

The sanctuary had no windows. The lampstand was the only light in the holy place, and Aaron trimmed its wicks daily. Its light fell on the table of the bread of the Presence opposite: the lamps did not illuminate themselves but what was in front of them. And the lampstand was not cast or assembled from parts but beaten out of a single block of gold, base, branches, blossoms and all.

The New Testament carries the picture forward. Jesus, probably at the Feast of Booths, when great lamps were lit in the temple courts, said I am the light of the world (John 8:12). And John sees seven golden lampstands with one like a son of man, robed as a priest, walking among them: the seven lampstands are the seven churches (Revelation 1:13, 20). The church’s light is kept burning by the great High Priest, and like the lamps of the holy place it shines on what is in front of it and never on itself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–22 — The Cleansing and Dedication of the Levites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites are sprinkled, shaved, and washed; the people lay hands on them; Aaron presents them as a wave offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: The servants of God must be cleansed and wholly given; the Levites are themselves the offering, dedicated entirely to God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Levites washed and offered to God. Now: believers present themselves as living sacrifices, cleansed by Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Take the Levites from among the people of Israel and cleanse them. Thus you shall do to them to cleanse them: sprinkle the water of purification upon them, and let them go with a razor over all their body, and wash their clothes and cleanse themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Levites, and before anything else they are cleansed, in three actions moving outward from the person. Water sprinkled on them, done to them, not by them. The razor over the whole body: every hair removed, the man as bare as a newborn. Then clothes washed, so that even what he wears into the tent is clean.

The order is the thing. Not one of these men has done a day’s work in the tabernacle. Israel’s servants did not become clean by serving; they were made clean in order to serve.

That order has never changed and is constantly inverted. People try to work their way into a fitness for God, and God has always done it the other way round: He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5). The washing comes first, and it is not something a man can do to himself while holding the razor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then let them take a bull from the herd and its grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, and you shall take another bull from the herd for a sin offering. And you shall bring the Levites before the tent of meeting and assemble the whole congregation of the people of Israel. When you bring the Levites before the LORD, the people of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites, and Aaron shall offer the Levites before the LORD as a wave offering from the people of Israel, that they may do the service of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a ceremony unlike anything else in the law, and two things in it are extraordinary.

First, the whole congregation lays hands on them. In the sacrifices that is what a worshipper does to an animal about to be killed, to say “this one goes in my place.” Israel does it to a tribe of living men.

Second, Aaron offers them as a wave offering: the portion lifted toward the altar, presented to God and received back for use. The Levites are not the men who bring the offering; they are the thing on the plate.

This is what Paul asks of an ordinary Christian, and he grounds it first in what God has done: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship (Rom. 12:1). The picture was acted out before the whole nation before it was ever written down.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Levites shall lay their hands on the heads of the bulls, and you shall offer the one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering to the LORD to make atonement for the Levites. And you shall set the Levites before Aaron and his sons, and shall offer them as a wave offering to the LORD. "Thus you shall separate the Levites from among the people of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Follow the hands and you see the whole system. The people put their hands on the Levites. The Levites put their hands on the bulls. The bulls die.

The men just presented to God as an offering need atonement themselves and cannot supply it. The substitutes need a substitute. Nothing in their washing, shaving or waving made them fit to stand where they stood.

There the chain runs out: it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Heb. 10:4). What was needed was one place where the hands could be laid and the chain could stop: someone who did not need a bull because he was the offering, and did not need a priest because he was the priest. The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isa. 53:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And after that the Levites shall go in to serve at the tent of meeting, when you have cleansed them and offered them as a wave offering. For they are wholly given to me from among the people of Israel. Instead of all who open the womb, the firstborn of all the people of Israel, I have taken them for myself. For all the firstborn among the people of Israel are mine, both of man and of beast. On the day that I struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt I consecrated them for myself, and I have taken the Levites instead of all the firstborn among the people of Israel. And I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the people of Israel, to do the service for the people of Israel at the tent of meeting and to make atonement for the people of Israel, that there may be no plague among the people of Israel when the people of Israel come near the sanctuary." Thus did Moses and Aaron and all the congregation of the people of Israel to the Levites. According to all that the LORD commanded Moses concerning the Levites, the people of Israel did to them. And the Levites purified themselves from sin and washed their clothes, and Aaron offered them as a wave offering before the LORD, and Aaron made atonement for them to cleanse them. And after that the Levites went in to do their service in the tent of meeting before Aaron and his sons; as the LORD had commanded Moses concerning the Levites, so they did to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sentences repay slow reading. The first: they are wholly given to me. The Hebrew doubles the word, given, given: not partly, not on certain days. And the ground of the claim goes back, as in chapter 3, to a night in Egypt and blood on a doorframe.

The second turns it round: I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons. What is handed over to God does not disappear into heaven; it comes back into the life of the people as provision for them.

And the purpose is blunt: that there may be no plague among the people of Israel when the people of Israel come near the sanctuary. Five times in one verse God says the people of Israel; he has his eye on the congregation. The Levites existed so that ordinary Israelites could come near and live, and so does every ministry God has established since.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — The Term of Levitical Service
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites serve from age twenty-five to fifty, after which they retire from heavy duty but may still assist.
verseByVerse.theology: God appoints seasons of service and of rest; even his servants are given a tender provision for their later years.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a fixed term of Levitical service. Now: faithful service in its season, resting in the God who appoints our times.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "This applies to the Levites: from twenty-five years old and upward they shall come to do duty in the service of the tent of meeting. And from the age of fifty years they shall withdraw from the duty of the service and serve no more. They minister to their brothers in the tent of meeting by keeping guard, but they shall do no service. Thus shall you do to the Levites in assigning their duties."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with a retirement policy, which nobody expects in the Pentateuch: service from twenty-five, and at fifty a hard stop.

Carrying the frames of the tabernacle across a desert is young men’s labour, and God does not ask a man of sixty to do it. Nor does he wait for the man to fail; the release is built into the law before anybody has an awkward conversation.

But the man is not finished. He stays in the tent, keeping guard alongside the men now doing the lifting. The heavy work stops; the presence does not. God retires his servants from the carrying and keeps them for the guarding, and a congregation with an older believer who prays, watches and knows where the dangers are has something the Levites had.

Twenty-five here, thirty in 4:3: Levites began service at twenty-five and took on the carrying of the holy things at thirty. David later lowered the age to twenty (1 Chr 23:24–27).

8.theology:
Wholly Given to God. The Levites are offered as a living wave offering, themselves the gift. So Romans 12:1: the servant of God is the offering.

Cleansing Before Service. The Levites are sprinkled, washed and atoned for, and only “after that” do they serve. Grace and cleansing first, then service: we labor from acceptance, not for it.

Given Twice, for the People. Given by the people to God, then by God to the priesthood, that there be “no plague” when Israel draws near. So Christ is given by the Father and gives himself, the Mediator whose work lets us approach God and live.
8.examples:
Then: The Levites were cleansed, atoned for and presented to God as a living offering, then sent to serve.

Now: Washed by Christ and made his by the Spirit, present yourself to God as a living sacrifice. Serve not to earn his favor but from grace already received, knowing that where your offering falls short, his did not. And rest in the God who appoints your seasons of labor and of rest, for you are wholly his.

9.title: The Passover Kept; the Cloud of Guidance
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the first month of the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Let the people of Israel keep the Passover at its appointed time.<sup>3</sup>On the fourteenth day of this month, at twilight, you shall keep it at its appointed time; according to all its statutes and all its rules you shall keep it."<sup>4</sup>So Moses told the people of Israel that they should keep the Passover.<sup>5</sup>And they kept the Passover in the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, at twilight, in the wilderness of Sinai; according to all that the LORD commanded Moses, so the people of Israel did.<sup>6</sup>And there were certain men who were unclean through touching a dead body, so that they could not keep the Passover on that day, and they came before Moses and Aaron on that day.<sup>7</sup>And those men said to him, "We are unclean through touching a dead body. Why are we kept from bringing the LORD's offering at its appointed time among the people of Israel?"<sup>8</sup>And Moses said to them, "Wait, that I may hear what the LORD will command concerning you."<sup>9</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If any one of you or of your descendants is unclean through touching a dead body, or is on a long journey, he shall still keep the Passover to the LORD.<sup>11</sup>In the second month on the fourteenth day at twilight they shall keep it. They shall eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.<sup>12</sup>They shall leave none of it until the morning, nor break any of its bones; according to all the statute for the Passover they shall keep it.<sup>13</sup>But if anyone who is clean and is not on a journey fails to keep the Passover, that person shall be cut off from his people because he did not bring the LORD's offering at its appointed time; that man shall bear his sin.<sup>14</sup>And if a stranger sojourns among you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, according to the statute of the Passover and according to its rule, so shall he do. You shall have one statute, both for the sojourner and for the native."<sup>15</sup>On the day that the tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the tent of the testimony. And at evening it was over the tabernacle like the appearance of fire until morning.<sup>16</sup>So it was always: the cloud covered it by day and the appearance of fire by night.<sup>17</sup>And whenever the cloud lifted from over the tent, after that the people of Israel set out, and in the place where the cloud settled down, there the people of Israel camped.<sup>18</sup>At the command of the LORD the people of Israel set out, and at the command of the LORD they camped. As long as the cloud rested over the tabernacle, they remained in camp.<sup>19</sup>Even when the cloud continued over the tabernacle many days, the people of Israel kept the charge of the LORD and did not set out.<sup>20</sup>Sometimes the cloud was a few days over the tabernacle, and according to the command of the LORD they remained in camp; then according to the command of the LORD they set out.<sup>21</sup>And sometimes the cloud remained from evening until morning. And when the cloud lifted in the morning, they set out, or if it continued for a day and a night, when the cloud lifted they set out.<sup>22</sup>Whether it was two days, or a month, or a longer time, that the cloud continued over the tabernacle, abiding there, the people of Israel remained in camp and did not set out, but when it lifted they set out.<sup>23</sup>At the command of the LORD they camped, and at the command of the LORD they set out. They kept the charge of the LORD, at the command of the LORD by Moses.
9.overview:
Chapter 9 holds together redemption remembered and presence experienced. Israel keeps the Passover in the wilderness, the second since Egypt; then the cloud and fire of God’s presence settle on the tabernacle to guide every step. Before Israel moves an inch toward the land, they remember the blood of the lamb: we travel as a redeemed people.

A tender provision lets the unclean or the traveller keep the feast a month later, yet the despiser who neglects it is cut off; grace is not license. And the cloud teaches the life of faith: going and staying at God’s word. It all points to Christ, our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7) and our guide, who leads his people home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Passover in the Wilderness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel keeps the Passover at Sinai; provision is made for the unclean and the traveler to keep it a month later.
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption is remembered before the journey begins; God makes a way for the excluded, yet the despiser is cut off.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Passover lamb remembered in the wilderness. Now: Christ our Passover, the redemption from which all pilgrimage flows.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the first month of the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, saying, "Let the people of Israel keep the Passover at its appointed time. On the fourteenth day of this month, at twilight, you shall keep it at its appointed time; according to all its statutes and all its rules you shall keep it." So Moses told the people of Israel that they should keep the Passover. And they kept the Passover in the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, at twilight, in the wilderness of Sinai; according to all that the LORD commanded Moses, so the people of Israel did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Israel takes a single step toward the promised land, God has them keep the Passover. The date puts this in the first month, before chapter 1: Numbers places it where it belongs theologically, so that a nation about to set out on the hardest journey of its life sits down first to eat a lamb and remember that it was bought out of slavery by blood.

It is the second Passover. The first was eaten in haste in Egypt, with the destroyer outside; this one a year later by people who are free, and it is the same meal. Redemption is not something you graduate from. The Christian of forty years comes to the Lord’s Table and eats the same bread as the man converted last Tuesday, because there is nothing further along than the blood of the Lamb.

It is also the last Passover on record for nearly forty years; the next is at Gilgal, after the whole generation has died (Josh. 5:10). The reader is given this scene to hold on to before the wilderness starts.

verseByVerse.quote: And there were certain men who were unclean through touching a dead body, so that they could not keep the Passover on that day, and they came before Moses and Aaron on that day. And those men said to him, "We are unclean through touching a dead body. Why are we kept from bringing the LORD's offering at its appointed time among the people of Israel?" And Moses said to them, "Wait, that I may hear what the LORD will command concerning you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a problem walks up to Moses: men unclean through touching a dead body. They have done nothing wrong. Somebody had to bury the dead, and anyone who did was unclean for seven days (ch. 19). An act of love had shut them out of the most important meal of the year.

And their question is a lovely sentence: Why are we kept from bringing the LORD’s offering at its appointed time?

They are grieved at not being able to give God what is his. A person can be shut out of the assembly for all sorts of reasons, illness, distance, shame, circumstance, and these men ached. That ache is itself evidence of a heart God has been at work in; nobody grieves over missing what they never wanted.

Moses’ answer is as good as their question: Wait, that I may hear what the LORD will command. He does not improvise a merciful ruling or send them away with the law as it stands. He says: I do not know, and I will ask. There is a kind of leader who would rather be wrong than say that.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If any one of you or of your descendants is unclean through touching a dead body, or is on a long journey, he shall still keep the Passover to the LORD. In the second month on the fourteenth day at twilight they shall keep it. They shall eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. They shall leave none of it until the morning, nor break any of its bones; according to all the statute for the Passover they shall keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s answer is to open a second door: a full second Passover a month later for anyone genuinely prevented, unclean or on a long journey.

God does not merely excuse them; he arranges a whole additional observance so that nobody who wanted to come goes without. And it is not a reduced version but according to all the statute for the Passover: the same meal.

Then a detail that will travel a long way: nor break any of its bones, from the original statute (Exod. 12:46), repeated here.

On a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem, soldiers broke the legs of the crucified men so the bodies could be taken down before the Sabbath, and finding Jesus already dead, did not break his. John, standing there, writes: For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “Not one of his bones will be broken” (John 19:36). He is quoting this law (and perhaps Psalm 34:20). A rule about handling a lamb in a wilderness described what a Roman execution squad would decline to do to the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone who is clean and is not on a journey fails to keep the Passover, that person shall be cut off from his people because he did not bring the LORD's offering at its appointed time; that man shall bear his sin. And if a stranger sojourns among you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, according to the statute of the Passover and according to its rule, so shall he do. You shall have one statute, both for the sojourner and for the native."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace has a hard edge, and both must be held: anyone clean and not travelling who fails to keep the Passover shall be cut off from his people.

The second month was a provision for the hindered, not a convenience for the indifferent. The men of verse 7 and the man of verse 13 differ not in circumstances but in hearts: one group ached to come and could not; this man could and did not bother.

That distinction comforts the right people and warns the rest. The believer who cannot get to church because he is ill, or nursing somebody, is not in the position of the man who could have gone and preferred not to. God knows which is which. And even the careless is not beyond the reach of the feast: the way back for the one who has despised it is to come, confessing, while the door is still open.

The last verse widens the door again: one statute, both for the sojourner and for the native. A foreigner who wanted in was in, on identical terms, once his household had joined the covenant by circumcision (Exodus 12:48). There has never been a second-class table in the house of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cloud covers the tabernacle, fire by night; Israel sets out when the cloud lifts and rests when it settles.
verseByVerse.theology: The life of faith is total dependence on the presence and guidance of God, moving and staying at his word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel led by cloud and fire. Now: believers led by the Spirit, following Christ wherever he goes.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day that the tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the tent of the testimony. And at evening it was over the tabernacle like the appearance of fire until morning. So it was always: the cloud covered it by day and the appearance of fire by night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take in the word always. Not sometimes, not at the great moments, not when Israel was behaving. Every single day and every single night for forty years, a visible sign of the presence of God stood over the middle of that camp, and any Israelite who woke in the dark and was frightened could put his head out of the tent and see fire burning over the tabernacle.

The two forms fit the two needs. A cloud by day, in a desert, is shade; fire by night is warmth and light. Isaiah says so of the age to come: a booth for shade by day from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain (Isa. 4:6).

Israel had that. We do not have a pillar of fire, and it is tempting to think ourselves the poorer for it. But the same God who hung a cloud over a tent has said to his people, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb. 13:5), and what was visible to Israel from the outside is now true of Christians from the inside. The camp had the fire over the tabernacle. The church is the tabernacle.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the cloud lifted from over the tent, after that the people of Israel set out, and in the place where the cloud settled down, there the people of Israel camped. At the command of the LORD the people of Israel set out, and at the command of the LORD they camped. As long as the cloud rested over the tabernacle, they remained in camp. Even when the cloud continued over the tabernacle many days, the people of Israel kept the charge of the LORD and did not set out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the rhythm of forty years, stated simply: when the cloud lifted they went; where it settled they camped. Israel had no itinerary, no map, no stopping places. There was a cloud, and you watched it.

For two million people with livestock, when the cloud lifted everything came down, tents, pens, the sick, and they went, convenient or not. When it settled they stopped, even if there was a better valley an hour on.

Verse 19 makes the harder half explicit: Even when the cloud continued over the tabernacle many days, the people of Israel kept the charge of the LORD and did not set out. Staying put was obedience too. Most people find that harder than moving. The waiting seasons — when nothing is happening, the cloud has not lifted, and every instinct says do something — are as much the will of God as the marching ones, and Israel could ruin her obedience just as thoroughly by going early as by refusing to go at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Sometimes the cloud was a few days over the tabernacle, and according to the command of the LORD they remained in camp; then according to the command of the LORD they set out. And sometimes the cloud remained from evening until morning. And when the cloud lifted in the morning, they set out, or if it continued for a day and a night, when the cloud lifted they set out. Whether it was two days, or a month, or a longer time, that the cloud continued over the tabernacle, abiding there, the people of Israel remained in camp and did not set out, but when it lifted they set out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The text goes out of its way to say the timings were unpredictable: a night, two days, a month, longer. It lists the possibilities so that no reader can extract a rule. Israel could never say, “We have been here three weeks, so we are due to move.”

Now translate that into what it did to a family. You pitch the tent and you have no idea whether you will be here for one night or half a year. Do you unpack properly? Do you dig in? Do you start something? The only way to live like that without going mad is to hold everything loosely and stay ready, and that is the deliberate design.

Which is precisely the condition of the Christian life and the reason this passage has comforted the church for centuries. We are not told the timings either. You do not know what tomorrow will bring… Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that” (Jas. 4:14–15). It is not the absence of a plan. It is a plan held by somebody else, revealed one lift of the cloud at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: At the command of the LORD they camped, and at the command of the LORD they set out. They kept the charge of the LORD, at the command of the LORD by Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with at the command of the LORD three times in one verse; literally, at the mouth of the LORD. And both halves get equal billing, camping listed first. There is no suggestion that travelling was the obedient part and sitting still dead time.

Nine chapters have been almost entirely about order, each arrangement ending with the same phrase: as the LORD commanded. In two chapters’ time they will be screaming for meat.

So read this verse while it is still true of them. A nation in a desert with no map, going only where God went, stopping only where God stopped, watching a fire over a tent every night. Whatever else they were, they were led. And so is everyone who belongs to him, not by a cloud outside but by the Spirit within: for all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (Rom. 8:14).

9.theology:
Redemption Before Pilgrimage. The wilderness life flows out of redemption accomplished. The Christian journeys not to be saved but because, in Christ our Passover, we already are.

Grace for the Excluded, Judgment for the Despiser. God opens a second Passover for those who long to draw near, even the foreign sojourner, yet the able despiser is cut off. The gospel makes a way for the hungry but is never license for the careless.

The Life of Guidance. Israel moves and rests only “at the command of the LORD”: total dependence on God’s leading, fulfilled in the believer led by the Spirit.
9.examples:
Then: Israel kept the Passover, made room for the longing outsider, and followed the cloud.

Now: Your journey flows from redemption — Christ, your Passover, sacrificed for you. If you feel excluded or defiled yet long to draw near, know that God makes a way. And live the cloud-led life: hold your plans loosely, watch for the Lord’s leading, and follow wherever the Spirit goes.

10.title: The Silver Trumpets; Israel Departs from Sinai

10.overview:
Chapter 10 sounds the trumpet and sets Israel marching. God gives two silver trumpets to summon the assembly, sound the alarm for war and announce the feasts, with the promise that “you shall be remembered before the LORD your God.” Then the cloud lifts, and Israel departs from Sinai, nearly a year after arriving, in the ordered ranks of chapters 1–2.

The departure is a hinge in the Pentateuch: the people carry the tabernacle, the law and the presence of God toward the land, Judah leading, the ark going before, and the cry ringing out, “Arise, O LORD!” The trumpets point to the last trumpet, when Christ will lead his people into the rest of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives two silver trumpets to summon the congregation, signal the march, sound the alarm for war, and announce the feasts.
verseByVerse.theology: The trumpet is the voice of God’s summons and a prayer that reaches heaven; God remembers his people when they call.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: silver trumpets calling Israel to gather and march. Now: the gospel call that gathers God’s people, and the last trumpet of Christ’s return.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Make two silver trumpets. Of hammered work you shall make them, and you shall use them for summoning the congregation and for breaking camp. And when both are blown, all the congregation shall gather themselves to you at the entrance of the tent of meeting. But if they blow only one, then the chiefs, the heads of the tribes of Israel, shall gather themselves to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two, not twelve; silver, not ram’s horn; beaten out of solid metal like the lampstand. A nation on the move needs a voice: two million people over several square miles cannot be shouted at. So God gives them a sound, and it is God’s, not a general’s. The trumpets announce the lifting of the cloud.

And the signals are precise: both trumpets means everybody; one means the leadership. An Israelite at his tent door could tell from the number of instruments whether the summons was for him. God did not leave his people guessing whether they had been called; he gave a signal clear enough to be read from half a mile away by a man who could not read. Everything in this chapter assumes that God intends to be understood by ordinary people.

verseByVerse.quote: When you blow an alarm, the camps that are on the east side shall set out. And when you blow an alarm the second time, the camps that are on the south side shall set out. An alarm is to be blown whenever they are to set out. But when the assembly is to be gathered together, you shall blow a long blast, but you shall not sound an alarm. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall blow the trumpets. The trumpets shall be to you for a perpetual statute throughout your generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An alarm, short and broken, means break camp; a long blast means assemble. Same instruments, opposite instruction, and a mistake plays out on a scale of hundreds of thousands. So verse 8 matters: the priests blow the trumpets. Not the army or the chiefs. Israel’s marching orders came out of the sanctuary.

That is why Paul reaches for a trumpet when he talks about preaching: if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle? (1 Cor. 14:8). A priest who blows an uncertain note leaves a nation standing in a field. The obligation to be clear is in the job description.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you go to war in your land against the adversary who oppresses you, then you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets, that you may be remembered before the LORD your God, and you shall be saved from your enemies. On the day of your gladness also, and at your appointed feasts and at the beginnings of your months, you shall blow the trumpets over your burnt offerings and over the sacrifices of your peace offerings. They shall be a reminder of you before your God: I am the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then two uses of the trumpet beyond signalling. The first is war, and the blast goes upward: that you may be remembered before the LORD your God, and you shall be saved from your enemies. It is a cry to God with a silver instrument, and the promised result is not morale but rescue.

The second is joy: at feasts and new moons, over the burnt offerings. The same instrument for the worst day and the best: terror and celebration go up on the same note.

And in both cases the phrase is the same: that you may be remembered. Not because God forgets — Scripture never means that when it uses the word. To be remembered in Hebrew is to be acted upon: God remembered Noah and the waters went down; God remembered Hannah and she conceived. It means his attention turning into action.

The church has the same permission in plainer words: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise (Jas. 5:13). Both directions: the same God, and the same reaching for him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cloud lifts; Israel sets out from Sinai in ordered ranks, tribe by tribe, Judah leading the march.
verseByVerse.theology: At last the redeemed people move toward the promised land, carrying God’s presence in ordered obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel marching out from Sinai. Now: the church on pilgrimage, moving toward the inheritance under Christ’s lead.

verseByVerse.quote: In the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, the cloud lifted from over the tabernacle of the testimony, and the people of Israel set out by stages from the wilderness of Sinai. And the cloud settled down in the wilderness of Paran. They set out for the first time at the command of the LORD by Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the hinge of the Pentateuch. Israel arrived at Sinai in the third month of the first year (Exod. 19:1) and has been camped there nearly a year: law, covenant, golden calf, tabernacle, priesthood, census. Fifty-nine chapters of the Bible take place at the foot of that mountain, and now, in a single sentence, the cloud moves.

Israel does not stay at Sinai. That is the point of the verse and it needs saying to Christians. The mountain where God spoke, where the glory came down, where the covenant was cut, was never meant to be the destination — it was where they were made ready. There is a kind of believer who wants to live permanently at the site of his best experience of God, and the cloud will not let him. When it lifts, the mountain is behind you.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been at Sinai almost a year. Paran was the wilderness south of Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: The standard of the camp of the people of Judah set out first by their companies, and over their company was Nahshon the son of Amminadab. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Issachar was Nethanel the son of Zuar. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Zebulun was Eliab the son of Helon. And when the tabernacle was taken down, the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari, who carried the tabernacle, set out. And the standard of the camp of Reuben set out by their companies, and over their company was Elizur the son of Shedeur. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Simeon was Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Gad was Eliasaph the son of Deuel. Then the Kohathites set out, carrying the holy things, and the tabernacle was set up before their arrival. And the standard of the camp of the people of Ephraim set out by their companies, and over their company was Elishama the son of Ammihud. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Manasseh was Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Benjamin was Abidan the son of Gideoni. Then the standard of the camp of the people of Dan, acting as the rear guard of all the camps, set out by their companies, and over their company was Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Asher was Pagiel the son of Ochran. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Naphtali was Ahira the son of Enan. This was the order of march of the people of Israel by their companies, when they set out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The march unfolds exactly as drawn up eight chapters earlier, and the writer’s point is that the plan worked. When the trumpet sounded, two million people, their livestock and a dismantled tabernacle moved off in the sequence God had specified, and nobody got lost and nobody argued.

Notice where the holy things travel: in the middle, behind Judah and Reuben and in front of Ephraim and Dan, with the strongest divisions at the head and the tail. The tabernacle is not at the front where it could be admired and not at the back where it could be forgotten. It is carried in the middle of the people, and every one of them is arranged around it, walking.

That was the whole of Israel’s life for forty years: a column of people with the presence of God moving in the middle of them. It is also a fair description of a church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — Hobab and the Cry of the Ark
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses urges Hobab to guide them, then the ark goes before, and Moses cries, “Arise, O LORD!” as it sets out and rests.
verseByVerse.theology: Even as God leads, the cry of faith rises with the ark; the LORD himself goes before his people to scatter their enemies.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: “Arise, O LORD!” as the ark led the way. Now: Christ, the true Ark, goes before us, scattering every foe.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to Hobab the son of Reuel the Midianite, Moses' father-in-law, "We are setting out for the place of which the LORD said, 'I will give it to you.' Come with us, and we will do good to you, for the LORD has promised good to Israel." But he said to him, "I will not go. I will depart to my own land and to my kindred." And he said, "Please do not leave us, for you know where we should camp in the wilderness, and you will serve as eyes for us. And if you do go with us, whatever good the LORD will do to us, the same will we do to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a small scene readers argue about. Moses asks Hobab, a Midianite related to him by marriage (the ESV says father-in-law; the Hebrew word can also mean brother-in-law), to come with them. Hobab refuses, and Moses presses him: you will serve as eyes for us.

The obvious question is whether Moses is faltering. He has a pillar of cloud. Why does he need a desert guide? Some readers see a lapse of faith, and the reading is not unreasonable.

But he does not ask Hobab to choose the route; the cloud does that. He asks for a man who knows the country: where the water is, which wadi floods, where a camp that size can pitch. God’s guidance settled the destination, not which side of a valley the wells were on. Divine direction has never made ordinary competence unnecessary, and a man who refuses good advice because he is being led by God has usually confused two different things.

And Moses offers not payment but partnership: Whatever good the LORD will do to us, the same will we do to you. A Midianite is invited into Israel’s promises on equal terms, the same good God had promised them. The text does not say whether he came, though his descendants, the Kenites, turn up among Judah after the conquest (Judg. 1:16), which suggests somebody in that family changed their mind.

verseByVerse.quote: So they set out from the mount of the LORD three days' journey. And the ark of the covenant of the LORD went before them three days' journey, to seek out a resting place for them. And the cloud of the LORD was over them by day, whenever they set out from the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something has changed. Elsewhere the ark travels in the middle of the column. Here it goes out in front, three days ahead, to seek out a resting place for them.

The image is of God going on ahead to find his people somewhere to stop. Not driving them from behind, not merely accompanying them, but out in front looking for the place where they can lie down. And the phrase — a resting place — is the one that will run through the whole Bible until it arrives at Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28).

Above them the cloud; ahead of them the ark: shade over their heads and a resting place chosen before they arrive. The Christian who wonders whether God has thought about tomorrow can start here: he was three days out in front of Israel, looking for somewhere for them to sleep.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the ark set out, Moses said, "Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee before you." And when it rested, he said, "Return, O LORD, to the ten thousand thousands of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then two lines Israel evidently sang for centuries, one for setting out and one for stopping. Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered. Whose enemies? Not “ours”: your enemies. The opposition in front of them was opposition to God. Psalm 68 opens with the same line, and the church has borrowed it ever since.

And at the end of the day’s march: Return, O LORD, to the ten thousand thousands of Israel. The prayer of a people who wanted God not merely to fight for them but to come home with them and stay.

Together they are the shape of the Christian hope. He arises and his enemies scatter; he returns and dwells with his people. Both are answered in one Man who disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col. 2:15), and of whom it is said, Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man (Rev. 21:3).

Sinai is behind them. The cloud is over them, the ark ahead of them, the trumpets in the priests’ hands, and Moses is singing. Israel has never looked more promising than on the twentieth day of the second month. The next chapter opens with the people complaining.

10.theology:
The Summons of God. The silver trumpets are the audible will of God for his people, sounded by the priests. The church still moves at the clear call of his word, and awaits the last trumpet.

God Goes Before and Abides. The ark leads the march to seek a resting place and returns to dwell in the midst: fulfilled in Christ, who has gone to prepare a place and dwells with us by the Spirit.

Arise, O LORD! The battles of God’s people are the LORD’s; the cry finds its answer in the risen Christ, who has scattered sin, death and the devil.
10.examples:
Then: The trumpets called Israel to march, the cloud lifted, and the ark led the host out from Sinai.

Now: You are a pilgrim, summoned by the gospel and following the One who goes before you to prepare your rest. When enemies oppress, cry, “Arise, O LORD!”, for the risen Christ has already scattered every foe. Invite others to come with you, for the Lord has promised good.

11.title: Grumbling and the Seventy Elders
11.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people complained in the hearing of the LORD about their misfortunes, and when the LORD heard it, his anger was kindled, and the fire of the LORD burned among them and consumed some outlying parts of the camp.<sup>2</sup>Then the people cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed to the LORD, and the fire died down.<sup>3</sup>So the name of that place was called Taberah, because the fire of the LORD burned among them.<sup>4</sup>Now the rabble that was among them had a strong craving. And the people of Israel also wept again and said, "Oh that we had meat to eat!<sup>5</sup>We remember the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic.<sup>6</sup>But now our strength is dried up, and there is nothing at all but this manna to look at."<sup>7</sup>Now the manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like that of bdellium.<sup>8</sup>The people went about and gathered it and ground it in handmills or beat it in mortars and boiled it in pots and made cakes of it. And the taste of it was like the taste of cakes baked with oil.<sup>9</sup>When the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell with it.<sup>10</sup>Moses heard the people weeping throughout their clans, everyone at the door of his tent. And the anger of the LORD blazed hotly, and Moses was displeased.<sup>11</sup>Moses said to the LORD, "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? And why have I not found favor in your sight, that you lay the burden of all this people on me?<sup>12</sup>Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth, that you should say to me, 'Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child,' to the land that you swore to give their fathers?<sup>13</sup>Where am I to get meat to give to all this people? For they weep before me and say, 'Give us meat, that we may eat.'<sup>14</sup>I am not able to carry all this people alone; the burden is too heavy for me.<sup>15</sup>If you will treat me like this, kill me at once, if I find favor in your sight, that I may not see my wretchedness."<sup>16</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and officers over them, and bring them to the tent of meeting, and let them take their stand there with you.<sup>17</sup>And I will come down and talk with you there. And I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you may not bear it yourself alone.<sup>18</sup>And say to the people, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat meat, for you have wept in the hearing of the LORD, saying, "Who will give us meat to eat? For it was better for us in Egypt." Therefore the LORD will give you meat, and you shall eat.<sup>19</sup>You shall not eat just one day, or two days, or five days, or ten days, or twenty days,<sup>20</sup>but a whole month, until it comes out at your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you, because you have rejected the LORD who is among you and have wept before him, saying, "Why did we come out of Egypt?"'"<sup>21</sup>But Moses said, "The people among whom I am number six hundred thousand on foot, and you have said, 'I will give them meat, that they may eat a whole month!'<sup>22</sup>Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, and be enough for them? Or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, and be enough for them?"<sup>23</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Is the LORD's hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not."<sup>24</sup>So Moses went out and told the people the words of the LORD. And he gathered seventy men of the elders of the people and placed them around the tent.<sup>25</sup>Then the LORD came down in the cloud and spoke to him, and took some of the Spirit that was on him and put it on the seventy elders. And as soon as the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied. But they did not continue doing it.<sup>26</sup>Now two men remained in the camp, one named Eldad, and the other named Medad, and the Spirit rested on them. They were among those registered, but they had not gone out to the tent, and so they prophesied in the camp.<sup>27</sup>And a young man ran and told Moses, "Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp."<sup>28</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun, the assistant of Moses from his youth, said, "My lord Moses, stop them."<sup>29</sup>But Moses said to him, "Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!"<sup>30</sup>And Moses and the elders of Israel returned to the camp.<sup>31</sup>Then a wind from the LORD sprang up, and it brought quail from the sea and let them fall beside the camp, about a day's journey on this side and a day's journey on the other side, around the camp, and about two cubits above the ground.<sup>32</sup>And the people rose all that day and all night and all the next day, and gathered the quail. Those who gathered least gathered ten homers. And they spread them out for themselves all around the camp.<sup>33</sup>While the meat was yet between their teeth, before it was consumed, the anger of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD struck down the people with a very great plague.<sup>34</sup>Therefore the name of that place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had the craving.<sup>35</sup>From Kibroth-hattaavah the people journeyed to Hazeroth, and they remained at Hazeroth.
11.overview:
Three days out from Sinai, the singing stops and the grumbling begins. Chapter 11 is the hinge of Numbers, where the obedient camp dissolves into discontent: the people complain, fire falls, and then they crave meat, despising the manna, the bread of heaven, and weeping for the garlic of slavery. Paul names it a warning written for us (1 Corinthians 10:6).

Moses, crushed by the weight of leadership, cries out to God, and God shares the burden by putting his Spirit on seventy elders. The craving is answered with quail and with judgment at “the graves of craving.” Discontent with God’s provision is a despising of God himself, and it drives us to Christ, the true Bread from heaven.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people complain of their misfortunes; the LORD’s fire burns the outskirts of the camp until Moses intercedes.
verseByVerse.theology: Grumbling against God’s providence kindles his anger; complaint is a serious sin against the goodness of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: fire at Taberah for complaining. Now: a warning against the grumbling heart that despises God’s providence.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people complained in the hearing of the LORD about their misfortunes, and when the LORD heard it, his anger was kindled, and the fire of the LORD burned among them and consumed some outlying parts of the camp. Then the people cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed to the LORD, and the fire died down. So the name of that place was called Taberah, because the fire of the LORD burned among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three days out from Sinai, the people complained in the hearing of the LORD about their misfortunes.

We are told almost nothing: no famine, no enemy, no hardship named. They had been walking for three days and were unhappy about it. The vagueness is the point: this is not a crisis but a temperature. And it happened inside the very three days in which the ark went ahead to find them a resting place (10:33).

Fire falls on the edge of the camp, Moses prays, and it stops. Taberah, Burning, is the first of the place-names this book leaves across a desert, each marking a moment when the people of God decided the God who was carrying them was not doing it well enough. Paul says these things were written for us (1 Cor. 10:11). His own call, Do all things without grumbling or disputing (Phil. 2:14), stands on the ground he has just laid: Christ’s own self-emptying obedience, and the God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Phil. 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: “Taberah” means “burning” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — Craving Meat and the Weight of Leadership
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people despise the manna and crave meat, weeping for Egypt; Moses, crushed by the burden, cries out to God.
verseByVerse.theology: Discontent with God’s provision despises God himself; the weight of leading God’s people is too heavy for one man alone.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: weeping for the food of Egypt. Now: the danger of despising God’s gifts and the need to share heavy burdens.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rabble that was among them had a strong craving. And the people of Israel also wept again and said, "Oh that we had meat to eat! We remember the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic. But now our strength is dried up, and there is nothing at all but this manna to look at."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The craving begins with the rabble at the fringe and spreads to the whole nation. Discontent is contagious, and it does not usually start at the centre.

What comes out of them is one of the great pieces of self-deception in Scripture: a menu of fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic, specific and mouth-watering.

Now read what is missing: the whips, the quota of bricks, the baby boys thrown into the Nile, a nation groaning so loudly that God heard their groaning (Exod. 2:24). None of that survives in the memory. What survives is the garlic.

And that cost nothing is the finest lie in the sentence. They were slaves; the fish came with the whip. Memory under present discomfort does not merely soften the past; it edits out precisely what God rescued them from.

Then the verdict on the present: nothing at all but this manna. Bread from the sky, six mornings a week, free, has become nothing at all. Anything God does daily and reliably will eventually stop being seen as a gift, and the surest test of a grumbling season is to ask what has quietly moved from the miracle column to the nothing column.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like that of bdellium. The people went about and gathered it and ground it in handmills or beat it in mortars and boiled it in pots and made cakes of it. And the taste of it was like the taste of cakes baked with oil. When the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell with it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the narrator interrupts the complaint to describe the manna, in three verses of quiet, affectionate detail, and every one contradicts what has just been said.

Israel said there was nothing to look at; the writer says it looked like bdellium, a pale precious resin. Israel implied monotony; the writer lists four ways of preparing it and says it tasted of cakes baked with oil. Israel despised it; the writer says it came down with the dew in the night while they slept. It is the gentlest rebuke in the book. He does not argue with them. He just describes what they have got.

And a Man took this bread and made a claim about himself with it: I am the bread of life… I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever (John 6:48, 51). The generation that called it worthless stood in a foreshadowing of Christ every morning and complained about the taste.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses heard the people weeping throughout their clans, everyone at the door of his tent. And the anger of the LORD blazed hotly, and Moses was displeased. Moses said to the LORD, "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? And why have I not found favor in your sight, that you lay the burden of all this people on me? Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth, that you should say to me, 'Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child,' to the land that you swore to give their fathers? Where am I to get meat to give to all this people? For they weep before me and say, 'Give us meat, that we may eat.' I am not able to carry all this people alone; the burden is too heavy for me. If you will treat me like this, kill me at once, if I find favor in your sight, that I may not see my wretchedness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The complaint reaches Moses and breaks him, in one of the rawest prayers in the Bible, and it should never be tidied up.

Why have you dealt ill with your servant? The meekest man on earth tells God he has been badly treated, asks whether the whole arrangement was fair, and finally asks to be killed rather than go on. His image is a mother’s: he is asked to carry a nation as a nurse carries an infant that will not stop screaming, and he did not give birth to it. God does not rebuke him for one word of it. Not one. He answers with help. And Moses took it to the right place: at the absolute end of himself, he said so to God, not to the elders and not to the congregation behind their backs. Every syllable of it is prayer, and that is why it could be answered.

Anyone in ministry, or caring for a parent, or holding a family together, who has thought things they would not dare say aloud, should notice that verse 15 is in the Bible. God can be told the truth about how it is going. Peter’s casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet. 5:7) comes with no list of anxieties too ugly to bring. And if you have prayed something like verse 15 and the wish to die has not lifted, tell a pastor, a doctor or a trusted friend today. God answered Moses by sending him people, and he often still does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — The Seventy Elders and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God places his Spirit on seventy elders to share Moses’ burden; Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp, and Moses rejoices.
verseByVerse.theology: God graciously distributes the Spirit to share the burden of leadership; Moses longs that all God’s people might be prophets.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Spirit on seventy elders. Now: the Spirit poured out on all God’s people, the longing of Moses fulfilled at Pentecost.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and officers over them, and bring them to the tent of meeting, and let them take their stand there with you. And I will come down and talk with you there. And I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you may not bear it yourself alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s answer to a despairing prayer is a personnel decision: seventy elders, and some of the Spirit that is on you put on them, so that you may not bear it yourself alone.

He does not tell Moses to pray harder or trust more. He concludes, as Moses had said, that the load is too big for one man, and divides it. Christians are often taught that admitting the work is too heavy is a failure of faith. God’s diagnosis here is structural, not spiritual, as Jethro’s had been: You are not able to do it alone (Exod. 18:18). Some burdens need not more grace for the individual but more shoulders.

And it is the same Spirit, extended, not a lesser one. Moses loses nothing by seventy others receiving it, and they do not get a discount version. What made Moses able to lead is what will make them able to help.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to the people, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat meat, for you have wept in the hearing of the LORD, saying, "Who will give us meat to eat? For it was better for us in Egypt." Therefore the LORD will give you meat, and you shall eat. You shall not eat just one day, or two days, or five days, or ten days, or twenty days, but a whole month, until it comes out at your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you, because you have rejected the LORD who is among you and have wept before him, saying, "Why did we come out of Egypt?"'" But Moses said, "The people among whom I am number six hundred thousand on foot, and you have said, 'I will give them meat, that they may eat a whole month!' Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, and be enough for them? Or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, and be enough for them?" And the LORD said to Moses, "Is the LORD's hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then God turns to the people, and his answer is frightening: meat for a whole month, until it comes out at your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you. That is not God losing his temper but a terrible form of judgment the Bible names in one line: he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Ps. 106:15). There are prayers it is a mercy not to have answered.

And God’s diagnosis: you have rejected the LORD who is among you. They thought they were complaining about food. Grumbling is never really about the circumstance; it is a verdict passed on the God who arranged it.

Moses cannot see how it could be done, and God’s reply is the sentence to carry out of the chapter: Is the LORD’s hand shortened? A shortened hand cannot reach far enough, and Isaiah insists the problem has never been at God’s end: Behold, the LORD’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save (Isa. 59:1).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses went out and told the people the words of the LORD. And he gathered seventy men of the elders of the people and placed them around the tent. Then the LORD came down in the cloud and spoke to him, and took some of the Spirit that was on him and put it on the seventy elders. And as soon as the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied. But they did not continue doing it. Now two men remained in the camp, one named Eldad, and the other named Medad, and the Spirit rested on them. They were among those registered, but they had not gone out to the tent, and so they prophesied in the camp. And a young man ran and told Moses, "Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp." And Joshua the son of Nun, the assistant of Moses from his youth, said, "My lord Moses, stop them." But Moses said to him, "Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!" And Moses and the elders of Israel returned to the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventy prophesy round the tent. But Eldad and Medad, on the list though not at the meeting, receive the Spirit where they are and prophesy in the middle of the camp.

Joshua reacts as a loyal assistant would: My lord Moses, stop them. Prophecy has broken out in the wrong place, without supervision, and it looks to him like a threat to his master’s standing.

Moses’ answer is one of the high points of his life: Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them! Offered a defence of his own uniqueness, he wishes the opposite as hard as he can. There is no trace in him of the instinct that guards its own position, and because he had no interest in being irreplaceable, God could trust him with what he was given.

And his wish was granted. In Jerusalem centuries later the Spirit fell on a hundred and twenty ordinary people at once, and Peter explained it from Joel: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy (Acts 2:17). Moses wished it; God said yes.

Does this mean prophecy continues today? The seventy prophesied once, as a sign that God had given them the Spirit for their task, But they did not continue doing it (v. 25). Moses’ wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets was fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Spirit was poured out on all believers (Acts 2:17–18). But the gift of new revelation belonged to the founding of the church (Eph 2:20), and Scripture is now complete; all believers have the Spirit, and all speak God’s completed word to one another. Many faithful Christians believe that prophecy in a lesser, tested sense continues today; this commentary holds the cessationist view because Ephesians 2:20 places prophets with the apostles in the church’s once-for-all foundation, and it holds that view charitably.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–35 — The Quail and the Graves of Craving
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends quail in vast quantity, but his anger burns and a plague strikes the greedy; the place is named Kibroth-hattaavah.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin granted is judgment; the craving fulfilled becomes the grave, a solemn warning against despising God’s provision.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the graves of craving. Now: a warning that to desire evil as they did invites the discipline of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a wind from the LORD sprang up, and it brought quail from the sea and let them fall beside the camp, about a day's journey on this side and a day's journey on the other side, around the camp, and about two cubits above the ground. And the people rose all that day and all night and all the next day, and gathered the quail. Those who gathered least gathered ten homers. And they spread them out for themselves all around the camp. While the meat was yet between their teeth, before it was consumed, the anger of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD struck down the people with a very great plague. Therefore the name of that place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had the craving. From Kibroth-hattaavah the people journeyed to Hazeroth, and they remained at Hazeroth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then God keeps his word about the meat, and the manner is dreadful: a wind brings quail for a day’s walk in every direction, about two cubits deep or, as many read the Hebrew, flying low at waist height. The people gather for thirty-six hours without sleeping, and the least of them gathers ten homers. They were not hungry any more. They were hoarding.

Then, while the meat was yet between their teeth, the plague. The craving and the judgment arrive in the same mouthful, and the place is named for it: Kibroth-hattaavah, the graves of craving. Israel buried its dead at a place whose name means what killed them.

Paul writes it to a church without softening: Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did (1 Cor. 10:6). The Greek Old Testament calls this place the graves of desire, and Paul’s word comes from the same root; he is very probably pointing at these graves.

So the chapter that opened three days from the mountain ends in a burial ground. God gave bread from heaven and they asked for meat; he gave them meat and they died of it. And one prayer in the whole episode he answered with unmixed kindness: the prayer of a man at the end of himself who said so.
verseByVerse.note: A homer was about 6 bushels (ESV note). Kibroth-hattaavah means “graves of craving” (ESV note).

11.theology:
The Sin of Grumbling. To scorn our circumstances is to accuse the God who ordains them; to despise the manna is to despise the Giver.

The Burden of Leadership and the Gift of the Spirit. God shares Moses’ burden by distributing his Spirit. The work of leading God’s people is borne by Spirit-gifted leaders together.

Sin Granted as Judgment. Getting what we sinfully demand can be the severest discipline. Yet Moses’ longing that all the LORD’s people were prophets is fulfilled at Pentecost.
11.examples:
