Then: Israel despised the bread of heaven and found their graves at Kibroth-hattaavah, while God shared Moses’ burden with seventy Spirit-filled elders.

Now: Where Israel grumbled in the wilderness, Christ, hungry in the wilderness, trusted his Father’s word (Matthew 4:4), and his faithfulness is counted to you who have grumbled too; confess it, and you will find the Father’s welcome, not the graves of craving. Feed on him, the true Bread, and ask the Spirit for a contented heart that sees the daily gifts. And if you lead God’s people, do not carry the burden alone or guard it jealously.

12.title: Miriam and Aaron Oppose Moses
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married, for he had married a Cushite woman.<sup>2</sup>And they said, "Has the LORD indeed spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?" And the LORD heard it.<sup>3</sup>Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth.<sup>4</sup>And suddenly the LORD said to Moses and to Aaron and Miriam, "Come out, you three, to the tent of meeting." And the three of them came out.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tent and called Aaron and Miriam, and they both came forward.<sup>6</sup>And he said, "Hear my words: If there is a prophet among you, I the LORD make myself known to him in a vision; I speak with him in a dream.<sup>7</sup>Not so with my servant Moses. He is faithful in all my house.<sup>8</sup>With him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles, and he beholds the form of the LORD. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?"<sup>9</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against them, and he departed.<sup>10</sup>When the cloud removed from over the tent, behold, Miriam was leprous, like snow. And Aaron turned toward Miriam, and behold, she was leprous.<sup>11</sup>And Aaron said to Moses, "Oh, my lord, do not punish us because we have done foolishly and have sinned.<sup>12</sup>Let her not be as one dead, whose flesh is half eaten away when he comes out of his mother's womb."<sup>13</sup>And Moses cried to the LORD, "O God, please heal her—please."<sup>14</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be shamed seven days? Let her be shut outside the camp seven days, and after that she may be brought in again."<sup>15</sup>So Miriam was shut outside the camp seven days, and the people did not set out on the march till Miriam was brought in again.<sup>16</sup>After that the people set out from Hazeroth, and camped in the wilderness of Paran.
12.overview:
Chapter 12 brings the rebellion home, not from the rabble now but from Moses’ own brother and sister. Miriam and Aaron challenge his unique authority, using his Cushite wife as a pretext but revealing their true grievance. At the heart of the chapter stands the remark that Moses was “very meek”: he does not defend himself; God defends him, descending in the cloud to declare that with Moses he speaks “mouth to mouth.”

Miriam is struck with leprosy, and the climax is breathtaking: Moses, the one wronged, cries out for his sister. The meek mediator intercedes for his accuser, a portrait of the heart of Christ, who prayed for those who crucified him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses over his Cushite wife, questioning his unique prophetic authority; Moses is exceedingly meek.
verseByVerse.theology: Envy of God-given authority is rebellion against God; true greatness is found in meekness, not self-assertion.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses’ siblings challenge his authority. Now: a warning against jealousy of others’ callings and a call to humble meekness.

verseByVerse.quote: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married, for he had married a Cushite woman. And they said, "Has the LORD indeed spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?" And the LORD heard it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The attack this time comes from inside the family: the sister who watched his basket in the reeds and the brother who spoke for him before Pharaoh.

The stated grievance is his wife. Cush is the region south of Egypt, and a Cushite woman was probably dark-skinned and certainly foreign. Whether this is Zipporah (Habakkuk 3:7 sets Cushan beside Midian) or a second marriage after her death, the text does not say. What it does say, at once, is that the wife was not what this was about.

The real thing comes out in the next breath: Has he not spoken through us also?

The marriage was the presentable objection; the complaint is that Moses has a standing they do not. Aaron was high priest and Miriam a prophetess (Exod. 15:20), the second and third most important people in the nation, and it was not enough.

That is how such things usually present themselves: a grievance raised on principled-sounding grounds, with the energy coming from somewhere else. The test is usually proportion: the reaction is far larger than the stated cause can explain.

And the LORD heard it. They said it privately, in a family. There is no such thing as a private conversation about the servants of God.

Was this racism? God never rebukes the marriage. Moses’ wife was a Cushite, and God sides with Moses; the sin was the jealousy and prejudice of his brother and sister. The law’s bans on marriage concerned idolatry, not ethnicity.
verseByVerse.note: Moses’ Cushite wife may be Zipporah or a second wife; Cush was the region south of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the narrator interrupts his own story with one of the strangest sentences in Scripture.

Readers have puzzled over Moses writing that about himself, and it may well be a note added later under the same inspiration, as the account of his death was (Deut. 34). The more important question is why it stands here. It is because of what Moses does not do next. Slandered by his own brother and sister, his marriage used against him, his call questioned, he says nothing. The silence is not weakness or shock. It is character.

Biblical meekness is not timidity; this is the man who faced down Pharaoh and ground the golden calf to powder. It is strength that has stopped needing to defend itself, because it has handed the defending to somebody else.

The New Testament gives this quality supremely to one person: learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt. 11:29), where the Greek Old Testament uses the same word for Moses’ meekness. And when he was accused, he opened not his mouth (Isa. 53:7). Moses saying nothing while his family attacks him faintly foreshadows the silence of Christ before Caiaphas.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God summons the three to the tent, descends in the cloud, and declares Moses’ unique standing: he speaks with him mouth to mouth.
verseByVerse.theology: God himself defends his servants and honors the offices he appoints; to speak against his chosen is to provoke his anger.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God vindicates Moses face to face. Now: trust God to defend your honor, and revere the callings he assigns.

verseByVerse.quote: And suddenly the LORD said to Moses and to Aaron and Miriam, "Come out, you three, to the tent of meeting." And the three of them came out. And the LORD came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tent and called Aaron and Miriam, and they both came forward. And he said, "Hear my words: If there is a prophet among you, I the LORD make myself known to him in a vision; I speak with him in a dream.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses said nothing. God does not. Suddenly the three are summoned like children called in from the garden, and the LORD comes down in the cloud to the door of his own house, before the whole camp, to speak about an hour of talk behind a brother’s back.

He begins with a general principle: to a prophet he speaks in a vision or in a dream. That is how he had dealt with Miriam and Aaron, and it is real revelation; neither is being demoted from it. It is simply not the whole of what God does.

Moses saw the form of the LORD. Yet no one can see God’s face and live (Exod 33:20). Moses saw a visible likeness of God’s glory, his back, not his unveiled face (Exod 33:23). The full sight of God is in Christ (John 1:18; 14:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Not so with my servant Moses. He is faithful in all my house. With him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles, and he beholds the form of the LORD. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?" And the anger of the LORD was kindled against them, and he departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every phrase raises the ground under Moses higher. Other prophets get visions; he gets God’s mouth. Others get riddles, the sideways, image-laden speech of Ezekiel and Zechariah; he gets it plainly. Others hear; he beholds the form of the LORD. And twice God calls him my servant Moses, in Scripture nearly a title.

And God’s question is not “why were you not kinder” but why then were you not afraid. Speaking against a man God had set where he set Moses was not a family disagreement; it was an act of nerve.

Then a chilling line: his anger is kindled, and he departed. No chance to answer. The cloud lifts, and only then do they find out what has happened.

One phrase travelled a long way: Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant… but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Heb. 3:5–6). The sentence that set Moses above everybody in Israel is used to say that Moses was, in the end, staff, and there is a Son over the house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — Miriam’s Leprosy and Moses’ Intercession
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Miriam is struck with leprosy; Aaron pleads, Moses intercedes, and after seven days outside the camp she is restored.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin bears bitter fruit, but the meek mediator intercedes for his accuser — a portrait of the heart of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses prays for the sister who wronged him. Now: Christ intercedes for sinners; we are called to forgive and pray for those who wrong us.

verseByVerse.quote: When the cloud removed from over the tent, behold, Miriam was leprous, like snow. And Aaron turned toward Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. And Aaron said to Moses, "Oh, my lord, do not punish us because we have done foolishly and have sinned. Let her not be as one dead, whose flesh is half eaten away when he comes out of his mother's womb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment is visible, immediate and terrible, and many have seen a grim aptness in it: she had spoken against a foreign woman, and now her own skin is white with disease. (“Like snow” may describe flaking skin rather than colour.)

Only Miriam is struck. Her name stands first in verse 1, and the verb there is feminine singular, marking her as the instigator. That does not leave Aaron innocent, and it may be that the high priest could not be made unclean without paralysing the nation’s worship. He is spared and made to watch his sister struck, which is its own punishment.

And Aaron breaks, pleading do not punish us.

He calls Moses my lord, the man whose authority he was questioning ten minutes ago, and he says “us,” not “her,” which is more than many men do when the consequences land on somebody else. And he goes to the brother he wronged, because there is nowhere else to go.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses cried to the LORD, "O God, please heal her—please."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five words in Hebrew: probably the shortest prayer Moses ever prays, with please at both ends.

This is the man they slandered, just vindicated by God in front of his accusers. Any ordinary man would have let it stand for a day. He does not wait an hour: a broken, doubled plea for the woman who tried to take his place. That is what the meekness of verse 3 consists of: given every right to enjoy the outcome, he wanted her well.

It is the shape of a command that would come from a hillside in Galilee: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matt. 5:44). Moses had no such command, and we who have it keep it poorly. But the One who gave it kept it on the cross, praying for his enemies, and we were among them. His Spirit now makes the same prayer possible in us.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to Moses, "If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be shamed seven days? Let her be shut outside the camp seven days, and after that she may be brought in again." So Miriam was shut outside the camp seven days, and the people did not set out on the march till Miriam was brought in again. After that the people set out from Hazeroth, and camped in the wilderness of Paran.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer is answered, though not entirely. A father spitting in his daughter’s face was the sharpest disgrace an ancient household knew, after which she would keep out of sight for a week; God says his displeasure is at least that serious. Miriam is healed and disciplined, and the two are not in conflict.

Christians need that distinction and often lose it. Forgiveness is not the removal of consequences. Miriam did not die or lose her place in Israel; she also sat seven days outside the camp in full view, the sin public and so the discipline public. The Lord disciplines the one he loves (Heb. 12:6): the discipline is evidence of the love, not a qualification of it.

And the loveliest detail in the chapter is the waiting. Two million people with a land to reach sat still for a week for one disgraced woman, and did not march till Miriam was brought in again. Israel had been stalled by rebellion before; this time the nation is stalled by mercy.

That tells you what kind of God had been offended. He had every right to be finished with her, and instead his people stopped until she could walk back in. It is a picture of how he treats those he has had to correct; when Miriam is next mentioned, she dies at Kadesh and is buried among her people (20:1), still one of them.

12.theology:
Meekness and Self-Forgetfulness. Moses does not defend himself but entrusts his cause to God: a portrait of Christ, who when reviled did not revile in return but entrusted himself to the righteous Judge.

God Vindicates His Servants. To attack God’s appointed servant is to provoke God himself. We need not scramble to justify ourselves; the Judge of all the earth will vindicate his own.

The Mediator Intercedes for his Accuser. The wronged mediator pleads for the guilty: the gospel in miniature, fulfilled when Christ prayed for those who crucified him and ever lives to intercede for sinners.
12.examples:
Then: Miriam and Aaron envied Moses’ authority and were rebuked by God; Moses interceded for his sister, and the camp waited until she was restored.

Now: Christ, the wronged Mediator, has interceded for you and brought you home. Out of that, beware envy of others’ callings, entrust your vindication to God, and when others wrong you, pray for their healing, asking the Spirit for the meekness you do not have by nature.

13.title: The Twelve Spies: The Sin of Unbelief
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Send men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel. From each tribe of their fathers you shall send a man, every one a chief among them."<sup>3</sup>So Moses sent them from the wilderness of Paran, according to the command of the LORD, all of them men who were heads of the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And these were their names: From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur;<sup>5</sup>from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori;<sup>6</sup>from the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh;<sup>7</sup>from the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph;<sup>8</sup>from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Nun;<sup>9</sup>from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu;<sup>10</sup>from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi;<sup>11</sup>from the tribe of Joseph (that is, from the tribe of Manasseh), Gaddi the son of Susi;<sup>12</sup>from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli;<sup>13</sup>from the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael;<sup>14</sup>from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vophsi;<sup>15</sup>from the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi.<sup>16</sup>These were the names of the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua.<sup>17</sup>Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan and said to them, "Go up into the Negeb and go up into the hill country,<sup>18</sup>and see what the land is, and whether the people who dwell in it are strong or weak, whether they are few or many,<sup>19</sup>and whether the land that they dwell in is good or bad, and whether the cities that they dwell in are camps or strongholds,<sup>20</sup>and whether the land is rich or poor, and whether there are trees in it or not. Be of good courage and bring some of the fruit of the land." Now the time was the season of the first ripe grapes.<sup>21</sup>So they went up and spied out the land from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob, near Lebo-hamath.<sup>22</sup>They went up into the Negeb and came to Hebron. Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak, were there. (Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)<sup>23</sup>And they came to the Valley of Eshcol and cut down from there a branch with a single cluster of grapes, and they carried it on a pole between two of them; they also brought some pomegranates and figs.<sup>24</sup>That place was called the Valley of Eshcol, because of the cluster that the people of Israel cut down from there.<sup>25</sup>At the end of forty days they returned from spying out the land.<sup>26</sup>And they came to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation of the people of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, at Kadesh. They brought back word to them and to all the congregation, and showed them the fruit of the land.<sup>27</sup>And they told him, "We came to the land to which you sent us. It flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit.<sup>28</sup>However, the people who dwell in the land are strong, and the cities are fortified and very large. And besides, we saw the descendants of Anak there.<sup>29</sup>The Amalekites dwell in the land of the Negeb. The Hittites, the Jebusites, and the Amorites dwell in the hill country. And the Canaanites dwell by the sea, and along the Jordan."<sup>30</sup>But Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said, "Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it."<sup>31</sup>Then the men who had gone up with him said, "We are not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are."<sup>32</sup>So they brought to the people of Israel a bad report of the land that they had spied out, saying, "The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that devours its inhabitants, and all the people that we saw in it are of great height.<sup>33</sup>And there we saw the Nephilim (the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim), and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them."
13.overview:
Chapter 13 brings Israel to the threshold of the promised land and to the great crisis of the book. Twelve spies see the same land, the same fruit, the same giants; ten see through the lens of fear, and two through faith. The land is everything God promised, its grapes carried on a pole between two men, yet the ten fixate on walled cities and the sons of Anak, and become grasshoppers in their own eyes.

Here is the anatomy of unbelief: measuring the giants against ourselves rather than against God. Hebrews 3–4 holds it up as the great warning, and points beyond Joshua, whose name in Greek is Jesus, to the Saviour who has entered the true rest and brings his people in (Hebrews 4:8–10, 14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the people’s request, twelve leaders are sent to spy out Canaan; Moses charges them to assess the land and its people.
verseByVerse.theology: God grants the people’s desire to scout the land, setting the stage for a test of faith at the very threshold of promise.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: twelve spies sent into Canaan. Now: the believer stands at the edge of obedience, called to trust God’s promise.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Send men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel. From each tribe of their fathers you shall send a man, every one a chief among them." So Moses sent them from the wilderness of Paran, according to the command of the LORD, all of them men who were heads of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things need settling before the story starts. First, whose idea was this? Numbers says God commanded it; Deuteronomy says the people asked (Deut. 1:22). Both are true: the request came from below and God permitted it, a pattern this book shows again with Balaam. There is a divine yes that is a concession rather than a plan, and it is often the beginning of trouble.

Second, God’s own clause: which I am giving. Present tense. The land is a gift already being handed over, settled since Abraham. The reconnaissance is about how, not whether, and forty days later ten men will come back and answer a question nobody had asked them.

Name that, because it is how a great deal of disobedience gets started among sincere people. God has spoken plainly, and we go away to gather information, and by the time we come back the plain word has quietly become one factor among several.

Which raises a fair question: was it wrong to send the spies at all? Not in itself. Joshua will send two into Jericho with God’s blessing and no rebuke (Josh. 2:1). Prudence is not unbelief, and the man who checks the road before he drives down it is not doubting God. The difference lies in what the information is being gathered for. Joshua’s spies went out to find the way in. These twelve were sent by a people who had not yet decided to go.

verseByVerse.quote: And these were their names: From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur; from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori; from the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh; from the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph; from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Nun; from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu; from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi; from the tribe of Joseph (that is, from the tribe of Manasseh), Gaddi the son of Susi; from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli; from the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael; from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vophsi; from the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi. These were the names of the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list is a roll of the finest men in Israel, every one a chief. This was not a failure of the second rank, which is what makes it devastating. Two names matter: Caleb of Judah, and Hoshea of Ephraim.

And Moses renames Hoshea Joshua, at the moment twelve men are about to find out whether they believe God can do what he promised. Ten will come back saying we are not able; the man with the new name will say God is. And that name, in Greek, is the one the angel gave a child in Nazareth: you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21).
verseByVerse.note: “Joshua” means “the LORD saves”; its Greek form is “Jesus.”

verseByVerse.quote: Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan and said to them, "Go up into the Negeb and go up into the hill country, and see what the land is, and whether the people who dwell in it are strong or weak, whether they are few or many, and whether the land that they dwell in is good or bad, and whether the cities that they dwell in are camps or strongholds, and whether the land is rich or poor, and whether there are trees in it or not. Be of good courage and bring some of the fruit of the land." Now the time was the season of the first ripe grapes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ briefing is practical: the land, the people, the cities, the soil, the timber. It is competent reconnaissance and nothing unspiritual. But the last two clauses are of a different order: Be of good courage and bring some of the fruit of the land.

Why say that? He has asked for facts, and facts do not require courage to collect. Moses evidently knew something about the men he was sending, or about human nature, and the sentence reads like a father saying something at a door that he is not sure will be remembered.

And he asks them to carry home not a map but fruit: a piece of the promise itself brought back into the wilderness, so that the nation would see evidence of God’s goodness before it heard anything else.

They brought it, and it made no difference. Evidence is not the same as faith; a man can hold the goodness of God in his own hands and still refuse to trust him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — The Survey of the Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The spies traverse the land from south to north, reaching Hebron and the Valley of Eshcol, where they cut a single cluster of grapes.
verseByVerse.theology: The land proves abundantly good, its fruit so heavy it must be carried between two men — the visible evidence of God’s gift.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a cluster of grapes borne on a pole. Now: God gives tangible evidence of his goodness to strengthen our faith.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went up and spied out the land from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob, near Lebo-hamath. They went up into the Negeb and came to Hebron. Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak, were there. (Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.) And they came to the Valley of Eshcol and cut down from there a branch with a single cluster of grapes, and they carried it on a pole between two of them; they also brought some pomegranates and figs. That place was called the Valley of Eshcol, because of the cluster that the people of Israel cut down from there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They go the whole length of the country, several hundred miles on foot through hostile territory. At Hebron they meet the descendants of Anak by name, a people of famous size, in a town the writer dates (seven years before Zoan in Egypt) to show it was an old, settled civilisation.

Eshcol means “cluster”. Picture the walk home: two grown men, a pole across their shoulders, and one bunch of grapes between them, all the way across the desert, to a camp that had eaten manna for over a year. It took two men to carry the fruit of one vine.

So two things will be set before Israel at once: three giants and a cluster of grapes. Both real, both accurately reported. Everything depends on which one a man measures against God.
verseByVerse.note: “Eshcol” means “cluster” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of forty days they returned from spying out the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forty days: one of Scripture’s heavy numbers, Noah’s rain, Moses on the mountain, Elijah to Horeb, almost always a period of testing.

Note that these were forty good days. Nothing went wrong on the journey. No one was caught, no one was killed, God brought all twelve of them safely through several hundred miles of enemy country and home again with the fruit. They had just experienced six weeks of unbroken providential care, in the very land they were about to say could not be taken.

The sentence in the next chapter is measured against this number: a year for each day (14:34). Six weeks of looking, four decades of walking in circles.

There is one other forty days in a wilderness, and it is the answer to this one: after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry (Matt. 4:1–2). Israel was tested with the fruit of the promise in their hands, and failed. He was tested with nothing in his hands, and did not. Where the nation called God’s gift impossible, he said Man shall not live by bread alone, and his trust stands in the place of ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–33 — The Report: Faith and Fear
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All twelve confirm the land is good, but ten magnify the giants while Caleb and Joshua urge faith; the people’s hearts melt in fear.
verseByVerse.theology: The same evidence produces faith in some and fear in others; unbelief measures the obstacles against self, faith against God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the grasshopper report of the ten. Now: the believer must measure every giant against the greatness of God, not self.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation of the people of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, at Kadesh. They brought back word to them and to all the congregation, and showed them the fruit of the land. And they told him, "We came to the land to which you sent us. It flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit. However, the people who dwell in the land are strong, and the cities are fortified and very large. And besides, we saw the descendants of Anak there. The Amalekites dwell in the land of the Negeb. The Hittites, the Jebusites, and the Amorites dwell in the hill country. And the Canaanites dwell by the sea, and along the Jordan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report begins truthfully, in God’s own words from the burning bush (Exod. 3:8): it flows with milk and honey. If it had stopped at verse 27, Israel would have marched that afternoon.

Then one word, However, and everything turns on it.

Not one word after it is false. The people were strong, the cities fortified, the Anakim there; Caleb will confirm every detail and take Hebron himself (Josh. 14:12–14). It is an accurate report arranged in an order that leads to despair.

Unbelief rarely needs to invent anything. It usually just needs to put the facts in a particular sequence, mention God first and briefly, and then spend the rest of the paragraph on the difficulties. By the end of verse 29 the giants and the fortifications and five named nations are filling the whole screen, and the God who had said which I am giving to the people of Israel has not been mentioned once.

verseByVerse.quote: But Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said, "Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one man interrupts: we are well able to overcome it. Caleb had seen the same walls, met the same giants and carried the same pole. He had precisely the information the other ten had.

What he has is a different denominator. The ten measured the giants against Israel and got a true answer: too big. Caleb measured them against God, and the arithmetic came out the other way. Both were doing sums. Only one of them had put the right number at the bottom.

And at once: not let us form a committee or wait for a better season. A nation that does not move now will talk itself out of it by morning, which is what happens.

Take the measure of the man. He is one voice against ten, in front of a crowd already frightened, and within a day they will be picking up stones to kill him for it. Forty-five years later, an old man of eighty-five walks up to Joshua and asks for the hill country of Hebron — the giants’ own town — with the sentence: I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me… So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day (Josh. 14:11–12). He had been waiting four decades to finish an argument he was right about, and God gave him the ground the giants were standing on.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men who had gone up with him said, "We are not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are." So they brought to the people of Israel a bad report of the land that they had spied out, saying, "The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that devours its inhabitants, and all the people that we saw in it are of great height. And there we saw the Nephilim (the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim), and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ten answer, and their reply is a study in how unbelief talks. It begins with something true, they are stronger than we are, correct and beside the point, because the question was never whether Israel was stronger than Canaan.

Then it slides: a land that devours its inhabitants. In verse 27 it flowed with milk and honey; now it eats people. The writer calls it a bad report, a slander: from reporting the facts to defaming the gift.

Then it exaggerates: all the people are of great height. That is fear talking, and fear speaks in totals.

Last comes the sentence that gives it away: we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them.

The first half is an honest report on their self-image. The second reports what was in the heads of men they never spoke to. Rahab will tell us how Israel actually appeared to Canaan: our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you (Josh. 2:11). The people the spies thought were laughing at them were terrified of them.

That is the mechanism, and it is a great deal more common than giants. A man decides what he is worth, and then assumes everybody else has reached the same verdict, and lives as though a judgment he passed on himself were a fact about the world. It ruined a nation. The only cure is to stop measuring against the giants and start measuring against God, which is the single difference between Caleb and the ten.

Who were the Nephilim and the sons of Anak? The Anakim were a real people of great stature (Deut 2:10–11), and Goliath probably came of the same stock (Josh 11:22 leaves Anakim in Gath). The spies’ claim that they came from the Nephilim echoes Genesis 6:4, but the spies were spreading a bad report (v. 32); most take it that the flood had ended that line (Genesis 6:4 itself is much debated), and that these men were simply very tall. The fear made them grasshoppers in their own eyes.

13.theology:
The Anatomy of Unbelief. Unbelief is rarely a denial of facts but a misreading of them, leaving God out of the equation, so that the obstacle eclipses the promise.

The Same Evidence, Two Responses. All twelve saw the same land, fruit and giants; the difference was in the heart. Evidence does not produce faith in an unbelieving heart; faith is a response to the trustworthiness of God.

Joshua. The faithful spy who will lead Israel in bears the name that in Greek is Jesus (Heb. 4:8), pointing to the One who brings his people into the true rest.
13.examples:
Then: Twelve spies saw the same land and giants; ten shrank like grasshoppers, but Caleb, factoring in God, cried, “Let us go up at once.”

Now: At the edge of every hard obedience, the question is the size of your God, who has already said “which I am giving.” Beware the “however” of unbelief, and measure your giants against the LORD who saves. Where your faith shrinks, Christ’s held firm for you in the wilderness, and his Spirit is given to make you, like Caleb, of “a different spirit” (14:24).

14.title: Israel’s Rebellion: The Wilderness Decreed
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Then all the congregation raised a loud cry, and the people wept that night.<sup>2</sup>And all the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, "Would that we had died in the land of Egypt! Or would that we had died in this wilderness!<sup>3</sup>Why is the LORD bringing us into this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and our little ones will become a prey. Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?"<sup>4</sup>And they said to one another, "Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt."<sup>5</sup>Then Moses and Aaron fell on their faces before all the assembly of the congregation of the people of Israel.<sup>6</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who were among those who had spied out the land, tore their clothes<sup>7</sup>and said to all the congregation of the people of Israel, "The land, which we passed through to spy it out, is an exceedingly good land.<sup>8</sup>If the LORD delights in us, he will bring us into this land and give it to us, a land that flows with milk and honey.<sup>9</sup>Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us. Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us; do not fear them."<sup>10</sup>Then all the congregation said to stone them with stones. But the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting to all the people of Israel.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them?<sup>12</sup>I will strike them with the pestilence and disinherit them, and I will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they."<sup>13</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Then the Egyptians will hear of it, for you brought up this people in your might from among them,<sup>14</sup>and they will tell the inhabitants of this land. They have heard that you, O LORD, are in the midst of this people. For you, O LORD, are seen face to face, and your cloud stands over them and you go before them, in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night.<sup>15</sup>Now if you kill this people as one man, then the nations who have heard your fame will say,<sup>16</sup>'It is because the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land that he swore to give to them that he has killed them in the wilderness.'<sup>17</sup>And now, please let the power of the Lord be great as you have promised, saying,<sup>18</sup>'The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, to the third and the fourth generation.'<sup>19</sup>Please pardon the iniquity of this people, according to the greatness of your steadfast love, just as you have forgiven this people, from Egypt until now."<sup>20</sup>Then the LORD said, "I have pardoned, according to your word.<sup>21</sup>But truly, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD,<sup>22</sup>none of the men who have seen my glory and my signs that I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and yet have put me to the test these ten times and have not obeyed my voice,<sup>23</sup>shall see the land that I swore to give to their fathers. And none of those who despised me shall see it.<sup>24</sup>But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land into which he went, and his descendants shall possess it.<sup>25</sup>Now, since the Amalekites and the Canaanites dwell in the valleys, turn tomorrow and set out for the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea."<sup>26</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,<sup>27</sup>"How long shall this wicked congregation grumble against me? I have heard the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against me.<sup>28</sup>Say to them, 'As I live, declares the LORD, what you have said in my hearing I will do to you:<sup>29</sup>your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness, and of all your number, listed in the census from twenty years old and upward, who have grumbled against me,<sup>30</sup>not one shall come into the land where I swore that I would make you dwell, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.<sup>31</sup>But your little ones, who you said would become a prey, I will bring in, and they shall know the land that you have rejected.<sup>32</sup>But as for you, your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness.<sup>33</sup>And your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years and shall suffer for your faithlessness, until the last of your dead bodies lies in the wilderness.<sup>34</sup>According to the number of the days in which you spied out the land, forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years, and you shall know my displeasure.'<sup>35</sup>I, the LORD, have spoken. Surely this will I do to all this wicked congregation who are gathered together against me: in this wilderness they shall come to a full end, and there they shall die."<sup>36</sup>And the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land, who returned and made all the congregation grumble against him by bringing up a bad report about the land—<sup>37</sup>the men who brought up a bad report of the land— died by plague before the LORD.<sup>38</sup>Of those men who went to spy out the land, only Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive.<sup>39</sup>When Moses told these words to all the people of Israel, the people mourned greatly.<sup>40</sup>And they rose early in the morning and went up to the heights of the hill country, saying, "Here we are. We will go up to the place that the LORD has promised, for we have sinned."<sup>41</sup>But Moses said, "Why now are you transgressing the command of the LORD, when that will not succeed?<sup>42</sup>Do not go up, for the LORD is not among you, lest you be struck down before your enemies.<sup>43</sup>For there the Amalekites and the Canaanites are facing you, and you shall fall by the sword. Because you have turned back from following the LORD, the LORD will not be with you."<sup>44</sup>But they presumed to go up to the heights of the hill country, although neither the ark of the covenant of the LORD nor Moses departed out of the camp.<sup>45</sup>Then the Amalekites and the Canaanites who lived in that hill country came down and defeated them and pursued them, even to Hormah.
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is the catastrophe toward which the book has been building. Swayed by the ten, the people rebel outright: weeping all night, longing for Egypt, proposing to stone Caleb and Joshua and choose a leader to take them back to slavery. It is the great refusal of grace, halted only by the appearing of the glory of the LORD.

Then comes Moses’ great intercession, pleading not his own glory but God’s name and God’s revealed character. God pardons, and yet justice falls: the faithless generation will wander forty years and die in the wilderness. Hebrews 3–4 makes this the great warning, and it drives us to the better Mediator, whose intercession secures not a forty-year reprieve but everlasting pardon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Rebellion and the Plea of Caleb and Joshua
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people weep, long for Egypt, and plot to return; Caleb and Joshua plead for faith, but the congregation moves to stone them.
verseByVerse.theology: Unbelief hardens into open rebellion and the rejection of God’s gift; faith pleads, but the rebellious heart reaches for stones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel longs to return to Egypt. Now: a warning against the heart that despises grace and shrinks back to bondage.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the congregation raised a loud cry, and the people wept that night. And all the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, "Would that we had died in the land of Egypt! Or would that we had died in this wilderness! Why is the LORD bringing us into this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and our little ones will become a prey. Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?" And they said to one another, "Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cry all night, and in the morning out comes the sentence formed in the dark: Would that we had died in this wilderness! God will take those words up in verse 29 and grant them. They asked to die in the wilderness because they could think of nothing worse to say, and God said: very well.

Then the accusation, the reverse of the truth: the God who split a sea for them is charged with bringing them here to fall by the sword, using their children as bait. That is what unbelief eventually says aloud about the character of God, and it began as a reasonable concern about fortified cities.

Then the bottom of it: Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt. A coup and an emigration, back to the brick pits where every family had buried somebody. They would rather have slavery they understand than a promise that requires them to trust somebody. People still make that trade, for the same reason.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron fell on their faces before all the assembly of the congregation of the people of Israel. And Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who were among those who had spied out the land, tore their clothes and said to all the congregation of the people of Israel, "The land, which we passed through to spy it out, is an exceedingly good land. If the LORD delights in us, he will bring us into this land and give it to us, a land that flows with milk and honey. Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us. Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us; do not fear them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four men respond. Moses and Aaron fall on their faces, and Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes, as a man does at a funeral or in the face of blasphemy.

Their plea is faith reasoning aloud. They deny not one fact the ten reported. They start from God’s pleasure in his people, If the LORD delights in us, rather than from the height of the walls.

And the people the ten said devour the land are bread for us: not because Joshua and Caleb thought Israel strong, but because they knew who was doing the eating.

The ground of it is the whole argument in one sentence: Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us. The Hebrew says their shadow has turned aside: whatever sheltered Canaan has moved off it, and whatever shelters Israel stands in the middle of the camp. If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom. 8:31) is not a new thought. Two men shouted it at a mob that was about to stone them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the congregation said to stone them with stones. But the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting to all the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is the answer of the whole congregation to the two men who believed God: not argument, rocks.

Unbelief, when it has run its course, does not merely disagree with faith; it wants faith silenced, because a man who trusts God is unbearable to a room that has decided not to. Stephen made exactly this point to the Sanhedrin, and the sequence of what happened next was the same: Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? (Acts 7:52). They picked up stones for him too.

And then, mid-sentence, God arrives: But the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting to all the people of Israel. The stones never leave their hands. There is a moment here that ought to be seen for what it is — two men standing in front of a crowd with rocks in its fists, entirely defenceless, and the glory of God interposing itself between them and the first throw.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God threatens to disinherit Israel; Moses pleads God’s name and revealed character, and God pardons, though judgment remains.
verseByVerse.theology: The mediator intercedes on the ground of God’s own glory and self-revelation; God pardons for his name’s sake.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses pleads God’s character back to him. Now: Christ intercedes on the ground of his own glory, securing our pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them? I will strike them with the pestilence and disinherit them, and I will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s verdict is two questions that go to the root: how long will they despise me, and not believe in me?

Two charges, and they are the same charge. To despise is the outward act; not to believe is the inward reality; and God names them in one breath because he sees no gap between them. That is a hard word for a religious culture that has learned to treat unbelief as an intellectual difficulty and contempt as a moral one. In God’s reading of this scene, refusing to trust him after everything he has done is not a failure of evidence. It is an insult.

And note the phrase in spite of all the signs. These are people who watched a sea open. They had eaten bread off the ground that morning and there was a pillar of fire over the tent behind them. More evidence would not have helped, which is the standing answer to anyone who says he would believe if only God did something visible. He did, for more than a year, in front of this congregation.

Then the offer: disinherit them, and I will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they. It is the offer of the golden calf again, a genuine test as well as a genuine threat.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the LORD, "Then the Egyptians will hear of it, for you brought up this people in your might from among them, and they will tell the inhabitants of this land. They have heard that you, O LORD, are in the midst of this people. For you, O LORD, are seen face to face, and your cloud stands over them and you go before them, in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night. Now if you kill this people as one man, then the nations who have heard your fame will say, 'It is because the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land that he swore to give to them that he has killed them in the wilderness.' And now, please let the power of the Lord be great as you have promised, saying, 'The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, to the third and the fourth generation.' Please pardon the iniquity of this people, according to the greatness of your steadfast love, just as you have forgiven this people, from Egypt until now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ answer is one of the great intercessions of the Old Testament, and what is striking is what he does not say. He does not defend the people, because there is no defence. He does not take the offer, though it would make him a patriarch, or appeal to his long service. Every argument is about God.

First, God’s reputation: the nations will conclude that the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land. Moses fears God’s name dishonoured in pagan mouths.

Then he quotes God back to himself, from Exodus 34:6–7: The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he will by no means clear the guilty. He is not telling God what he ought to be like; he holds up what God said he was and asks him to be it.

That is the method of praying with confidence: not “I have been good” or “they are worth it,” but this is who you have said you are. And Moses quotes the hard half too, which is why his prayer is honest, not sentimental. He asks mercy from a God who does not pretend sin is nothing.

Did Moses change God’s mind? God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind (23:19). The threat was real, and God used it to draw out Moses’ prayer, which pleads God’s own name and promise (vv. 17–19). God forgives according to your word (v. 20) because the prayer asked for what God had always purposed. He ordains prayer as one of the means by which he does his will.

Is it fair that children suffer for their fathers’ sin? Each person is judged for his own sin (Deut 24:16; Ezek 18:20). The consequences of sin run through families, and children who carry on their fathers’ hatred of God share their judgment (Exod 20:5, of those who hate me). Here the children who were spared entered the land (v. 31).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "I have pardoned, according to your word. But truly, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD, none of the men who have seen my glory and my signs that I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and yet have put me to the test these ten times and have not obeyed my voice, shall see the land that I swore to give to their fathers. And none of those who despised me shall see it. But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land into which he went, and his descendants shall possess it. Now, since the Amalekites and the Canaanites dwell in the valleys, turn tomorrow and set out for the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer is answered. The nation is not destroyed, the covenant stands, and Israel lived on because one man stood in the gap.

Yet in the same paragraph none of the men who saw his glory and tested him shall see the land.

Pardoned, and excluded. Both, in five verses, from the same mouth. Any reader who wants to understand the Bible has to be able to hold those two together, because they are not in tension — they are the shape of everything God does with sin. He forgives, fully and for ever, and forgiveness is not the abolition of consequences. David is told the LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die, and in the same breath told what will happen to his household (2 Sam. 12:13–14).

These ten times may be a round figure for “again and again” (as in Genesis 31:7). Either way it was not one bad afternoon; the file goes back to the Red Sea.

And one exception: Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully. Not better information or a braver temperament. Something else was in him, and God put it there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–38 — The Sentence of Forty Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God decrees forty years of wandering, a year for each day; the ten faithless spies die by plague, but Caleb and Joshua live.
verseByVerse.theology: The faithless generation forfeits the rest because of unbelief; faith alone enters the inheritance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: forty years in the wilderness for unbelief. Now: Hebrews warns the church not to fail to enter God’s rest through unbelief.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, "How long shall this wicked congregation grumble against me? I have heard the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against me. Say to them, 'As I live, declares the LORD, what you have said in my hearing I will do to you: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness, and of all your number, listed in the census from twenty years old and upward, who have grumbled against me, not one shall come into the land where I swore that I would make you dwell, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun. But your little ones, who you said would become a prey, I will bring in, and they shall know the land that you have rejected. But as for you, your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness. And your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years and shall suffer for your faithlessness, until the last of your dead bodies lies in the wilderness. According to the number of the days in which you spied out the land, forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years, and you shall know my displeasure.' I, the LORD, have spoken. Surely this will I do to all this wicked congregation who are gathered together against me: in this wilderness they shall come to a full end, and there they shall die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the sentence, and its terrible symmetry. God hands back what they shouted in verse 2: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness. They said they wished to die here. They will.

Then the reversal of their accusation: your little ones, who you said would become a prey, I will bring in. Their unbelief was dressed up as concern for their families, and God answers by taking better care of their families than they would.

And the arithmetic: a year for each day. Forty days of looking at the promise, forty years of walking away from it.

Consider what those forty years actually were. Not a punishment inflicted on them from outside so much as their own choice extended and given room. They said they would rather be in the wilderness than in the land; God let them have the wilderness. Hell is God’s just sentence on sin, and it is never passed on anyone who wanted him: in the end it grants the sinner what he chose.

And verse 33 is unbearable: your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years and shall suffer for your faithlessness. The children inherit, but they carried it, spending their youth burying their parents in a desert. Nobody sins in a way that stops with themselves.

Hebrews uses this generation as a warning (Heb 3:16–4:2). Can a true believer lose salvation? Arminian Christians, whose love for Christ is not in doubt, say yes. But Hebrews also says we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end (Heb 3:14): holding firm shows who truly belongs. The warning is real, and it is one of the means by which God keeps his own (John 10:28–29). Some of this generation, like Moses and Aaron, were true believers who were kept from Canaan but not from God. This commentary holds with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (both chapter 17) that those truly born again will persevere, while recognising that faithful Christians differ. And a troubled believer who fears he is like this generation should see the difference: they wanted Egypt and reached for stones, while he grieves that he has not trusted God more. That grief is hearing his voice today, and the throne of grace is open (Hebrews 4:16).
verseByVerse.note: Forty years, a year for each day of spying.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land, who returned and made all the congregation grumble against him by bringing up a bad report about the land— the men who brought up a bad report of the land— died by plague before the LORD. Of those men who went to spy out the land, only Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer says it twice in one sentence, so that nobody mistakes the grounds: the ten died for the bad report.

The whole nation was under sentence, but these ten die first, because they put the words into everyone else’s mouth. There is a heavier accounting for those who form what a community believes: we who teach will be judged with greater strictness (Jas. 3:1).

And of the twelve, only Joshua and Caleb remain alive. The two threatened with stoning the day before are still standing; the crowd had been entirely wrong about who was in danger.

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses told these words to all the people of Israel, the people mourned greatly. And they rose early in the morning and went up to the heights of the hill country, saying, "Here we are. We will go up to the place that the LORD has promised, for we have sinned." But Moses said, "Why now are you transgressing the command of the LORD, when that will not succeed? Do not go up, for the LORD is not among you, lest you be struck down before your enemies. For there the Amalekites and the Canaanites are facing you, and you shall fall by the sword. Because you have turned back from following the LORD, the LORD will not be with you." But they presumed to go up to the heights of the hill country, although neither the ark of the covenant of the LORD nor Moses departed out of the camp. Then the Amalekites and the Canaanites who lived in that hill country came down and defeated them and pursued them, even to Hormah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they mourn and set out at dawn: we have sinned. It is the right sentence. It is not repentance, and Moses says so.

Look at what has actually changed. Yesterday God said go and they would not; today God says do not go and they will. The direction has reversed and the disposition has not moved an inch. They are still doing what they have decided, and God’s word is still the thing being overridden. That is the definition of the problem, and the fact that their preference now happens to look more obedient makes no difference at all.

Moses names it: the LORD will not be with you. And verse 44 is devastating: they went up although neither the ark of the covenant of the LORD nor Moses departed out of the camp. They marched off to fight for God’s promises while the ark stayed and watched them go.

They are routed even to Hormah, a name to keep: Israel returns to that spot in chapter 21, with God, and wins.

Hebrews preaches this chapter to Christians without softening: So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief (Heb. 3:19). Its point is not that Israel was uniquely bad but that the same promise stands before its readers and the same refusal is available. And the remedy is the one thing this generation would not do: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion (Heb. 3:15). Go in, trusting not our own steadfastness but the High Priest who has passed through the heavens for us (Heb. 4:14).

14.theology:
Unbelief Forfeits the Inheritance. The faithless generation is barred from the rest. The promised rest is received by faith alone.

Intercession on the Ground of God’s Glory. Moses refuses his own exaltation and prays God’s self-disclosure back to him: gospel praying, fulfilled in Christ, who intercedes not on our merit but on the ground of his glory and the Father’s love.

Pardon and Discipline Together. God spares the nation yet bars the unbelieving. Forgiveness does not always remove consequences; mercy and holiness meet in the discipline of a faithful God.
14.examples:
Then: Israel wept for Egypt and reached for stones; Moses interceded, and God pardoned the nation yet decreed forty years in the wilderness.

Now: Christ, your Joshua, trusted the Father where this generation would not, and his faithfulness is counted as yours. So take heed lest an unbelieving heart draw you back from grace; hear his voice today, and lean on the Spirit who keeps you trusting. Pray as Moses did, pleading not your worthiness but God’s revealed character, and when you have shrunk back, come to the throne of grace again.

all the congregation shall stone him with stones outside the camp."<sup>36</sup>And all the congregation brought him outside the camp and stoned him to death with stones, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>37</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>38</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, and tell them to make tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and to put a cord of blue on the tassel of each corner.<sup>39</sup>And it shall be a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD, to do them, not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes, which you are inclined to whore after.<sup>40</sup>So you shall remember and do all my commandments, and be holy to your God.<sup>41</sup>I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God: I am the LORD your God."
15.overview:
After the judgment of chapter 14, chapter 15 opens with a surprising word: “When you come into the land...” The generation barred from the land is given laws for life in it. Grace persists after judgment; the promise stands, though this generation forfeits it.

The chapter gives laws for offerings, one law for native and sojourner alike, and atonement for unintentional sin, then draws a sharp line at the “high-handed” sin of defiance, illustrated by the man gathering sticks on the Sabbath. It closes with tassels of blue, reminders to obey grounded in redemption. And it points to Christ, who bore both our failings and our rebellion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Offerings in the Land; One Law for All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives laws for grain and drink offerings when Israel enters the land, with one statute for native and sojourner alike.
verseByVerse.theology: Grace persists after judgment; the promise of the land stands, and God’s welcome extends equally to the foreigner.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: laws for offerings in the promised land. Now: the gospel’s welcome to all peoples on equal terms in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you, and you offer to the LORD from the herd or from the flock a food offering or a burnt offering or a sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering or at your appointed feasts, to make a pleasing aroma to the LORD, then he who brings his offering shall offer to the LORD a grain offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil; and you shall offer with the burnt offering, or for the sacrifice, a quarter of a hin of wine for the drink offering for each lamb. Or for a ram, you shall offer for a grain offering two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil. And for the drink offering you shall offer a third of a hin of wine, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And when you offer a bull as a burnt offering or sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or for peace offerings to the LORD, then one shall offer with the bull a grain offering of three tenths of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with half a hin of oil. And you shall offer for the drink offering half a hin of wine, as a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read this chapter’s first sentence straight after the last one, because the placing is the point. Chapter 14 ended with a generation sentenced to die and an army running from Hormah. Then: When you come into the land. Not “if.” God has just told these people they will never see Canaan, and the next thing he gives is instruction for when they get there: how much flour, oil and wine go with a lamb, a ram, a bull.

In effect he is talking to the children. The men listening will die in the wilderness; the boys beside them are being given the liturgy of a country they will inherit, and the fathers hear in detail about a life their sons will have.

That is how God deals with failure. Judgment is real, and it is not the end of the sentence. Israel’s worst day is followed at once by legislation for a future she does not deserve, because the promise never depended on the generation it passed through. If we are faithless, he remains faithful—for he cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus it shall be done for each bull or ram, or for each lamb or young goat. As many as you offer, so shall you do with each one, as many as there are. Every native Israelite shall do these things in this way, in offering a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And if a stranger is sojourning with you, or anyone is living permanently among you, and he wishes to offer a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD, he shall do as you do. For the assembly, there shall be one statute for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you, a statute forever throughout your generations. You and the sojourner shall be alike before the LORD. One law and one rule shall be for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And twice in six verses, as though God is determined it will not be missed: You and the sojourner shall be alike before the LORD.

The ger is the resident foreigner, with no tribe, land or ancestry in the covenant. He could not inherit a field. He could inherit everything that mattered: the same offerings, access and standing at the altar, with no second-class rite and no probation.

That was extraordinary in the ancient world, where religion was ethnic by definition. Israel’s law says: if he will come, he comes on identical terms.

So Paul can tell Gentiles, without any sense of novelty, you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Eph. 2:19). The arrangement made for the outsider in Numbers 15 has become their address.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Provision is made for atoning unintentional sin, but the one who sins defiantly, with a high hand, is cut off.
verseByVerse.theology: There is atonement for the sin of weakness and ignorance, but defiant rebellion against God despises his word and finds no sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the line between weakness and defiance. Now: grace covers our failings, but presumptuous rebellion despises the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land to which I bring you and when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall present a contribution to the LORD. Of the first of your dough you shall present a loaf as a contribution; like a contribution from the threshing floor, so shall you present it. Some of the first of your dough you shall give to the LORD as a contribution throughout your generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the first of the dough: not of the harvest, which is elsewhere, but at the kitchen end. A woman kneading bread in her own house takes a piece off the batch before it is baked and gives it away.

The harvest offering happens once a year at the sanctuary with everybody watching. This one happens on baking day, several times a month, in front of nobody: the smallest act of worship touching the most ordinary object. And it comes off the top, before the loaf goes in the oven, while it still costs something to give.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you sin unintentionally, and do not observe all these commandments that the LORD has spoken to Moses, all that the LORD has commanded you by Moses, from the day that the LORD gave commandment, and onward throughout your generations, then if it was done unintentionally without the knowledge of the congregation, all the congregation shall offer one bull from the herd for a burnt offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD, with its grain offering and its drink offering, according to the rule, and one male goat for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for all the congregation of the people of Israel, and they shall be forgiven, because it was a mistake, and they have brought their offering, a food offering to the LORD, and their sin offering before the LORD for their mistake. And all the congregation of the people of Israel shall be forgiven, and the stranger who sojourns among them, because the whole population was involved in the mistake. "If one person sins unintentionally, he shall offer a female goat a year old for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement before the LORD for the person who makes a mistake, when he sins unintentionally, to make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven. You shall have one law for him who does anything unintentionally, for him who is native among the people of Israel and for the stranger who sojourns among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a gracious provision for sin committed unintentionally, first for the whole nation, then for the single person.

Two things are clear. First, unintentional sin is still sin, requiring blood, a priest and atonement. Israel was not permitted the modern assumption that what a man did not mean does not count; the person harmed is really harmed.

Second, God legislated for it in advance, on both scales, including the case where the whole nation is wrong together and nobody notices. A community can be sincerely, collectively mistaken, and Scripture assumes it will happen.

And each case ends: they shall be forgiven. Not excused: forgiven, which means something was genuinely wrong. This is why a person can live with the knowledge that much of the damage he has done was done without knowing it. Declare me innocent from hidden faults (Ps. 19:12) is a prayer with an answer.

verseByVerse.quote: But the person who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native or a sojourner, reviles the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised the word of the LORD and has broken his commandment, that person shall be utterly cut off; his iniquity shall be on him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the sharp line: the one who sins with a high hand reviles the LORD and is cut off.

The high hand is a raised fist: not sin in weakness, or in a moment, or in ignorance, but defiance, knowing what God has said and doing it anyway as a gesture. For that one category the chapter offers no sacrifice. There is no goat listed.

This frightens sensitive Christians, and it must be handled carefully. Have I committed it? The text gives the shape of the answer: the high-handed man reviles and despises. He is not sorry. A person lying awake afraid he has sinned beyond forgiveness has already shown that he has not, because the high-handed man does not lie awake.

Peter denied Christ three times with oaths, about as deliberate as sin gets (Matt. 26:74), and was restored on a beach over breakfast (John 21:15-17). What is described here is not the seriousness of a sin but the direction of a life, a settled contempt with no intention of returning. Hebrews says the same: if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins (Heb. 10:26). Not because the blood of Christ is insufficient, but because a man who has decided to despise it will not come and be washed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–41 — The Sabbath-Breaker and the Tassels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man gathering sticks on the Sabbath is stoned as a case of high-handed sin; Israel is given tassels with a cord of blue as reminders to obey.
verseByVerse.theology: Defiant sin is deadly serious, but God graciously provides visible reminders to keep his commandments and resist wandering hearts.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: tassels of blue to prompt obedience. Now: the believer needs constant reminders of grace to walk in holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: While the people of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. And those who found him gathering sticks brought him to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation. They put him in custody, because it had not been made clear what should be done to him. And the LORD said to Moses, "The man shall be put to death; all the congregation shall stone him with stones outside the camp." And all the congregation brought him outside the camp and stoned him to death with stones, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, without warning, a story: a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath is held in custody and stoned outside the camp at God’s command. The severity is shocking, and the reader should not be talked out of the shock. But it comes straight after the definition of high-handed sin, as its case study.

He was gathering fuel in the open, in a camp under the pillar of fire, and the Sabbath had been given at Sinai with the mountain shaking as the sign of the covenant itself (Exod. 31:13–17). And he was held because it had not been made clear what should be done to him. Nobody improvised; Moses waited and asked.

What was on trial was not firewood but whether God’s word meant anything in that camp, at the moment a nation under sentence was deciding how seriously to take him. The man had raised his fist in public, and the whole congregation had to see what that meant.

And remember who was later accused of breaking this same Sabbath: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (Mark 2:27–28). The Lord of the Sabbath took the weight of its broken commandment on himself and was executed outside a city for crimes he had not committed.

Should Sabbath-breakers be put to death today? The penalty belonged to Israel’s civil law, where the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant itself, and it ended with that theocracy.

Does the Sabbath bind Christians today? It was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exod 31:13), and the New Testament calls Sabbaths a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Col 2:16–17). Many godly Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment, and their view deserves respect; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. The better reading is that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Heb 4:9–10), so no day binds the conscience (Rom 14:5); rest and gathering for worship on the Lord’s Day remain good gifts. Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy rather than under rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience; faithful believers differ here.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Speak to the people of Israel, and tell them to make tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and to put a cord of blue on the tassel of each corner. And it shall be a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD, to do them, not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes, which you are inclined to whore after. So you shall remember and do all my commandments, and be holy to your God. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God: I am the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, after the stoning, God does something tender: a cord of blue on the tassel of every cloak in Israel. Blue was the colour of the tabernacle curtains and the high priest’s robe, one of the costliest dyes of the ancient world, and now a strand of it on a shepherd’s coat.

The tassel is to look at and remember, and God knows how forgetting works. A man seldom decides to disobey; his eye falls on something and he follows it, and by the time he thinks of God the thing is done. So God puts something at the bottom edge of his vision, where he glances a hundred times a day. He cannot look down without seeing blue.

And the order in the last verse: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Rescue first, commandments second. Israel does not obey in order to be brought out; she was brought out, and the tassel reminds her whose she already is.

These are the tassels a desperate woman reached for, twelve years ill, when she touched the fringe of his garment (Matt. 9:20). A thread sewn into a hem to recall the commandments, and the power went out of the one who had kept them all, and he turned and called her daughter.

15.theology:
Grace After Judgment. The promise outlasts the failure; God’s covenant is more durable than his people’s unbelief, and his discipline never cancels his grace.

Weakness and Defiance. Grace abounds for the stumbling believer; presumptuous contempt for God spurns the very provision of mercy, a warning Hebrews presses on the church.

Reminders of Grace and Holiness. The tassels are God’s provision for forgetful hearts, grounded in redemption. We obey because we have been redeemed.
15.examples:
Then: The generation barred from the land was given laws for the land, a defiant Sabbath-breaker was stoned, and Israel wore tassels of blue to remember.
