Now: Christ suffered outside the gate, bearing the law-breaker’s curse, and kept the commandments you forget. Rest in that grace, beware the high-handed heart, and use the reminders he gives, the Word, the table, the saints, through which his Spirit turns your wandering eyes back to the Lord who redeemed you.

16.title: Korah’s Rebellion: The One Mediator
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Korah the son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and On the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took men.<sup>2</sup>And they rose up before Moses, with a number of the people of Israel, 250 chiefs of the congregation, chosen from the assembly, well-known men.<sup>3</sup>They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron and said to them, "You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?"<sup>4</sup>When Moses heard it, he fell on his face,<sup>5</sup>and he said to Korah and all his company, "In the morning the LORD will show who is his, and who is holy, and will bring him near to him. The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him.<sup>6</sup>Do this: take censers, Korah and all his company;<sup>7</sup>put fire in them and put incense on them before the LORD tomorrow, and the man whom the LORD chooses shall be the holy one. You have gone too far, sons of Levi!"<sup>8</sup>And Moses said to Korah, "Hear now, you sons of Levi:<sup>9</sup>is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself, to do service in the tabernacle of the LORD and to stand before the congregation to minister to them,<sup>10</sup>and that he has brought you near him, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you? And would you seek the priesthood also?<sup>11</sup>Therefore it is against the LORD that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"<sup>12</sup>And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and they said, "We will not come up.<sup>13</sup>Is it a small thing that you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, that you must also make yourself a prince over us?<sup>14</sup>Moreover, you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, nor given us inheritance of fields and vineyards. Will you put out the eyes of these men? We will not come up."<sup>15</sup>And Moses was very angry and said to the LORD, "Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, and I have not harmed one of them."<sup>16</sup>And Moses said to Korah, "Be present, you and all your company, before the LORD, you and they, and Aaron, tomorrow.<sup>17</sup>And let every one of you take his censer and put incense on it, and every one of you bring before the LORD his censer, 250 censers; you also, and Aaron, each his censer."<sup>18</sup>So every man took his censer and put fire in them and laid incense on them and stood at the entrance of the tent of meeting with Moses and Aaron.<sup>19</sup>Then Korah assembled all the congregation against them at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And the glory of the LORD appeared to all the congregation.<sup>20</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,<sup>21</sup>"Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment."<sup>22</sup>And they fell on their faces and said, "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?"<sup>23</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>24</sup>"Say to the congregation, Get away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram."<sup>25</sup>Then Moses rose and went to Dathan and Abiram, and the elders of Israel followed him.<sup>26</sup>And he spoke to the congregation, saying, "Depart, please, from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest you be swept away with all their sins."<sup>27</sup>So they got away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. And Dathan and Abiram came out and stood at the door of their tents, together with their wives, their sons, and their little ones.<sup>28</sup>And Moses said, "Hereby you shall know that the LORD has sent me to do all these works, and that it has not been of my own accord.<sup>29</sup>If these men die as all men die, or if they are visited by the fate of all mankind, then the LORD has not sent me.<sup>30</sup>But if the LORD creates something new, and the ground opens its mouth and swallows them up with all that belongs to them, and they go down alive into Sheol, then you shall know that these men have despised the LORD."<sup>31</sup>And as soon as he had finished speaking all these words, the ground under them split apart.<sup>32</sup>And the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households and all the people who belonged to Korah and all their goods.<sup>33</sup>So they and all that belonged to them went down alive into Sheol, and the earth closed over them, and they perished from the midst of the assembly.<sup>34</sup>And all Israel who were around them fled at their cry, for they said, "Lest the earth swallow us up!"<sup>35</sup>And fire came out from the LORD and consumed the 250 men offering the incense.<sup>36</sup>Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>37</sup>"Tell Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest to take up the censers out of the blaze. Then scatter the fire far and wide, for they have become holy.<sup>38</sup>As for the censers of these men who have sinned at the cost of their lives, let them be made into hammered plates as a covering for the altar, for they offered them before the LORD, and they became holy. Thus they shall be a sign to the people of Israel."<sup>39</sup>So Eleazar the priest took the bronze censers, which those who were burned had offered, and they were hammered out as a covering for the altar,<sup>40</sup>to be a reminder to the people of Israel, so that no outsider, who is not of the descendants of Aaron, should draw near to burn incense before the LORD, lest he become like Korah and his company—as the LORD said to him through Moses.<sup>41</sup>But on the next day all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, "You have killed the people of the LORD."<sup>42</sup>And when the congregation had assembled against Moses and against Aaron, they turned toward the tent of meeting. And behold, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the LORD appeared.<sup>43</sup>And Moses and Aaron came to the front of the tent of meeting,<sup>44</sup>and the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>45</sup>"Get away from the midst of this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment." And they fell on their faces.<sup>46</sup>And Moses said to Aaron, "Take your censer, and put fire on it from off the altar and lay incense on it and carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the LORD; the plague has begun."<sup>47</sup>So Aaron took it as Moses said and ran into the midst of the assembly. And behold, the plague had already begun among the people. And he put on the incense and made atonement for the people.<sup>48</sup>And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.<sup>49</sup>Now those who died in the plague were 14,700, besides those who died in the affair of Korah.<sup>50</sup>And Aaron returned to Moses at the entrance of the tent of meeting, when the plague was stopped.
16.overview:
Chapter 16 records the most serious challenge yet to God’s appointed order: Korah, a Levite, with Dathan and Abiram, leading 250 chiefs against Moses and Aaron. Their slogan sounds almost pious, “all in the congregation are holy,” but at root it is a rejection of mediation itself: access to God without the priest God appointed.

The judgment is swift and terrible: the earth swallows the ringleaders and fire consumes the 250. Yet the next day the people grumble and a plague breaks out, until Aaron, with his censer, “stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.” Here is the gospel in a single picture, pointing to Christ, our great High Priest, who stands between us and the wrath of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and 250 chiefs challenge Moses and Aaron, claiming all are holy; Moses calls for a test before the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: Rebellion against God’s appointed mediation, however pious its rhetoric, is rebellion against God himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Korah despises the appointed priesthood. Now: a warning against rejecting the one Mediator God has appointed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Korah the son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and On the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took men. And they rose up before Moses, with a number of the people of Israel, 250 chiefs of the congregation, chosen from the assembly, well-known men. They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron and said to them, "You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coalition is formidable. Korah is a Kohathite, of the highest-ranking Levitical family, the men who carried the ark. Dathan, Abiram and On are Reubenites, from the tribe of the demoted firstborn. And with them 250 chiefs, well-known men, the most respected in Israel.

Their slogan must be taken seriously, because it is almost entirely true.

Is the congregation holy? Yes — God had said so at Sinai: you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exod. 19:6). Is the LORD among them? Yes; the cloud is over the tent as they speak. Every premise is orthodox and quotable.

And the conclusion is a lie. From “we are all holy” Korah infers that no one may be set over us, which does not follow, and which conveniently puts Korah at the head of the movement to abolish leadership.

Dangerous errors are rarely built from falsehoods; they are true statements arranged to reach a desired destination. The surest tell is personal: watch who ends up better off if the argument wins. Korah wanted the priesthood, and total equality was the vehicle. Diotrephes did the same in a New Testament church, and John names the motive: he likes to put himself first (3 John 9).

Is this a warning never to question a leader? Moses and Aaron were appointed directly by God and vindicated by miracle; Korah wanted their place. Today’s elders are fallible men, to be honoured (Heb 13:17) but also tested by Scripture (Acts 17:11) and corrected when they err (1 Tim 5:19–20). And “all the congregation are holy” sounds like the priesthood of all believers (1 Pet 2:9); but that rests on the one Mediator, Christ, not on anyone appointing himself to approach God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses heard it, he fell on his face, and he said to Korah and all his company, "In the morning the LORD will show who is his, and who is holy, and will bring him near to him. The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him. Do this: take censers, Korah and all his company; put fire in them and put incense on them before the LORD tomorrow, and the man whom the LORD chooses shall be the holy one. You have gone too far, sons of Levi!" And Moses said to Korah, "Hear now, you sons of Levi: is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself, to do service in the tabernacle of the LORD and to stand before the congregation to minister to them, and that he has brought you near him, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you? And would you seek the priesthood also? Therefore it is against the LORD that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses falls on his face again, flat on the ground rather than on his feet arguing: the most consistent thing about the man.

Then his question goes past the theology to the appetite: Is it too small a thing for you that God has brought you near to himself, And would you seek the priesthood also? Of all the men in that camp, Korah belonged to the clan entrusted with the holiest object on earth, and it was not enough.

Discontent of this kind rarely afflicts the people with least. It grows in men who already have much and can see one thing more. Korah was in the presence of God every day, and his eye was on the one door still shut. Is it too small a thing is a question to put to yourself when aggrieved about a position, because the honest answer exposes how much has stopped counting.

And Moses names the real defendant: it is against the LORD that you and all your company have gathered together. Aaron did not appoint himself.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek Old Testament reads “The Lord knows those who are his” (ESV note) — words Paul quotes.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and they said, "We will not come up. Is it a small thing that you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, that you must also make yourself a prince over us? Moreover, you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, nor given us inheritance of fields and vineyards. Will you put out the eyes of these men? We will not come up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dathan and Abiram will not even come: We will not come up bookends their reply.

And they apply God’s own phrase for Canaan, a land flowing with milk and honey, to Egypt. The place of slavery, infanticide and the lash has become the promised land, and the God who brought them out is charged with murder. One of the most brazen inversions in the Bible.

Then the sneer that he has given them no fields or vineyards: true, because of the verdict of chapter 14, which fell because they refused to go in. They blame Moses for the consequence of their own rebellion.

And the last line, Will you put out the eyes of these men?, accuses of deception the man who once offered to be blotted out of God’s book for them (Exod. 32:32). There is no arguing with this. It is not a position; it is a mood that has found words.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s glory appears; the earth opens and swallows the rebels and their households, and fire consumes the 250 offering incense.
verseByVerse.theology: God vindicates his appointed mediation with terrible judgment; to usurp the priesthood is to perish before the holy God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the earth swallows the rebels. Now: the fearful seriousness of rejecting God’s appointed way of approach.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses was very angry and said to the LORD, "Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, and I have not harmed one of them." And Moses said to Korah, "Be present, you and all your company, before the LORD, you and they, and Aaron, tomorrow. And let every one of you take his censer and put incense on it, and every one of you bring before the LORD his censer, 250 censers; you also, and Aaron, each his censer." So every man took his censer and put fire in them and laid incense on them and stood at the entrance of the tent of meeting with Moses and Aaron. Then Korah assembled all the congregation against them at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And the glory of the LORD appeared to all the congregation. And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, "Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment." And they fell on their faces and said, "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?" And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Say to the congregation, Get away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is finally angry, I have not taken one donkey from them: a man defending not his dignity but his integrity, and to God rather than to them.

Then the test, exactly designed: each man with a censer and incense. Incense was reserved to the priest alone. Korah claimed there was no such reservation; very well, let him do it. The test is simply the disputed claim acted out, and two hundred and fifty men agreed to find out.

And when God says that I may consume them in a moment, the two brothers fall on their faces: shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation? They plead for the people gathered against them, and win a reprieve for all but the ringleaders.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses rose and went to Dathan and Abiram, and the elders of Israel followed him. And he spoke to the congregation, saying, "Depart, please, from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest you be swept away with all their sins." So they got away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. And Dathan and Abiram came out and stood at the door of their tents, together with their wives, their sons, and their little ones. And Moses said, "Hereby you shall know that the LORD has sent me to do all these works, and that it has not been of my own accord. If these men die as all men die, or if they are visited by the fate of all mankind, then the LORD has not sent me. But if the LORD creates something new, and the ground opens its mouth and swallows them up with all that belongs to them, and they go down alive into Sheol, then you shall know that these men have despised the LORD." And as soon as he had finished speaking all these words, the ground under them split apart. And the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households and all the people who belonged to Korah and all their goods. So they and all that belonged to them went down alive into Sheol, and the earth closed over them, and they perished from the midst of the assembly. And all Israel who were around them fled at their cry, for they said, "Lest the earth swallow us up!" And fire came out from the LORD and consumed the 250 men offering the incense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses puts it on record beforehand, the mark of a genuine prophet: if these men die a natural death, then the LORD has not sent me. He stakes his commission on an event he cannot manufacture, announced before everybody. And the moment he finishes speaking, the ground splits.

He had said if the LORD creates something new, with the verb of Genesis 1:1, used only of God: nothing already in the world would do. Then fire from the LORD consumes the two hundred and fifty with censers in their hands.

The horror should not be smoothed over, nor its point. The question was whether a man may approach God on his own terms if he is sincere, respected and part of a majority. These men were not irreligious; they were holding incense, doing the most spiritual thing available to them, and it killed them. There is a way of coming to God worse than not coming at all, as Nadab and Abihu had shown.

Jude puts it among the standing warnings of Scripture: men who walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion (Jude 11). Korah has become a category: the man who will not have the mediator God appointed, and appoints himself.

Why did the households die with them? In the Old Testament a family often stood or fell with its head (cf. Josh 7:24), and God as Judge has the right to take any life. It is not a pattern for human justice (Deut 24:16). And not all perished: the sons of Korah did not die (26:11), and their descendants wrote psalms (Pss 42–49).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–50 — Aaron Between the Dead and the Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rebels’ censers are made into altar plating as a warning; the people grumble again, a plague breaks out, and Aaron’s incense halts it.
verseByVerse.theology: The priest interposes himself between the wrath of God and the people — the gospel in a single image, fulfilled in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Aaron stands between the dead and the living. Now: Christ stands between us and the wrath of God, halting our destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Tell Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest to take up the censers out of the blaze. Then scatter the fire far and wide, for they have become holy. As for the censers of these men who have sinned at the cost of their lives, let them be made into hammered plates as a covering for the altar, for they offered them before the LORD, and they became holy. Thus they shall be a sign to the people of Israel." So Eleazar the priest took the bronze censers, which those who were burned had offered, and they were hammered out as a covering for the altar, to be a reminder to the people of Israel, so that no outsider, who is not of the descendants of Aaron, should draw near to burn incense before the LORD, lest he become like Korah and his company—as the LORD said to him through Moses. But on the next day all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, "You have killed the people of the LORD." And when the congregation had assembled against Moses and against Aaron, they turned toward the tent of meeting. And behold, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the LORD appeared. And Moses and Aaron came to the front of the tent of meeting,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The censers of the dead men are hammered flat to plate the altar as a sign. For the rest of that generation, every Israelite approached the place of sacrifice over bronze that had been in the hands of men who died claiming they did not need a priest.

Then the sentence that shows how little had gone in: on the next day the whole congregation accuses Moses and Aaron, You have killed the people of the LORD.

One day after the earth opened before the entire nation, they had reinterpreted it as a leadership problem. The heart does not deny evidence it does not want; it re-explains it. That is why more signs would not have saved this generation, and why the rich man was told his brothers neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31).

verseByVerse.quote: and the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Get away from the midst of this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment." And they fell on their faces. And Moses said to Aaron, "Take your censer, and put fire on it from off the altar and lay incense on it and carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the LORD; the plague has begun." So Aaron took it as Moses said and ran into the midst of the assembly. And behold, the plague had already begun among the people. And he put on the incense and made atonement for the people. And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped. Now those who died in the plague were 14,700, besides those who died in the affair of Korah. And Aaron returned to Moses at the entrance of the tent of meeting, when the plague was stopped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plague begins, and people die where they stand. What follows is one of the great scenes of the book.

Moses sends Aaron out because wrath has begun, and every detail counts. He takes a censer, the very object two hundred and fifty men had died holding the day before. He takes fire from off the altar, the place of sacrifice. And an old man past eighty runs, into a plague, toward the people who had spent the morning accusing him of murder, and stands between the dead and the living until it stops.

There is the priesthood the rebels said was unnecessary, doing what nobody else in the camp could do. Fourteen thousand seven hundred were dead, and the only thing standing between the rest and the same end was one man with a censer.

Not on a mountain or behind a curtain, but out in the open with corpses on one side and the living on the other, holding back the wrath of God with his own body and an offering. That is what a priest is for. And the true Priest did not carry the offering in his hands. He is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:2): he stood between the dead and the living by being the dead, and rose, and the plague was stopped for ever.

16.theology:
Rebellion Against the Mediator Is Rebellion Against God. Korah’s pious slogan masked a refusal of God’s appointed mediation. To reject the one Mediator God appoints, supremely Christ, is to perish before the holy God.

The Holiness That Consumes. God alone determines how he may be approached. The same glory that blesses can consume; we are spared only because a better Mediator bore the fire in our place.

The Priest Between the Dead and the Living. The mediator interposes himself to halt the wrath: fulfilled in Christ our High Priest, who stands forever between us and the judgment of God.
16.examples:
Then: Korah grasped for the priesthood and was swallowed; the people grumbled and a plague broke out; and Aaron stood between the dead and the living.

Now: Christ, your great High Priest, has run into the midst of your death and stands between you and the wrath of God; because he stands, you live. In that security, and by his Spirit, you need not grasp for what God has withheld or despise the place he has given you, and when envy rises, bring it to the Priest who prays for you.

17.title: Aaron’s Staff Buds: Resurrection and the Confirmed Priesthood
17.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, and get from them staffs, one for each fathers' house, from all their chiefs according to their fathers' houses, twelve staffs. Write each man's name on his staff,<sup>3</sup>and write Aaron's name on the staff of Levi. For there shall be one staff for the head of each fathers' house.<sup>4</sup>Then you shall deposit them in the tent of meeting before the testimony, where I meet with you.<sup>5</sup>And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you."<sup>6</sup>Moses spoke to the people of Israel. And all their chiefs gave him staffs, one for each chief, according to their fathers' houses, twelve staffs. And the staff of Aaron was among their staffs.<sup>7</sup>And Moses deposited the staffs before the LORD in the tent of the testimony.<sup>8</sup>On the next day Moses went into the tent of the testimony, and behold, the staff of Aaron for the house of Levi had sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds.<sup>9</sup>Then Moses brought out all the staffs from before the LORD to all the people of Israel. And they looked, and each man took his staff.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Put back the staff of Aaron before the testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebels, that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die."<sup>11</sup>Thus did Moses; as the LORD commanded him, so he did.<sup>12</sup>And the people of Israel said to Moses, "Behold, we perish, we are undone, we are all undone.<sup>13</sup>Everyone who comes near, who comes near to the tabernacle of the LORD, shall die. Are we all to perish?"
17.overview:
After Korah’s rebellion, God gives a quiet sign to settle the question of the priesthood for good. Twelve staffs are laid up before the LORD overnight, and in the morning only Aaron’s has come alive, budding, blossoming and bearing ripe almonds.

A dead stick bearing fruit is resurrection logic: God confirms his chosen priest not by power or argument but by bringing life out of death. The staff is then kept before the testimony as a sign against rebellion, and it points ahead to Christ, whose priesthood is confirmed by the empty tomb.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Twelve Staffs Laid Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands a staff from each tribe, with Aaron’s name on Levi’s, to be placed before the testimony to settle the question of the priesthood.
verseByVerse.theology: God will end the grumbling not by argument but by a sign, choosing his priest through a demonstration of life.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: twelve dead staffs laid before the LORD. Now: God settles disputes by his own vindicating act, not human contention.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, and get from them staffs, one for each fathers' house, from all their chiefs according to their fathers' houses, twelve staffs. Write each man's name on his staff, and write Aaron's name on the staff of Levi. For there shall be one staff for the head of each fathers' house. Then you shall deposit them in the tent of meeting before the testimony, where I meet with you. And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fourteen thousand seven hundred people have just died, and God’s next move is not another judgment but a gentle sign: one staff per tribe, each with its owner’s name, and the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout.

The test is scrupulously fair. Every tribe is represented, each staff is named so nobody can claim a mix-up, and all lie in the same place overnight with nobody in the room. God is not asking Israel to take Moses’ word for it.

And a staff was a shepherd’s rod or a chief’s badge of office: a length of dead wood, cut years ago and leaned on daily. So the question is not "which of these men is most capable?" but "on which of these dead sticks will life appear?" The priesthood will not be settled by ability or by the majority who backed Korah, but by a miracle, because nothing else can settle it.

The stated purpose is mercy: Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings. God wants the arguing to stop because the arguing was killing them.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to the people of Israel. And all their chiefs gave him staffs, one for each chief, according to their fathers' houses, twelve staffs. And the staff of Aaron was among their staffs. And Moses deposited the staffs before the LORD in the tent of the testimony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two quiet details. The staff of Aaron was among their staffs: not marked out, not placed nearer the ark, but in the pile with the other eleven. And the staffs are left before the LORD overnight, in an empty, dark room.

That is exactly what God had asked for. There is no possible human contribution to what comes next. Twelve dead sticks in a dark room, and the only variable in the entire experiment is God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Budding Staff and the Fear of the People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Aaron’s staff alone sprouts, buds, blossoms, and bears almonds; it is kept as a sign, and the people cry out in fear of the holy God.
verseByVerse.theology: God confirms his priest by bringing life from dead wood — resurrection logic that points to Christ’s vindication.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a dead staff bears living fruit. Now: Christ’s priesthood confirmed by resurrection, the living High Priest forever.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day Moses went into the tent of the testimony, and behold, the staff of Aaron for the house of Levi had sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four verbs: sprouted, budded, blossomed, bore ripe almonds. That is not merely a sign of life but a whole growing season compressed into one night, on wood that had been dead for years, with no soil, root or water.

And it was an almond. In Israel the almond is the first tree to wake in the year, flowering in winter before anything else has stirred, and its Hebrew name sounds like the Hebrew for watching, as the ESV note at Jeremiah 1:11 explains. So God answered Jeremiah: “I see an almond branch.” Then the LORD said to me, “You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it” (Jer. 1:11–12). The almond is the tree of the God who is awake first.

Eleven staffs came out as they went in; one came out carrying fruit. God’s chosen priest is not the man with the most support but the one on whom life appeared where there was none.

The New Testament never mentions the budding rod when it speaks of Jesus’ priesthood, but it argues along the same line. Christ was declared to be the Son of God in power… by his resurrection from the dead (Rom. 1:4), and his priesthood rests not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life (Heb. 7:16). Twelve dead sticks and one that blossomed; a hillside of graves and one empty tomb. God settles who may stand between him and us in only one way, and he has now done it twice.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses brought out all the staffs from before the LORD to all the people of Israel. And they looked, and each man took his staff. And the LORD said to Moses, "Put back the staff of Aaron before the testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebels, that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die." Thus did Moses; as the LORD commanded him, so he did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Picture that morning. Twelve chiefs collect their rods before the nation, each taking back the same dry stick he handed in, while one man walks away holding a branch in blossom. There was no verdict to announce and no argument to have. They looked, and it was over.

Then God turns the sign into a permanent fixture, kept before the testimony; Hebrews 9:4 lists it with the tablets and the jar of manna. The reason given is kindness: lest they die. The memorial is not a trophy for Aaron; it exists so that nobody else will have to learn this lesson the way Korah did.

Hebrews says the ark held Aaron’s rod (Heb 9:4), but by Solomon’s day only the tablets were inside (1 Kgs 8:9). The rod was kept with the ark in the wilderness; it had probably been lost or removed by Solomon’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel said to Moses, "Behold, we perish, we are undone, we are all undone. Everyone who comes near, who comes near to the tabernacle of the LORD, shall die. Are we all to perish?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends on a cry nobody expects: we are all undone. They have got it half right, and it is the terrifying half. After the earth opening, the fire, the plague and the blossoming rod, they have finally understood that God is holy and that coming near him is lethal, and the lesson has landed as despair.

What they have not understood is the other half: that the whole point of the priesthood is that somebody may come near on their behalf. They are standing outside a tent that exists precisely so that they will not perish.

Many who take God seriously stop just here. They know their sin and his holiness, and from those two facts alone they rightly conclude that they are undone. It is not the end of the matter. The next words in the Bible are God’s answer: chapter 18 opens with him telling Aaron that this is what the priest is for. You and your sons… shall bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary.

Israel cried out that everyone who comes near will die. It was true. So a priest came near, and did die, and now the invitation reads: let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb. 4:16). The coming near that they dreaded is now the gospel’s welcome.

17.theology:
Resurrection Vindicates the Priest. God confirms his chosen priest not by argument but by bringing life from dead wood. So Christ’s priesthood is confirmed by the empty tomb; he was “declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection.”

The Almond, Herald of Life. The first tree to bloom, whose name sounds like watching, marks the true priest as the one God awakens to life: the High Priest who, having died, lives forever to make intercession.

The Terror of Holiness and the Need for a Mediator. The people cry, “Are we all to perish?” Apart from a mediator, to approach the holy God is death. Their dread presses toward the gospel: through the appointed priest, supremely Christ, we draw near and live.
17.examples:
Then: Aaron’s staff alone blossomed overnight, confirming God’s chosen priest by life from the dead, while the people trembled before the holy God.

Now: Your High Priest is confirmed by a greater sign than a budding staff: the empty tomb. The risen Christ lives forever to intercede for you, so draw near to the holy God not in terror but in confidence.

18.title: Duties of Priests and Levites: ‘I Am Your Portion’
18.text: <sup>1</sup>So the LORD said to Aaron, "You and your sons and your father's house with you shall bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary, and you and your sons with you shall bear iniquity connected with your priesthood.<sup>2</sup>And with you bring your brothers also, the tribe of Levi, the tribe of your father, that they may join you and minister to you while you and your sons with you are before the tent of the testimony.<sup>3</sup>They shall keep guard over you and over the whole tent, but shall not come near to the vessels of the sanctuary or to the altar lest they, and you, die.<sup>4</sup>They shall join you and keep guard over the tent of meeting for all the service of the tent, and no outsider shall come near you.<sup>5</sup>And you shall keep guard over the sanctuary and over the altar, that there may never again be wrath on the people of Israel.<sup>6</sup>And behold, I have taken your brothers the Levites from among the people of Israel. They are a gift to you, given to the LORD, to do the service of the tent of meeting.<sup>7</sup>And you and your sons with you shall guard your priesthood for all that concerns the altar and that is within the veil; and you shall serve. I give your priesthood as a gift, and any outsider who comes near shall be put to death."<sup>8</sup>Then the LORD spoke to Aaron, "Behold, I have given you charge of the contributions made to me, all the consecrated things of the people of Israel. I have given them to you as a portion and to your sons as a perpetual due.<sup>9</sup>This shall be yours of the most holy things, reserved from the fire: every offering of theirs, every grain offering of theirs and every sin offering of theirs and every guilt offering of theirs, which they render to me, shall be most holy to you and to your sons.<sup>10</sup>In a most holy place shall you eat it. Every male may eat it; it is holy to you.<sup>11</sup>This also is yours: the contribution of their gift, all the wave offerings of the people of Israel. I have given them to you, and to your sons and daughters with you, as a perpetual due. Everyone who is clean in your house may eat it.<sup>12</sup>All the best of the oil and all the best of the wine and of the grain, the firstfruits of what they give to the LORD, I give to you.<sup>13</sup>The first ripe fruits of all that is in their land, which they bring to the LORD, shall be yours. Everyone who is clean in your house may eat it.<sup>14</sup>Every devoted thing in Israel shall be yours.<sup>15</sup>Everything that opens the womb of all flesh, whether man or beast, which they offer to the LORD, shall be yours. Nevertheless, the firstborn of man you shall redeem, and the firstborn of unclean animals you shall redeem.<sup>16</sup>And their redemption price (at a month old you shall redeem them) you shall fix at five shekels in silver, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, which is twenty gerahs.<sup>17</sup>But the firstborn of a cow, or the firstborn of a sheep, or the firstborn of a goat, you shall not redeem; they are holy. You shall sprinkle their blood on the altar and shall burn their fat as a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>18</sup>But their flesh shall be yours, as the breast that is waved and as the right thigh are yours.<sup>19</sup>All the holy contributions that the people of Israel present to the LORD I give to you, and to your sons and daughters with you, as a perpetual due. It is a covenant of salt forever before the LORD for you and for your offspring with you."<sup>20</sup>And the LORD said to Aaron, "You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel.<sup>21</sup>"To the Levites I have given every tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in return for their service that they do, their service in the tent of meeting,<sup>22</sup>so that the people of Israel do not come near the tent of meeting, lest they bear sin and die.<sup>23</sup>But the Levites shall do the service of the tent of meeting, and they shall bear their iniquity. It shall be a perpetual statute throughout your generations, and among the people of Israel they shall have no inheritance.<sup>24</sup>For the tithe of the people of Israel, which they present as a contribution to the LORD, I have given to the Levites for an inheritance. Therefore I have said of them that they shall have no inheritance among the people of Israel."<sup>25</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>26</sup>"Moreover, you shall speak and say to the Levites, 'When you take from the people of Israel the tithe that I have given you from them for your inheritance, then you shall present a contribution from it to the LORD, a tithe of the tithe.<sup>27</sup>And your contribution shall be counted to you as though it were the grain of the threshing floor, and as the fullness of the winepress.<sup>28</sup>So you shall also present a contribution to the LORD from all your tithes, which you receive from the people of Israel. And from it you shall give the LORD's contribution to Aaron the priest.<sup>29</sup>Out of all the gifts to you, you shall present every contribution due to the LORD; from each its best part is to be dedicated.'<sup>30</sup>Therefore you shall say to them, 'When you have offered from it the best of it, then the rest shall be counted to the Levites as produce of the threshing floor, and as produce of the winepress.<sup>31</sup>And you may eat it in any place, you and your households, for it is your reward in return for your service in the tent of meeting.<sup>32</sup>And you shall bear no sin by reason of it, when you have contributed the best of it. But you shall not profane the holy things of the people of Israel, lest you die.'"
18.overview:
Chapter 18 answers the terrified cry of chapter 17, “Are we all to perish?”, with a gracious provision: the priests and Levites will bear the danger of the sanctuary on the people’s behalf, and both are supported not by land but by the people’s offerings.

The crown of the chapter is verse 20: “I am your portion and your inheritance.” The tribe that owns no fields possesses the LORD, a portion Asaph would later sing (Ps 73:26) and the New Testament makes the inheritance of every believer in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Charge of the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests and Levites bear the responsibility for the sanctuary, guarding it so that wrath may not fall on the people.
verseByVerse.theology: The mediators bear the danger of holiness on the people’s behalf, answering the people’s fear of perishing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: priests guard the sanctuary lest wrath fall. Now: Christ our High Priest bears the danger of holiness for us.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD said to Aaron, "You and your sons and your father's house with you shall bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary, and you and your sons with you shall bear iniquity connected with your priesthood. And with you bring your brothers also, the tribe of Levi, the tribe of your father, that they may join you and minister to you while you and your sons with you are before the tent of the testimony. They shall keep guard over you and over the whole tent, but shall not come near to the vessels of the sanctuary or to the altar lest they, and you, die. They shall join you and keep guard over the tent of meeting for all the service of the tent, and no outsider shall come near you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel has just cried out that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die (17:13). God’s answer is not reassurance. It is an appointment.

To bear iniquity means to carry the liability, to be the one held answerable when something goes wrong. The danger of the holy place is real, and God has assigned it to somebody: Aaron will carry it.

That is the priesthood in one sentence, and it is not a promotion. It is the transfer of risk. Every arrangement that follows exists so that the weight falls on a named man instead of on the congregation.

That is why the New Testament can describe Christ’s work in exactly these terms: he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Pet. 2:24). Aaron carried the liability for what went wrong at the sanctuary; there is a Priest who carried it for everything that has ever gone wrong in his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall keep guard over the sanctuary and over the altar, that there may never again be wrath on the people of Israel. And behold, I have taken your brothers the Levites from among the people of Israel. They are a gift to you, given to the LORD, to do the service of the tent of meeting. And you and your sons with you shall guard your priesthood for all that concerns the altar and that is within the veil; and you shall serve. I give your priesthood as a gift, and any outsider who comes near shall be put to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never again points back to the fourteen thousand seven hundred graves of chapter 16. This whole arrangement is God answering a disaster.

Then a startling phrase, used twice in three verses: the Levites are a gift to you, and I give your priesthood as a gift. The very thing Korah wanted to seize can only be given. Nobody in Israel could take the priesthood, and nobody had to earn it; Aaron did not qualify for it and was not consulted about it.

Hebrews makes exactly this argument: no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was. So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son” (Heb. 5:4–5). The rule that killed Korah is the rule the Son of God submitted to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–19 — The Provision for the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests are supported by the offerings, firstfruits, and devoted things of the people — their portion from the LORD’s table.
verseByVerse.theology: Those who serve at the altar live from the altar; God provides for his ministers through the gifts of his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: priests fed from the offerings. Now: those who preach the gospel live from the gospel, as God provides for his servants.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD spoke to Aaron, "Behold, I have given you charge of the contributions made to me, all the consecrated things of the people of Israel. I have given them to you as a portion and to your sons as a perpetual due. This shall be yours of the most holy things, reserved from the fire: every offering of theirs, every grain offering of theirs and every sin offering of theirs and every guilt offering of theirs, which they render to me, shall be most holy to you and to your sons. In a most holy place shall you eat it. Every male may eat it; it is holy to you. This also is yours: the contribution of their gift, all the wave offerings of the people of Israel. I have given them to you, and to your sons and daughters with you, as a perpetual due. Everyone who is clean in your house may eat it. All the best of the oil and all the best of the wine and of the grain, the firstfruits of what they give to the LORD, I give to you. The first ripe fruits of all that is in their land, which they bring to the LORD, shall be yours. Everyone who is clean in your house may eat it. Every devoted thing in Israel shall be yours.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests own nothing, so God arranges their living: the grain, sin, guilt and wave offerings and the firstfruits all become food on the priest’s table.

A priest ate what had been given to God; his dinner was somebody else’s act of worship. He had no harvest of his own, and if Israel stopped bringing offerings the priests went hungry, which tied the nation’s spiritual health directly to the survival of the men who served it.

Paul applies this arrangement to Christian ministers without embarrassment: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Cor. 9:13–14). In the apostle’s reading, a congregation paying its pastor is making the same provision made for Aaron.

verseByVerse.quote: Everything that opens the womb of all flesh, whether man or beast, which they offer to the LORD, shall be yours. Nevertheless, the firstborn of man you shall redeem, and the firstborn of unclean animals you shall redeem. And their redemption price (at a month old you shall redeem them) you shall fix at five shekels in silver, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, which is twenty gerahs. But the firstborn of a cow, or the firstborn of a sheep, or the firstborn of a goat, you shall not redeem; they are holy. You shall sprinkle their blood on the altar and shall burn their fat as a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. But their flesh shall be yours, as the breast that is waved and as the right thigh are yours. All the holy contributions that the people of Israel present to the LORD I give to you, and to your sons and daughters with you, as a perpetual due. It is a covenant of salt forever before the LORD for you and for your offspring with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The firstborn sons of Israel belonged to God because he had spared them on the night of the Passover (Exodus 13:2, 15), so each was bought back for five shekels, and unclean animals were redeemed in the same way. Every family with a firstborn son carried a reminder that its child was alive because a lamb had died.

And the standard is the best: not the surplus, but the top of the harvest, which God passed to the men who served at the tent.

Then a memorable phrase: a covenant of salt forever. Salt does not rot; it was rubbed into sacrifices and used across the ancient Near East to seal an agreement that would not go off. God is telling a landless family that this arrangement will outlast every harvest.

That forever held for as long as the Levitical order stood, and Hebrews says that order was always waiting for a better one. Its priests died and were replaced, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Hebrews 7:24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–32 — ‘I Am Your Portion’ and the Levites’ Tithe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests receive no land, for the LORD himself is their portion; the Levites receive the tithe and in turn tithe to the priests.
verseByVerse.theology: To have God himself as one’s inheritance is the highest treasure; the landless tribe possesses the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priests’ portion is the LORD himself. Now: in Christ, God himself is the believer’s inheritance forever.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Aaron, "You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel. "To the Levites I have given every tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in return for their service that they do, their service in the tent of meeting, so that the people of Israel do not come near the tent of meeting, lest they bear sin and die. But the Levites shall do the service of the tent of meeting, and they shall bear their iniquity. It shall be a perpetual statute throughout your generations, and among the people of Israel they shall have no inheritance. For the tithe of the people of Israel, which they present as a contribution to the LORD, I have given to the Levites for an inheritance. Therefore I have said of them that they shall have no inheritance among the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward, spoken directly to Aaron: I am your portion.

Picture the day this came true. The land is divided, and eleven tribes walk away holding a map: this valley, that ridge, the olive terraces, the boundary stone with a grandfather’s name on it. Levi is handed only towns to live in, scattered among the other tribes (35:1–8). No tribal acres, no field to leave to a son.

By every visible measure they got the worst of the settlement, and the text says so twice: no inheritance… no portion. Then the exchange. Everything the other tribes received, God had made. Levi received God.

Scripture keeps putting a test to us. Suppose you were given everything you have ever wanted, and God himself were not there. Would that be heaven? Asaph got to the right answer after nearly losing his faith over the prosperity of the wicked: Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps. 73:25–26).

And the comfort on the reverse side: every acre those tribes received could be taken from them, and eventually was, by drought, debt, Assyria and time. A portion that is God cannot be repossessed.

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Cor 16:2; 2 Cor 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Gal 6:6; 1 Cor 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Moreover, you shall speak and say to the Levites, 'When you take from the people of Israel the tithe that I have given you from them for your inheritance, then you shall present a contribution from it to the LORD, a tithe of the tithe. And your contribution shall be counted to you as though it were the grain of the threshing floor, and as the fullness of the winepress. So you shall also present a contribution to the LORD from all your tithes, which you receive from the people of Israel. And from it you shall give the LORD's contribution to Aaron the priest. Out of all the gifts to you, you shall present every contribution due to the LORD; from each its best part is to be dedicated.' Therefore you shall say to them, 'When you have offered from it the best of it, then the rest shall be counted to the Levites as produce of the threshing floor, and as produce of the winepress. And you may eat it in any place, you and your households, for it is your reward in return for your service in the tent of meeting. And you shall bear no sin by reason of it, when you have contributed the best of it. But you shall not profane the holy things of the people of Israel, lest you die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One last provision, and the most searching. The Levites live on the nation’s tithe, and God tells them to tithe it, from its best part, not a tenth of whatever was hardest to eat.

So the men supported by other people’s giving are themselves givers. The Levite could easily have concluded that his whole life was already a contribution and that the tithe was somebody else’s duty. God does not allow the arithmetic. The man who lives off the offerings still brings one, because everything he has was first given to him.

Then the closing warning: lest you die. A priest could grow so used to holy things that they became merely his supper. Familiarity with sacred things is its own danger, and the men closest to the altar were the ones warned about it. No minister guards that perfectly. The way back for one who has grown cold is the mercy he handles every week, offered by the Priest who never once treated the holy things lightly, and the Spirit who first gave him a heart for them can rekindle it.

Chapter 17 ended with a nation crying Are we all to perish? Chapter 18 answers in two parts: a priest will bear the liability, so that the people may live; and that priest will have no possessions on earth, because he has God. The man who came near for them owned nothing at all, which is exactly what the true Priest turned out to be like: Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matt. 8:20).

18.theology:
The Mediators Bear the Danger of Holiness. The priests “bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary,” guarding it so that wrath may not fall on the people. This points to Christ, who bore our sins in his body, taking the full danger of holiness upon himself.

Those Who Serve the Altar Live from the Altar. The landless priests and Levites are supported by the best of the offerings, sealed by a covenant of salt. Paul applies this to gospel ministry: God’s people support those who serve them spiritually.

God himself the Portion. The landless priests possess the LORD, and so are richer than all the landed tribes. In Christ this becomes the inheritance of every believer: not merely God’s gifts but God himself.
18.examples:
Then: The priests bore the danger of the sanctuary so that wrath would not fall on the people, lived from the offerings, and received the LORD himself as their portion.

Now: Christ has borne the danger of holiness and the weight of your sin, so you may draw near and live. Out of what he has given you, and by the Spirit who makes a stingy heart generous, support those who minister God’s word among you. And treasure your true inheritance: not merely God’s gifts, but God himself, “my portion forever.”

19.title: The Red Heifer: The Paradox of Purification
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,<sup>2</sup>"This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded: Tell the people of Israel to bring you a red heifer without defect, in which there is no blemish, and on which a yoke has never come.<sup>3</sup>And you shall give it to Eleazar the priest, and it shall be taken outside the camp and slaughtered before him.<sup>4</sup>And Eleazar the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger, and sprinkle some of its blood toward the front of the tent of meeting seven times.<sup>5</sup>And the heifer shall be burned in his sight. Its skin, its flesh, and its blood, with its dung, shall be burned.<sup>6</sup>And the priest shall take cedarwood and hyssop and scarlet yarn, and throw them into the fire burning the heifer.<sup>7</sup>Then the priest shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp. But the priest shall be unclean until evening.<sup>8</sup>The one who burns the heifer shall wash his clothes in water and bathe his body in water and shall be unclean until evening.<sup>9</sup>And a man who is clean shall gather up the ashes of the heifer and deposit them outside the camp in a clean place. And they shall be kept for the water for impurity for the congregation of the people of Israel; it is a sin offering.<sup>10</sup>And the one who gathers the ashes of the heifer shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening. And this shall be a perpetual statute for the people of Israel, and for the stranger who sojourns among them.<sup>11</sup>"Whoever touches the dead body of any person shall be unclean seven days.<sup>12</sup>He shall cleanse himself with the water on the third day and on the seventh day, and so be clean. But if he does not cleanse himself on the third day and on the seventh day, he will not become clean.<sup>13</sup>Whoever touches a dead person, the body of anyone who has died, and does not cleanse himself, defiles the tabernacle of the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from Israel; because the water for impurity was not thrown on him, he shall be unclean. His uncleanness is still on him.<sup>14</sup>"This is the law when someone dies in a tent: everyone who comes into the tent and everyone who is in the tent shall be unclean seven days.<sup>15</sup>And every open vessel that has no cover fastened on it is unclean.<sup>16</sup>Whoever in the open field touches someone who was killed with a sword or who died naturally, or touches a human bone or a grave, shall be unclean seven days.<sup>17</sup>For the unclean they shall take some ashes of the burnt sin offering, and fresh water shall be added in a vessel.<sup>18</sup>Then a clean person shall take hyssop and dip it in the water and sprinkle it on the tent and on all the furnishings and on the persons who were there and on whoever touched the bone, or the slain or the dead or the grave.<sup>19</sup>And the clean person shall sprinkle it on the unclean on the third day and on the seventh day. Thus on the seventh day he shall cleanse him, and he shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water, and at evening he shall be clean.<sup>20</sup>"If the man who is unclean does not cleanse himself, that person shall be cut off from the midst of the assembly, since he has defiled the sanctuary of the LORD. Because the water for impurity has not been thrown on him, he is unclean.<sup>21</sup>And it shall be a statute forever for them. The one who sprinkles the water for impurity shall wash his clothes, and the one who touches the water for impurity shall be unclean until evening.<sup>22</sup>And whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean, and anyone who touches it shall be unclean until evening."
19.overview:
Chapter 19 gives one of the strangest rituals in the law: the red heifer. An unblemished red cow, never yoked, is slaughtered outside the camp and burned entirely, and its ashes are mixed with water to cleanse anyone defiled by contact with death. In a wilderness where a whole generation is dying, the need is constant.

The ritual is full of paradox: the ashes that purify the unclean defile the clean who prepare them. The means of cleansing bears the uncleanness it removes. Hebrews seizes on this rite (Heb 9:13–14; Heb 13:12): the heifer purified the outside, Christ purifies the conscience. The red heifer asks the question; the cross of Christ is the answer.
19.theology:
Death and defilement. Death is the great contaminator, the wage of sin. The red heifer provides cleansing from death's stain so the people may remain near the living God.

The paradox of substitution. The means of purification bears the uncleanness it removes, a shadow of Christ who became sin for us.

Cleansing of the conscience. The heifer purified the flesh; the blood of Christ purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Heb 9:13–14).
19.examples:
Then: The heifer’s ashes cleansed the death-defiled, while the one who prepared them became unclean himself.

Now: Christ suffered outside the gate, took on your defilement, and by his blood purifies the conscience. The riddle of the red heifer is answered at the cross; come and be clean.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A red heifer, without blemish and never yoked, is burned outside the camp, and its ashes are kept to make the water of purification: God’s remedy, in a wilderness full of graves, for the most common defilement of all, contact with death.
verseByVerse.theology: Death is the great defiler, the wage of sin (Rom 6:23), and the heifer’s ashes are God’s provision to cleanse those death has touched. The one who prepares the purifying water himself becomes unclean (vv.7-8), yet the ashes cleanse others: the sin-bearer bears defilement so the defiled may be clean.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a people surrounded by death had a God-given way to be cleansed and restored to worship.

Now: we are defiled by “dead works” (Heb 9:14), and the blood of Christ cleanses the conscience and restores us to the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, "This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded: Tell the people of Israel to bring you a red heifer without defect, in which there is no blemish, and on which a yoke has never come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This one is called the statute of the law, and what follows is one of the strangest rituals in the Bible. Jewish tradition has always admitted as much; the rabbis classed the red heifer as the one commandment whose reason God kept to himself, and applied to it Solomon’s confession, I said, “I will be wise,” but it was far from me (Eccl. 7:23). It is meant to pose a question the ritual itself cannot answer.

A red heifer, perhaps because red is the colour of blood, without defect, the standard requirement for a sacrifice. But then a requirement almost never made: on which a yoke has never come. The law asks for an unworked animal only in a handful of the gravest rites, the heifer of the unsolved murder (Deut. 21:3) and later the cows that carried the ark home (1 Sam. 6:7), and in each case it marks something set apart from ordinary use altogether.

Every other beast in Israel had spent its life pulling somebody’s plough; this one had never worn a collar. The law does not explain the detail, and we should not press it into a code. But it is a fitting picture of the One who offered himself without blemish to God (Hebrews 9:14), never harnessed to sin as every other son of Adam has been. Only a pure offering can cleanse.

Is the red heifer still relevant? Its ashes cleansed from contact with death, and Hebrews says it purified only the flesh, while the blood of Christ purifies the conscience (Heb 9:13–14). Some who expect a rebuilt temple look for a new red heifer, but the shadow is fulfilled; it is not to be revived.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall give it to Eleazar the priest, and it shall be taken outside the camp and slaughtered before him. And Eleazar the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger, and sprinkle some of its blood toward the front of the tent of meeting seven times. And the heifer shall be burned in his sight. Its skin, its flesh, and its blood, with its dung, shall be burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The animal is handed not to Aaron but to his son Eleazar, probably because what is about to happen defiles the man who does it, and the high priest must not be defiled. Then the detail the New Testament seizes on: outside the camp. Not at the altar, but out past the last tent, where the rubbish went and the lepers lived, the place that meant rejection.

Yet the blood is sprinkled toward the front of the tent of meeting seven times, seven being completeness. The priest stands on the waste ground, facing the tabernacle he is not entering, flicking blood toward it across the distance. The sacrifice is rejected by the camp and accepted by heaven at the same moment.

Then the whole animal goes into the fire. Nothing is eaten or saved for the priests; it is given entirely to the flame. Hebrews makes the point from the Day of Atonement, whose sin offerings were also burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27), and the red heifer shares the pattern: the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb. 13:11–12). Golgotha was outside the city wall. They put him where they put the heifer.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest shall take cedarwood and hyssop and scarlet yarn, and throw them into the fire burning the heifer. Then the priest shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp. But the priest shall be unclean until evening. The one who burns the heifer shall wash his clothes in water and bathe his body in water and shall be unclean until evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cedarwood and hyssop and scarlet yarn are not decoration. They are the cleansing kit of the whole law: the same three items cleanse a healed leper (Lev. 14:4–6), hyssop painted lamb’s blood on the doorposts in Egypt (Exod. 12:22), and the same plant was lifted to Jesus’ lips at the cross (John 19:29). Cedar may stand for what resists decay, and scarlet for blood. Everything Israel possessed for making foul things clean is burned down into this one ash.

Then the sentence that turns the chapter over: the priest shall be unclean until evening. So is the man who burned the carcass. They have done exactly what God commanded, and it has cost them their standing in the camp for the rest of the day.

Think of the last genuinely costly thing you did for someone else’s good: the mess you cleaned up that you had not made, the relative you cared for at the end. Some of it stuck to you. That is the small, ordinary shadow of this verse. Cleansing is never free for the one who provides it. Somebody stands outside the camp until evening so that somebody else may go in.

verseByVerse.quote: And a man who is clean shall gather up the ashes of the heifer and deposit them outside the camp in a clean place. And they shall be kept for the water for impurity for the congregation of the people of Israel; it is a sin offering. And the one who gathers the ashes of the heifer shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening. And this shall be a perpetual statute for the people of Israel, and for the stranger who sojourns among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ashes are stored in a clean place, and the text says something remarkable: it is a sin offering. Not it was. The heifer is dead and burned; the jar of grey ash is the sin offering still, one animal killed once, its value held in reserve for whoever needs it, generation after generation.

No other sacrifice in the law is shaped like that, and it is precisely the shape of the gospel. Christ was offered once, on one Friday, and that one offering has been applied to sinners every day since and is not used up. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Heb. 10:14).

Why was the provision needed permanently? Chapter 14 had sentenced a generation to die in the wilderness: six hundred thousand men over thirty-eight years is something like forty funerals a day. Israel was walking through a rolling graveyard. And the closing line includes the stranger who sojourns among them. The foreigner got the same water as the Israelite. God did not make a cleansing for insiders only, and he never has. Israel itself had been a sojourner in Egypt when God took it up (Deut. 10:19).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ashes are mixed with running water and sprinkled on the death-defiled on the third and seventh days. To refuse the cleansing is to stay cut off and to defile the sanctuary: God provides the remedy, but it must be received.
verseByVerse.theology: Cleansing is provided but must be applied: the one who refuses it “defiles the tabernacle of the LORD” and is cut off (v.13, 20). The sprinkled water points to “the sprinkled blood” of Christ (Hebrews 12:24; 1 Pet 1:2), a cleansing freely given that must be personally received by faith. God’s remedy does no good to the one who will not come to be washed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the one who touched death was sprinkled and restored, but the one who refused stayed unclean and cut off.

Now: the cleansing blood of Christ is offered freely: “Let us draw near... with our hearts sprinkled clean” (Hebrews 10:22). Provision made is not the same as pardon received.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever touches the dead body of any person shall be unclean seven days. He shall cleanse himself with the water on the third day and on the seventh day, and so be clean. But if he does not cleanse himself on the third day and on the seventh day, he will not become clean. Whoever touches a dead person, the body of anyone who has died, and does not cleanse himself, defiles the tabernacle of the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from Israel; because the water for impurity was not thrown on him, he shall be unclean. His uncleanness is still on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the defilement the whole chapter was built for: a full week outside the worship of God, cleansed on the third day and the seventh, or not cleansed at all.

An honest reader asks: was it a sin to bury your father? It was not, and the distinction matters. Sin is guilt and needs forgiveness; uncleanness is contamination and needs washing. Burying your mother was love, and somebody had to do it. But the law would not let Israel walk away from a graveside as though nothing had happened, because it was teaching one lesson in the body: death is not natural, not neutral, and not fine. It is the wage of sin (Rom. 6:23) and the mark of a wrecked world. Every funeral cost a week, so that nobody could quietly get used to burying people.

The warning in verse 13 is heavier than it looks. The man who will not be cleansed defiles the tabernacle of the LORD; his uncleanness reaches the sanctuary, and he is cut off. Sin is never as private as it feels.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the law when someone dies in a tent: everyone who comes into the tent and everyone who is in the tent shall be unclean seven days. And every open vessel that has no cover fastened on it is unclean. Whoever in the open field touches someone who was killed with a sword or who died naturally, or touches a human bone or a grave, shall be unclean seven days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law works outward from the body, and the detail is strangely tender: even every open vessel in the tent is unclean. Anyone who has cleared out a house after a death knows the half-drunk tea, the reading glasses on the arm of the chair. Death does not stay in the body. It seeps into the room.

Then verse 16 goes out of doors: a human bone or a grave in the open field. An unmarked grave you walked across without knowing it was there. You could be defiled by something you never chose, never saw, and would never remember.

That is the reader’s actual condition. A man may know the sins he intended. What he cannot inventory is what he has walked through: the words absorbed, the habits caught, the damage done to people he never learned about. David prayed the only sane prayer about it: Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults (Ps. 19:12). Israel needed a cleansing that reached further than her memory. So do we.

verseByVerse.quote: For the unclean they shall take some ashes of the burnt sin offering, and fresh water shall be added in a vessel. Then a clean person shall take hyssop and dip it in the water and sprinkle it on the tent and on all the furnishings and on the persons who were there and on whoever touched the bone, or the slain or the dead or the grave. And the clean person shall sprinkle it on the unclean on the third day and on the seventh day. Thus on the seventh day he shall cleanse him, and he shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water, and at evening he shall be clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every detail of the mechanics preaches. The ESV note gives "fresh water" as "living" water, from a spring, not standing in a cistern. The death of the heifer and the life of the spring are mixed in one bowl: a sacrifice that died, joined to water that is alive. Christ gives both, for he is the offering made and the one who says the water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life (John 4:14).

Then the point on which the chapter turns: the clean person shall sprinkle it on the unclean. The unclean man may not sprinkle himself or pick up the hyssop and put himself right. He must wait for a clean person to come and do for him what he cannot do for himself.

Every religion of self-improvement dies on that sentence. David, who knew the ritual, does not offer to perform it but asks God to do it to him: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow (Ps. 51:7). It is applied on the third day and again on the seventh, and then at evening he shall be clean. The man is not left to guess whether it worked. The law names the hour when he is clean, and he is.
verseByVerse.note: “Fresh water” is literally “living water” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "If the man who is unclean does not cleanse himself, that person shall be cut off from the midst of the assembly, since he has defiled the sanctuary of the LORD. Because the water for impurity has not been thrown on him, he is unclean. And it shall be a statute forever for them. The one who sprinkles the water for impurity shall wash his clothes, and the one who touches the water for impurity shall be unclean until evening. And whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean, and anyone who touches it shall be unclean until evening."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saddest verse in the chapter is the man who simply will not come. His tragedy is not that there was no remedy: the ashes stood ready, the spring was running, a clean man was willing. He stayed unclean within reach of the cure. There is a way to be lost that involves nothing more dramatic than declining to be washed.

Then the riddle is stated flatly: the water that makes the unclean clean makes the clean unclean. Every man who handles it pays for it. No ritual can explain itself, and this one was built to hold a question open for fourteen centuries until a Man came who was the answer.

He was the clean One who came to the unclean and touched them. At Nain he laid his hand on the bier of a widow’s only son, where this chapter said death’s defilement would run up his arm; instead life ran down it, and the young man sat up (Luke 7:14–15). He took a dead girl by the hand, and she rose (Mark 5:41–42). And at the last, outside the gate, the One who had never worn the yoke was made unclean with a world’s defilement. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor. 5:21). The red heifer asks how the defiled can ever be purified. The cross of Christ is the answer, and there is no other.

20.title: Water from the Rock; the Death of Aaron: When the Mediator Fails
20.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people of Israel, the whole congregation, came into the wilderness of Zin in the first month, and the people stayed in Kadesh. And Miriam died there and was buried there.<sup>2</sup>Now there was no water for the congregation. And they assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron.<sup>3</sup>And the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Would that we had perished when our brothers perished before the LORD!<sup>4</sup>Why have you brought the assembly of the LORD into this wilderness, that we should die here, both we and our cattle?<sup>5</sup>And why have you made us come up out of Egypt to bring us to this evil place? It is no place for grain or figs or vines or pomegranates, and there is no water to drink."<sup>6</sup>Then Moses and Aaron went from the presence of the assembly to the entrance of the tent of meeting and fell on their faces. And the glory of the LORD appeared to them,<sup>7</sup>and the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>8</sup>"Take the staff, and assemble the congregation, you and Aaron your brother, and tell the rock before their eyes to yield its water.
