So you shall bring water out of the rock for them and give drink to the congregation and their cattle."<sup>9</sup>And Moses took the staff from before the LORD, as he commanded him.<sup>10</sup>Then Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly together before the rock, and he said to them, "Hear now, you rebels: shall we bring water for you out of this rock?"<sup>11</sup>And Moses lifted up his hand and struck the rock with his staff twice, and water came out abundantly, and the congregation drank, and their livestock.<sup>12</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them."<sup>13</sup>These are the waters of Meribah, where the people of Israel quarreled with the LORD, and through them he showed himself holy.<sup>14</sup>Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom: "Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the hardship that we have met:<sup>15</sup>how our fathers went down to Egypt, and we lived in Egypt a long time. And the Egyptians dealt harshly with us and our fathers.<sup>16</sup>And when we cried to the LORD, he heard our voice and sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt. And here we are in Kadesh, a city on the edge of your territory.<sup>17</sup>Please let us pass through your land. We will not pass through field or vineyard, or drink water from a well. We will go along the King's Highway. We will not turn aside to the right hand or to the left until we have passed through your territory."<sup>18</sup>But Edom said to him, "You shall not pass through, lest I come out with the sword against you."<sup>19</sup>And the people of Israel said to him, "We will go up by the highway, and if we drink of your water, I and my livestock, then I will pay for it. Let me only pass through on foot, nothing more."<sup>20</sup>But he said, "You shall not pass through." And Edom came out against them with a large army and with a strong force.<sup>21</sup>Thus Edom refused to give Israel passage through his territory, so Israel turned away from him.<sup>22</sup>And they journeyed from Kadesh, and the people of Israel, the whole congregation, came to Mount Hor.<sup>23</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron at Mount Hor, on the border of the land of Edom,<sup>24</sup>"Let Aaron be gathered to his people, for he shall not enter the land that I have given to the people of Israel, because you rebelled against my command at the waters of Meribah.<sup>25</sup>Take Aaron and Eleazar his son and bring them up to Mount Hor.<sup>26</sup>And strip Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. And Aaron shall be gathered to his people and shall die there."<sup>27</sup>Moses did as the LORD commanded. And they went up Mount Hor in the sight of all the congregation.<sup>28</sup>And Moses stripped Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. And Aaron died there on the top of the mountain. Then Moses and Eleazar came down from the mountain.<sup>29</sup>And when all the congregation saw that Aaron had perished, all the house of Israel wept for Aaron thirty days.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 marks the beginning of the end of the wilderness generation, and it is heavy with loss. Miriam dies. Aaron dies. And Moses commits the sin that bars him from the Promised Land. At Kadesh the people again have no water and grumble exactly as their parents had done, but the tragedy here belongs to Moses.

Told to speak to the rock, Moses calls the people “you rebels,” takes the glory to himself, and strikes the rock twice. God is gracious to the thirsty people, but his verdict on Moses is severe: he did not believe God or uphold him as holy. The severity matches the privilege: Moses had misrepresented the holiness of God before the whole nation.

Paul says “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). At the first rock (Exod 17) Moses was told to strike; this time only to speak, for Christ was “offered once to bear the sins of many” (Hebrews 9:28). Moses’ failure magnifies the true Mediator, who never failed to uphold God’s holiness and alone leads his people into the rest Moses could not enter.
20.theology:
The smitten Rock. The rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4), struck once for sin. Moses’ second striking marred the gospel picture, though the reason God gives is Moses’ unbelief.

The holiness of God in leadership. Those who represent God bear a weighty responsibility not to misrepresent his character.

The mortal priesthood. Aaron dies outside the land, his office passed on. The dying priests of the old order magnify the undying priesthood of Christ.
20.examples:
Then: Moses struck the rock in anger and was barred from the land, and Aaron died on Mount Hor, his priesthood passing to his son.

Now: The Rock has been struck once for you. Drink freely of the living water that flows from the smitten Savior, and follow the Priest who never fails and never dies.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new generation, the same old grumbling. Miriam dies, the people quarrel over water, and Moses, told to speak to the rock, strikes it twice in anger. God is faithful even to a faithless people, but Moses’ disobedience costs him the promised land.
verseByVerse.theology: God said “tell the rock”; Moses struck it and took the glory (“shall we bring water”), and God’s verdict was severe (v.12). Leaders are held to account, and God’s holiness matters more than a servant’s reputation. The rock, struck once already (Ex 17), pictures Christ (1 Cor 10:4), struck once for all and now need only be asked.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: even Moses, the meekest man on earth, was barred from Canaan for one act of unbelieving, self-exalting anger.

Now: we come to our Rock not by striking but by asking, and the living water flows (John 7:37-38). And God takes the holiness of his leaders seriously.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel, the whole congregation, came into the wilderness of Zin in the first month, and the people stayed in Kadesh. And Miriam died there and was buried there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between chapter 19 and this verse probably lie some thirty-eight years (the first month here seems to be in the fortieth year; compare 33:38), and the Bible gives them a paragraph break. A generation grew old and died, and Scripture does not think the years worth narrating, because nothing was going anywhere.

And they are at Kadesh, where the spies came back (Num. 13:26) and the nation wept all night. Nearly four decades later Israel is camped on the same ground, having travelled several hundred miles to arrive where it started. Unbelief does not take you backwards. It takes you in a circle, and then hands you the bill.

Here Miriam dies. The last time we saw her in a good light she was on the far shore of the Red Sea with a tambourine, leading the song: Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously (Exod. 15:20–21). Now, a grave in the wilderness of Zin. Within twelve months Miriam, Aaron and Moses will all be dead, and none of the three will cross the Jordan.
verseByVerse.note: Kadesh lay on the southern edge of Canaan. This is the last year of the wilderness wanderings.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was no water for the congregation. And they assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron. And the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Would that we had perished when our brothers perished before the LORD! Why have you brought the assembly of the LORD into this wilderness, that we should die here, both we and our cattle? And why have you made us come up out of Egypt to bring us to this evil place? It is no place for grain or figs or vines or pomegranates, and there is no water to drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the oldest crisis in the book and it produces the oldest reaction. They assembled themselves together against Moses, the language of a mob forming, and their words echo their parents’ at Rephidim (Exod. 17:2–3). A new generation, and an old script.

Look at what they complain about: no place for grain or figs or vines or pomegranates. Those are the fruits the spies carried back to Kadesh (13:23). They are complaining that the wilderness is not Canaan, the land their parents refused at this very spot. They want the fruit without the crossing.

And Egypt, slavery and the lash, has become in the telling somewhere with pomegranates. Complaint has a memory, and the memory edits. The first symptom is always the same: we start to speak of what God rescued us from as though it were what we lost.

But their thirst was real, and God does not scold them for saying so; in a moment he will give them everything they asked for. A third of the Psalms tell God the situation is unbearable. The difference is one preposition. They assembled against Moses instead of crying to the LORD. Lament carries the trouble to God and stays in the room; grumbling carries it to everyone else and puts God in the dock. A Christian who has grumbled can still turn it into lament, because the God who redeemed him still listens, and the Spirit helps us in our weakness when we do not know what to pray (Rom. 8:26).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron went from the presence of the assembly to the entrance of the tent of meeting and fell on their faces. And the glory of the LORD appeared to them, and the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Take the staff, and assemble the congregation, you and Aaron your brother, and tell the rock before their eyes to yield its water. So you shall bring water out of the rock for them and give drink to the congregation and their cattle."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Moses and Aaron do next is exactly right. They walk away from the shouting to the tent of meeting and fall on their faces. They do not argue or defend their record; they take the crowd to God. And God answers not with a rebuke but with splendour: the glory of the LORD appeared.

Then the instruction, with two commands pulling in different directions. The staff is the one kept before the LORD, very probably Aaron’s staff that budded (17:10), and it recalls the rod that struck the rock at Horeb nearly forty years before (Exod. 17:5–6). It is an instrument of striking. Moses is told to carry it in front of the nation and not use it. He is to tell the rock.

Why does that matter enough to build a chapter around? Because the rock at Horeb was struck once, and God is now teaching Israel that it is never to be struck again. Water for the thirsty is not obtained by hitting the rock a second time. It is obtained by asking. The staff in Moses’ hand is a memorial of a blow already struck; the word in Moses’ mouth is all that is needed now. Hold on to that, because in three verses a good man is going to smash it.

And notice the comfort in the order: the water was promised before the rock was struck. God had decided to give this mutinous crowd everything they were shouting for before his servant lost his temper. What happened at the rock could spoil the picture of that grace. Nothing could stop its flow.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses took the staff from before the LORD, as he commanded him. Then Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly together before the rock, and he said to them, "Hear now, you rebels: shall we bring water for you out of this rock?" And Moses lifted up his hand and struck the rock with his staff twice, and water came out abundantly, and the congregation drank, and their livestock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He takes the staff. So far, so obedient. Then the whole thing collapses in a single sentence.

Two things are wrong with it, and both are fatal. The first is the name: rebels. A true word, but God had given no rebuke at all; he had offered water. Moses presents a generous God as a furious one, and the people learn something false about their Maker. The second is the pronoun: shall we bring water, not "shall the LORD." Somewhere between the tent and the rock, the mediator has slipped into the middle of the sentence. Then he strikes the rock twice, in temper, doing what he was not told to do.

And the water came out abundantly. Every person and animal in that camp drank through a man who was at that moment sinning against God. God’s kindness to his people is not throttled by the state of his servant’s heart. A church can be fed under a preacher who is in the wrong. That is a mercy for the people and a trap for the servant, because the gushing water felt exactly like approval, and it was not.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them." These are the waters of Meribah, where the people of Israel quarreled with the LORD, and through them he showed himself holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verdict falls on both brothers. Forty years of bearing this nation, and it ends here. Every honest reader feels the objection: is that not out of all proportion? He hit a rock.

Three things answer it. First, God names the sin, and it is not bad temper but you did not believe in me. Moses did not trust that a spoken word would be enough. Second, the charge is public: in the eyes of the people. Moses was the lens through which the nation saw God, and he smeared it. The higher the platform, the less private the failure, which is why teachers will be judged with greater strictness (Jas. 3:1). Third, Paul tells us what the rock was: they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10:4). At Horeb the Rock was struck once, and life poured out; here he was to be spoken to, because Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many (Heb. 9:28), is now approached with words, not blows. God’s stated reason is Moses’ unbelief, but many Reformed readers have heard this further note too: Moses took a hammer to that picture in front of the whole nation.

Then verse 13: he showed himself holy. He would be shown holy at those waters one way or the other; if his servant would not do it, his servant would become the occasion of it. Yet Moses was not lost. Fourteen centuries later a man appears in glory inside the land he was refused, talking with Jesus about his exodus (Luke 9:30–31). Moses was kept out of Canaan. He was never kept out of Christ, who upheld his Father as holy at every point where Moses failed.
verseByVerse.note: “Meribah” means “quarreling” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses asks Edom, Israel’s kinsmen through Esau, for peaceful passage. Edom refuses with an army, and Israel, forbidden to fight their brother nation (Deut 2:4-5), turns away.
verseByVerse.theology: Edom’s refusal continues the long estrangement of Esau’s line from Jacob’s (Gen 25-27; cf. Obadiah). God restrains Israel from retaliating against a brother nation, teaching submission to his timing rather than force.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel swallowed the insult and took the long way around, trusting God’s route.

Now: the way to our inheritance is often blocked, even by those who should be kin. Secure in what God has promised, we need not repay hostility with hostility (Rom 12:18-19).

verseByVerse.quote: Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom: "Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the hardship that we have met: how our fathers went down to Egypt, and we lived in Egypt a long time. And the Egyptians dealt harshly with us and our fathers. And when we cried to the LORD, he heard our voice and sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt. And here we are in Kadesh, a city on the edge of your territory. Please let us pass through your land. We will not pass through field or vineyard, or drink water from a well. We will go along the King's Highway. We will not turn aside to the right hand or to the left until we have passed through your territory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your brother Israel is chosen with care. Edom is Esau; Israel is Jacob (Gen. 36:1). These are twins who fought in the womb, and centuries later their descendants are still on opposite sides of a border. Old family wounds do not heal by being outlived. They get inherited.

Moses tells an outsider the gospel of the exodus: slavery, and when we cried to the LORD, he heard our voice. Then a painfully modest request: not a field, not a drink from a well, only the King’s Highway, walked straight down the middle.

A nation with some six hundred thousand fighting men could have taken it. But God had told them not to: Do not contend with them, for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession (Deut. 2:4–5). Esau despised his birthright, and God still kept a promise to him. The God who chooses is not therefore careless of those he did not choose.
verseByVerse.note: The King’s Highway was the main trade road east of the Jordan.

verseByVerse.quote: But Edom said to him, "You shall not pass through, lest I come out with the sword against you." And the people of Israel said to him, "We will go up by the highway, and if we drink of your water, I and my livestock, then I will pay for it. Let me only pass through on foot, nothing more." But he said, "You shall not pass through." And Edom came out against them with a large army and with a strong force. Thus Edom refused to give Israel passage through his territory, so Israel turned away from him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel sweetens the offer, and Edom answers with one sentence and an army. The brother came out in force to stop his brother walking down a public road.

Then the sentence that shows what forty years have produced: so Israel turned away from him. They had the numbers and every human reason to force the crossing, and they walked away because God had said the land was Esau’s. That is obedience with nothing in it for the obedient, and it makes no sense unless you believe God is running the map.

And look where the detour goes. Because Edom said no, Israel takes the long road around Seir, and on that road, in the next chapter, God lifts up the bronze serpent that Jesus would claim as a picture of his own cross (John 3:14). Israel could not see the bronze serpent from Kadesh. The detour was not the loss of the plan. It was the plan.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Mount Hor, Moses strips Aaron of his priestly garments and puts them on Eleazar, and Aaron dies on the mountain. The first high priest passes; the office continues.
verseByVerse.theology: Aaron dies outside the land, under the same judgment as Moses (v.24), and the garments pass to Eleazar: the office outlives the man. The old priesthood was marked by death, and this very weakness magnifies Christ, who “holds his priesthood permanently” (Hebrews 7:24), never passes his garments to a successor, and “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Aaron’s garments were laid on his son; the high priest died, and the people mourned him thirty days.

Now: our High Priest never dies and never hands off his office; his ministry for us can never be interrupted by death.

verseByVerse.quote: And they journeyed from Kadesh, and the people of Israel, the whole congregation, came to Mount Hor. And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron at Mount Hor, on the border of the land of Edom, "Let Aaron be gathered to his people, for he shall not enter the land that I have given to the people of Israel, because you rebelled against my command at the waters of Meribah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence passed at Meribah is now to be carried out, and Aaron hears it announced over his own head.

But notice the phrase: not "Aaron shall die," though he will, but let Aaron be gathered to his people. Abraham was gathered to his people (Gen. 25:8), and plainly that means more than burial, because Abraham was buried in a cave in a foreign country while his kin lay far away in Ur and Haran. To be gathered is to be brought in to a company already assembled somewhere else. The Old Testament says this quietly, the way a family speaks of someone going home.

And Aaron does nothing with the news. No protest is recorded, no plea that forty years had earned a better ending. He is told to climb a mountain he will not come down from, and he climbs it. That, not the golden calf, is the last thing Scripture shows us Aaron doing.

So the God who shuts the land against Aaron opens something else in the same breath: not a border crossing, but a gathering. That is the shape of a Christian funeral, where loss and welcome are announced together, and why Paul can say that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Cor. 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Take Aaron and Eleazar his son and bring them up to Mount Hor. And strip Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. And Aaron shall be gathered to his people and shall die there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the most affecting scenes in the Torah, and it is easy to walk past.

An old man climbs a mountain in the full dress of the high priest: the blue robe with bells and pomegranates round the hem, the breastpiece with the twelve engraved stones over the heart, and on the turban the gold plate that read Holy to the LORD (Exod. 28). He has worn it for forty years. At the summit Moses takes it off him piece by piece, until the greatest priest Israel has had stands on a bare rock with nothing to show for any of it. Then he dies.

The garments go onto Eleazar, and Israel comes down with a high priest. But the man is gone, and that is the limitation Hebrews names: the former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Heb. 7:23–24). There was another hill, and another priest’s garments taken off him, and soldiers who threw dice for them (John 19:23–24). But that priest had no successor and needed none. He came back for his own office. He is wearing it still.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses did as the LORD commanded. And they went up Mount Hor in the sight of all the congregation. And Moses stripped Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. And Aaron died there on the top of the mountain. Then Moses and Eleazar came down from the mountain. And when all the congregation saw that Aaron had perished, all the house of Israel wept for Aaron thirty days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole nation watched. Three men went up and two came down, and the second was wearing the robes of the first. Israel read what had happened off the shoulders of the man walking back toward them.

Then thirty days of mourning, the same the nation would later give Moses (Deut. 34:8). And look who they were weeping for: the man who made the golden calf and told the feeblest lie in Scripture, that he threw the gold in the fire and out came this calf (Exod. 32:24), the man who spoke against his own brother (Num. 12:1–2). God had not merely tolerated Aaron; he had made him the man Israel could not bear to lose. That is what grace does with a failure who is not thrown away.

The chapter has been an inventory of endings: Miriam buried, Moses barred, Aaron stripped, a door slammed by a brother. And here Hebrews shows what is different now: because our priest lives forever, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25). The church will never gather at the foot of a mountain to weep for him.

21.title: The Bronze Serpent: Look and Live
21.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb, heard that Israel was coming by the way of Atharim, he fought against Israel, and took some of them captive.<sup>2</sup>And Israel vowed a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will indeed give this people into my hand, then I will devote their cities to destruction."<sup>3</sup>And the LORD heeded the voice of Israel and gave over the Canaanites, and they devoted them and their cities to destruction. So the name of the place was called Hormah.<sup>4</sup>From Mount Hor they set out by the way to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom. And the people became impatient on the way.<sup>5</sup>And the people spoke against God and against Moses, "Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food."<sup>6</sup>Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, so that many people of Israel died.<sup>7</sup>And the people came to Moses and said, "We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD and against you. Pray to the LORD, that he take away the serpents from us." So Moses prayed for the people.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live."<sup>9</sup>So Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. And if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live.<sup>10</sup>And the people of Israel set out and camped in Oboth.<sup>11</sup>And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness that is opposite Moab, toward the sunrise.<sup>12</sup>From there they set out and camped in the Valley of Zered.<sup>13</sup>From there they set out and camped on the other side of the Arnon, which is in the wilderness that extends from the border of the Amorites, for the Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites.<sup>14</sup>Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the LORD, "Waheb in Suphah, and the valleys of the Arnon,<sup>15</sup>and the slope of the valleys that extends to the seat of Ar, and leans to the border of Moab."<sup>16</sup>And from there they continued to Beer; that is the well of which the LORD said to Moses, "Gather the people together, so that I may give them water."<sup>17</sup>Then Israel sang this song: "Spring up, O well!—Sing to it!—<sup>18</sup>the well that the princes made, that the nobles of the people dug, with the scepter and with their staffs." And from the wilderness they went on to Mattanah,<sup>19</sup>and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth,<sup>20</sup>and from Bamoth to the valley lying in the region of Moab by the top of Pisgah that looks down on the desert.<sup>21</sup>Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, saying,<sup>22</sup>"Let me pass through your land. We will not turn aside into field or vineyard. We will not drink the water of a well. We will go by the King's Highway until we have passed through your territory."<sup>23</sup>But Sihon would not allow Israel to pass through his territory. He gathered all his people together and went out against Israel to the wilderness and came to Jahaz and fought against Israel.<sup>24</sup>And Israel defeated him with the edge of the sword and took possession of his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, as far as to the Ammonites, for the border of the Ammonites was strong.<sup>25</sup>And Israel took all these cities, and Israel settled in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon, and in all its villages.<sup>26</sup>For Heshbon was the city of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land out of his hand, as far as the Arnon.<sup>27</sup>Therefore the ballad singers say, "Come to Heshbon, let it be built; let the city of Sihon be established.<sup>28</sup>For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon. It devoured Ar of Moab, and swallowed the heights of the Arnon.<sup>29</sup>Woe to you, O Moab! You are undone, O people of Chemosh! He has made his sons fugitives, and his daughters captives, to an Amorite king, Sihon.<sup>30</sup>So we overthrew them; Heshbon, as far as Dibon, perished; and we laid waste as far as Nophah; fire spread as far as Medeba."<sup>31</sup>Thus Israel lived in the land of the Amorites.<sup>32</sup>And Moses sent to spy out Jazer, and they captured its villages and dispossessed the Amorites who were there.<sup>33</sup>Then they turned and went up by the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against them, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.<sup>34</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Do not fear him, for I have given him into your hand, and all his people, and his land. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon."<sup>35</sup>So they defeated him and his sons and all his people, until he had no survivor left. And they possessed his land.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 holds one of the brightest gospel lights in Numbers, for our Lord himself pointed to it: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). The people grumble yet again, despising even the manna, and God sends fiery serpents among them. A people who spit venom at God are bitten by venom.

When they repent, God does not remove the serpents. He has a bronze serpent lifted on a pole, and whoever looks at it lives. The dying are not told to fight the serpents or to be worthy, only to look: salvation by faith alone in its purest Old Testament form. And what was lifted up was an image of the very thing killing them. So Christ came “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8:3) and was made sin and a curse for us (2 Cor 5:21; Gal 3:13), lifted up on the cross, and every dying sinner who looks to him shall live.
21.theology:
Look and live. The bronze serpent saves by sight, not effort, the purest Old Testament picture of justification by faith (John 3:14–15).

The curse lifted up. The serpent, emblem of the curse, was raised on a pole. So Christ became a curse for us (Gal 3:13), bearing the very judgment that was killing us.

Judgment that fits the sin. Venomous words met venomous serpents. God's judgments hold up a mirror, yet his mercy provides a remedy in the midst of the curse.
21.examples:
Then: God sent fiery serpents for Israel's grumbling, then a bronze serpent on a pole, so that everyone bitten who looked would live.

Now: You have been bitten by sin and are dying. Do not look to yourself or your worthiness. Look to Christ lifted up, who became the curse for you, and live. The weakest look of faith saves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king of Arad attacks Israel and takes captives. Israel vows to the LORD, God gives victory, and the place is named Hormah: a first taste of the conquest, granted in answer to dependence on God.
verseByVerse.theology: Victory comes not by Israel’s might but by the LORD’s gift, sought in prayer and vow (vv.2-3). It is a small firstfruit of the conquest, a sign that the God who disciplines his people has not abandoned his promise.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: attacked and taking losses, Israel turned to God with a vow, and he gave the victory.

Now: our battles are won the same way, by casting ourselves on God, who “gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57).

verseByVerse.quote: When the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb, heard that Israel was coming by the way of Atharim, he fought against Israel, and took some of them captive. And Israel vowed a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will indeed give this people into my hand, then I will devote their cities to destruction." And the LORD heeded the voice of Israel and gave over the Canaanites, and they devoted them and their cities to destruction. So the name of the place was called Hormah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first thing to happen after Aaron’s funeral is a raid. And Israel’s response is the most surprising sentence in the book so far: Israel vowed a vow to the LORD. Not a complaint, not a mob at the tent door. In twenty chapters trouble has rarely produced prayer from the people, and the change is the whole point of the verse.

Then the name: Hormah. In chapter 14 the people invaded without God, and the enemy came down and defeated them and pursued them, even to Hormah (14:45). That rout was the low-water mark of the nation, on the very ground where they now win.

Same place, same enemy, opposite outcome. The one variable is whether God went with them. If there is ground in your own history where you were beaten a hundred times, a besetting sin or a fear, this verse says the ground is not the reason. Israel did not need a different battlefield. She needed a different way of going up: they asked first.

Was it just? To devote to destruction (Hebrew herem) meant handing a city over wholly to God, usually by destroying it. This was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Gen 15:16; Deut 9:4–5), including child sacrifice (Deut 12:31), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Lev 18:24–28). It was a unique command, carried out through Israel at one moment in redemptive history. It is no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36), and the church’s weapons are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4).
verseByVerse.note: “Devote to destruction” means to set apart to the LORD for destruction (ESV note); “Hormah” means “destruction” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — The Bronze Serpent: Look and Live
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the long detour around Edom, the people despise the manna as “worthless food,” and God sends fiery serpents. When they confess and Moses prays, God’s remedy is startling: a bronze serpent on a pole, and whoever looks at it lives. Jesus himself made it a picture of his cross.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus makes this the great type of his cross (John 3:14-15). The cure is by looking, not by working. The bronze serpent, made in the image of the very thing killing them, pictures Christ, whom God “made... to be sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21) and who became “a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), lifted up so that all who look to him might live.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the dying Israelite had only to turn his eyes to the pole, and he lived.

Now: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth!” (Isaiah 45:22). Salvation is by looking to Christ crucified, not by trying to cure ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: From Mount Hor they set out by the way to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom. And the people became impatient on the way. And the people spoke against God and against Moses, "Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the map behind this sentence. Canaan is north, and they are marching south, back toward the Red Sea, because a brother nation would not let them use its road. They have just buried Aaron. And the people became impatient, literally their soul became short: the fraying that comes three-quarters of the way through, when the end was supposed to be in sight and the road turns the wrong way.

The complaint contradicts itself in one breath: there is no food, and we cannot stand the food. Grumbling does not have to be coherent, only loud, because the point was never the food.

And this worthless food is the manna, the bread God rained down every morning for forty years, which the Psalms call the grain of heaven… the bread of the angels (Ps. 78:24–25). Israel, standing in it, calls it contemptible. It is a verdict on the goodness of God by people whose mouths are full of his generosity, and it is nearer to us than we would like. Anything given daily stops registering as a gift. Ask what you have stopped thanking God for, and you will usually find it is whatever he has been most faithful about. The cure is not to manufacture gratitude but to look again at the giver, who has kept giving through every complaint.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, so that many people of Israel died. And the people came to Moses and said, "We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD and against you. Pray to the LORD, that he take away the serpents from us." So Moses prayed for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment is fitted to the crime with terrible precision: a people whose words had turned venomous are answered by venom. The word rendered fiery is seraphim, burning ones, most likely for the fire the poison put in the wound; the desert south of Edom is real snake country, and the horror was literal: swelling, thirst, and hours to live.

Then the second surprise of the chapter. This time the people do not bargain, excuse or blame: We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD and against you. They name the sin and both parties they wronged, and ask for the one thing they cannot do for themselves: Pray to the LORD.

So Moses prayed for the people. This is the man they had just attacked, who one chapter ago lost the land because his patience with them snapped. He prays. There is a love that is not exhausted by rejection, and there is only one place it comes from, and Israel is about to be shown it, hammered out of bronze and hoisted on a pole.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch what God does not do. They asked him to take away the serpents, and he does not; so far as the chapter tells us, the snakes are still in the sand when Israel breaks camp. He leaves the danger in the world and puts a remedy in the middle of it.

Anyone who has begged God to remove something and watched him not remove it knows this ground. Paul asked three times for a thorn to be taken out and was told instead, My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor. 12:8–9). That is not a smaller answer than the one requested. It is a costlier one, and it leaves the sufferer with God himself rather than merely with relief.

And on the pole God puts not a lamb or an angel but a serpent: an image of the very thing killing them, lifted up dead and harmless where every dying man can see it. The cure is a look. Not a pilgrimage to the pole, not a fee, not a period of improvement first. A man too far gone to stand can still turn his head. God set the price of life at the one thing a dying man is still able to do.

Was the bronze serpent magic? The image had no power in itself; those who looked were healed because God promised it, and later, when Israel worshipped the image, Hezekiah broke it in pieces (2 Kgs 18:4). Jesus says that whoever looks to him in faith lives (John 3:14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. And if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fourteen centuries later a rabbi came to Jesus by night with questions about being born again, and Jesus reached past every other text for this one: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up (John 3:14). Of all the pictures available, the lamb, the manna, the mercy seat, this is the one the Lord chose to explain his own cross.

See why. The serpent had stood for the enemy and the curse since Eden (Genesis 3:14–15), and to hang it on a pole was to display it defeated. Paul describes Calvary in the same terms: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Gal. 3:13). He became, in the sight of the whole camp, the thing that was killing us, and drew every dying eye to himself. Not look and then earn it; not look after cleaning up. Look, and live, in that order and no other.

One postscript. Seven hundred years later Hezekiah broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it (2 Kgs. 18:4). It was called Nehushtan, a name that, as the ESV note explains, sounds like the Hebrew for both bronze and serpent. Anything God gives you as a window, a church, a teacher, a way of praying, you can turn into a wall, and the tell is always the same: you begin to love the means more than the Christ it was pointing at.

Break the bronze, then, and keep the Christ. The serpent on the pole was only ever an arrow pointing to a hill outside Jerusalem, where the Son of God hung with the whole curse of the world on him, and did not come down, and let the dying look at him. Every eye that has ever turned to him has lived, and not one that turned has been refused.
verseByVerse.note: Centuries later King Hezekiah destroyed the bronze serpent because people were burning incense to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — The Journey and the Song of the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel journeys on toward Moab, and along the way sings a joyful little song over a well God gives them: after the venom and the grumbling, thanks instead of complaint.
verseByVerse.theology: The Song of the Well (vv.17-18) is a rare, bright note of grateful worship in a book full of murmuring. The itinerary marks real progress toward the land, and joy over God’s gifts is the fitting response of those being brought home.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: instead of grumbling over water, this time Israel sang over it.

Now: a grumbling life and a grateful one often receive the same gift two ways. The God who brought you through the serpents gives the well too; “give thanks in all circumstances” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel set out and camped in Oboth. And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness that is opposite Moab, toward the sunrise. From there they set out and camped in the Valley of Zered. From there they set out and camped on the other side of the Arnon, which is in the wilderness that extends from the border of the Amorites, for the Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the serpents, the text goes quiet. Set out and camp, set out and camp: four verses of a nation simply travelling.

That is not filler. Most of the Christian life is these verses rather than the ones before them: long stretches of ordinary obedience where nothing happens except that you keep going in the right direction. God records both. The Holy Spirit thought the campsite at Oboth was worth a line in the Bible.

And the geography is quietly hopeful. The Arnon is the northern border of Moab, so Israel has finally stopped going south. They are moving up the eastern side of the Dead Sea, and every camp from here on is closer to the Jordan than the last.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the LORD, "Waheb in Suphah, and the valleys of the Arnon, and the slope of the valleys that extends to the seat of Ar, and leans to the border of Moab."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the writer quotes a book we do not have. Nothing else in Scripture mentions the Book of the Wars of the LORD, and no copy has been found. It appears to have been a collection of victory poems, cited here as a geographer might cite a gazetteer, to fix the Arnon crossing. Some think the citation shows the book was edited after Moses; others that such a collection was already being made in his day.

Does a lost book mean the Bible is missing something? It does not. Scripture quotes outside sources fairly often: the Book of Jashar in Joshua and 2 Samuel, court annals in Kings, and pagan Greek poets in Paul (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). Inspiration has never been the claim that every source an inspired writer consulted was itself inspired. It is the claim that what God caused to be written is true, and that what he has given is enough: able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (2 Tim. 3:15).

So the lost book is not a hole in the Bible but a footnote in it: evidence that these events happened in a real country with real rivers, and that the writer expected his readers to be able to check.

verseByVerse.quote: And from there they continued to Beer; that is the well of which the LORD said to Moses, "Gather the people together, so that I may give them water." Then Israel sang this song: "Spring up, O well!—Sing to it!— the well that the princes made, that the nobles of the people dug, with the scepter and with their staffs." And from the wilderness they went on to Mattanah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beer means "well," as the ESV note explains. Set this beside the last chapter. At Meribah there was no water, a mob formed, a mediator lost his temper and a rock was struck twice. Here God announces the water before anyone has complained. He gathers them, and gives.

And Israel does something she has not done since the Red Sea. She sings. It is a working song, the kind men chant while they dig, with the leaders down in the pit swinging their staffs at the sand alongside everybody else. God provides the water; the nobles dig; the camp sings. Grace and effort in one verse, and neither crowding out the other.

The nation that called God’s bread worthless twelve verses ago is now singing at a hole in the ground. Judgment fell, mercy was lifted up on a pole, and the survivors came out singing. That is what God is doing in the wilderness: making, out of complainers, a people who sing.
verseByVerse.note: “Beer” means “well” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth, and from Bamoth to the valley lying in the region of Moab by the top of Pisgah that looks down on the desert.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are ordinary place-names, and the writer is not preaching from them. But after the serpents and the long detour, a list of camps that runs steadily forward is itself good news: the road has stopped turning back.

And it ends at the top of Pisgah, the ridge from which Moses will be shown the whole land before he dies (Deut. 34:1), that looks down on the desert. For thirty-eight years the wilderness was the horizon in every direction. Now they stand above it. It is not yet the promised land, but it is the first time Israel has seen the wilderness from the outside, and every believer who has come out the far side of a long, disciplined stretch knows what that morning felt like.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–35 — Victory over Sihon and Og
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan refuse Israel passage and come out to fight, and Israel defeats them both, taking their lands east of the Jordan. After forty years of wandering, God begins to give his people the land.
verseByVerse.theology: The defeat of Sihon and Og is the first great conquest, celebrated for generations (Ps 135:11; 136:19-20). Unbelief had delayed the promise but could not cancel it. These victories are the down payment on the whole inheritance, a reminder that God finishes what he begins (Phil 1:6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Sihon and Og fell before Israel, and the long-promised land began at last to be theirs.

Now: the God who kept his word to a wandering, faithless people keeps it still; “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, saying, "Let me pass through your land. We will not turn aside into field or vineyard. We will not drink the water of a well. We will go by the King's Highway until we have passed through your territory." But Sihon would not allow Israel to pass through his territory. He gathered all his people together and went out against Israel to the wilderness and came to Jahaz and fought against Israel. And Israel defeated him with the edge of the sword and took possession of his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, as far as to the Ammonites, for the border of the Ammonites was strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel sends Sihon almost word for word the message she sent Edom. The courtesy has not changed; God’s instruction has. Edom was protected (Deut. 2:5), so Israel turned away from an insult without drawing a sword. Of Sihon God had said, Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon… Begin to take possession, and contend with him in battle (Deut. 2:24).

And Sihon marched out into open desert to attack a nation that had asked to use a road. Deuteronomy adds the hardest line: the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate (Deut. 2:30). We should not soften that, nor overreach it. Sihon wanted this war; God did not manufacture an appetite that was not already his own. He declined to restrain a man bent on violence, and used it: a sovereignty that runs underneath human wickedness without ever becoming its author.

The result is the first territory Israel has ever owned, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, taken by a people who forty years earlier had been too frightened to cross a border.

verseByVerse.quote: And Israel took all these cities, and Israel settled in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon, and in all its villages. For Heshbon was the city of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land out of his hand, as far as the Arnon. Therefore the ballad singers say, "Come to Heshbon, let it be built; let the city of Sihon be established. For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon. It devoured Ar of Moab, and swallowed the heights of the Arnon. Woe to you, O Moab! You are undone, O people of Chemosh! He has made his sons fugitives, and his daughters captives, to an Amorite king, Sihon. So we overthrew them; Heshbon, as far as Dibon, perished; and we laid waste as far as Nophah; fire spread as far as Medeba."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the chapter does something sly. Sihon had taken Heshbon from Moab not long before, and the Amorite poets had written a victory ballad about it. That is the song quoted here: the conqueror’s taunt, gloating over Moab’s ruin.

And Israel, it seems, sings it over the rubble of Heshbon. The winner’s taunt-song is chanted at the winner’s funeral. Every empire composes its ballad; the ballad outlives the empire and is sung by somebody else on the ruins. Scripture keeps a copy of the lyrics to prove it.

One line especially: You are undone, O people of Chemosh! Chemosh was Moab’s national god, and the song says he turned his own worshippers into refugees. That is the difference between an idol and God. An idol takes everything you have and then cannot hold the ground you gave it for. Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases. Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands (Ps. 115:3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Israel lived in the land of the Amorites. And Moses sent to spy out Jazer, and they captured its villages and dispossessed the Amorites who were there. Then they turned and went up by the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against them, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei. But the LORD said to Moses, "Do not fear him, for I have given him into your hand, and all his people, and his land. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon." So they defeated him and his sons and all his people, until he had no survivor left. And they possessed his land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One more kingdom stands between Israel and the Jordan, and it is the worst one. Og was a giant, the last of the Rephaim, and his iron bed was over thirteen feet long; you could go and look at it in Rabbah (Deut. 3:11).

Now remember chapter 13: there we saw the Nephilim… and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers (13:33), and a generation died in the sand rather than face them. Here is that terror wearing a crown, coming down the road at Edrei. And God says, Do not fear him, for I have given him into your hand. The new generation fights the giant their parents ran from, and wins. The fear that killed the fathers no longer holds the sons.

Israel never forgot that day. Centuries later a psalm sings it with a refrain on every second line: to him who struck down great kings, for his steadfast love endures forever… Sihon, king of the Amorites… and Og, king of Bashan, for his steadfast love endures forever (Ps. 136:17–20). Israel learned to read her military history not as a record of her courage but as an inventory of his mercy. The God who hung a serpent on a pole for a camp of dying grumblers walks in front of them against giants. He does not save halfway.

Was the destruction of Og’s people just? Sihon and Og attacked Israel (vv. 23, 33), and the Amorites’ sin had reached its full measure (Gen 15:16). It was part of God’s unique judgment on Canaan, not a licence for later wars.
verseByVerse.note: Bashan lay east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for its cattle.

22.title: Balak and Balaam: The Sovereign God over a Pagan Prophet
22.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the people of Israel set out and camped in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho.<sup>2</sup>And Balak the son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites.<sup>3</sup>And Moab was in great dread of the people, because they were many. Moab was overcome with fear of the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And Moab said to the elders of Midian, "This horde will now lick up all that is around us, as the ox licks up the grass of the field." So Balak the son of Zippor, who was king of Moab at that time,<sup>5</sup>sent messengers to Balaam the son of Beor at Pethor, which is near the River in the land of the people of Amaw, to call him, saying, "Behold, a people has come out of Egypt. They cover the face of the earth, and they are dwelling opposite me.<sup>6</sup>Come now, curse this people for me, since they are too mighty for me. Perhaps I shall be able to defeat them and drive them from the land, for I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed."<sup>7</sup>So the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian departed with the fees for divination in their hand. And they came to Balaam and gave him Balak's message.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, "Lodge here tonight, and I will bring back word to you, as the LORD speaks to me." So the princes of Moab stayed with Balaam.<sup>9</sup>And God came to Balaam and said, "Who are these men with you?"<sup>10</sup>And Balaam said to God, "Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, has sent to me, saying,<sup>11</sup>'Behold, a people has come out of Egypt, and it covers the face of the earth. Now come, curse them for me. Perhaps I shall be able to fight against them and drive them out.'"<sup>12</sup>God said to Balaam, "You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed."<sup>13</sup>So Balaam rose in the morning and said to the princes of Balak, "Go to your own land, for the LORD has refused to let me go with you."<sup>14</sup>So the princes of Moab rose and went to Balak and said, "Balaam refuses to come with us."<sup>15</sup>Once again Balak sent princes, more in number and more honorable than these.<sup>16</sup>And they came to Balaam and said to him, "Thus says Balak the son of Zippor: 'Let nothing hinder you from coming to me,<sup>17</sup>for I will surely do you great honor, and whatever you say to me I will do. Come, curse this people for me.'"<sup>18</sup>But Balaam answered and said to the servants of Balak, "Though Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go beyond the command of the LORD my God to do less or more.<sup>19</sup>So you, too, please stay here tonight, that I may know what more the LORD will say to me."<sup>20</sup>And God came to Balaam at night and said to him, "If the men have come to call you, rise, go with them; but only do what I tell you."<sup>21</sup>So Balaam rose in the morning and saddled his donkey and went with the princes of Moab.<sup>22</sup>But God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the LORD took his stand in the way as his adversary. Now he was riding on the donkey, and his two servants were with him.<sup>23</sup>And the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road, with a drawn sword in his hand. And the donkey turned aside out of the road and went into the field. And Balaam struck the donkey, to turn her into the road.<sup>24</sup>Then the angel of the LORD stood in a narrow path between the vineyards, with a wall on either side.<sup>25</sup>And when the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she pushed against the wall and pressed Balaam's foot against the wall. So he struck her again.<sup>26</sup>Then the angel of the LORD went ahead and stood in a narrow place, where there was no way to turn either to the right or to the left.<sup>27</sup>When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she lay down under Balaam. And Balaam's anger was kindled, and he struck the donkey with his staff.<sup>28</sup>Then the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey, and she said to Balaam, "What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?"<sup>29</sup>And Balaam said to the donkey, "Because you have made a fool of me. I wish I had a sword in my hand, for then I would kill you."<sup>30</sup>And the donkey said to Balaam, "Am I not your donkey, on which you have ridden all your life long to this day? Is it my habit to treat you this way?" And he said, "No."<sup>31</sup>Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, with his drawn sword in his hand. And he bowed down and fell on his face.<sup>32</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why have you struck your donkey these three times? Behold, I have come out to oppose you because your way is perverse before me.<sup>33</sup>The donkey saw me and turned aside before me these three times. If she had not turned aside from me, surely just now I would have killed you and let her live."<sup>34</sup>Then Balaam said to the angel of the LORD, "I have sinned, for I did not know that you stood in the road against me. Now therefore, if it is evil in your sight, I will turn back."<sup>35</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to Balaam, "Go with the men, but speak only the word that I tell you." So Balaam went on with the princes of Balak.<sup>36</sup>When Balak heard that Balaam had come, he went out to meet him at the city of Moab, on the border formed by the Arnon, at the extremity of the border.<sup>37</sup>And Balak said to Balaam, "Did I not send to you to call you? Why did you not come to me? Am I not able to honor you?"<sup>38</sup>Balaam said to Balak, "Behold, I have come to you! Have I now any power of my own to speak anything? The word that God puts in my mouth, that must I speak."<sup>39</sup>Then Balaam went with Balak, and they came to Kiriath-huzoth.<sup>40</sup>And Balak sacrificed oxen and sheep, and sent for Balaam and for the princes who were with him.<sup>41</sup>And in the morning Balak took Balaam and brought him up to Bamoth-baal, and from there he saw a fraction of the people.
22.overview:
With chapters 22–24 the narrative pulls back to show something Israel could not see: while they camp on the plains of Moab, a spiritual battle is being waged over their destiny. Balak king of Moab hires the renowned pagan seer Balaam to curse them, and God so overrules this hireling that he can speak nothing but blessing over the people God has blessed.

The talking donkey is not comic relief but theology in story form. The seer who claims to see what others cannot is blind to the angel with a drawn sword, while his donkey sees plainly. The God who can open a donkey's mouth can open or shut any mouth he pleases.

Here is the comfort of the chapter: God’s people are surrounded by enemies who plot their ruin, unaware, and God is in control of the plot. “No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed” (Isaiah 54:17). The God who would not let Balaam curse his people works all things, even his enemies’ schemes, for the good of those he has blessed in Christ (Rom 8:28, 31).
22.theology:
Sovereignty over enemies. God so controls the pagan Balaam that he cannot curse the people God has blessed.

The security of the blessed. The blessing of God cannot be reversed by any curse. If God is for us, who can be against us (Rom 8:31)?

God humbles the proud. The seer is blinder than his donkey; all true sight is God's gift.
22.examples:
Then: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, but God forbade the curse, opened a donkey's mouth to rebuke the blind seer, and decreed that only blessing would fall.

Now: You are surrounded by enemies you cannot see, yet God holds their curses in his hand and turns them to blessing. Those whom God has blessed in Christ cannot be cursed. Rest in the sovereign Lord who is for you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel camps on the plains of Moab, and Balak, terrified, sends for the famous diviner Balaam to curse them. The enemy of God’s people, unable to defeat them by the sword, reaches for a curse.
verseByVerse.theology: Balak’s strategy assumes what the pagan world believed: that a skilled diviner could bend a deity’s power to curse. The whole narrative will dismantle that lie: no curse can touch those the LORD has blessed (Rom 8:31, 33).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: unable to conquer Israel in battle, Moab hired a curse against the people God had blessed.

Now: the enemy still resorts to schemes, but no curse prospers against those the LORD has blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Israel set out and camped in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho. And Balak the son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites. And Moab was in great dread of the people, because they were many. Moab was overcome with fear of the people of Israel. And Moab said to the elders of Midian, "This horde will now lick up all that is around us, as the ox licks up the grass of the field." So Balak the son of Zippor, who was king of Moab at that time,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After forty years, this is where they stop: on the flat ground of the east bank, with the river in front of them and Jericho visible across it. Everything from here to the end of the book happens in this one camp, within sight of the land.

And the first thing that happens is that somebody is terrified. Balak had watched Sihon and Og disappear in a single campaign, and his own image is the best line in the chapter: as the ox licks up the grass of the field. Not a battle but a grazing: an animal with its head down, working steadily across a meadow, and when it lifts its head the field is gone.

What Balak cannot see is that God had forbidden Israel to touch him: Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle, for I will not give you any of their land for a possession (Deut. 2:9). The king lies awake planning against a nation ordered to leave him alone. That is what fear does when it will not consult God. It manufactures the disaster it was trying to avoid.

verseByVerse.quote: sent messengers to Balaam the son of Beor at Pethor, which is near the River in the land of the people of Amaw, to call him, saying, "Behold, a people has come out of Egypt. They cover the face of the earth, and they are dwelling opposite me. Come now, curse this people for me, since they are too mighty for me. Perhaps I shall be able to defeat them and drive them from the land, for I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Balak sends for a specialist. The River is the Euphrates, which puts Pethor in upper Mesopotamia, roughly four hundred miles away: the best part of a month’s travel each way, because Balak has heard of a man whose word works. Fear is expensive, and it will pay for anything.

And Balak wants not an army but a curse. He believes what most of the ancient world believed: that words spoken by the right man with the right ritual have force in themselves. What is missing from his reason, he whom you bless is blessed, is God. Balak imagines blessing and cursing as a technique for hire.

That is why the next three chapters are not really about Balaam. They are about what happens when the machinery of pagan religion is aimed at a people the living God has already spoken over. Balak will build twenty-one altars, kill forty-two animals and climb three mountains, and every time he opens his hired mouth, out will come a blessing.
verseByVerse.note: “The River” is the Euphrates (ESV note): Balaam was a well-known diviner from far away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Balaam plainly not to go or curse the people, for they are blessed. But when a grander delegation comes, Balaam, mouthing pious words, clearly wants to go, and God lets him go on a short leash. The diviner’s heart is being exposed.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s first word is unmistakable: Israel “is blessed” (v.12). Balaam’s second inquiry reveals a heart looking for a loophole (cf. 2 Pet 2:15). God’s permission to go (v.20) is not approval but the giving-over of a man to the desire he will not surrender, while God stays sovereign over what Balaam may say.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God had already said no, but Balaam, hungry for the reward, kept asking for a different answer.

Now: when we know God’s will but keep asking, hoping he will bless what our hearts are set on, we walk “the way of Balaam.” Beware the prayer that is really a search for permission.

verseByVerse.quote: So the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian departed with the fees for divination in their hand. And they came to Balaam and gave him Balak's message. And he said to them, "Lodge here tonight, and I will bring back word to you, as the LORD speaks to me." So the princes of Moab stayed with Balaam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fee tells us what Balaam is: not a prophet of Israel but a freelance seer, of the kind archaeologists have since found named in a plaster inscription at Deir Alla, in the Jordan valley not far from this camp: “Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods”, written about 800 BC, centuries after these events. A seer of that name was long remembered across the region, and men of his trade blessed and cursed for money.

Then he says something startling: as the LORD speaks to me. The covenant name, Yahweh. This pagan diviner uses it, and God actually answers him. That unsettles readers, and it should be faced rather than tidied away.

God is not restricted to speaking through good men. He spoke through Caiaphas, who did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied (John 11:49–51), and through Saul after the Spirit had left him (1 Sam. 19:23–24). The gift is not the proof of the man. The New Testament calls Balaam a man who loved gain from wrongdoing (2 Pet. 2:15), but God will use a hireling’s mouth rather than let one word be spoken against his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And God came to Balaam and said, "Who are these men with you?" And Balaam said to God, "Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, has sent to me, saying, 'Behold, a people has come out of Egypt, and it covers the face of the earth. Now come, curse them for me. Perhaps I shall be able to fight against them and drive them out.'" God said to Balaam, "You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is not gathering information. It is like his question in Eden, Where are you?, asked to make a man say out loud what he is doing. Balaam’s summary is accurate as far as it goes, though he leaves out the fee.

Then two sentences, each shutting a door, and the last four words are the foundation of chapters 23 and 24: for they are blessed. Not "they are good," not "they deserve it." God has spent twenty-one chapters recording their grumbling, idolatry and rebellion. They are blessed because he blessed them, and for no other reason on earth.

That is the security of the people of God, stated to an enemy. The blessing does not rest on Israel’s conduct, so Israel’s conduct cannot cancel it. It rests on a promise made to Abraham, and Paul says where that promise finally lands: Christ redeemed us so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles (Galatians 3:14). So Paul can pile up every enemy and ask, almost with a laugh, Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Rom. 8:33). A professional curser sat with a purse of gold in the next room, and heaven had already ruled. He was too late by some six centuries.

verseByVerse.quote: So Balaam rose in the morning and said to the princes of Balak, "Go to your own land, for the LORD has refused to let me go with you." So the princes of Moab rose and went to Balak and said, "Balaam refuses to come with us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At first glance Balaam looks obedient. Then compare. God said: You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed. Balaam reports only: the LORD has refused to let me go with you.

The whole heart of the man is in that edit. He passes on the travel restriction and suppresses the reason. One closes the matter forever; the other is an invitation to try again, and the messengers hear it that way, reporting that Balaam refuses, as though the man himself were the obstacle.

This is how a divided heart talks: nothing technically untrue, and the door left ajar. We all know the answer that is accurate in every particular and dishonest in its whole effect, given so that the thing we still want remains available. When you decline something you would rather have accepted, do you shut the door, or leave it looking as though a better offer might open it?

verseByVerse.quote: Once again Balak sent princes, more in number and more honorable than these. And they came to Balaam and said to him, "Thus says Balak the son of Zippor: 'Let nothing hinder you from coming to me, for I will surely do you great honor, and whatever you say to me I will do. Come, curse this people for me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak reads the gap exactly as it was left for him: a bigger delegation, higher-ranking men, and the offer raised in both currencies, honour and a blank cheque.

He does not try to persuade Balaam that cursing Israel is right. He simply raises the price, because he has correctly judged that this man has one. Nobody sends a better offer to someone who has genuinely said no.

Here the reader should stop being a spectator. There are things we have refused once and would refuse again at that price, and the honest question is what would have to be added to the offer: a little more money, a little more standing, the one person whose good opinion still governs us. Satan keeps the file open. When the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time (Luke 4:13). That verse is also our hope. The One tempted in the wilderness had no price at all, and he refused every offer in our place; his faithfulness is counted to those who have sold out cheaply, and his Spirit now strengthens them to say a cleaner no.

verseByVerse.quote: But Balaam answered and said to the servants of Balak, "Though Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go beyond the command of the LORD my God to do less or more. So you, too, please stay here tonight, that I may know what more the LORD will say to me." And God came to Balaam at night and said to him, "If the men have come to call you, rise, go with them; but only do what I tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam’s reply is magnificent, and it will be quoted against him for ever after: I could not go beyond the command of the LORD my God to do less or more. Theologically it is flawless. In his mouth it is also a lie, not in what it asserts but in what it conceals, because the next sentence is that I may know what more the LORD will say to me.

What more? God had already said it, plainly, twice over. There is nothing more to know. A man who says he cannot be bought and then asks the buyer to wait overnight while he checks again has told you everything about himself. He wants the money and he wants God to authorise it, and he is prepared to keep asking until the answer improves. Peter names the disease with brutal economy: he loved gain from wrongdoing (2 Pet. 2:15). The lips are orthodox; the appetite is for hire.

So God gives him what he keeps asking for: rise, go with them; but only do what I tell you. Has God changed his mind? He has not. This is permission, and permission is not approval. Israel demanded a king until God gave them one (1 Sam. 8:7–9); of an earlier generation the psalm says, he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Ps. 106:15). There is a stage at which the most frightening thing God can do to a man who will not stop asking is to say yes. Verse 22 will tell us what God thought of the trip.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–35 — The Donkey and the Angel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road the angel of the LORD stands in the way with a drawn sword, unseen by the prophet but seen by his donkey. Three times she swerves to save him and three times he beats her, until God opens her mouth, and then his eyes. The famous seer is blinder than his beast.
verseByVerse.theology: The talking donkey is God’s gentle mockery of a “seer” who cannot see (vv.23-31). If God can make a donkey speak, he can certainly put his words in Balaam’s mouth. God “catches the wise in their craftiness” (1 Corinthians 3:19) and can use the lowliest instrument to reveal his will.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the renowned seer, riding blindly toward danger, was saved and rebuked by the beast he despised.

Now: God still humbles our pride with unlikely instruments (1 Cor 1:27). Beware being so sure of your own sight that a donkey sees more than you.

verseByVerse.quote: So Balaam rose in the morning and saddled his donkey and went with the princes of Moab. But God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the LORD took his stand in the way as his adversary. Now he was riding on the donkey, and his two servants were with him. And the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road, with a drawn sword in his hand. And the donkey turned aside out of the road and went into the field. And Balaam struck the donkey, to turn her into the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two sentences sit side by side without explanation, and the reader is meant to feel the jolt. He had permission. He went. God was angry. Permission had never been the same thing as pleasure, and Balaam knew it; he had spent two nights trying to convert one into the other.

The Hebrew word for adversary here is satan, in its ordinary sense: one who stands in the road to oppose. Heaven has come out onto the highway with a drawn sword to stop a man going where heaven has just said he may go. That is not a contradiction. It is an obstacle in the path of a man God is determined to use, a kindness that looks, from the saddle, exactly like an obstruction.

And the joke that runs through the chapter begins. The donkey saw. A seer whose livelihood rests on perceiving what others cannot is sitting on the only creature in the story with functioning eyes, and he beats her for having them.

Who is the angel of the LORD? He speaks as God, speak only the word that I tell you (v. 35), and many Reformed interpreters think he is the Son before his incarnation, as in other appearances; others see a created angel bearing God’s name and authority.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel of the LORD stood in a narrow path between the vineyards, with a wall on either side. And when the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she pushed against the wall and pressed Balaam's foot against the wall. So he struck her again. Then the angel of the LORD went ahead and stood in a narrow place, where there was no way to turn either to the right or to the left. When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she lay down under Balaam. And Balaam's anger was kindled, and he struck the donkey with his staff.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The road narrows three times: open country, where the donkey can swing into a field; a path between vineyard walls, where she crushes his foot against the stone; then a place with no way to turn, where she simply lies down.

Read it as the diagram of a man going the wrong way. God does not usually stop us with a wall at the first step. He allows a wide place with a small inconvenience, then a tighter place with a real cost, then no room at all, so that the man might look up before the sword. Balaam does not look up. He escalates: a slap, a second blow, and finally the staff.

Three times an animal saved his life, and three times he beat her for it. A man who has decided where he is going cannot tell an obstacle from a rescue, so he attacks whatever slows him down, which is why a man being warned off a course so often turns on the person warning him. Before you next lose your temper with an interruption, ask whether you know what is standing in the road ahead of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey, and she said to Balaam, "What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?" And Balaam said to the donkey, "Because you have made a fool of me. I wish I had a sword in my hand, for then I would kill you." And the donkey said to Balaam, "Am I not your donkey, on which you have ridden all your life long to this day? Is it my habit to treat you this way?" And he said, "No."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Readers sometimes handle this verse apologetically, so let us not. The text says God did it, and the New Testament treats it as history: a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet’s madness (2 Pet. 2:16). The God who made throats and language was not stretched by this. And the miracle draws the eye, which is the point: everything else is a man behaving as he has behaved all along.

What she says is quietly devastating. She accuses him of nothing; she appeals to their whole shared life, years of faithful service offered as evidence. And Balaam, who has not noticed he is arguing with a donkey, must answer the one word that dismantles his case: No.

His own words are the most revealing he speaks in three chapters: you have made a fool of me. Not "you have hurt me" but "you have humiliated me," in front of the princes he is trying to impress. And he wishes for a sword, with no idea that there is one a few feet in front of his face, held by somebody who has been considering using it on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, with his drawn sword in his hand. And he bowed down and fell on his face. And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why have you struck your donkey these three times? Behold, I have come out to oppose you because your way is perverse before me. The donkey saw me and turned aside before me these three times. If she had not turned aside from me, surely just now I would have killed you and let her live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had been three paces from that sword for the whole argument. It did not appear when his eyes were opened; it was there all along, and he was riding straight at it, shouting at his donkey.

That is how things stand with a man going his own way who thinks nothing much is happening. Heaven is not idle while we are busy; it is standing in the road. The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good (Prov. 15:3). Balaam’s opened eyes changed nothing about the situation and everything about the man, which is what every genuine awakening does.
