Then the angel’s first concern is a detail we might skip: Why have you struck your donkey these three times? The Lord of hosts, sword drawn, takes time to defend a beaten animal, and tells her owner she was the one worth sparing. God notices what is done to creatures with no voice.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Balaam said to the angel of the LORD, "I have sinned, for I did not know that you stood in the road against me. Now therefore, if it is evil in your sight, I will turn back." And the angel of the LORD said to Balaam, "Go with the men, but speak only the word that I tell you." So Balaam went on with the princes of Balak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three words in, it sounds like repentance. Read the whole sentence and it falls apart in the hand.

First, the excuse is smuggled into the confession: I have sinned, for I did not know. If not knowing is the reason, the blame belongs elsewhere, with the angel for being invisible or the donkey for being unclear. Second, and worse, the little word if. He has just been told by an armed angel that his way is perverse; there is no "if" left. A man who wanted to turn back would have turned the donkey round. It is Pharaoh’s repentance and Saul’s: sorrow for the sword in the road, not for the road. Paul draws the line exactly: godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Cor. 7:10). The door of godly grief was open to Balaam as it is to us, and the mercy behind it does not ask for excuses, only for the truth.

The angel’s reply is chilling in its brevity: Go with the men, but speak only the word that I tell you. He is sent on, muzzled, a hired mouth with a sword behind it, travelling all the way to Moab to bless the people he was paid to curse. God has harnessed the man to his purposes, which is a far more terrifying thing to happen to anybody.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Balaam arrives and warns Balak at once that he can speak only what God puts in his mouth. Balak takes him to a high place over Israel, expecting curses. He will get blessings instead.
verseByVerse.theology: Balaam’s words at verse 38 set the theme of all that follows: God, not the diviner, controls the outcome. Balak’s careful ritual preparations (v.41) are about to be overturned, proving that no human scheme can reverse the blessing of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the king who paid for curses was warned, before a word was spoken, that only God’s word would come out of the prophet’s mouth.

Now: “No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD” (Proverbs 21:30). God’s purposes for his people cannot be reversed.

verseByVerse.quote: When Balak heard that Balaam had come, he went out to meet him at the city of Moab, on the border formed by the Arnon, at the extremity of the border. And Balak said to Balaam, "Did I not send to you to call you? Why did you not come to me? Am I not able to honor you?" Balaam said to Balak, "Behold, I have come to you! Have I now any power of my own to speak anything? The word that God puts in my mouth, that must I speak." Then Balaam went with Balak, and they came to Kiriath-huzoth. And Balak sacrificed oxen and sheep, and sent for Balaam and for the princes who were with him. And in the morning Balak took Balaam and brought him up to Bamoth-baal, and from there he saw a fraction of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak rides out to the border to meet him, and his greeting is all wounded vanity: Am I not able to honor you? He has staked his kingdom on a superstition and his pride on a purchase, and he is offended that the merchandise was slow.

Balaam answers with the same flawless orthodoxy, every syllable true. Then he accepts the hospitality and lets Balak walk him up to Bamoth-baal, the high places of Baal, to look at the people he has just said he cannot curse. A man can hold a sound doctrine of God in his mouth and be led up a pagan mountain by the elbow.

The last clause is exquisite: he saw a fraction of the people. From the highest ground Moab has, the enemies of Israel can take in only a corner of the camp. Balak has spent a fortune and climbed a mountain, and cannot even get the whole nation into his field of view, let alone into his curse. So the chapter closes with a king and a hired seer on a pagan height at dawn, plotting against a people asleep in their tents, while over their heads the verdict has already been given: they are blessed. Nobody on any mountain in the world can unsay it.

23.title: Balaam's First and Second Oracles: God Is Not Man, That He Should Lie
23.text: <sup>1</sup>And Balaam said to Balak, "Build for me here seven altars, and prepare for me here seven bulls and seven rams."<sup>2</sup>Balak did as Balaam had said. And Balak and Balaam offered on each altar a bull and a ram.<sup>3</sup>And Balaam said to Balak, "Stand beside your burnt offering, and I will go. Perhaps the LORD will come to meet me, and whatever he shows me I will tell you." And he went to a bare height,<sup>4</sup>and God met Balaam. And Balaam said to him, "I have arranged the seven altars and I have offered on each altar a bull and a ram."<sup>5</sup>And the LORD put a word in Balaam's mouth and said, "Return to Balak, and thus you shall speak."<sup>6</sup>And he returned to him, and behold, he and all the princes of Moab were standing beside his burnt offering.<sup>7</sup>And Balaam took up his discourse and said, "From Aram Balak has brought me, the king of Moab from the eastern mountains: 'Come, curse Jacob for me, and come, denounce Israel!'<sup>8</sup>How can I curse whom God has not cursed? How can I denounce whom the LORD has not denounced?<sup>9</sup>For from the top of the crags I see him, from the hills I behold him; behold, a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations!<sup>10</sup>Who can count the dust of Jacob or number the fourth part of Israel? Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!"<sup>11</sup>And Balak said to Balaam, "What have you done to me? I took you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have done nothing but bless them."<sup>12</sup>And he answered and said, "Must I not take care to speak what the LORD puts in my mouth?"<sup>13</sup>And Balak said to him, "Please come with me to another place, from which you may see them. You shall see only a fraction of them and shall not see them all. Then curse them for me from there."<sup>14</sup>And he took him to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah, and built seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.<sup>15</sup>Balaam said to Balak, "Stand here beside your burnt offering, while I meet the LORD over there."<sup>16</sup>And the LORD met Balaam and put a word in his mouth and said, "Return to Balak, and thus shall you speak."<sup>17</sup>And he came to him, and behold, he was standing beside his burnt offering, and the princes of Moab with him. And Balak said to him, "What has the LORD spoken?"<sup>18</sup>And Balaam took up his discourse and said, "Rise, Balak, and hear; give ear to me, O son of Zippor:<sup>19</sup>God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it?<sup>20</sup>Behold, I received a command to bless: he has blessed, and I cannot revoke it.<sup>21</sup>He has not beheld misfortune in Jacob, nor has he seen trouble in Israel. The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of a king is among them.<sup>22</sup>God brings them out of Egypt and is for them like the horns of the wild ox.<sup>23</sup>For there is no enchantment against Jacob, no divination against Israel; now it shall be said of Jacob and Israel, 'What has God wrought!'<sup>24</sup>Behold, a people! As a lioness it rises up and as a lion it lifts itself; it does not lie down until it has devoured the prey and drunk the blood of the slain."<sup>25</sup>And Balak said to Balaam, "Do not curse them at all, and do not bless them at all."<sup>26</sup>But Balaam answered Balak, "Did I not tell you, 'All that the LORD says, that I must do'?"<sup>27</sup>And Balak said to Balaam, "Come now, I will take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God that you may curse them for me from there."<sup>28</sup>So Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the desert.<sup>29</sup>And Balaam said to Balak, "Build for me here seven altars and prepare for me here seven bulls and seven rams."<sup>30</sup>And Balak did as Balaam had said, and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.
23.overview:
Balak builds altars and offers sacrifices again and again, trying to make the spiritual machinery produce a curse. But every time Balaam opens his mouth, blessing pours out. The pagan prophet, against his own financial interest and his employer's fury, can only say what God puts in his mouth.

The first oracle marvels at a people set apart, innumerable as the dust: the Abrahamic promise confirmed by an enemy's mouth. The second rises to the bedrock truth of verse 19: “God is not man, that he should lie.” It is one of Scripture's great statements of God's unchanging faithfulness (what theologians call his immutability). The blessing he has spoken over his people cannot be revoked, because the God who spoke it cannot lie.

Then verse 21: God “has not beheld misfortune in Jacob,” words older versions render as iniquity. On that reading, how can God say this of a people who have grumbled and rebelled? Many have found the answer in what theologians call imputation, God reckoning to his people a standing not theirs by nature, looking on them according to his covenant grace. If so, here faintly is justification. The full answer comes in Christ, in whom there is no condemnation (Rom 8:1), for God laid our sin on his Son and clothes us in his righteousness.
23.theology:
God's immutability and faithfulness. God is not man, that he should lie or change his mind. His blessing cannot be revoked.

Imputed blamelessness. On the older reading of 23:21, God beholds no iniquity in Jacob, not because they are sinless, but because of covenant grace, anticipating justification in Christ.

The futility of opposition. Every altar and high place fails to produce a curse. The enemies of God's people exhaust themselves against an unchangeable decree.
23.examples:
Then: Balak built altars and demanded curses, but God turned every oracle into blessing.

Now: The God who cannot lie has spoken his blessing over you in Christ, and it cannot be revoked. Rest in promises that are Yes and Amen in Jesus, sealed by a God who does not change.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Balaam performs the rituals, and God puts words in his mouth, but not the words Balak paid for. Looking over Israel, Balaam blesses them, and Balak is horrified.
verseByVerse.theology: The first oracle states the theme: “How can I curse whom God has not cursed?” (v.8). Israel’s security rests not in its own merit but in God’s electing choice. What God has blessed stands blessed, and no purchased curse can reach it (cf. Rom 8:33-34).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the hired curse came out as blessing.

Now: no accusation, curse or scheme can stand against those God has set apart as his own, for it is God who justifies.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balaam said to Balak, "Build for me here seven altars, and prepare for me here seven bulls and seven rams." Balak did as Balaam had said. And Balak and Balaam offered on each altar a bull and a ram. And Balaam said to Balak, "Stand beside your burnt offering, and I will go. Perhaps the LORD will come to meet me, and whatever he shows me I will tell you." And he went to a bare height,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam is setting up his equipment. Seven altars with a bull and a ram on each is the heaviest ritual apparatus he knows, and he will do it on three summits: twenty-one altars, forty-two animals, a fortune in livestock.

In Balaam’s world the gods were responsive to correct procedure. Get the numbers, the species, the height and the direction of view right, and the power could be tapped and pointed. It is religion as engineering, which is why Balak is paying by the mountain.

And one word gives the enterprise away: Perhaps the LORD will come to meet me. After all that expenditure, the man is not sure anyone is there. Every religion of technique ends in that word, because a god who can be operated cannot be trusted; you never know whether it worked. The believer does not build an altar and hope. He comes to a Father who has already said Come to me, and the whole apparatus of getting God’s attention was finished at a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: and God met Balaam. And Balaam said to him, "I have arranged the seven altars and I have offered on each altar a bull and a ram." And the LORD put a word in Balaam's mouth and said, "Return to Balak, and thus you shall speak." And he returned to him, and behold, he and all the princes of Moab were standing beside his burnt offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God met Balaam, not because the altars worked, but because he had business of his own with this man and would have come to an empty hillside had he chosen.

What Balaam says is quietly damning. No worship, not even a request. He files his return: here is what I built, it is all correct, now let us proceed to the transaction. It is the Pharisee in the temple thanking God for his own record (Luke 18:11–12), the oldest religious instinct there is. The honest question is whether the sentence underneath your prayers is ever "Look what I have done" rather than God, be merciful to me, a sinner! (Luke 18:13), the prayer Jesus says went home heard.

God does not answer the invoice: the LORD put a word in Balaam’s mouth. The same words describe true prophecy (Deut. 18:18), and here they are deliberately physical. He is not given a vision to interpret. A word is placed in him, and he will carry it down the hill and say it whether he likes it or not. Balak has hired a man. God has requisitioned a mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balaam took up his discourse and said, "From Aram Balak has brought me, the king of Moab from the eastern mountains: 'Come, curse Jacob for me, and come, denounce Israel!' How can I curse whom God has not cursed? How can I denounce whom the LORD has not denounced?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oracle opens by reading the contract into the record in front of the client: the distance, the commission, Come, curse Jacob for me.

Then, instead of the curse, two questions: How can I curse whom God has not cursed? Not "I will not" but How can I: not a moral refusal but a report of impossibility, like a man saying he cannot lift a mountain.

Everything the New Testament says about a Christian’s security is in the shape of those questions. Paul asks them almost word for word in a courtroom: Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died (Rom. 8:33–34). Somebody has paid a great deal to accuse. But the verdict has already been entered by the only court there is. A curse has to come from somewhere, and there is nowhere left for this one to come from.

verseByVerse.quote: For from the top of the crags I see him, from the hills I behold him; behold, a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations! Who can count the dust of Jacob or number the fourth part of Israel? Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking down at a camp laid out in a square around a tent, Balaam is struck that they do not blend in. Israel was not distinct because she was better; she was distinct because God had put his name on her. That distinctness continues, you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession (1 Pet. 2:9), though it has never meant retreat from the world. Israel dwelt alone in full view of the nations, so that they would look, and a hired pagan on a hilltop is doing just that.

Then the line that ought to stop every reader: Let me die the death of the upright.

He says it on a pagan height, beside smoking altars, in the pay of a king who wants this people destroyed. He wants their funeral without their life, to end up where the people of God end up having spent his career going somewhere else. It is the most honest thing he ever says and the most useless, because a man does not get to choose his last hour separately from the years before it. Balaam was killed with the sword among the Midianites, the enemies of the people he had just blessed (Num. 31:8): the opposite of what he asked for, chosen one small compromise at a time. Wanting a Christian death is not the same as wanting Christ. But Christ is offered freely to anyone who does want him, and the death of the upright belongs to all who come.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak said to Balaam, "What have you done to me? I took you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have done nothing but bless them." And he answered and said, "Must I not take care to speak what the LORD puts in my mouth?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What have you done to me? I took you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have done nothing but bless them. Balak has just watched his four-hundred-mile investment stand on a mountain and pronounce a benediction over the people it was hired to destroy, and the cry is one of pure commercial outrage. Not "what is God doing?" but What have you done to me? Even here, at the moment he brushes against the will of the Almighty, the king can only see a supplier who has failed to deliver.

Balaam’s reply is technically perfect and spiritually empty. Yes, he must speak what the LORD puts in his mouth, and having said so he will at once agree to try again from a different hill. Orthodoxy of speech is not loyalty of heart; a man can be perfectly sound and thoroughly for sale.

Underneath the comedy, hold on to the arithmetic. Every mouth opened against the people of God in these chapters is compelled to bless them. No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed, and you shall refute every tongue that rises against you in judgment (Isa. 54:17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Balak tries a new vantage point, hoping a different view will yield a curse. But the second oracle is stronger still: God does not lie or change his mind, and Balaam cannot reverse his blessing.
verseByVerse.theology: Numbers 23:19 is a summit of biblical theology: God does not lie or change his mind as men do (cf. 1 Sam 15:29; Mal 3:6; Titus 1:2). The oracle grounds Israel’s security in that faithfulness: “The LORD their God is with them” (v.21). Because God cannot lie, his promises to his people are unbreakable (Heb 6:17-18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Balak learned that a God who cannot lie will not un-bless what he has blessed.

Now: our hope rests on the same unchanging God. His promises do not expire.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak said to him, "Please come with me to another place, from which you may see them. You shall see only a fraction of them and shall not see them all. Then curse them for me from there." And he took him to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah, and built seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each altar. Balaam said to Balak, "Stand here beside your burnt offering, while I meet the LORD over there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak’s next idea is superstition dressed as strategy. He has diagnosed the problem as a sightline: perhaps a smaller view will produce a smaller blessing. He is trying to change God’s verdict by changing the angle, and the whole ruinous ritual is repeated on the top of Pisgah, on the assumption that the failure was technical.

People do this in church. When God has plainly said no, the temptation is not usually to defy him outright but to seek a different vantage point, another counsellor, another passage, another congregation, until the view is narrow enough that the answer we wanted looks defensible. Balak was not a stupid man. He simply could not accept that the obstacle was not the arrangement but the Almighty.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD met Balaam and put a word in his mouth and said, "Return to Balak, and thus shall you speak." And he came to him, and behold, he was standing beside his burnt offering, and the princes of Moab with him. And Balak said to him, "What has the LORD spoken?" And Balaam took up his discourse and said, "Rise, Balak, and hear; give ear to me, O son of Zippor: God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king of Moab is made to stand up beside his own burnt offering and be lectured, and what follows is one of the towering statements about God in the Old Testament, delivered by a man who has been trying to get round it for three days.

Two things are denied, and they are the two things men do constantly: we say what is not so, and we say what we mean and then go back on it. God does neither. He is God, who never lies (Titus 1:2), and he confirmed his promise with an oath so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement (Heb. 6:18).

A fair question arises: does Scripture not also say that God relented, over Nineveh, or after Moses interceded at Sinai (Exod. 32:14; Jonah 3:10)? It does, and those passages describe something different. They speak of God’s settled and unchanging character meeting a changed human situation: he had always been the God who spares the repentant, and Nineveh repented. What this verse denies is that God is fickle, that his word can be renegotiated, or that his promise might quietly lapse. And the living proof is standing on the mountain: Balaam has asked twice for a different answer, at enormous cost, and God has not moved an inch.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I received a command to bless: he has blessed, and I cannot revoke it. He has not beheld misfortune in Jacob, nor has he seen trouble in Israel. The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of a king is among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing is not Balaam’s to give, and so not his to withdraw. Nobody can revoke it, because nobody issued it but God, and the man who most wishes otherwise is the one who says so.

Then verse 21, the hardest sentence in the chapter. The line can be read as disaster and hardship, as the ESV takes it, or as iniquity and perverseness, as the King James and other older versions read it. Read the first way, no calamity can overtake this people because the LORD their God is with them. Read the second, God does not look upon iniquity in his covenant people. Godly readers have taken it both ways, and the sentence is genuinely open.

On either reading the verse points forward. God had spent twenty-two chapters recording what was wrong with this nation. He knew. Yet to an outsider hired to find a fault he could exploit, the answer is that there is nothing there to be used. Behind it stands what Paul makes explicit: Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin (Rom. 4:7–8). That is not because sin does not matter. It is because God had already determined what he would do about it, on a hill of his own choosing, fourteen centuries later.

verseByVerse.quote: God brings them out of Egypt and is for them like the horns of the wild ox. For there is no enchantment against Jacob, no divination against Israel; now it shall be said of Jacob and Israel, 'What has God wrought!' Behold, a people! As a lioness it rises up and as a lion it lifts itself; it does not lie down until it has devoured the prey and drunk the blood of the slain."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wild ox, the aurochs, the great untamed bull nobody yoked, is a picture not of Israel but of God for Israel. Their power is on loan, and the loan is the point.

Then the flat demolition of Balak’s business plan: there is no enchantment against Jacob. The professional diviner announces from his own altars that divination does not work on these people. And so the nations say, not "what has Israel achieved," but What has God wrought!, a line so charged that it was the first message Samuel Morse sent by telegraph in 1844.

The last image is the fiercest. Balak had described Israel as an ox grazing (22:4); God describes them as a lion getting up. It echoes Jacob’s blessing of Judah, a lion’s cub (Genesis 49:9), a line that ends in the last book of the Bible: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered (Rev. 5:5). The strength the nations feared in the camp was never really the camp’s. It was the strength of the One who would one day be born inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak said to Balaam, "Do not curse them at all, and do not bless them at all." But Balaam answered Balak, "Did I not tell you, 'All that the LORD says, that I must do'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having failed to purchase a curse, Balak tries to purchase silence, and cannot get that either.

There is genuine comedy here, and Scripture means us to see it: a king with an army and a treasury trying to switch off the word of God like a man slapping a radio, while the blessings keep coming. He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision (Ps. 2:4).

Balaam’s answer is once again perfectly correct and once again spoken by a man still on the payroll and willing to walk up one more hill. He is three for three on telling Balak the truth and three for three on staying for the fee.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–30 — Preparing for a Third Attempt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Balak takes Balaam to yet another height, Peor, and builds seven more altars, hoping this time the curse will come. His stubbornness against God is almost pitiable, and futile.
verseByVerse.theology: Balak keeps changing locations and rebuilding altars, as if the problem were the setting rather than the sovereign God: stubborn opposition that will not learn and cannot win (Prov 21:30).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twice refused, Balak tried a third hilltop and seven more altars.

Now: fighting against God’s settled purpose only wastes the fighter. A God who does not change his mind about blessing us can be trusted when he says no; “whoever knows the right thing to do” (James 4:17) need not keep looking for a hill from which it might turn out differently.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak said to Balaam, "Come now, I will take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God that you may curse them for me from there." So Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the desert. And Balaam said to Balak, "Build for me here seven altars and prepare for me here seven bulls and seven rams." And Balak did as Balaam had said, and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Astonishingly, they go again, and Perhaps returns, the word Balaam used on the first mountain. Two men who have watched God override them twice are still trying the same door, and their whole theology is in that adverb.

And the place should make the reader go cold: Peor. In two chapters Israel will be camped below this hill, drawn into the sacrifices of Baal of Peor, and twenty-four thousand will die of a plague (25:3, 9). Everything Balak wanted will happen, here, with Balaam’s fingerprints on it, because he will go home by way of one last piece of advice about how to get at a nation you cannot curse (31:16; Rev. 2:14).

So the altars go up a third time on the one hill where the enemy will eventually get what he came for. Balak is standing on the answer to his problem and looking the wrong way, waiting for a curse out of the sky, while the thing that will actually work is in the valley under his feet.

The arrangement of these chapters is deliberate: three chapters of God refusing, four times over, to let a word be spoken against his people, and one chapter of what happens next. Whatever Israel had to fear, it was never Balaam.

24.title: Balaam's Final Oracles: A Star Shall Come Out of Jacob
24.text: <sup>1</sup>When Balaam saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens, but set his face toward the wilderness.<sup>2</sup>And Balaam lifted up his eyes and saw Israel camping tribe by tribe. And the Spirit of God came upon him,<sup>3</sup>and he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened,<sup>4</sup>the oracle of him who hears the words of God, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered:<sup>5</sup>How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel!<sup>6</sup>Like palm groves that stretch afar, like gardens beside a river, like aloes that the LORD has planted, like cedar trees beside the waters.<sup>7</sup>Water shall flow from his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters; his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted.<sup>8</sup>God brings him out of Egypt and is for him like the horns of the wild ox; he shall eat up the nations, his adversaries, and shall break their bones in pieces and pierce them through with his arrows.<sup>9</sup>He crouched, he lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him up? Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you."<sup>10</sup>And Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together. And Balak said to Balaam, "I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times.<sup>11</sup>Therefore now flee to your own place. I said, 'I will certainly honor you,' but the LORD has held you back from honor."<sup>12</sup>And Balaam said to Balak, "Did I not tell your messengers whom you sent to me,<sup>13</sup>'If Balak should give me his house full of silver and gold, I would not be able to go beyond the word of the LORD, to do either good or bad of my own will. What the LORD speaks, that will I speak'?<sup>14</sup>And now, behold, I am going to my people. Come, I will let you know what this people will do to your people in the latter days."<sup>15</sup>And he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened,<sup>16</sup>the oracle of him who hears the words of God, and knows the knowledge of the Most High, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered:<sup>17</sup>I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the forehead of Moab and break down all the sons of Sheth.<sup>18</sup>Edom shall be dispossessed; Seir also, his enemies, shall be dispossessed. Israel is doing valiantly.<sup>19</sup>And one from Jacob shall exercise dominion and destroy the survivors of cities!"<sup>20</sup>Then he looked on Amalek and took up his discourse and said, "Amalek was the first among the nations, but its end is utter destruction."<sup>21</sup>And he looked on the Kenite, and took up his discourse and said, "Enduring is your dwelling place, and your nest is set in the rock.<sup>22</sup>Nevertheless, Kain shall be burned when Asshur takes you away captive."<sup>23</sup>And he took up his discourse and said, "Alas, who shall live when God does this?<sup>24</sup>But ships shall come from Kittim and shall afflict Asshur and Eber; and he too shall come to utter destruction."<sup>25</sup>Then Balaam rose and went back to his place. And Balak also went his way.
24.overview:
The Balaam saga reaches its climax. Balaam no longer resorts to omens; the Spirit of God comes upon him, and the third oracle pours out a vision of Israel's beauty, “How lovely are your tents, O Jacob” (v. 5), words still sung at the door of synagogues. The hireling who came to curse stands transfixed by the loveliness of the people of God.

The fourth oracle soars into outright Messianic prophecy: “a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel” (v. 17). Balaam sees, across the centuries, a King who will arise from Israel and triumph over her enemies, and many have heard its echo when the magi followed a star to Bethlehem (Matt 2).

The wonder is who speaks it: a pagan, mercenary seer, overruled by the Spirit of God. The God who would not let Balaam curse his people compelled him to prophesy the King who would save them. The security of God's people rests on the coming of God's King, who now reigns as “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Revelation 19:16).
24.theology:
The Star out of Jacob. Balaam prophesies a coming royal King from Israel, fulfilled in Christ, the Star and Scepter.

God's sovereign freedom. God overrules even a pagan, mercenary prophet to proclaim the coming Messiah.

The King secures his people. The security of God's people rests on the coming of God's King, who reigns over every hostile nation.
24.examples:
Then: The Spirit overcame Balaam, who beheld the loveliness of Israel and prophesied a Star out of Jacob.

Now: The Star has risen, and the King foretold by a pagan seer reigns. Your security rests not in yourself but in Christ the Scepter of Israel, before whom every enemy will bow and every curse be turned to blessing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Balaam no longer resorts to omens; the Spirit of God comes upon him, and he blesses Israel with a vision of beauty and abundance, ending with the words of the Abrahamic promise.
verseByVerse.theology: The third oracle echoes the Abrahamic covenant almost verbatim (v.9; cf. Gen 12:3; 27:29), God confirming through a pagan’s mouth the promise he swore to the patriarchs, and portraying Israel’s flourishing as his own planting (v.6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a diviner hired to curse Israel pronounced over them the blessing of Abraham.

Now: the promise still stands over God’s people in Christ, the true offspring of Abraham (Gal 3:16, 29), and no curse can undo it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Balaam saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens, but set his face toward the wilderness. And Balaam lifted up his eyes and saw Israel camping tribe by tribe. And the Spirit of God came upon him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something has finally broken through. Three times he has built the altars, and the answer has been the same every time. He gives up the apparatus and simply turns and looks at the camp.

And then one of the strangest sentences in the Old Testament: the Spirit of God came upon him. The Spirit of God, on a man for hire.

That needs explaining. In the Old Testament the Spirit characteristically comes upon a man to equip him for a task, Samson for strength, Bezalel for craftsmanship, Saul for prophecy after God had rejected him (1 Sam. 19:23–24), and that is not the same thing as a new heart. It can be given to a man who is not saved. What Christians are promised is better: not the Spirit descending on them for a job, but taking up residence in them for ever, the Spirit of God dwells in you (Rom. 8:9), will be in you (John 14:17). Balaam was used. He was never indwelt, and this chapter shows the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: and he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened, the oracle of him who hears the words of God, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oracle opens with a professional’s letterhead, repeated at verse 15, and it drips with irony. The man whose eye is opened is the man who two chapters ago could not see an armed angel in front of him while his donkey could. Whatever sight he now has is not native to him; God opened his eyes then and is opening them now.

Falling down with his eyes uncovered pictures a man flat on the ground and wide awake: not in a trance, not working himself into anything, but prostrate, conscious, and being spoken through. The apparatus of pagan religion has been stripped away until there is nothing left but a man on his face and a word coming out of him that he did not choose and cannot stop.

verseByVerse.quote: How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel! Like palm groves that stretch afar, like gardens beside a river, like aloes that the LORD has planted, like cedar trees beside the waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of all the sentences in Numbers, this is the one the Jewish people have loved most; it opens the morning liturgy, and for centuries a Jew entering the synagogue has begun with these words. They were composed by a pagan diviner in the pay of a man who wanted the whole camp dead.

Notice what the pictures have in common: every one is wet. Palm groves, a river, planted aloes, cedars by the water, and Balaam is looking down at a tent city in a desert where the nation has spent forty years arguing about the next drink. He is describing not what is in front of his eyes but what God sees, and intends to make of them.

The middle image gives the reason: aloes that the LORD has planted. Not a people who turned out well, but planted by hand, in ground the gardener chose. Israel’s loveliness is entirely derivative, and so is the church’s: You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit (John 15:16). What the enemy saw that morning was God’s gardening, seen from a distance, and it was beautiful.

verseByVerse.quote: Water shall flow from his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters; his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted. God brings him out of Egypt and is for him like the horns of the wild ox; he shall eat up the nations, his adversaries, and shall break their bones in pieces and pierce them through with his arrows. He crouched, he lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him up? Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oracle runs past anything Balaam could have known. His king: Israel will have no king for nearly four centuries and is at this moment a refugee column with a tent for a capital. Agag appears to be the royal title of the Amalekites, and the coming king will overtop him, as happened when Saul and then David broke Amalek (1 Sam. 15). The Septuagint, the early Greek translation of the Old Testament, reads this verse differently: a man will come from his seed and rule many nations, with Gog in place of Agag. It shows that Jews before Christ already heard a coming ruler here.

Then the strength images intensify. The lion here is not on the hunt but lying down, which is more frightening, because it means the lion is not worried. Israel is asleep in the valley. Nobody is going to wake her.

Last comes the most delicious sentence in the Balaam narrative: Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you. That is God’s promise to Abraham, I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse (Gen. 12:3), and Balak has paid a fortune to have it reversed. Instead he hears it recited over him by his own employee at his own expense. The curse he purchased has turned in the air and come down on the man who bought it. Nobody outbids God for the last word about his people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Balak explodes and drives Balaam away unpaid. But before he goes, Balaam warns that he has one more thing to say: what Israel will do to Moab “in the latter days.”
verseByVerse.theology: Balak can withhold Balaam’s fee but cannot alter God’s decree. Balaam’s insistence that he can speak only God’s word (vv.12-13), though self-serving, is true, and sets up a word about “the latter days” (v.14) that reaches far beyond Moab to the coming King.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Balak sent the prophet home in a fury, raging against a verdict he could not change.

Now: those who set themselves against God’s purposes for his people may rage, but they cannot prevail.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together. And Balak said to Balaam, "I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times. Therefore now flee to your own place. I said, 'I will certainly honor you,' but the LORD has held you back from honor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Striking the hands together is a gesture of furious contempt, a slow, savage clap, and it is all Balak has left. The contract is torn up, and Balaam is dismissed unpaid and told to run.

Then Balak says one true thing, as an accusation: the LORD has held you back from honor. He is right. The silver and the standing at a royal court were within reach, and God stood in the road again, as on the road from Pethor.

So a man who has just delivered two of the most magnificent oracles in the Old Testament has lost everything he came for, and Peter tells us he loved gain from wrongdoing (2 Pet. 2:15). That is what makes what happens next so terrible. Before he leaves the district he will find another way to earn the money, one that does not need God’s permission, and it will kill twenty-four thousand Israelites and eventually him (31:8, 16). A man who wants the wages badly enough will find a route to them his conscience can sign. The New Testament calls it the way of Balaam.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balaam said to Balak, "Did I not tell your messengers whom you sent to me, 'If Balak should give me his house full of silver and gold, I would not be able to go beyond the word of the LORD, to do either good or bad of my own will. What the LORD speaks, that will I speak'? And now, behold, I am going to my people. Come, I will let you know what this people will do to your people in the latter days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam defends himself by quoting himself, and once again every word is impeccable. He has said it three times in three chapters, it is true three times, and it has never once described his heart. There is such a thing as a man whose doctrine is his alibi.

I am going to my people. He does not go; seven chapters later the sword finds him still among the Midianites (31:8). Men announce their departure from a compromising situation far more often than they leave it.

Then the greatest thing he ever says, given unpaid: he owes Balak nothing now, and gives the oracle anyway, because it is not his to withhold. The crowning prophecy of the Pentateuch outside Genesis is delivered by a dismissed hireling to a furious pagan king, for no fee at all. God had said he would put a word in this man’s mouth, and it came out whether anyone was paying or not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–25 — The Fourth Oracle: A Star out of Jacob
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greatest oracle comes last: Balaam sees, far off, a coming ruler, a star and a scepter out of Jacob who will crush his enemies and reign. It points beyond David to the Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology: The “star... out of Jacob” and “scepter... out of Israel” (v.17) is a messianic prophecy, fulfilled in part in David but pointing ultimately to Christ. Ancient Jewish interpretation read it messianically, and many see its echo in the star that brought the Magi to “he who has been born king of the Jews” (Matthew 2:2). This clearest messianic hope in the Pentateuch comes through a hostile prophet.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: from a distant hilltop a pagan seer glimpsed a rising King, centuries before he came.

Now: the King Balaam saw from afar we know by name: Jesus, the bright morning star, reigning forever.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened, the oracle of him who hears the words of God, and knows the knowledge of the Most High, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered: I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the forehead of Moab and break down all the sons of Sheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take the near horizon first. Four centuries later David subdued Moab and garrisoned Edom (2 Sam. 8:2, 14), the two nations named here, and any honest reading has David in view. But the oracle will not sit down inside David. Not now… not near is a strange way to describe a king four hundred years off in a book dating events to the month, and verse 19 widens the horizon to a dominion with no stated end. Something larger is coming through a smaller frame.

A scepter is the ruler’s staff, and Jacob had said on his deathbed that the scepter shall not depart from Judah… and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples (Gen. 49:10). A star is a king in the language of the ancient East, and it is what Jesus called himself at the end of the Bible: I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star (Rev. 22:16). The Star shall crush the forehead of the enemy, and many Christians have heard an echo of the first promise, that the seed of the woman would bruise the serpent’s head (Gen. 3:15). The Hebrew words differ, but the hope is one: a son of the promised line who crushes the enemy of God’s people, and Christ is that Son.

Israel never forgot this verse. The community at Qumran read it of the Messiah; when a rebel leader rose against Rome in AD 132 his followers named him Bar Kokhba, "son of a star"; and readers from the earliest centuries have wondered about the wise men who came from the east following a star (Matt. 2:1–2), from the east, as Balaam had come. Matthew does not cite this oracle, and we should not pretend he does. But a seer from the east saw a Star rise out of Jacob and could not say when, and fourteen hundred years later men from the east saw a star and went to find out. Balaam glimpsed a King he would never meet, from a hill he had climbed for money, and could only say what he saw.

How Jewish readers take it. Targum Onkelos renders the oracle of a king arising from Jacob and the Messiah anointed from Israel. Maimonides cites it among the Torah's promises of the King Messiah, applying its lines in turn to David and to the Messiah (Laws of Kings 11:1); others read it of David alone. So Jewish and Christian readers share the conviction that a king from Jacob is in view, and many in both traditions have looked beyond David for him. This commentary sees that King in Jesus, the root and descendant of David (Revelation 22:16).
verseByVerse.note: A star and a sceptre from Israel: understood as a promise of the Messiah, the true King.

verseByVerse.quote: Edom shall be dispossessed; Seir also, his enemies, shall be dispossessed. Israel is doing valiantly. And one from Jacob shall exercise dominion and destroy the survivors of cities!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom is the brother who slammed the door four chapters ago. Israel asked for a road, was met with an army, and turned away without a fight because God told them to. Now, in an oracle they never heard, God answers Edom for them. Hold on to that when you have taken an injustice quietly and walked the long way round. Israel’s silence at the border was not the end of the matter but its transfer to somebody better placed to settle it: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom. 12:19). We can let go of the grievance because the God who has settled our own account will also settle this one.

And the last line lifts off the local map: not Israel collectively, but one from Jacob, a single figure out of this family, ruling. The whole Bible is bending toward a Person here, and a hired diviner in the pay of Moab is announcing it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he looked on Amalek and took up his discourse and said, "Amalek was the first among the nations, but its end is utter destruction." And he looked on the Kenite, and took up his discourse and said, "Enduring is your dwelling place, and your nest is set in the rock. Nevertheless, Kain shall be burned when Asshur takes you away captive." And he took up his discourse and said, "Alas, who shall live when God does this? But ships shall come from Kittim and shall afflict Asshur and Eber; and he too shall come to utter destruction." Then Balaam rose and went back to his place. And Balak also went his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three short oracles close the account, widening until the whole world is in view. Amalek was first because it was the first nation to attack Israel after the exodus, striking at the stragglers (Exod. 17:8; Deut. 25:17–18). Being first to raise a hand against the people of God is a distinction nobody should want.

Then the Kenites, Jethro’s people, friends of Israel, whose nest is set in the rock, high and not high enough, for Asshur will carry them off. Then Asshur itself falls to ships from the western coastlands. Balaam is naming the rise and fall of empires he has no earthly means of knowing, and stops to say what a man ought to say from that height: Alas, who shall live when God does this?

Then verse 25, the flattest, saddest verse in the story. No repentance, no worship. The man who saw the Star out of Jacob goes home, and on his way out hands Balak the advice that does what three mountains of sorcery could not (31:16). It is possible to see more of God than almost anyone in your generation and be lost, because the eye can be opened while the heart is not. The only question at the end of a chapter like this is not what Balaam saw but whether the Star he saw at a distance is the one you have come to. And if you have come, however weakly, you have his own word: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

25.title: Baal of Peor: The Seduction Balaam's Curse Could Not Achieve
25.text: <sup>1</sup>While Israel lived in Shittim, the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab.<sup>2</sup>These invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods.<sup>3</sup>So Israel yoked himself to Baal of Peor. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Take all the chiefs of the people and hang them in the sun before the LORD, that the fierce anger of the LORD may turn away from Israel."<sup>5</sup>And Moses said to the judges of Israel, "Each of you kill those of his men who have yoked themselves to Baal of Peor."<sup>6</sup>And behold, one of the people of Israel came and brought a Midianite woman to his family, in the sight of Moses and in the sight of the whole congregation of the people of Israel, while they were weeping in the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>7</sup>When Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose and left the congregation and took a spear in his hand<sup>8</sup>and went after the man of Israel into the chamber and pierced both of them, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly. Thus the plague on the people of Israel was stopped.<sup>9</sup>Nevertheless, those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>11</sup>"Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned back my wrath from the people of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I did not consume the people of Israel in my jealousy.<sup>12</sup>Therefore say, 'Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace,<sup>13</sup>and it shall be to him and to his descendants after him the covenant of a perpetual priesthood, because he was jealous for his God and made atonement for the people of Israel.'"<sup>14</sup>The name of the slain man of Israel, who was killed with the Midianite woman, was Zimri the son of Salu, chief of a father's house belonging to the Simeonites.<sup>15</sup>And the name of the Midianite woman who was killed was Cozbi the daughter of Zur, who was the tribal head of a father's house in Midian.<sup>16</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>17</sup>"Harass the Midianites and strike them down,<sup>18</sup>for they have harassed you with their wiles, with which they beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of the chief of Midian, their sister, who was killed on the day of the plague on account of Peor."
25.overview:
What Balaam could not accomplish by cursing, he accomplished by seduction. Numbers 31:16 reveals that he counseled Balak to lure Israel into sexual immorality and idolatry with the women of Moab, and it works where the curse failed. Israel survives the sorcerer's curse only to fall to the temptress's smile.

The people join themselves to Baal of Peor until the wrath of God breaks out in a plague, and Paul holds this very episode before the Corinthian church (1 Cor 10:8). A people who survived Egypt, the wilderness and Balaam can still be destroyed by their own appetites. The church is rarely defeated by persecution; far more often she is hollowed out by accommodation to the world's sensuality and idolatry.

The chapter turns on the zeal of Phinehas, who drives a spear through a brazen Israelite and his Midianite partner, and the plague is stopped. God grants him “my covenant of peace” because “he was jealous for his God.” His zeal is not cruelty but holy jealousy that reflects God's own, and his turning away of wrath foreshadows Christ, the truly zealous One (John 2:17), who turns away the wrath of God from his people forever, not by another's death but by his own.
25.theology:
Seduction from within. What Balaam's curse could not do, immorality and idolatry accomplished. The church is rarely defeated from without but often hollowed out by compromise within (1 Cor 10:8).

Holy jealousy. Phinehas was jealous with God's jealousy for the purity of his people, not with human cruelty.

Turning away wrath. Phinehas stood in the breach and stopped the plague, foreshadowing Christ the zealous Priest who turns away God's wrath by his own atoning death.
25.examples:
Then: Israel, unable to be cursed, was seduced into immorality and idolatry at Peor; the plague raged until Phinehas's zeal turned away God's wrath.

Now: The world will try to corrupt by pleasure what it cannot defeat by force. You belong to the Christ who turned God's wrath away forever, so flee sexual immorality and idolatry, walking by the Spirit he has given you (Gal 5:16), and when you fall, run back to him rather than away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What Balaam could not do by cursing, the enemy accomplishes by seduction. At Shittim Israel falls into sexual sin with the women of Moab and is drawn into worshiping Baal of Peor, and a plague breaks out. The greatest danger to God’s people was never the enemy’s curse but their own hearts.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the dark sequel to Balaam’s blessing. Unable to curse Israel, Balaam advised Balak to seduce them into idolatry (Num 31:16; Rev 2:14). What no external curse could achieve, internal compromise did: God’s people are far more endangered by seduction than by opposition (1 Cor 10:8, 12).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the nation no curse could touch was nearly undone by a few tents and a false god.

Now: “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). The enemy’s most effective weapon is not persecution but the slow drift into compromise.

verseByVerse.quote: While Israel lived in Shittim, the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab. These invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods. So Israel yoked himself to Baal of Peor. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the end of chapter 24 and the start of chapter 25 together, because the join is the point. Balaam went back to his place, and immediately Israel began to whore with the daughters of Moab. Scripture tells us the two are connected: Behold, these, on Balaam’s advice, caused the people of Israel to act treacherously against the LORD in the incident of Peor (31:16), and the risen Christ names Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality (Rev. 2:14).

So this is the same campaign, by the same consultant, with the weapon changed. Three rounds of sorcery produced nothing but blessing, because a people God has blessed cannot be cursed. So Balaam, sacked and unpaid, told Balak in effect: you cannot get at them from outside; invite them to dinner.

Watch the order of the collapse, because it is the ordinary order: first the women, then the sacrifices, then the people ate, and only then bowed down to their gods. Nobody got up that morning intending to worship Baal. The idolatry came in last, through the appetite, when the man was already at the table and it would have been awkward to leave. Sin rarely opens by asking for your allegiance. It asks for your evening. And then Israel yoked himself to Baal of Peor: joined at the neck, no longer able to turn without the other. Paul uses a similar picture: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers (2 Cor. 6:14).
verseByVerse.note: Shittim lay on the plains of Moab across from Jericho. Balaam had advised this plan (31:16).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Take all the chiefs of the people and hang them in the sun before the LORD, that the fierce anger of the LORD may turn away from Israel." And Moses said to the judges of Israel, "Each of you kill those of his men who have yoked themselves to Baal of Peor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The response is immediate and terrible. The Hebrew of hang them in the sun is difficult, and the exact form of execution is uncertain (impaling and public exposure are both likely), but the sense is not: the ringleaders are put to death in the open, in daylight. The sin was public; the judgment is public.

And the chiefs are named: not the young or the weak, but the heads of families who had watched for forty years what happened to those who despised the Lord. When a nation falls apart at the top, God does not begin his reckoning at the bottom.

Then Moses passes the order to the judges, and it matters for what happens three verses later. There is now a lawful, public, standing order in Israel that the men who have joined themselves to Baal are to be executed. What Phinehas does in verse 8 is not a private outburst. It is the only recorded instance of anyone actually doing what Moses had just told the whole judiciary to do.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As the plague rages and the people weep, an Israelite brazenly brings a Midianite woman into the camp. Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, drives a spear through them both, the plague is stopped, and God gives him a covenant of peace and a perpetual priesthood.
verseByVerse.theology: Phinehas’s zeal “made atonement for the people” and stayed the plague (vv.11-13); Psalm 106:30-31 says it “was counted to him as righteousness.” This is not a warrant for private vengeance but a picture, in a unique redemptive-historical moment, of holy zeal that confronts flagrant, plague-bringing sin, pointing to the greater Priest whose self-offering turns away wrath forever.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: one man’s holy zeal, in a moment of national apostasy, halted the plague.

Now: we are called not to the spear but to the same jealousy for God’s honor: to hate sin, first in ourselves. And we rest in the Priest whose blood made the atonement Phinehas only foreshadowed.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, one of the people of Israel came and brought a Midianite woman to his family, in the sight of Moses and in the sight of the whole congregation of the people of Israel, while they were weeping in the entrance of the tent of meeting. When Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose and left the congregation and took a spear in his hand and went after the man of Israel into the chamber and pierced both of them, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly. Thus the plague on the people of Israel was stopped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene is staged with terrible care. The congregation is at the tabernacle door weeping, the plague already running through the camp, the order to execute the guilty already given. And into that, in broad daylight, a man walks a Midianite woman past a weeping nation and a grieving prophet, up to the tents, while his own people’s funeral goes on around him. It is defiance staged as theatre.

And nobody moves. Not Moses, not the judges who were given the order. Israel stands at the tent door and cries and does nothing, and every second of that paralysis is more people dead in the camp behind them.

Then Phinehas, the high priest’s son and grandson, rises and takes a spear, and the text says with brutal directness: the plague on the people of Israel was stopped.

Modern readers find this passage almost unbearable, and they should not be talked out of that. But be clear what it is and what it is not. It is not vigilantism: Moses had just ordered the execution of those who joined themselves to Baal, and Phinehas was a member of the priestly house charged with guarding the holiness of the camp. It is not racial: Moses himself had married a Midianite (Exod. 2:21), Israel had welcomed foreigners from the start, and the red heifer’s cleansing was explicitly for the stranger who sojourns among them (19:10). It is a lawful capital sentence carried out, by the one official in a paralysed nation who was prepared to act, on a man who was committing the crime in public while the sentence was being announced.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set that number against the whole book. Nothing in Numbers, not the serpents nor the earth swallowing Korah, killed on this scale in a single episode. And it happened in the last camp, in sight of the river, to the generation that had survived everything else. The enemy that had failed with armies and with sorcery succeeded with hospitality.

Paul cites this plague as a live warning to a church: We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day (1 Cor. 10:8). The difference in the figures deserves a straight answer. Paul says in a single day, which Numbers does not; the most natural reading is that the twenty-three thousand fell on the worst day, and twenty-four thousand is the total of a plague that plainly ran longer, since the executions of verses 4–5 preceded it. Both writers use the round thousands ordinary in ancient reckoning. Faithful readers have long offered these explanations, and neither figure requires us to think the other writer careless.

Paul writes it to baptised, communing, confident Christians and adds, these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction (1 Cor. 10:11). The men who died at Peor had seen the sea open. Past experience of God is no immunity against present sin.

And for the reader who has already fallen this way, the same letter carries the comfort. Of people guilty of exactly these sins Paul writes, such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 6:11), and he adds and by the Spirit of our God, who is the power of a new life. Peor is a warning to the confident, not a closed door to the repentant.
verseByVerse.note: Paul gives 23,000, perhaps those who died in one day, or a rounded figure.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned back my wrath from the people of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I did not consume the people of Israel in my jealousy. Therefore say, 'Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace, and it shall be to him and to his descendants after him the covenant of a perpetual priesthood, because he was jealous for his God and made atonement for the people of Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s verdict on Phinehas troubles readers most, and it should be read exactly as it stands: he was jealous with my jealousy.

The word is easily misheard. God’s jealousy is not envy; envy wants what belongs to another. Jealousy in Scripture is a husband’s proper refusal to share his wife, the opposite of indifference. God had married this nation at Sinai, and Israel had gone to Baal’s table; his jealousy is not a blemish on his love but its temperature. Phinehas, alone in the camp, felt what God felt. The commendation is not that he was violent, but that his heart matched God’s when every other heart in Israel had gone numb.

Then the startling reward: my covenant of peace, granted for bloodshed that had stopped a slaughter. And made atonement is the priest’s own word. Phinehas stood between a holy God and a doomed people, and the wrath stopped at him. The psalm remembers it in the language of the gospel: Then Phinehas stood up and intervened, and the plague was stayed. And that was counted to him as righteousness (Ps. 106:30–31), the phrase used of Abraham’s faith (Gen. 15:6). The deed did not earn his acceptance with God; God publicly owned it as the act of a righteous man, faith in motion when everyone else had stopped believing God meant it.

Now say plainly what must be said. This is not a licence for anybody today. Phinehas held a priestly office in a theocratic nation under a specific standing order through Moses; no Christian holds that office or that order. The church’s zeal is armed differently, the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4), and when Paul faces the identical sin in Corinth, the remedy he commands is exclusion from the fellowship, not a spear (1 Cor. 5:1–5). Zeal for God is still required of us. Its instruments have changed entirely.

And this is why the chapter is in the Bible at all. Phinehas turned away wrath by the death of the guilty. A greater Priest stood in the same breach and turned away the same wrath by his own death, having done nothing to deserve it; his covenant of peace was bought with his own body, and his priesthood is perpetual in his own person. He himself is our peace (Eph. 2:14). At Peor the priest struck the guilty. At Calvary the Priest was struck himself.

verseByVerse.quote: The name of the slain man of Israel, who was killed with the Midianite woman, was Zimri the son of Salu, chief of a father's house belonging to the Simeonites. And the name of the Midianite woman who was killed was Cozbi the daughter of Zur, who was the tribal head of a father's house in Midian.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only now does the text give the names, with full genealogy. These were not two young people who lost their heads. Zimri was a clan chief of Simeon; Cozbi was a Midianite princess. It looks far more like a deliberate alliance than a romance, two leading families sealing a connection in the most public way available, in open contempt of the God whose plague was running through the camp. Verse 18 confirms it: Cozbi is part of Midian’s wiles. Moab and Midian were acting together throughout (22:4, 7), which is why verse 1 speaks of the daughters of Moab and Cozbi is a Midianite.

And the names are written down. Zimri could have died anonymously, one among twenty-four thousand; instead his name and tribe are in the permanent record of the people of God, attached to the worst thing he ever did. There is a book, and things get written in it, which is why the mercy of Christ is described as a record dealt with: God canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands… nailing it to the cross (Col. 2:14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies for their part in the seduction at Peor. The reckoning, carried out in chapter 31, begins here.
verseByVerse.theology: The command against Midian (vv.17-18) is God’s judgment on those who deliberately engineered Israel’s downfall. It shows how seriously God takes those who lead his people into sin (cf. Matt 18:6-7). Peor becomes a byword for apostasy (Ps 106:28-29; Hos 9:10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: those who plotted to corrupt God’s people came under God’s judgment.

Now: God still regards with the utmost gravity those who deliberately lead others into sin. “It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck” (Luke 17:2).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Harass the Midianites and strike them down, for they have harassed you with their wiles, with which they beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of the chief of Midian, their sister, who was killed on the day of the plague on account of Peor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes by turning to the people who set the trap, and two things stand in God’s sentence.

First, God does not accept the excuse of the seducer. Israel sinned freely and was judged for it, and the men who engineered the temptation are also held to account. Nobody at Peor could plead that they were only tempted, and nobody in Midian that they only offered. Jesus holds both together: cut off your own hand rather than sin, and of the one who causes a little one to stumble, it would be better for him to have a great millstone fastened around his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea (Matt. 18:6–8).

Second, the word wiles. Midian did not defeat Israel; Midian beguiled her. Paul uses the same vocabulary of the enemy the church faces, the schemes of the devil (Eph. 6:11), and it is the plain lesson of chapters 22 to 25 read as one story. Balak tried a curse and failed, and never dared an army. Balaam could not raise a syllable against them from three mountains. Then a dinner invitation on a warm evening at Shittim brought down more of Israel than every enemy in the book combined.

The people of God have never been in real danger from the mountain; the blessing was God’s and no one could reach it. What ruined them walked into the camp smiling and was invited to stay. That is why the Lord Jesus, praying for his own on the last night, did not ask for them to be taken off the field. He asked for the one thing Israel lacked at Shittim: I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one (John 17:15).

26.title: The Second Census: A New Generation, an Old Faithfulness

The people of Israel who came out of the land of Egypt were:<sup>5</sup>Reuben, the firstborn of Israel; the sons of Reuben: of Hanoch, the clan of the Hanochites; of Pallu, the clan of the Palluites;<sup>6</sup>of Hezron, the clan of the Hezronites; of Carmi, the clan of the Carmites.<sup>7</sup>These are the clans of the Reubenites, and those listed were 43,730.<sup>8</sup>And the sons of Pallu: Eliab.<sup>9</sup>The sons of Eliab: Nemuel, Dathan, and Abiram. These are the clans of Dan according to their clans.<sup>43</sup>All the clans of the Shuhamites, as they were listed, were 64,400.<sup>44</sup>The sons of Asher according to their clans: of Imnah, the clan of the Imnites; of Ishvi, the clan of the Ishvites; of Beriah, the clan of the Beriites.<sup>45</sup>Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the clan of the Heberites; of Malchiel, the clan of the Malchielites.<sup>46</sup>And the name of the daughter of Asher was Serah.<sup>47</sup>These are the clans of the sons of Asher as they were listed, 53,400.<sup>48</sup>The sons of Naphtali according to their clans: of Jahzeel, the clan of the Jahzeelites; of Guni, the clan of the Gunites;<sup>49</sup>of Jezer, the clan of the Jezerites; of Shillem, the clan of the Shillemites.<sup>50</sup>These are the clans of Naphtali according to their clans, and those listed were 45,400.<sup>51</sup>This was the list of the people of Israel, 601,730.<sup>52</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>53</sup>"Among these the land shall be divided for inheritance according to the number of names.<sup>54</sup>To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance; every tribe shall be given its inheritance in proportion to its list.<sup>55</sup>But the land shall be divided by lot. According to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit.<sup>56</sup>Their inheritance shall be divided according to lot between the larger and the smaller."<sup>57</sup>This was the list of the Levites according to their clans: of Gershon, the clan of the Gershonites; of Kohath, the clan of the Kohathites; of Merari, the clan of the Merarites.<sup>58</sup>These are the clans of Levi: the clan of the Libnites, the clan of the Hebronites, the clan of the Mahlites, the clan of the Mushites, the clan of the Korahites. And Kohath was the father of Amram.<sup>59</sup>The name of Amram's wife was Jochebed the daughter of Levi, who was born to Levi in Egypt. And she bore to Amram Aaron and Moses and Miriam their sister.<sup>60</sup>And to Aaron were born Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.<sup>61</sup>But Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD.<sup>62</sup>And those listed were 23,000, every male from a month old and upward. For they were not listed among the people of Israel, because there was no inheritance given to them among the people of Israel.<sup>63</sup>These were those listed by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who listed the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.<sup>64</sup>But among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron the priest, who had listed the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai.<sup>65</sup>For the LORD had said of them, "They shall die in the wilderness." Not one of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.
26.overview:
A second census bookends the book. Forty years after the first counting at Sinai, a new generation is numbered on the plains of Moab, at the edge of the Promised Land. The first census numbered the generation that would die in the wilderness for unbelief; this one numbers the generation that will enter. The whole tragic interval of chapters 11–25 lies between the two countings.

The most moving verses are the last (vv. 64–65): not one of the first list was left except Caleb and Joshua. The sentence of chapter 14 has been carried out in full. Yet God did not give up on Israel. He raised a new generation and brought them back to the border of promise: the severity and the kindness of God (Rom 11:22) side by side.

This is the comfort of the chapter: God's faithfulness spans the generations. The covenant did not die with the rebels in the sand; the church too is carried forward by the faithfulness of God, not the constancy of men. That same faithfulness carried the promise on to the Son of David, in whom believers have obtained an inheritance that no grave can take (Eph 1:11).
26.theology:
God's faithfulness across generations. The covenant did not die with the unbelieving generation. God raised up a new people and kept his promise.

Severity and kindness. Both are displayed (Rom 11:22): judgment fully carried out on the rebels, kindness extended to the new generation.

Grace in unexpected places. The sons of Korah did not die; the rebel's line was preserved to sing God's praises.
26.examples:
Then: A new generation was numbered at the border, nearly matching the first, while not one of the unbelieving generation remained except Caleb and Joshua.

Now: God's promises outlive every failure and span every generation. The inheritance is sure because it rests on his faithfulness, not yours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–51 — The Census of the New Generation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second census is taken, tribe by tribe, but not of the generation counted in chapter 1, which has died in the wilderness. This is their children, who will enter the land: the long lists are a monument to God’s faithfulness.
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment fell (the fathers died), but the promise endured (the children are numbered for the conquest). God’s purposes are not defeated by one generation’s unbelief; even the roll-call of tribes preaches that God keeps covenant to a thousand generations (Deut 7:9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the sons of the men who died in the desert stood counted and ready.

Now: where one generation fails, God raises up another; his promise never dies with those who forfeit it (Ps 145:4).

verseByVerse.quote: After the plague, the LORD said to Moses and to Eleazar the son of Aaron, the priest, "Take a census of all the congregation of the people of Israel, from twenty years old and upward, by their fathers' houses, all in Israel who are able to go to war." And Moses and Eleazar the priest spoke with them in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying, "Take a census of the people, from twenty years old and upward," as the LORD commanded Moses. The people of Israel who came out of the land of Egypt were:
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the plague: the saddest and the most hopeful words in the chapter. The counting begins over twenty-four thousand fresh graves.

The purpose is stated twice: those able to go to war, and in verse 53, the land divided for inheritance. So the document is both a muster roll and a deed register, and it is the same list, because in God’s arrangement the people who receive the inheritance are the people who go in for it.

And it has been done before. Chapter 1 counted a nation for a march that should have taken eleven days (Deut. 1:2) and collapsed at Kadesh. This is the same procedure, with an entirely different set of men, every one of the first list now dead except two. God is not repeating himself. He is starting again, with the sons of the people who would not go, and this time they will cross.
verseByVerse.note: The second census, of the new generation.

verseByVerse.quote: Reuben, the firstborn of Israel; the sons of Reuben: of Hanoch, the clan of the Hanochites; of Pallu, the clan of the Palluites; of Hezron, the clan of the Hezronites; of Carmi, the clan of the Carmites. These are the clans of the Reubenites, and those listed were 43,730. And the sons of Pallu: Eliab. The sons of Eliab: Nemuel, Dathan, and Abiram. These are the Dathan and Abiram, chosen from the congregation, who contended against Moses and Aaron in the company of Korah, when they contended against the LORD and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up together with Korah, when that company died, when the fire devoured 250 men, and they became a warning. But the sons of Korah did not die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The register opens with Reuben and almost at once stops being a list, pausing to retell Dathan and Abiram and the earth that swallowed them (26:9–10). A roll of the covenant people is also a memorial, and God writes into it both the mercy and the warning.

Then eight words that change everything: But the sons of Korah did not die.

Korah went down alive into the ground, and his sons were not in the pit. The text does not explain the mechanics; it records the survival, and Scripture spends five hundred years showing what God did with it. Of the Sons of Korah stands over eleven psalms, among them the one every homesick believer knows: As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God (Ps. 42:1), and How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts (Ps. 84:1). The descendants of the man who resented Aaron’s priesthood became the singers who taught Israel to long for God.

That is the gospel written into a genealogy.
