The rebel’s sin did not settle his children’s destiny, the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezek. 18:20), and God did not merely spare that family; he gave it the music. If you carry a family name you would rather not have, and a history you did not choose, this verse is in the Bible for you. The sons of Korah did not die. They sang.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Simeon according to their clans: of Nemuel, the clan of the Nemuelites; of Jamin, the clan of the Jaminites; of Jachin, the clan of the Jachinites; of Zerah, the clan of the Zerahites; of Shaul, the clan of the Shaulites. These are the clans of the Simeonites, 22,200. The sons of Gad according to their clans: of Zephon, the clan of the Zephonites; of Haggi, the clan of the Haggites; of Shuni, the clan of the Shunites; of Ozni, the clan of the Oznites; of Eri, the clan of the Erites; of Arod, the clan of the Arodites; of Areli, the clan of the Arelites. These are the clans of the sons of Gad as they were listed, 40,500. The sons of Judah were Er and Onan; and Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. And the sons of Judah according to their clans were: of Shelah, the clan of the Shelanites; of Perez, the clan of the Perezites; of Zerah, the clan of the Zerahites. And the sons of Perez were: of Hezron, the clan of the Hezronites; of Hamul, the clan of the Hamulites. These are the clans of Judah as they were listed, 76,500.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read past the figures for a moment, because two of them tell a story.

Simeon has collapsed: 59,300 fighting men at Sinai, here 22,200, a loss of nearly two thirds when several tribes grew. And the man who paraded a Midianite woman past a weeping nation was chief of a father’s house belonging to the Simeonites (25:14). Scripture does not draw the line between those facts, and we should not draw it harder than it does. But the plague seems to have fallen heaviest on the tribe whose chief led the way into it, and the ruin of a people can begin with one man of standing who decides the rules are for other people.

Judah is the largest tribe at 76,500, as in chapter 1. Jacob had said that the scepter shall not depart from Judah… and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples (Gen. 49:10). Fourteen hundred years before Bethlehem, the tribe that will carry the King is quietly the strongest name on the list, and nobody counting that morning knew why.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Issachar according to their clans: of Tola, the clan of the Tolaites; of Puvah, the clan of the Punites; of Jashub, the clan of the Jashubites; of Shimron, the clan of the Shimronites. These are the clans of Issachar as they were listed, 64,300. The sons of Zebulun, according to their clans: of Sered, the clan of the Seredites; of Elon, the clan of the Elonites; of Jahleel, the clan of the Jahleelites. These are the clans of the Zebulunites as they were listed, 60,500. The sons of Joseph according to their clans: Manasseh and Ephraim. The sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the clan of the Machirites; and Machir was the father of Gilead; of Gilead, the clan of the Gileadites. These are the sons of Gilead: of Iezer, the clan of the Iezerites; of Helek, the clan of the Helekites; and of Asriel, the clan of the Asrielites; and of Shechem, the clan of the Shechemites; and of Shemida, the clan of the Shemidaites; and of Hepher, the clan of the Hepherites. Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters. And the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. These are the clans of Manasseh, and those listed were 52,700.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of a military register, the text does something no ancient muster roll does. At verse 33 it stops and names five women: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah.

This is a list of men who can fight, kept for dividing land among men. These five cannot fight and, under every custom of the ancient world, cannot inherit; their father is dead and his line has run out. By the logic of the document they should not appear in it, and God has their names written down in full, one chapter before they walk up to Moses and ask for what nobody thought they could have. The next chapter has been prepared for here, by a God who counted them before they asked.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Ephraim according to their clans: of Shuthelah, the clan of the Shuthelahites; of Becher, the clan of the Becherites; of Tahan, the clan of the Tahanites. And these are the sons of Shuthelah: of Eran, the clan of the Eranites. These are the clans of the sons of Ephraim as they were listed, 32,500. These are the sons of Joseph according to their clans. The sons of Benjamin according to their clans: of Bela, the clan of the Belaites; of Ashbel, the clan of the Ashbelites; of Ahiram, the clan of the Ahiramites; of Shephupham, the clan of the Shuphamites; of Hupham, the clan of the Huphamites. And the sons of Bela were Ard and Naaman: of Ard, the clan of the Ardites; of Naaman, the clan of the Naamites. These are the sons of Benjamin according to their clans, and those listed were 45,600. These are the sons of Dan according to their clans: of Shuham, the clan of the Shuhamites. These are the clans of Dan according to their clans. All the clans of the Shuhamites, as they were listed, were 64,400. The sons of Asher according to their clans: of Imnah, the clan of the Imnites; of Ishvi, the clan of the Ishvites; of Beriah, the clan of the Beriites. Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the clan of the Heberites; of Malchiel, the clan of the Malchielites. And the name of the daughter of Asher was Serah. These are the clans of the sons of Asher as they were listed, 53,400.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Clan after clan, in the same unvarying formula. Modern readers skim these paragraphs. Ask why God did not.

A census is an act of ownership; nobody counts carefully what they do not intend to keep. The repetition that makes the chapter tedious is the point: God goes through this nation clan by clan and misses nobody. He had done it at Sinai, and every man on that list was now dead; he does it again, unhurried, as though the losses had changed nothing about his method.

That is how the Lord Jesus describes his own care: He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out… I know my own and my own know me (John 10:3, 14). There is no such thing, in Scripture, as being lost in the crowd of the redeemed.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Naphtali according to their clans: of Jahzeel, the clan of the Jahzeelites; of Guni, the clan of the Gunites; of Jezer, the clan of the Jezerites; of Shillem, the clan of the Shillemites. These are the clans of Naphtali according to their clans, and those listed were 45,400. This was the list of the people of Israel, 601,730.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set the total beside Sinai’s 603,550. The difference is 1,820 men, less than a third of one per cent. In between, an entire adult generation died under a sentence of judgment, and the nation arriving at the Jordan is very nearly the size of the one that left the mountain.

God carried the most severe judgment in the book through to the last man over thirty-eight years, and at the end his promise to Abraham stood exactly where it had stood. Judgment fell in full; the promise did not shrink by a thousandth. The numbers are the arithmetic of Romans: Note then the kindness and the severity of God (Rom. 11:22). Both, neither cancelling the other, printed in the same column of a census.

Are the numbers literal? Over 600,000 fighting men implies two million people in the wilderness, and readers rightly ask how. Some propose that the word for “thousand” means a clan or military unit, which would make the army a few thousand. But the totals add up as thousands, and the census silver of Exodus 38:25–26 matches 603,550 men at half a shekel each exactly. Many conservative scholars therefore take the numbers as written, and this commentary does too, while acknowledging that others who hold Scripture just as high read the word as a unit and that the question is still debated. On the plain reading, the wilderness did not feed them; God did, with manna for forty years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 52–56 — The Land Divided by Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land is divided according to each tribe’s size, but assigned by lot, which is to say, by God: fairness and divine sovereignty together.
verseByVerse.theology: The inheritance is proportioned by size but distributed by lot (vv.54-56), and “the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). The inheritance is a gift received by God’s appointment, a foretaste of the one “kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: each tribe’s portion was both fair and God-given; no tribe could boast, none was cheated.

Now: our inheritance too is God’s gift, assigned by his hand, not earned by our merit.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Among these the land shall be divided for inheritance according to the number of names. To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance; every tribe shall be given its inheritance in proportion to its list. But the land shall be divided by lot. According to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit. Their inheritance shall be divided according to lot between the larger and the smaller."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two principles are held together that look as though they must fight. The size of each portion is decided by the census, fair and proportionate, so that no family is crowded or given more than it can work. The location is decided by the lot, that is, by God (Prov. 16:33). Human arithmetic settles how much; divine sovereignty settles where. Nobody lobbied for the good valleys, and nobody was cheated of acreage.

That combination runs into the New Testament as a great comfort: in him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Eph. 1:11), and Paul’s verb carries the idea of an allotment. Your portion is not a leftover, not drawn by chance, and not awarded on the strength of your performance. It was measured out by a Father who knows the size of you, and placed by a hand that never slips.
verseByVerse.note: The total was 601,730 men (v. 51) — almost the same as forty years before.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 57–65 — The Levites, and the Old Generation Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites are counted separately, for their portion is the LORD himself. And the chapter ends solemnly: not one of the generation counted at Sinai is left, except Caleb and Joshua. God’s word, in judgment as in mercy, comes exactly true.
verseByVerse.theology: The end of the old generation (vv.64-65) is the precise fulfillment of God’s word of judgment (14:29-30). God’s threatenings are as sure as his promises. Yet grace shines here: the two men who believed God are spared, living proof that “whoever does the will of God abides forever” (1 John 2:17). And the Levites’ portion, the LORD himself (cf. 18:20), is the richest inheritance of all.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the whole unbelieving generation fell, exactly as God had warned, but Caleb and Joshua, who trusted him, still stood.

Now: God’s warnings are as certain as his promises (Heb 3:16-19). Faith is the difference between those who fall in the wilderness and those who enter the rest (Heb 4:1-2), and it rests not on our strength but on the God who keeps his word to the last letter.

verseByVerse.quote: This was the list of the Levites according to their clans: of Gershon, the clan of the Gershonites; of Kohath, the clan of the Kohathites; of Merari, the clan of the Merarites. These are the clans of Levi: the clan of the Libnites, the clan of the Hebronites, the clan of the Mahlites, the clan of the Mushites, the clan of the Korahites. And Kohath was the father of Amram. The name of Amram's wife was Jochebed the daughter of Levi, who was born to Levi in Egypt. And she bore to Amram Aaron and Moses and Miriam their sister. And to Aaron were born Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. But Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD. And those listed were 23,000, every male from a month old and upward. For they were not listed among the people of Israel, because there was no inheritance given to them among the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites are counted from a month old, babies included, because this tribe is not mustered for war. And they are kept off the main roll because there was no inheritance given to them.

So the tribe counted most carefully receives least. Twelve names on the list are attached to territory; Levi’s is attached to a tent. God had explained the exchange to Aaron, I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel (18:20), and here it is on paper: a separate column, a separate criterion, and no acreage at the end. The other tribes are listed by what they can do, because they will fight for land. Levi is listed by who they are.

The list also pauses over Amram’s family, Aaron, Moses and Miriam, two already dead and the third about to be, and over Nadab and Abihu, who died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD. Even the priestly genealogy carries its graves. The tribe nearest the holiness of God had learned most painfully what that nearness costs.

verseByVerse.quote: These were those listed by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who listed the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho. But among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron the priest, who had listed the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai. For the LORD had said of them, "They shall die in the wilderness." Not one of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with an audit, and it is devastating. Two lists taken forty years apart, six hundred thousand men on each, and the overlap is two names. God had said They shall die in the wilderness, a sentence pronounced at Kadesh that may have sounded like words said in the heat of the moment, and this verse is the receipt. Every word came true, one funeral at a time, over thirty-eight years.

But read the exception, because the same faithfulness is in it. Caleb and Joshua had stood before a nation that wanted to stone them and said the LORD is with us; do not fear them (14:9), and God had promised those two men they would go in. Four decades later, with everyone they had known buried behind them, they are standing on the plains of Moab being counted. The God who is exact about his warnings is exact about his promises, and it is the same exactness. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa. 40:8), and a chapter of names and numbers turns out to be the proof of it.

27.title: The Daughters of Zelophehad; Joshua Commissioned
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Then drew near the daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of Manasseh the son of Joseph. The names of his daughters were: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.<sup>2</sup>And they stood before Moses and before Eleazar the priest and before the chiefs and all the congregation, at the entrance of the tent of meeting, saying,<sup>3</sup>"Our father died in the wilderness. He was not among the company of those who gathered themselves together against the LORD in the company of Korah, but died for his own sin. And he had no sons.<sup>4</sup>Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son? Give to us a possession among our father's brothers."<sup>5</sup>Moses brought their case before the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>7</sup>"The daughters of Zelophehad are right. You shall give them possession of an inheritance among their father's brothers and transfer the inheritance of their father to them.<sup>8</sup>And you shall speak to the people of Israel, saying, 'If a man dies and has no son, then you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter.<sup>9</sup>And if he has no daughter, then you shall give his inheritance to his brothers.<sup>10</sup>And if he has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to his father's brothers.<sup>11</sup>And if his father has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to the nearest kinsman of his clan, and he shall possess it. And it shall be for the people of Israel a statute and rule, as the LORD commanded Moses.'"<sup>12</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Go up into this mountain of Abarim and see the land that I have given to the people of Israel.<sup>13</sup>When you have seen it, you also shall be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was,<sup>14</sup>because you rebelled against my word in the wilderness of Zin when the congregation quarreled, failing to uphold me as holy at the waters before their eyes." (These are the waters of Meribah of Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin.)<sup>15</sup>Moses spoke to the LORD, saying,<sup>16</sup>"Let the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation<sup>17</sup>who shall go out before them and come in before them, who shall lead them out and bring them in, that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd."<sup>18</sup>So the LORD said to Moses, "Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him.<sup>19</sup>Make him stand before Eleazar the priest and all the congregation, and you shall commission him in their sight.<sup>20</sup>You shall invest him with some of your authority, that all the congregation of the people of Israel may obey.<sup>21</sup>And he shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD. At his word they shall go out, and at his word they shall come in, both he and all the people of Israel with him, the whole congregation."<sup>22</sup>And Moses did as the LORD commanded him. He took Joshua and made him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation,<sup>23</sup>and he laid his hands on him and commissioned him as the LORD directed through Moses.
27.overview:
Chapter 27 holds two stories that seem unrelated: a daughters' appeal for inheritance, and the commissioning of Israel's next leader. Both turn on the future of the people of God: as the new generation prepares to enter Canaan, God settles who will inherit and who will lead.

Five daughters whose father died without sons stand before Moses, the priest and the whole congregation and ask for his inheritance. It is an act of courage and of faith in a promised land they have not yet entered, and God's verdict is striking: “The daughters of Zelophehad are right.” Their claim is honored and the law amended to provide for them.

Then God tells Moses to see the land he will not enter because of Meribah. Moses' concern is not for himself but that the congregation “may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” (v. 17), and God appoints Joshua, “a man in whom is the Spirit.” The name Joshua is Yeshua, the Hebrew form of “Jesus,” and the Joshua who led the people into the earthly rest points to the greater Joshua, who leads his people into the true rest that Moses and the law could never give (Heb 4:8–9).
27.theology:
God hears the faithful appeal. The daughters of Zelophehad, bold in faith, are vindicated by God himself, who honors the overlooked.

The limit of the law. Moses sees the land but cannot enter it. The law-giver cannot bring the people into rest, pointing beyond himself to a greater Leader.

The greater Joshua. Spirit-filled Joshua leads Israel into the land, foreshadowing Jesus, who leads his people into eternal rest (Heb 4:8–9).
27.examples:
Then: God vindicated the daughters' appeal and secured their inheritance, then commissioned Joshua to shepherd the people into the land Moses could only see.

Now: God hears the bold faith of the overlooked and secures your inheritance in Christ. The greater Joshua leads you into the rest the law could never give, and you will never be left as sheep without a shepherd.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Five sisters whose father died without sons ask Moses for a share of his inheritance. Moses brings their case before the LORD, and God rules in their favor: a precedent is set, and the inheritance rights of daughters are written into Israel’s law.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s ruling (v.7) establishes a lasting statute protecting daughters’ inheritance where there is no son, a striking dignity in the ancient world. God’s justice hears the voiceless (cf. Ps 68:5), and Moses’ habit of bringing hard cases “before the LORD” (v.5) models leadership that seeks God’s will.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: five sisters with no brother and no power brought their case to God, and God declared them right.

Now: God still hears the appeal of those the world overlooks. Bring your hard cases “before the LORD” (v.5), as Moses did.

verseByVerse.quote: Then drew near the daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of Manasseh the son of Joseph. The names of his daughters were: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. And they stood before Moses and before Eleazar the priest and before the chiefs and all the congregation, at the entrance of the tent of meeting, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stage the scene properly, because everything depends on it. The whole nation assembled, the leadership drawn up at the tabernacle door: Moses, the high priest, the tribal chiefs. Every person with standing is a man. And out of the crowd walk five unmarried women with no father, no brothers, no legal representative and no precedent, and they keep walking until they are at the front.

The text names them twice, here and in the census: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah, listed as carefully as any chief in the muster roll. And they drew near, the word Numbers uses for approaching God at the tent. They did not lobby an uncle. They came to the front and stood there until somebody asked them what they wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our father died in the wilderness. He was not among the company of those who gathered themselves together against the LORD in the company of Korah, but died for his own sin. And he had no sons. Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son? Give to us a possession among our father's brothers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What they say is careful legal reasoning, plainly long thought out, in three moves. Their father died under the general sentence at Kadesh, no better and no worse than six hundred thousand others. Crucially, he was not with Korah, whose rebellion probably carried a forfeiture: they rule out the one ground on which the claim could be refused. And he left no sons, which by the custom of every nation around them meant the family was finished.

Then the plea, not what a modern reader expects. Not "this is unfair to us," but Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan? In Israel land and name were one thing. To hold no portion was to have no place in the covenant people and, after a generation, no memory. They are fighting for a dead man’s place among the people of God.

And nobody in that assembly has crossed the Jordan. These women are pressing a claim to a field in a country nobody has set foot in, because they believe God will give it. That is faith of a practical kind, the sort that makes arrangements, and it rests not on their strength but on his promise. Set your own praying beside it. Do you ask God for things you have already begun to plan for, or only for things you would be quietly unsurprised not to receive?

verseByVerse.quote: Moses brought their case before the LORD. And the LORD said to Moses, "The daughters of Zelophehad are right. You shall give them possession of an inheritance among their father's brothers and transfer the inheritance of their father to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is the lawgiver of Israel, who has spoken with God face to face, the most competent man alive on what the law requires, and he does not know the answer. He does not improvise a ruling to protect his authority. He takes their case to God.

Anyone who leads anything should read that verse twice. The temptation of office is not to be wrong but to appear to know. The greatest leader in the Old Testament handled a question he could not answer by admitting it and going to God with it.

Then the verdict, startling in its bluntness: right. God does not merely make a compassionate exception; he says their reading of what the covenant required was correct, and the leadership had not thought it through. Five women with no standing understood the mind of God on a point of law better than the chiefs of the twelve tribes: God chose what is low and despised in the world… so that no human being might boast in the presence of God (1 Cor. 1:28–29).

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall speak to the people of Israel, saying, 'If a man dies and has no son, then you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter. And if he has no daughter, then you shall give his inheritance to his brothers. And if he has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to his father's brothers. And if his father has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to the nearest kinsman of his clan, and he shall possess it. And it shall be for the people of Israel a statute and rule, as the LORD commanded Moses.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now watch what God does with the answer. Instead of granting the petition and moving on, he gives a complete order of succession, daughter, brothers, uncles, nearest kinsman, a statute and rule for the nation.

One family’s grievance becomes permanent law. Because five women were brave enough to walk to the front, every daughter in Israel for a thousand years had a right she would not otherwise have had. The ruling covered daughters where there was no son, and chapter 36 adds that such heiresses marry within their tribe; it did not make sons and daughters equal heirs, but in its world it was a real protection. God does not merely relieve the person in front of him; he alters the arrangements so that the next person never has to ask.

And the chain ends with the nearest kinsman: a relative close enough and willing enough to keep a lost family’s portion in the family. That is the institution that saves a widow in Bethlehem when Boaz stands up for Ruth, and many Christians have seen in it a picture of what the Son of God did about the inheritance we had forfeited: he had to be made like his brothers in every respect (Heb. 2:17). A kinsman was needed. He became one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–23 — Joshua Appointed to Succeed Moses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Moses to climb a mountain and look at the land he will not enter. Moses responds not with self-pity but with concern that the people have a shepherd, and God appoints Joshua, a man “in whom is the Spirit,” commissioned before all the people.
verseByVerse.theology: Moses’ prayer that Israel not be “as sheep that have no shepherd” (v.17) is the compassion Jesus felt for the crowds (Matt 9:36), answered by the Good Shepherd (John 10:11). Joshua, “a man in whom is the Spirit” (v.18), is God’s provision of continuity: the work is bigger than any one servant.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: knowing he would die outside the land, Moses’ first thought was for the flock, and God provided Joshua.

Now: we have the Shepherd who never dies, Jesus, whose name is Joshua, who leads his people all the way into the promised rest (Heb 4:8-9; John 10:11).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Go up into this mountain of Abarim and see the land that I have given to the people of Israel. When you have seen it, you also shall be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was, because you rebelled against my word in the wilderness of Zin when the congregation quarreled, failing to uphold me as holy at the waters before their eyes." (These are the waters of Meribah of Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer has put these paragraphs side by side deliberately. Moses has just settled the inheritance law of a land he will never own a foot of, and the moment the case is closed, God tells him to climb a hill, look at it, and die.

There is severity in this and real tenderness, and both must be kept. The severity is unsoftened: failing to uphold me as holy. One episode, decades of faithfulness either side of it, and the sentence stands. God is not sentimental about his own glory, least of all when his friends obscure it.

But look at what he gives. Not simply "you shall die," but see the land. Moses is shown the whole of it, Gilead, Dan, Judah, the Negeb, right to the sea (Deut. 34:1–3), refused the possession and granted the view, and then gathered to his people, Scripture’s quiet word for a homecoming. Fourteen centuries later Peter, James and John look up on a mountain and there he is, inside the land at last, in glory, talking with Jesus about his departure (Luke 9:30–31). God’s no to Moses was real, and it was not the last word he spoke to him.
verseByVerse.note: Abarim was the mountain range of Moab; its peak Nebo overlooks Jericho.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to the LORD, saying, "Let the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation who shall go out before them and come in before them, who shall lead them out and bring them in, that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man has just been told the date of his own death. Read what he says next.

Not one word about himself. No appeal against the sentence, no request that his own sons be considered, and they never are. His entire concern is that this exasperating nation, which broke his heart for forty years and cost him the land, should not be left without someone to walk in front of them. That is the measure of the man, and why God trusted him with them.

He calls on the God of the spirits of all flesh, the only one who knows what is inside every human being, because no man can see far enough into another to make this appointment safely. And he asks for a leader who will go out before them, whose place is in front, taking first whatever is coming.

Sheep that have no shepherd does not stay in Numbers. It becomes the prophets’ indictment of Israel’s failed leaders (Ezek. 34:5), and then a man goes through Galilee and sees the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matt. 9:36). God answered Moses’ prayer for one generation with Joshua, and finally, for every generation, in the one who said I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Moses asked for a man who would go out before the flock. God sent a Shepherd who went out before them all the way to a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD said to Moses, "Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Make him stand before Eleazar the priest and all the congregation, and you shall commission him in their sight. You shall invest him with some of your authority, that all the congregation of the people of Israel may obey. And he shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD. At his word they shall go out, and at his word they shall come in, both he and all the people of Israel with him, the whole congregation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The qualification named is not experience, though Joshua had forty years of it, nor courage, though he had stood with Caleb against a nation. It is that the Spirit is in him. Every servant of God since has been equipped the same way, and the Spirit Joshua had is now given to all who belong to Christ. The ceremony is public, in their sight, with Moses’ hands laid on him, the pattern the church still follows in setting people apart (Acts 6:6; 1 Tim. 4:14).

Then a phrase that repays attention: some of your authority. Some, not all. Moses spoke with God face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exod. 33:11); Joshua must stand before the priest, who will inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim, the means kept in the high priest’s breastpiece by which Israel sought a yes or no from God. For decisions of national moment Joshua will inquire through the priest.

So the authority Moses held alone is deliberately split, prophet and priest, and never again given whole to one man in Israel. It is a gap left open on purpose: the office of the one who both speaks God’s word and stands in God’s presence for the people stayed vacant for fourteen centuries, until a man walked out of the Jordan who was Prophet, Priest and King at once, and needed nobody to inquire for him, because the word he spoke was his own.

And the name: Joshua is Yehoshua, the same name, in its later form, that an angel would give to a child in Nazareth. Hebrews makes the comparison and leaves it deliberately unfinished: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on (Heb. 4:8). One Joshua took them into Canaan. The other takes his people into rest.
verseByVerse.note: The Urim was used by the priest to learn God’s will (see Exod 28:30).

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses did as the LORD commanded him. He took Joshua and made him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation, and he laid his hands on him and commissioned him as the LORD directed through Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider what that obedience cost. A dying man hands over, in public, with his own hands, to the one who will do what he has wanted for forty years and been refused. Every step of the ceremony rehearses his own exclusion, and Scripture records not a syllable of reluctance, no wistful speech, no attempt to keep a little authority back. Moses did as the LORD commanded him.

Two parties are handed something in this chapter they were not entitled to: five women who should have inherited nothing, and a servant who should not have followed Moses. And the same chapter takes from the greatest man in Israel the one thing he most wanted. God gives to those with no claim and withholds from the man with every claim, and in both directions he is entirely good, and the outcome was better than anyone could see. Moses, who failed once at Meribah, did not enter Canaan; he entered glory, because his standing rested on the God who forgives and not on his record. And he never lost the flock. He handed them to a Joshua, and God would one day hand them to another, who never failed at any rock.

28.title: The Continual Offerings: The Rhythm of Worship
28.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel and say to them, 'My offering, my food for my food offerings, my pleasing aroma, you shall be careful to offer to me at its appointed time.'<sup>3</sup>And you shall say to them, This is the food offering that you shall offer to the LORD: two male lambs a year old without blemish, day by day, as a regular offering.<sup>4</sup>The one lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight;<sup>5</sup>also a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with a quarter of a hin of beaten oil.<sup>6</sup>It is a regular burnt offering, which was ordained at Mount Sinai for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Its drink offering shall be a quarter of a hin for each lamb. In the Holy Place you shall pour out a drink offering of strong drink to the LORD.<sup>8</sup>The other lamb you shall offer at twilight. Like the grain offering of the morning, and like its drink offering, you shall offer it as a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"On the Sabbath day, two male lambs a year old without blemish, and two tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, and its drink offering:<sup>10</sup>this is the burnt offering of every Sabbath, besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.<sup>11</sup>"At the beginnings of your months, you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish;<sup>12</sup>also three tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for each bull, and two tenths of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for the one ram;<sup>13</sup>and a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering for every lamb; for a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>Their drink offerings shall be half a hin of wine for a bull, a third of a hin for a ram, and a quarter of a hin for a lamb. This is the burnt offering of each month throughout the months of the year.<sup>15</sup>Also one male goat for a sin offering to the LORD; it shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.<sup>16</sup>"On the fourteenth day of the first month is the LORD's Passover,<sup>17</sup>and on the fifteenth day of this month is a feast. Seven days shall unleavened bread be eaten.<sup>18</sup>On the first day there shall be a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work,<sup>19</sup>but offer a food offering, a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old; see that they are without blemish;<sup>20</sup>also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil; three tenths of an ephah shall you offer for a bull, and two tenths for a ram;<sup>21</sup>a tenth shall you offer for each of the seven lambs;<sup>22</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you.<sup>23</sup>You shall offer these besides the burnt offering of the morning, which is for a regular burnt offering.<sup>24</sup>In the same way you shall offer daily, for seven days, the food of a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. It shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.<sup>25</sup>And on the seventh day you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work.<sup>26</sup>"On the day of the firstfruits, when you offer a grain offering of new grain to the LORD at your Feast of Weeks, you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work,<sup>27</sup>but offer a burnt offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old;<sup>28</sup>also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each bull, two tenths for one ram,<sup>29</sup>a tenth for each of the seven lambs;<sup>30</sup>with one male goat, to make atonement for you.<sup>31</sup>Besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, you shall offer them and their drink offering. See that they are without blemish.
28.overview:
As the new generation prepares to enter the land, God renews the calendar of worship: the daily, weekly, monthly and seasonal offerings that are to mark the rhythm of their life with him. Beneath what reads like a liturgical timetable lies a glad truth: God means to be worshipped continually, woven into the fabric of time.

The foundation is the “regular” or “continual” burnt offering: a lamb every morning and a lamb at twilight, never interrupted. Fellowship with God was not occasional but constant. Upon this daily foundation are layered the Sabbath, new-moon and festival offerings, an ascending rhythm that filled the whole calendar.

Hebrews gathers up these endless offerings and shows their meaning: they had to be repeated because they could never finish the work (Heb 10:11–12). Yet the continual offering also points to the continual intercession of Christ, our Great High Priest, who “always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25). The altar never went cold, because the love of God never sleeps.
28.theology:
Continual worship. The daily morning and evening offering taught that fellowship with God is constant, not occasional. Worship is to be the heartbeat of daily life, the altar never going cold.

The continual intercession of Christ. The unceasing offering foreshadows our Great High Priest who always lives to make intercession (Heb 7:25), pleading his finished sacrifice without interruption.

Time made holy. Day, week, month, and season are all consecrated to God. The whole calendar is filled with worship, anticipating eternal worship before the throne.
28.examples:
Then: Israel offered the continual morning and evening sacrifice, with added offerings for Sabbaths, new moons, and feasts, so that worship filled the whole calendar.

Now: The endless offerings that could never finish are fulfilled in Christ's one finished sacrifice and his unceasing intercession. Day and night your Mediator pleads for you, and his Spirit in you is what turns a distracted day into an offering. Your worship will never be as constant as the old altar was meant to be; his intercession is, and that is what keeps you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God restates the rhythm of worship for life in the land, beginning with the daily offering: a lamb every morning and every evening. Before any festival there is this steady heartbeat of approach to God.
verseByVerse.theology: The tamid, the continual daily offering (vv.3-6), frames all of Israel’s worship: before the feasts and festivals, there is the unbroken daily approach to God, morning and evening. It teaches that communion with God is meant to be constant, not occasional (cf. Ps 55:17; Dan 6:10). The daily lamb points to “the Lamb of God” (John 1:29), whose one offering is continually sufficient, so that we now “draw near” at every hour (Heb 10:19-22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: every single morning and evening, without fail, a lamb was offered — the steady heartbeat of a life lived before God.

Now: worship is daily, not just Sunday. “Evening and morning... I utter my complaint” (Ps 55:17). Through the once-for-all Lamb, we draw near continually (Heb 10:22).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel and say to them, 'My offering, my food for my food offerings, my pleasing aroma, you shall be careful to offer to me at its appointed time.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a single animal is named, God says four times in one sentence whose these offerings are: my offering, my food… my pleasing aroma. That is the frame for the next two chapters, and without it the calendar reads as religious bookkeeping. This is not Israel arranging her devotional life; it is a covenant Lord telling the people he redeemed what belongs to him. Worship in Scripture is first a response to a claim, not an expression of feeling.

The language of my food needs a word, because Israel’s neighbours meant it literally: their gods were fed by sacrifice. Scripture flatly denies that: If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine (Ps. 50:12). God empties the vocabulary of the pagan idea while keeping the warmth: the rising smoke is not nourishment, it is pleasure. Paul lifts the phrase onto the cross, Christ gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Eph. 5:2), and then onto a gift sent to a missionary in prison, a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God (Phil. 4:18).

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall say to them, This is the food offering that you shall offer to the LORD: two male lambs a year old without blemish, day by day, as a regular offering. The one lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight; also a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with a quarter of a hin of beaten oil. It is a regular burnt offering, which was ordained at Mount Sinai for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. Its drink offering shall be a quarter of a hin for each lamb. In the Holy Place you shall pour out a drink offering of strong drink to the LORD. The other lamb you shall offer at twilight. Like the grain offering of the morning, and like its drink offering, you shall offer it as a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The foundation of the whole calendar is its smallest item. Regular translates tamid, continual: whatever else was happening in Israel (harvest, war, plague, a good king or a bad one), a lamb died at dawn and a lamb died at dusk. Every feast in the chapter is offered besides the regular burnt offering; the special days are added on top and never replace it.

Two things follow. First, the cost: seven hundred and thirty lambs a year, for centuries, and none of them ever finished the matter, which is the argument of Hebrews. Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down (Heb. 10:11–12). The old altar never sat down because the work was never done.

Second, assurance. Israel lived each ordinary hour under a sacrifice at each end of the day; nobody had to wonder at three in the afternoon whether God had been approached. Christians have that assurance permanently, not because we keep the rhythm, but because he always lives to make intercession (Heb. 7:25). The tamid was silenced more than once by exile and war (Dan. 8:11). His intercession has never stopped.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Sabbath and New Moon Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the Sabbath the offering is doubled; each new moon brings a fuller set of sacrifices. Day, week and month are all consecrated to God.
verseByVerse.theology: The Sabbath and new-moon offerings (vv.9-15) build worship into the very structure of time — day, week, and month all marked by approach to God. Israel’s calendar was designed so that time itself belonged to the LORD, its rhythms punctuated by worship. It trains God’s people to sanctify their days, receiving each season from his hand (cf. Ps 31:15, “my times are in your hand”).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the week and the month, not just the day, were consecrated to God — time itself woven through with worship.

Now: we still sanctify our time to God — the Lord’s Day set apart, our weeks and seasons received from his hand. “My times are in your hand” (Ps 31:15).

verseByVerse.quote: "On the Sabbath day, two male lambs a year old without blemish, and two tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, and its drink offering: this is the burnt offering of every Sabbath, besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering. "At the beginnings of your months, you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish; also three tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for each bull, and two tenths of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for the one ram; and a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering for every lamb; for a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. Their drink offerings shall be half a hin of wine for a bull, a third of a hin for a ram, and a quarter of a hin for a lamb. This is the burnt offering of each month throughout the months of the year. Also one male goat for a sin offering to the LORD; it shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sabbath correction comes first: the day of rest is the day worship increases, not slackens. Ceasing from work was cleared ground, so that a nation could turn to God without the plough in the way.

Then the months. God claims the day at dawn and dusk, the week at its seventh day, the month at its first, and in the next chapter the year at its climax, until no unit of time is left unconsecrated. Isaiah throws the same two markers forward to the end of all things: From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD (Isa. 66:23).

And note the sober detail: one male goat for a sin offering. Every month, as Israel marked the turning of the season, sin was named again. The calendar of a redeemed people had a sin offering built into it, because God knew what a month does to his people and made provision in advance.

Does the Sabbath bind Christians today? It was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exod 31:13), and the New Testament calls Sabbaths a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Col 2:16–17). Many godly Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment, and this commentary honours them; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. The better reading is that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Heb 4:9–10), so no day binds the conscience (Rom 14:5); rest and gathering for worship on the Lord’s Day remain good gifts, gladly taken up out of joy and wisdom rather than as a law. Faithful Christians differ on this, and should differ charitably.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–31 — Passover, Unleavened Bread, and Firstfruits
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The annual feasts follow: Passover and Unleavened Bread, remembering the exodus, and the Feast of Weeks at the wheat harvest. Israel’s year retells the gospel, fulfilled in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: The feasts are prophecy on a calendar (cf. Lev 23). Passover proclaims redemption by the lamb’s blood — “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor 5:7); Unleavened Bread calls for purity, sweeping out the leaven of sin (1 Cor 5:8); Firstfruits/Weeks becomes Pentecost, the firstfruits of the Spirit’s harvest (Acts 2). The prescribed offerings surround each feast with worship, but their deepest meaning is the redemption they rehearse, now accomplished in Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: year by year Israel kept Passover and Firstfruits, retelling the story of their rescue and thanking God for the harvest.

Now: our Passover Lamb has been sacrificed (1 Cor 5:7); the firstfruits of the Spirit have come (Acts 2). The feasts pointed forward; in Christ they are kept.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the fourteenth day of the first month is the LORD's Passover, and on the fifteenth day of this month is a feast. Seven days shall unleavened bread be eaten. On the first day there shall be a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, but offer a food offering, a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old; see that they are without blemish; also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil; three tenths of an ephah shall you offer for a bull, and two tenths for a ram; a tenth shall you offer for each of the seven lambs; also one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you. You shall offer these besides the burnt offering of the morning, which is for a regular burnt offering. In the same way you shall offer daily, for seven days, the food of a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. It shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering. And on the seventh day you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The year opens where the nation opened: with the night in Egypt when the blood was on the doorposts. Israel’s calendar is a memory system. Every feast re-tells a saving act, so that a child born forty years after the exodus lived through it annually. The New Testament applies both halves of this spring feast in a single verse: Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump… For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7).

The order must not be reversed. First the lamb, then the leaven: the sacrifice is not the reward for the housecleaning, it is the reason for it. Israel did not earn Passover by removing the yeast; she removed the yeast because the lamb had died and she was leaving Egypt in the morning. A Christian who puts the purging first has misread the feast, and will spend his life sweeping.

Must Christians keep these feasts? They were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17): Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor 5:7), and the Lord’s Supper has taken the Passover’s place. Keeping them is a matter of freedom, not obligation (Rom 14:5–6), and never a condition of standing with God (Gal 4:10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: "On the day of the firstfruits, when you offer a grain offering of new grain to the LORD at your Feast of Weeks, you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, but offer a burnt offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old; also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each bull, two tenths for one ram, a tenth for each of the seven lambs; with one male goat, to make atonement for you. Besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, you shall offer them and their drink offering. See that they are without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Firstfruits came fifty days after Passover, offered before any of the new grain was eaten. A farmer brings the first sheaf, not the last, before the harvest is safely in: a pledge that the rest is coming. Strictly, the first barley sheaf was waved during Unleavened Bread, on the day after the Sabbath (Lev. 23:10–11), the day of the week Jesus rose; Weeks brought the firstfruits of the wheat. The logic is the same, and Paul reaches for it at the empty tomb: Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor. 15:20). His resurrection is the first sheaf, the guarantee of every believer’s body rising behind him.

And the date: fifty days after the Passover at which Jesus died, on the day Israel had brought her first grain for centuries, the Spirit fell and three thousand were gathered (Acts 2:41). Israel kept harvesting a field. God was keeping an appointment.

The chapter ends where it began, with the regular offering and animals without blemish. For a thousand years Israel searched her flocks for something perfect enough to offer, and never found anything better than a lamb. Then John the Baptist looked at Jesus and said the sentence the whole calendar had been waiting for: Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29).

29.title: The Feasts of the Seventh Month: The Climax of the Worship Year
29.text: <sup>1</sup>"On the first day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work. It is a day for you to blow the trumpets,<sup>2</sup>and you shall offer a burnt offering, for a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish;<sup>3</sup>also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the ram,<sup>4</sup>and one tenth for each of the seven lambs;<sup>5</sup>with one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you;<sup>6</sup>besides the burnt offering of the new moon, and its grain offering, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offering, according to the rule for them, for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>"On the tenth day of this seventh month you shall have a holy convocation and afflict yourselves. You shall do no work,<sup>8</sup>but you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old: see that they are without blemish.<sup>9</sup>And their grain offering shall be of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the one ram,<sup>10</sup>a tenth for each of the seven lambs:<sup>11</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the sin offering of atonement, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings.<sup>12</sup>"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, and you shall keep a feast to the LORD seven days.<sup>13</sup>And you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD, thirteen bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old; they shall be without blemish;<sup>14</sup>and their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each of the thirteen bulls, two tenths for each of the two rams,<sup>15</sup>and a tenth for each of the fourteen lambs;<sup>16</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>17</sup>"On the second day twelve bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>18</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>19</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings.<sup>20</sup>"On the third day eleven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>21</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>22</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>23</sup>"On the fourth day ten bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>24</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>25</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>26</sup>"On the fifth day nine bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>27</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>28</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>29</sup>"On the sixth day eight bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>30</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>31</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offerings.<sup>32</sup>"On the seventh day seven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>33</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>34</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offering.<sup>35</sup>"On the eighth day you shall have a solemn assembly. You shall not do any ordinary work,<sup>36</sup>but you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>37</sup>and the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bull, for the ram, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>38</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>39</sup>"These you shall offer to the LORD at your appointed feasts, in addition to your vow offerings and your freewill offerings, for your burnt offerings, and for your grain offerings, and for your drink offerings, and for your peace offerings."<sup>40</sup>So Moses told the people of Israel everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
29.overview:
Chapter 29 carries the calendar into the seventh month, the holiest and fullest of Israel's year: the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the great Feast of Booths. If chapter 28 established the daily rhythm, chapter 29 brings it to its climax, and the sheer abundance of sacrifice proclaims the lavish worship God's redemption deserves.

At the center stands the Day of Atonement (vv. 7–11), when the people afflicted their souls and atonement was made for the whole nation: a sinful people can dwell with a holy God only through blood. Hebrews shows that the high priest's yearly blood could never finally cleanse, until Christ “entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12).

The month ends with Booths, the harvest festival of joy, when Israel dwelt in shelters to remember the wilderness. The sweep of the chapter, trumpets sounding, atonement made, harvest joy overflowing, points to the consummation, when the trumpet shall sound, atonement is complete in Christ, and the redeemed from every nation dwell with God. “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).
29.theology:
The lavishness of worship. The abundance of offerings in the seventh month proclaims that God's redemption deserves extravagant, joyful worship, the climax of the whole sacred calendar.

Atonement at the center. The Day of Atonement points to Christ, who entered once for all with his own blood to secure eternal redemption (Heb 9:12), fulfilling what the annual day could only foreshadow.

A rehearsal for eternity. Trumpets, atonement, and the ingathering of booths anticipate the last trumpet, the finished work of Christ, and the nations gathered to dwell forever with God.
29.examples:
Then: Israel's holiest month overflowed with worship — trumpets sounding, atonement made for the nation, and the joyful Feast of Booths recalling their pilgrimage and looking to the harvest.

Now: The trumpet will sound, atonement is finished in Christ who entered once for all, and the redeemed of every nation will dwell forever in the booth of God's presence. Worship the God whose every feast was a rehearsal for the eternal joy now yours in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Trumpets and the Day of Atonement
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The seventh month opens with the Feast of Trumpets and reaches its solemn peak on the Day of Atonement. The trumpet calls the nation to attention; the Day of Atonement cleanses it.
verseByVerse.theology: The trumpet blast (v.1) summons God’s people to holy attention — a call to wake and gather before God (cf. the last trumpet, 1 Cor 15:52; 1 Thess 4:16). The Day of Atonement (vv.7-11), with its affliction of soul and its sin offering, is the yearly cleansing of the nation (Lev 16), fulfilled once for all when Christ “entered... by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Heb 9:12). The extra offerings here surround with worship what the blood accomplishes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the trumpet woke the nation to worship, and the Day of Atonement humbled and cleansed them before God.

Now: the trumpet still summons (1 Cor 15:52), and the atonement is finished — Christ has entered the true sanctuary with his own blood, once for all (Heb 9:12). We are cleansed, and we wait for the trumpet.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work. It is a day for you to blow the trumpets, and you shall offer a burnt offering, for a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish; also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the ram, and one tenth for each of the seven lambs; with one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you; besides the burnt offering of the new moon, and its grain offering, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offering, according to the rule for them, for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh month is to Israel’s year what the seventh day is to her week, and it opens with noise. Numbers has already said what trumpets are for: they summon the congregation, sound the alarm in war, and are blown over the sacrifices, a reminder of you before your God (10:9–10). A trumpet is not music; it is an interruption, telling a man that something has begun and he is required.

So the holiest month opens not with a sacrifice or a fast but with a sound ordering a nation to stop and pay attention. The trumpet keeps that meaning to the end of the Bible: at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable (1 Cor. 15:52); the Lord himself will descend from heaven… with the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thess. 4:16). Every autumn Israel heard a blast over the camp and stopped. One day a blast will go out over the whole earth, and everyone who ever lived will stop.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the tenth day of this seventh month you shall have a holy convocation and afflict yourselves. You shall do no work, but you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old: see that they are without blemish. And their grain offering shall be of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the one ram, a tenth for each of the seven lambs: also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the sin offering of atonement, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afflict yourselves is the standing phrase for fasting and self-humbling, and this is the only fast the law of Moses commanded. Once a year the nation stopped eating and working and attended to its sin while the high priest went behind the curtain with blood. Leviticus 16 gives the ceremony; Numbers adds only the offerings, assuming the reader knows what the day means.

Hebrews builds its central argument on this day. Into the second room only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood (Heb. 9:7): the way in was not yet open. Then the contrast: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20).

The day’s two commands have both been transformed. The affliction has been answered, for the sin mourned every autumn has been dealt with once; and the rest has been deepened, for the Christian rests from his own work permanently: whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his (Heb. 4:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The month closes with the Feast of Booths, seven days celebrating the harvest and God’s care in the wilderness. It required more offerings than any other feast: abundant worship for abundant joy.
verseByVerse.theology: Booths (Tabernacles) celebrated both the ingathering harvest and God’s faithful care in the wilderness (Lev 23:42-43), Israel dwelling in temporary shelters as a reminder of their pilgrim past. Its lavish offerings express overflowing gratitude. It looked forward to the final ingathering, and Jesus used its great water ceremony to cry, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). Ultimately it anticipates the day God will “tabernacle” with his people forever (Rev 21:3), when the harvest is home and the pilgrimage is done.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: for seven joyful days Israel dwelt in booths, giving thanks for the harvest and remembering God’s care through the desert.

Now: we are still pilgrims in temporary tents (2 Cor 5:1), giving thanks, longing for the day God will dwell with us forever and “wipe away every tear” (Rev 21:3-4). The great feast is still ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, and you shall keep a feast to the LORD seven days. And you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD, thirteen bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old; they shall be without blemish; and their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each of the thirteen bulls, two tenths for each of the two rams, and a tenth for each of the fourteen lambs; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five days after the fast comes the greatest celebration of the year, opening with the largest single day of sacrifice in the calendar. Leviticus gives the command that names it: You shall dwell in booths for seven days… that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt (Lev. 23:42–43).

Consider who was told to do this. A generation on the edge of a land full of houses they did not build (Deut. 6:10–11) is instructed to camp out annually, for ever. God knew what settled prosperity does to memory. He built in one week a year when a wealthy farmer slept under leaves and remembered that his family once had nothing and was carried. It is the instinct behind the Lord’s Supper: a small, physical, repeated act that keeps a people from forgetting what saved them.

Abraham, Hebrews says, never stopped living that way: living in tents with Isaac and Jacob… For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Heb. 11:9–10). One week a year Israel lived like a pilgrim again, which is what she still was, and what the church has never stopped being.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the second day twelve bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings. "On the third day eleven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering. "On the fourth day ten bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering. "On the fifth day nine bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering. "On the sixth day eight bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offerings. "On the seventh day seven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eighteen verses in which almost nothing changes except one thing, deliberately: the bulls count down, thirteen to seven, and the week’s total is exactly seventy. Jewish interpreters connected this with the seventy nations of Genesis 10, reading the week as Israel offering on behalf of the world. Numbers does not say so, and no honest reader should claim more than the text gives. But the instinct is biblical, because this is the feast Zechariah says the nations will come and keep: Then everyone who survives of all the nations that have come against Jerusalem shall go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of hosts, and to keep the Feast of Booths (Zech. 14:16).

The repetition teaches too. This was the most expensive week of the year, a herd of cattle burned in seven days at the busiest point of harvest, and it was the week of greatest joy. Costly worship and glad worship are not opposites here; they are the same week.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the eighth day you shall have a solemn assembly. You shall not do any ordinary work, but you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish, and the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bull, for the ram, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An extra day is added after the seven: quieter, one bull instead of thirteen, a final gathering before everyone goes home.

By Jesus’ time the feast had acquired a ceremony not in the law, described in the Mishnah (the early Jewish law code). Each morning a priest filled a golden pitcher at the pool of Siloam and poured it out at the base of the altar, while the people sang: With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation (Isa. 12:3). It was a prayer for rain, and many think it also recalled the water from the rock in Numbers 20.

John records what happened one year at that moment: On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water’” (John 7:37–38). Interpreters differ on whether John’s last day is the seventh day or this eighth one; either way it was the feast’s climax. Soon afterward, with the great lamps of the feast still in memory, he said, I am the light of the world (John 8:12). The feast had been asking a question every autumn since Moses. He answered it out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: "These you shall offer to the LORD at your appointed feasts, in addition to your vow offerings and your freewill offerings, for your burnt offerings, and for your grain offerings, and for your drink offerings, and for your peace offerings." So Moses told the people of Israel everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The calendar closes with a clause that keeps it from becoming a cage: in addition to your vow offerings and your freewill offerings. Chapters 28 and 29 are the floor, not the ceiling. God has specified what is due, and then makes room for everything a grateful Israelite might bring beyond it. A freewill offering is what its name says: nobody commanded it and nobody counted it.

That balance is easy to lose either way. A believer can reduce his life with God to the appointed times and never come to him uninvited; or he can despise the appointed times as routine and worship only when he feels like it. Israel was given both, in the same paragraph. The freewill offering grew from a redeemed people’s gratitude, and the Spirit who now lives in believers is the one who stirs that gladness beyond duty.

The last verse is the quietest: everything just as the LORD had commanded. An old man with weeks to live read out every bull, every ram, every tenth of an ephah, exactly as given. Israel’s whole calendar reached the people because one man refused to abbreviate what God had said.

30.title: Vows: The Integrity of the Word
30.text: <sup>1</sup>Moses spoke to the heads of the tribes of the people of Israel, saying, "This is what the LORD has commanded.<sup>2</sup>If a man vows a vow to the LORD, or swears an oath to bind himself by a pledge, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.<sup>3</sup>"If a woman vows a vow to the LORD and binds herself by a pledge, while within her father's house in her youth,<sup>4</sup>and her father hears of her vow and of her pledge by which she has bound herself and says nothing to her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand.<sup>5</sup>But if her father opposes her on the day that he hears of it, no vow of hers, no pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand. And the LORD will forgive her, because her father opposed her.<sup>6</sup>"If she marries a husband, while under her vows or any thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she has bound herself,<sup>7</sup>and her husband hears of it and says nothing to her on the day that he hears, then her vows shall stand, and her pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand.<sup>8</sup>But if, on the day that her husband comes to hear of it, he opposes her, then he makes void her vow that was on her, and the thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she bound herself. And the LORD will forgive her.<sup>9</sup>(But any vow of a widow or of a divorced woman, anything by which she has bound herself, shall stand against her.)<sup>10</sup>And if she vowed in her husband's house or bound herself by a pledge with an oath,<sup>11</sup>and her husband heard of it and said nothing to her and did not oppose her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she bound herself shall stand.<sup>12</sup>But if her husband makes them null and void on the day that he hears them, then whatever proceeds out of her lips concerning her vows or concerning her pledge of herself shall not stand. Her husband has made them void, and the LORD will forgive her.<sup>13</sup>Any vow and any binding oath to afflict herself, her husband may establish, or her husband may make void.<sup>14</sup>But if her husband says nothing to her from day to day, then he establishes all her vows or all her pledges that are upon her. He has established them, because he said nothing to her on the day that he heard of them.<sup>15</sup>But if he makes them null and void after he has heard of them, then he shall bear her iniquity."<sup>16</sup>These are the statutes that the LORD commanded Moses about a man and his wife and about a father and his daughter while she is in her youth within her father's house.
30.overview:
From the festal calendar the book turns to something quieter but no less serious: the binding nature of vows. In a world where promises are broken without a second thought, this chapter recovers the weight of human speech. A vow made before God binds.

Words matter to God because he is a God of his word. He keeps his promises, and his people, redeemed by his faithfulness, are to be people of their word. Ecclesiastes warns, “When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it… It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay” (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5).
