The remaining laws address vows made by a daughter under her father or a wife under her husband, which the head of the household may affirm or annul on the day he hears it. To modern ears this sounds strange, but its intent is protective: it guards against rash or harmful vows and locates accountability in the household. Jesus presses the point further: let your yes be yes (Matthew 5:37). And the chapter’s last clause, in which a husband bears his wife’s iniquity, leads the Christian reader to the One who carried the debt of promises his people could not keep.
30.theology:
The sanctity of speech. A vow to God binds; the word once given must be kept. Faithfulness in speech reflects the integrity of the God of truth, who keeps every promise.

Words matter to God. Because God is a God of his word, his people are to be people of their word. To break a vow to God is to lie before the One who is Truth itself. And he has kept his own word in the fullest way: all the promises of God find their Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Yes be yes. Jesus calls his people to such transparent integrity (Matt 5:37) that their plain word is as trustworthy as any oath, for they serve the God who cannot lie.
30.examples:
Then: Israel was bound to keep every vow made to the LORD, with the household head able to confirm or annul vows made by dependents, guarding against rash pledges.

Now: Your word is sacred because you serve the God whose word never fails, and his Spirit in you is the Spirit of truth, who makes a truthful tongue possible. Let your yes be yes. And when you find you have broken your word, confess it and make it right where you can: Christ kept every word he spoke in your place, and his faithfulness, not yours, is your standing with God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A chapter on the seriousness of vows, with provisions for vows made by women within a household and the role of a father or husband in confirming or annulling them. Behind the detail is one principle: words spoken to God bind, and integrity of speech matters to him.
verseByVerse.theology:
“He shall not break his word” (v.2) — a vow to God is a serious, binding thing (cf. Deut 23:21-23; Eccl 5:4-5, “When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it”). God cares deeply about the integrity of our speech; a promise made in his hearing is not to be treated lightly. The provisions for annulling a woman’s vow within the household reflect the ordered authority structures of that society, yet the governing principle — keep your word to God — is timeless. Jesus deepens it: let your “yes be yes” (Matthew 5:37), so that vows become almost unnecessary among truthful people.

Does a Christian husband hold this power today? No. The annulment procedure belonged to Israel’s household law, and the New Testament does not carry it into the church. A believing wife answers to the Lord for her own promises. Headship, where Scripture speaks of it, is Christ’s kind of self-giving love, never control; a man who uses religion to dominate or harm his wife has abandoned it, and abuse is never to be tolerated.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a vow to God was no light matter; the one who made it was bound to keep it.

Now: God still weighs our words. Be slow to promise and faithful to perform, for “it is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay” (Ecclesiastes 5:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to the heads of the tribes of the people of Israel, saying, "This is what the LORD has commanded. If a man vows a vow to the LORD, or swears an oath to bind himself by a pledge, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything else in the chapter is measured against this. For a man there is no release clause: no father can annul his vow, no elder can review it, no circumstance is listed under which it lapses. He said it; he does it. The chapter so often read as a restriction on women opens by binding men absolutely.

The reason is not that words are magic but that God keeps his. A vow was made to the LORD, and breaking it implied that the God who hears lets things slide, a lie about his character told with your life.

Scripture has grim examples of what the absence of a release clause could mean. Jephthah made a rash vow and destroyed his own daughter with it (Judg. 11:30–39). Herod made a rash promise at a birthday party and beheaded John the Baptist rather than look weak before his guests (Mark 6:23–26). Both would have done better to break their word. There is a pride that dresses up as integrity, and it is most dangerous when it refuses to admit it should never have spoken.

Should Christians make vows or oaths? Jesus forbids the evasive swearing that tried to dodge obligations: Let what you say be simply “Yes” or “No” (Matt 5:37). He does not forbid solemn promises before God: marriage vows, oaths in court, ordination vows. God himself swore an oath (Heb 6:17), and Paul called God to witness (2 Cor 1:23). What a Christian promises, he must keep.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a woman vows a vow to the LORD and binds herself by a pledge, while within her father's house in her youth, and her father hears of her vow and of her pledge by which she has bound herself and says nothing to her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand. But if her father opposes her on the day that he hears of it, no vow of hers, no pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand. And the LORD will forgive her, because her father opposed her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The qualified cases are misread constantly, and four things govern them, every one of which limits the father rather than the daughter. First, the window is a single day; after that the vow is fixed and he has no power over it. Second, it applies only to an unmarried girl still in her father’s household (v. 16), which in that economy meant a young woman with no property of her own, who might have pledged goods or labour that were not hers to pledge. Third, he can only annul; he can never impose a vow. Fourth, the release is not grudging: the LORD will forgive her. God will not hold a woman liable for a promise she has been prevented from keeping.

Read plainly, the provision is a protection: household law for a society organised around the family as one economic unit, not a pronouncement on the worth of women. And it comes three chapters after five women with no legal standing walked to the front of the assembly and God said the daughters of Zelophehad are right, changing Israel’s inheritance law because of them. Same book, same Lawgiver, same season on the plains of Moab. Whatever chapter 30 is doing, contempt is not available as a reading.

verseByVerse.quote: "If she marries a husband, while under her vows or any thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she has bound herself, and her husband hears of it and says nothing to her on the day that he hears, then her vows shall stand, and her pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand. But if, on the day that her husband comes to hear of it, he opposes her, then he makes void her vow that was on her, and the thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she bound herself. And the LORD will forgive her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second case is a woman who marries while a vow is already on her, with the same single day, the same limited power, and the same gracious clause.

The law’s phrase is thoughtless utterance of her lips: a word blurted out before the cost was counted. Everyone knows that situation from the inside. Things get promised at gravesides and in hospital corridors on the worst night of a person’s life: “If you will only do this, I will never again…” Such a vow can be sincere, godly in motive, and completely unpayable.

The law neither mocks such promises nor treats them as unbreakable chains. Someone who loves the person and stands outside the emotion of the moment may say within a day: this must not bind you for forty years. And God underwrites the release himself. That is not a loophole; it is mercy written into the statute book. He is not looking for ways to hold his people to their worst moments.

verseByVerse.quote: (But any vow of a widow or of a divorced woman, anything by which she has bound herself, shall stand against her.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This bracketed verse carries more than it looks. A widow and a divorced woman have no father over them and no husband beside them; nobody can annul what they say. Their word goes straight to God and binds them exactly as a man’s does.

Both sides of that are true. It is a statement of full standing: whatever the surrounding culture thought of a woman alone, Israel’s law treats her promises as those of an adult who answers to God directly. It is also a real exposure: she has nobody to catch a rash word before it hardens.

Which is why Scripture insists these are the people God watches over personally: Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation (Ps. 68:5). She is not less protected. Her protection has been taken up by somebody higher than a household.

verseByVerse.quote: And if she vowed in her husband's house or bound herself by a pledge with an oath, and her husband heard of it and said nothing to her and did not oppose her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she bound herself shall stand. But if her husband makes them null and void on the day that he hears them, then whatever proceeds out of her lips concerning her vows or concerning her pledge of herself shall not stand. Her husband has made them void, and the LORD will forgive her. Any vow and any binding oath to afflict herself, her husband may establish, or her husband may make void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third case is a wife who vows while in her husband’s house. The pattern holds, and verse 13 names the kind of vow chiefly in view: vows to afflict herself.

That changes the picture. The vows the law is most concerned about are vows of self-denial: fasting, abstaining, going without. So the authority here is mainly a power to stop somebody hurting herself, not to stop her serving God. A wife who in grief or guilt pledges to fast for a year, or to give away what the household needs to live on, can be relieved of it. It is a brake on self-punishment.

That guard is still needed. Religious people try to settle an account with God by taking something from themselves, and the more ashamed they are the heavier the pledge. The gospel has no place for it: These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (Col. 2:23). God never made self-punishment the price of forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: But if her husband says nothing to her from day to day, then he establishes all her vows or all her pledges that are upon her. He has established them, because he said nothing to her on the day that he heard of them. But if he makes them null and void after he has heard of them, then he shall bear her iniquity." These are the statutes that the LORD commanded Moses about a man and his wife and about a father and his daughter while she is in her youth within her father's house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two clauses close the chapter, and they decide how it should be read.

The first: silence is not neutrality. A husband who says nothing establishes all her vows. A man who declines to engage with what is happening in his household has not avoided responsibility for it; he has taken it on by default.

The second is the sentence the chapter turns on: he shall bear her iniquity. If he lets the vow stand and later prevents her keeping it, the guilt transfers to him. Everything that sounds like unchecked male authority dies on that clause. The power is bounded by a day, can only release and never impose, and its misuse is charged to the man’s account before God. That is the biblical shape of headship wherever it appears: never a licence, always a liability, measured by Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph. 5:25).

Read that phrase once more: a husband carrying his wife’s guilt because of a promise. Here it happens through his failure. The phrase is an echo, not a prophecy, but Christians can hardly miss it: another Husband did it by deliberate choice, who heard what his bride had bound herself to and could not pay, and did not annul it but assumed it: the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isa. 53:6). The church was released from an unpayable debt by a Man who took it and bore it away.

31.title: War Against Midian: Holy War and the Seriousness of Sin
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Avenge the people of Israel on the Midianites. Afterward you shall be gathered to your people."<sup>3</sup>So Moses spoke to the people, saying, "Arm men from among you for the war, that they may go against Midian to execute the LORD's vengeance on Midian.<sup>4</sup>You shall send a thousand from each of the tribes of Israel to the war."<sup>5</sup>So there were provided, out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand from each tribe, twelve thousand armed for war.<sup>6</sup>And Moses sent them to the war, a thousand from each tribe, together with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, with the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for the alarm in his hand.<sup>7</sup>They warred against Midian, as the LORD commanded Moses, and killed every male.<sup>8</sup>They killed the kings of Midian with the rest of their slain, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the five kings of Midian. And they also killed Balaam the son of Beor with the sword.<sup>9</sup>And the people of Israel took captive the women of Midian and their little ones, and they took as plunder all their cattle, their flocks, and all their goods.<sup>10</sup>All their cities in the places where they lived, and all their encampments, they burned with fire,<sup>11</sup>and took all the spoil and all the plunder, both of man and of beast.<sup>12</sup>Then they brought the captives and the plunder and the spoil to Moses, and to Eleazar the priest, and to the congregation of the people of Israel, at the camp on the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.<sup>13</sup>Moses and Eleazar the priest and all the chiefs of the congregation went to meet them outside the camp.<sup>14</sup>And Moses was angry with the officers of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, who had come from service in the war.<sup>15</sup>Moses said to them, "Have you let all the women live?<sup>16</sup>Behold, these, on Balaam's advice, caused the people of Israel to act treacherously against the LORD in the incident of Peor, and so the plague came among the congregation of the LORD.<sup>17</sup>Now therefore, kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known man by lying with him.<sup>18</sup>But all the young girls who have not known man by lying with him keep alive for yourselves.<sup>19</sup>Encamp outside the camp seven days. Whoever of you has killed any person and whoever has touched any slain, purify yourselves and your captives on the third day and on the seventh day.<sup>20</sup>You shall purify every garment, every article of skin, all work of goats' hair, and every article of wood."<sup>21</sup>Then Eleazar the priest said to the men in the army who had gone to battle: "This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded Moses:<sup>22</sup>only the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron, the tin, and the lead,<sup>23</sup>everything that can stand the fire, you shall pass through the fire, and it shall be clean. Nevertheless, it shall also be purified with the water for impurity. And whatever cannot stand the fire, you shall pass through the water.<sup>24</sup>You must wash your clothes on the seventh day, and you shall be clean. And afterward you may come into the camp."<sup>25</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>26</sup>"Take the count of the plunder that was taken, both of man and of beast, you and Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers' houses of the congregation,<sup>27</sup>and divide the plunder into two parts between the warriors who went out to battle and all the congregation.<sup>28</sup>And levy for the LORD a tribute from the men of war who went out to battle, one out of five hundred, of the people and of the oxen and of the donkeys and of the flocks.<sup>29</sup>Take it from their half and give it to Eleazar the priest as a contribution to the LORD.<sup>30</sup>And from the people of Israel's half you shall take one drawn out of every fifty, of the people, of the oxen, of the donkeys, and of 31.overview:
Chapter 31 records God's judgment on Midian, the nation that, on Balaam's counsel, seduced Israel into the deadly sin of Peor (ch. 25). It is one of the hardest chapters in Numbers, a chapter of holy war, to be read with care and trembling. The Midianites were not innocent bystanders; they had deliberately set out to corrupt the people of God, and twenty-four thousand Israelites had died as a result.

We must resist two errors. The first is to make ourselves God’s judges. The horror a reader feels at verses 17–18 is not wrong, and this commentary will not ask anyone to lose it, but the deeper wonder is not that God judges sin but that he is so patient with it. The second error is to make this a charter for human violence; it is not. These were unique, God-commanded acts of judgment in redemptive history, never a model for the church, whose warfare is not “against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12) and whose weapons are the gospel and prayer.

The chapter records the death of Balaam (v. 8) and gives great attention to the purification of warriors and plunder, for even righteous warfare brings the defilement of death. Its deepest note is the holiness of God and the seriousness of sin, which drives us to the cross, where the judgment our sin deserves fell on Christ.
31.theology:
The seriousness of sin. The judgment on Midian responds to a calculated seduction that nearly destroyed Israel. God's holiness means sin is graver than we dare imagine; the wonder is his patience.

Death defiles. Even righteous warriors must be purified, for contact with death contaminates. Holiness is required to dwell with God, pointing to the deeper cleansing of Christ's blood.

The corrupter judged. Balaam, who could not curse but taught seduction, perishes in the judgment. The one who loves the wages of unrighteousness reaps its end (2 Pet 2:15).
31.examples:
Then: God judged Midian for seducing Israel into the sin of Peor; Balaam perished, the warriors were purified from death's defilement, and a portion of the spoil was given to the LORD.

Now: Read this trembling text in its setting, never as a charter for violence, and let it drive you to the cross, where the judgment your sin deserved fell on Christ that you might be spared and cleansed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s command from chapter 25 is carried out: judgment on Midian for scheming to destroy God’s people at Peor. Among the slain is Balaam, who fell under the judgment his own counsel unleashed.
verseByVerse.theology: The Midian war is judgment on those who engineered Israel’s fall at Peor (25:16-18; 31:16). Balaam’s death (v.8) closes his tragic story: gifted with true oracles, he loved “gain from wrongdoing” (2 Pet 2:15) and perished with God’s enemies. These conquest-era judgments belong to a unique moment in redemptive history and must not be made a template for the church, whose “weapons... are not of the flesh” (2 Cor 10:4); yet they reveal the real severity of God against those who deliberately lead his people into sin (Luke 17:1-2).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the seducers of Peor faced God’s judgment, and Balaam, who sold his gift for profit, died among them.

Now: we war not with swords but against sin and the schemes that corrupt (Eph 6:12; 2 Cor 10:4), in the strength of the Spirit Christ has given, not our own. Yet the warning stands: God takes with deadly seriousness those who lead his people astray, and the love of gain can ruin even a gifted soul (2 Pet 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Avenge the people of Israel on the Midianites. Afterward you shall be gathered to your people." So Moses spoke to the people, saying, "Arm men from among you for the war, that they may go against Midian to execute the LORD's vengeance on Midian. You shall send a thousand from each of the tribes of Israel to the war." So there were provided, out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand from each tribe, twelve thousand armed for war. And Moses sent them to the war, a thousand from each tribe, together with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, with the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for the alarm in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the last thing God gives Moses to do, and Moses passes it on not as avenge yourselves but to execute the LORD’s vengeance on Midian. It is not tribal payback but a judicial sentence, and the judge is God.

The size of the force says the same: twelve thousand out of a nation that had just counted 601,730 fighting men. Two per cent. Nobody conquers a country with two per cent of an army. This is a punitive expedition of fixed size against a fixed target, and a priest, Phinehas, goes at its head carrying holy things. Israel is not being turned loose.

The target is precise. Moab began the seduction at Shittim (25:1) and is not touched, because God had forbidden it: Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle (Deut. 2:9). Midian, which worked with Balaam to engineer the whole thing, is judged. God’s judgments land where the guilt is and stop.

verseByVerse.quote: They warred against Midian, as the LORD commanded Moses, and killed every male. They killed the kings of Midian with the rest of their slain, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the five kings of Midian. And they also killed Balaam the son of Beor with the sword. And the people of Israel took captive the women of Midian and their little ones, and they took as plunder all their cattle, their flocks, and all their goods. All their cities in the places where they lived, and all their encampments, they burned with fire, and took all the spoil and all the plunder, both of man and of beast. Then they brought the captives and the plunder and the spoil to Moses, and to Eleazar the priest, and to the congregation of the people of Israel, at the camp on the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The battle is reported in a sentence, and the text pauses over the five kings. One should be familiar: Zur, the father of Cozbi, the woman Phinehas killed in the tent (25:15). The men at the top of Midian had put their own daughters into the plan.

Then, almost in passing, Balaam. This is the man who stood on a mountain with the Spirit of God upon him and said Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his (23:10). He set off home (24:25), yet when the sword came he was among the enemies of the nation he had blessed four times. He could not sell a curse, so he sold a strategy, and the fee killed him.

The New Testament never mentions him without the money: he loved gain from wrongdoing (2 Pet. 2:15); men abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error (Jude 11); the risen Christ names the teaching of Balaam as a live danger in a congregation (Rev. 2:14). A man may hold flawless doctrine and receive real revelation and still be lost, because none of that is the same as loving God more than what God’s enemies offer to pay.

If every male was killed, how is Midian strong again in Judges 6? Because this war touched only part of Midian. These were the Midianite clans near Moab, under five kings; Midian was a widespread nomadic people across the desert, and “every male” is the language of decisive victory over this group, not of the whole people. Judges 6 comes perhaps two centuries later. The captive girls (vv. 32–41) were taken as servants or wives under the law’s protections (Deut 21:10–14), and thirty-two were given to the sanctuary’s service.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The returning soldiers, and all they have touched, must be purified before re-entering the camp. Nothing touched by death comes casually back into the presence of a holy God.
verseByVerse.theology: Even a divinely commanded war leaves death-defilement that must be cleansed (vv.19-24; cf. Num 19). Death is the enemy and the wage of sin (Romans 6:23), never something God’s people handle lightly, and holiness is not suspended even in righteous conflict.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: even victorious soldiers, and their plunder, had to be cleansed of death’s defilement before returning to the camp.

Now: we never handle sin and death casually, even when we must confront them. The one who has touched what defiles comes back to be cleansed (1 John 1:7-9), for holiness is never suspended.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Eleazar the priest and all the chiefs of the congregation went to meet them outside the camp. And Moses was angry with the officers of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, who had come from service in the war. Moses said to them, "Have you let all the women live? Behold, these, on Balaam's advice, caused the people of Israel to act treacherously against the LORD in the incident of Peor, and so the plague came among the congregation of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The army comes home victorious and Moses is furious. Verse 16 is the hinge of the chapter and must be read before the next two verses: the women were the means by which, on Balaam’s advice, Israel was led into treachery at Peor.

This finally tells us what happened at Shittim. It was not an accident of proximity but a designed operation. Balaam had discovered on three mountains what no fee could buy, and drew the conclusion: what cannot be reached from outside can be invited in. Midian executed the plan using their own women, a chief’s daughter among them, and twenty-four thousand Israelites died. The women before Moses are, in the text’s own account, the people through whom that plan was carried out.

That does not make what follows easy. It does mean that a reader who treats this as an unprovoked massacre of bystanders has not read verse 16.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known man by lying with him. But all the young girls who have not known man by lying with him keep alive for yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the two hardest verses in Numbers, and there is no honest way to make them comfortable. If they appal you, you are reading them correctly. Scripture does not ask anyone to feel nothing here, and to hurry past them or pretend the words say something gentler would not be honest. So let us say what can honestly be said, and then say plainly what cannot.

First, what the passage is. This is the devoted judgment of God (the kind the Old Testament elsewhere calls herem, the handing over of something wholly to God, here for destruction) on a particular people, at a particular moment, through a specific command, in the unrepeatable period when God governed one nation directly as its king. It is dated, bounded and explicitly commanded, and Scripture never generalises it. Moses treats the married women as the group through whom the plan of verse 16 was carried out; the text does not sort them one by one, and we should not pretend it does. The command is given to a levied force under a priest, not a mob, and it is over within days.

Second, what the passage is not, and this cannot be said too strongly: a model for anyone, anywhere, ever again. No church, nation, movement or individual has the authority Israel had here, and the New Testament removes the possibility: My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36); For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:3–4). Every Christian who has reached for this chapter to justify violence has read it against the plain teaching of his own Lord.

Third, the girls who were spared. Keep alive for yourselves reads horribly in English and needs its legal context. The law governing a woman taken captive in war is Deuteronomy 21:10–14, unlike anything else in the ancient world: she is given a full month to mourn her father and mother, may then be married, not used, and if the man does not want her she must be let go free; he may never sell her or treat her as property, since you have humiliated her. It is not our world and not painless, but it is far from what a modern reader assumes.

But why the boys? This is the part that stays with every honest reader, and Scripture does not give a full reason. The likeliest one is that in the ancient world a clan’s sons carried on its name and its feuds, and God was ending the line of the Midianite houses that had set out to destroy Israel; the same reasoning lies behind the judgment of Amalek in 1 Samuel 15. This commentary will not invent more than that. What can be said is that no child who died that day passed out of the hands of the Judge of all the earth, and Christians have long confessed that little ones who die are not beyond his mercy in Christ (the Westminster Confession 10.3 speaks of elect infants dying in infancy being saved by Christ).

Fourth, the question underneath the question. What troubles us is really not Israel but God. Does God have the right to end human lives? He does, and exercises it in every generation; everyone who dies, dies at a time he appointed: See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; I kill and I make alive (Deut. 32:39). What is unusual in Numbers 31 is not that God judges, but that he does it visibly, through a named instrument, where we can watch.

And here an honest reader is left. Abraham’s question stands, asked as a confidence rather than an accusation: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Gen. 18:25). We are not given a full account of this chapter. We are given proof, from elsewhere, of what kind of God is judging. He did not settle the question of his justice by explaining Numbers 31. He settled it by coming himself, standing under the judgment his justice required, and dying of it: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8). A reader who cannot see the bottom of this chapter is asked to trust the character of the One who bled at Calvary. That is the only ground on which anyone has been able to look at the severity of God without despair.

verseByVerse.quote: Encamp outside the camp seven days. Whoever of you has killed any person and whoever has touched any slain, purify yourselves and your captives on the third day and on the seventh day. You shall purify every garment, every article of skin, all work of goats' hair, and every article of wood." Then Eleazar the priest said to the men in the army who had gone to battle: "This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded Moses: only the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron, the tin, and the lead, everything that can stand the fire, you shall pass through the fire, and it shall be clean. Nevertheless, it shall also be purified with the water for impurity. And whatever cannot stand the fire, you shall pass through the water. You must wash your clothes on the seventh day, and you shall be clean. And afterward you may come into the camp."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What comes next is easy to miss and morally enormous. The army has carried out a God-commanded judgment, and God does not send them home as heroes. He sends them outside the camp for seven days, to be cleansed with the water made from the ashes of the red heifer (ch. 19), the provision for defilement by death. Hebrews names this rite as a picture of Christ: if the ashes of a heifer made the defiled clean outwardly, how much more will the blood of Christ purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:13–14).

Israel’s soldiers came back from obeying God unclean. Not guilty; unclean. There is no garland, no parade, no suggestion that killing at God’s command left a man untouched. He had handled death, and had to be washed before he could worship. A religion that sends its soldiers to a week outside the camp and a sprinkling of water is not a religion that glories in blood.

Eleazar adds the rule for the plunder: what can stand the fire goes through the fire, everything else through the water. Nothing comes into the camp unpurified, and the test is the material’s capacity to survive. Paul uses a similar image for the day every Christian’s work is examined: each one’s work will become manifest… because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done (1 Cor. 3:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The plunder is divided between soldiers and congregation, with a tribute for the LORD and the Levites. Then the officers, finding not one man missing, bring an offering of gold. Even victory is met with worship.
verseByVerse.theology: A portion of everything is set apart “as a contribution to the LORD” (vv.28-29) — even the spoils of war belong first to God, who gave the victory (cf. 1 Chr 29:14). The officers’ freewill offering after finding no soldier lost (vv.48-50) is thanksgiving for God’s protecting hand. Victory is received as grace and returned in worship; the God who wins the battle is given the glory and the firstfruits of its reward.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: not a single Israelite soldier had fallen, and the grateful officers brought their gold to the LORD in thanks for his protection.

Now: every victory, every safe deliverance, calls for worship and thanksgiving. What we receive from God’s hand we return to him in gratitude, for “all things come from you, and of your own have we given you” (1 Chr 29:14).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Take the count of the plunder that was taken, both of man and of beast, you and Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers' houses of the congregation, and divide the plunder into two parts between the warriors who went out to battle and all the congregation. And levy for the LORD a tribute from the men of war who went out to battle, one out of five hundred, of the people and of the oxen and of the donkeys and of the flocks. Take it from their half and give it to Eleazar the priest as a contribution to the LORD. And from the people of Israel's half you shall take one drawn out of every fifty, of the people, of the oxen, of the donkeys, and of the flocks, of all the cattle, and give them to the Levites who keep guard over the tabernacle of the LORD." And Moses and Eleazar the priest did as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two principles govern the division, both fairer than anyone would have arranged alone.

First, half goes to the twelve thousand who fought and half to the congregation who stayed home. David will make the same ruling centuries later: as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage; they shall share alike (1 Sam. 30:24). God’s people share the outcome of a work only some of them could do.

Second, the tribute is levied unequally, in the direction nobody would expect: the fighters give one in five hundred, the congregation one in fifty, ten times as much. God’s arithmetic takes account of what a thing cost the giver, the principle Jesus applies watching a widow’s two coins: they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had (Mark 12:44).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the plunder remaining of the spoil that the army took was 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys, and 32,000 persons in all, women who had not known man by lying with him. And the half, the portion of those who had gone out in the army, numbered 337,500 sheep, and the LORD's tribute of sheep was 675. The cattle were 36,000, of which the LORD's tribute was 72. The donkeys were 30,500, of which the LORD's tribute was 61. The persons were 16,000, of which the LORD's tribute was 32 persons. And Moses gave the tribute, which was the contribution for the LORD, to Eleazar the priest, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Modern readers skim the accounts. Consider instead who does the counting: Moses, Eleazar and the heads of the fathers’ houses together, in public, with the figures written down to the last animal. No single man handles it and nothing is taken on trust. The figures are very large, and, as with the census totals, some careful scholars think ancient conventions of counting may be at work; either way the point is precision in the open.

That is Paul’s standard with the church’s money: We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (2 Cor. 8:20–21). Wherever God’s people handle wealth, the books are to be open. A ledger is a spiritual document.

verseByVerse.quote: From the people of Israel's half, which Moses separated from that of the men who had served in the army— now the congregation's half was 337,500 sheep, 36,000 cattle, and 30,500 donkeys, and 16,000 persons— from the people of Israel's half Moses took one of every 50, both of persons and of beasts, and gave them to the Levites who kept guard over the tabernacle of the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary: Out of the congregation’s half Moses takes one in fifty for the Levites. They did not fight and own no land, and out of a war they took no part in they are given a portion. The tribe with no inheritance is provided for by everyone else’s, so that men can serve at the tabernacle full time. The arrangement of chapter 18 does not lapse because the nation is at war. God’s provision for those who serve at his tent is not funded out of what is left over; it is a line item.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officers who were over the thousands of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, came near to Moses and said to Moses, "Your servants have counted the men of war who are under our command, and there is not a man missing from us. And we have brought the LORD's offering, what each man found, articles of gold, armlets and bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and beads, to make atonement for ourselves before the LORD." And Moses and Eleazar the priest received from them the gold, all crafted articles. And all the gold of the contribution that they presented to the LORD, from the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, was 16,750 shekels. (The men in the army had each taken plunder for himself.) And Moses and Eleazar the priest received the gold from the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and brought it into the tent of meeting, as a memorial for the people of Israel before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers come with a report and an offering, and both are remarkable. Twelve thousand men went out against five kings and twelve thousand came back. In an ancient war that is not luck, and they did not think it was.

Then the surprising part: they bring their gold to make atonement for ourselves before the LORD. Not thanksgiving, atonement. They had lost nobody, and their instinct was that they needed covering. These men had spent a week outside the camp being sprinkled, and had understood: coming home alive is not a verdict on your worthiness. Twenty-four thousand had died at Peor and these had not, and the difference was mercy.

The gold was laid up in the tent of meeting as a memorial, not spent. So the last act of the last war Moses ordered was a pile of enemy jewellery in the tabernacle, put there by soldiers who could say nothing except that they had been spared and had not earned it. There is no better posture for anyone who has come through something they did not deserve to come through.

32.title: The Tribes East of Jordan: The Danger of Settling for Less
32.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the people of Reuben and the people of Gad had a very great number of livestock. And they saw the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead, and behold, the place was a place for livestock.<sup>2</sup>So the people of Gad and the people of Reuben came and said to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the chiefs of the congregation,<sup>3</sup>"Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon,<sup>4</sup>the land that the LORD struck down before the congregation of Israel, is a land for livestock, and your servants have livestock."<sup>5</sup>And they said, "If we have found favor in your sight, let this land be given to your servants for a possession. Do not take us across the Jordan."<sup>6</sup>But Moses said to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben, "Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here?<sup>7</sup>Why will you discourage the heart of the people of Israel from going over into the land that the LORD has given them?<sup>8</sup>Your fathers did this, when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to see the land.<sup>9</sup>For when they went up to the Valley of Eshcol and saw the land, they discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land that the LORD had given them.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD's anger was kindled on that day, and he swore, saying,<sup>11</sup>'Surely none of the men who came up out of Egypt, from twenty years old and upward, shall see the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, because they have not wholly followed me,<sup>12</sup>none except Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and Joshua the son of Nun, for they have wholly followed the LORD.'<sup>13</sup>And the LORD's anger was kindled against Israel, and he made them wander in the wilderness forty years, until all the generation that had done evil in the sight of the LORD was gone.<sup>14</sup>And behold, you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the LORD against Israel!<sup>15</sup>For if you turn away from following him, he will again abandon them in the wilderness, and you will destroy all this people."<sup>16</sup>Then they came near to him and said, "We will build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones,<sup>17</sup>but we will take up arms, ready to go before the people of Israel, until we have brought them to their place. And our little ones shall live in the fortified cities because of the inhabitants of the land.<sup>18</sup>We will not return to our homes until each of the people of Israel has gained his inheritance.<sup>19</sup>For we will not inherit with them on the other side of the Jordan and beyond, because our inheritance has come to us on this side of the Jordan to the east."<sup>20</sup>So Moses said to them, "If you will do this, if you will take up arms to go before the LORD for the war,<sup>21</sup>and every armed man of you will pass over the Jordan before the LORD, until he has driven out his enemies from before him<sup>22</sup>and the land is subdued before the LORD; then after that you shall return and be free of obligation to the LORD and to Israel, and this land shall be your possession before the LORD.<sup>23</sup>But if you will not do so, behold, you have sinned against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out.<sup>24</sup>Build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep, and do what you have promised."<sup>25</sup>And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben said to Moses, "Your servants will do as my lord commands.<sup>26</sup>Our little ones, our wives, our livestock, and all our cattle shall remain there in the cities of Gilead,<sup>27</sup>but your servants will pass over, every man who is armed for war, before the LORD to battle, as my lord orders."<sup>28</sup>So Moses gave command concerning them to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel.<sup>29</sup>And Moses said to them, "If the people of Gad and the people of Reuben, every man who is armed to battle before the LORD, will pass with you over the Jordan and the land shall be subdued before you, then you shall give them the land of Gilead for a possession.<sup>30</sup>However, if they will not pass over with you armed, they shall have possessions among you in the land of Canaan."<sup>31</sup>And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben answered, "What the LORD has said to your servants, we will do.<sup>32</sup>We will pass over armed before the LORD into the land of Canaan, and the possession of our inheritance shall remain with us beyond the Jordan."<sup>33</sup>And Moses gave to them, to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben and to the half-tribe of Manasseh the son of Joseph, the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, the land and its cities with their territories, the cities of the land throughout the country.<sup>34</sup>And the people of Gad built Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer,<sup>35</sup>Atroth-shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah,<sup>36</sup>Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran, fortified cities, and folds for sheep.<sup>37</sup>And the people of Reuben built Heshbon, Elealeh, Kiriathaim,<sup>38</sup>Nebo, and Baal-meon (their names were changed), and Sibmah. And they gave other names to the cities that they built.<sup>39</sup>And the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead and captured it, and dispossessed the Amorites who were in it.<sup>40</sup>And Moses gave Gilead to Machir the son of Manasseh, and he settled in it.<sup>41</sup>And Jair the son of Manasseh went and captured their villages, and called them Havvoth-jair.<sup>42</sup>And Nobah went and captured Kenath and its villages, and called it Nobah, after his own name.
32.overview:
At the edge of the Promised Land, Reuben and Gad, owners of great herds, look at the rich grazing east of the Jordan and ask to settle there, short of the inheritance across the river. Moses is troubled, for it echoes the sin that doomed the previous generation: reluctance to enter the land God had given.

His rebuke is sharp, because he fears a repeat of Kadesh-barnea, where unbelief spread like a contagion. The danger is not always open rebellion; sometimes it is quiet contentment with a lesser good that keeps us from the greater one God intends.

Yet the chapter resolves not in condemnation but in a covenant of responsibility. Reuben and Gad pledge that their fighting men will cross and fight alongside their brothers until the whole land is subdued. The people of God advance together, and no tribe may enjoy its rest while its brothers still fight. And the warning rings out as one of Scripture's most memorable lines: “Be sure your sin will find you out” (v. 23), sin pictured as a pursuer that tracks down the one who broke his word.
32.theology:
The danger of settling for less. Reuben and Gad nearly settle short of the inheritance. We are tempted to be content with a lesser good rather than press into the fullness God promises in Christ.

Solidarity in the battle. No tribe may enjoy rest while the brothers still fight. The people of God advance together, keeping faith with one another until the whole work is done.

Your sin will find you out. Sin is pictured as a pursuer on the road behind the promise-breaker. A broken vow before God is never left behind; it catches up.
32.examples:
Then: Reuben and Gad sought to settle east of the Jordan but were bound by covenant to fight alongside their brothers until all Israel received its inheritance.

Now: The inheritance across the river is already secured for you by Christ, who did not stop short for his own comfort; that is why you need not settle on the near bank. His Spirit is given to carry you on and to keep you faithful to your brothers and sisters in the battle. And where you have stopped short or broken your word, the sin that pursues you has a place to stop: it was laid on him, and it is answered by confession, not by hiding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Request of Reuben and Gad
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Reuben and Gad ask to settle in the grazing land east of the Jordan rather than cross into Canaan. Moses fears a repeat of the spies’ unbelief: a refusal to share in the conquest that would discourage the whole nation.
verseByVerse.theology: Moses’ alarm (vv.6-15) is that settling short of the promise, and leaving the brothers to fight alone, would “discourage the heart of the people” as the spies once did (v.7-9). The great sin of the wilderness generation was unbelief that would not enter and that spread its fear to others. The passage warns against contentment with a lesser inheritance and against a self-interest that abandons the family of God to struggle alone (cf. Gal 6:2, “bear one another’s burdens”).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses feared that seeking their own comfort while their brothers fought would repeat the spies’ sin and infect the whole camp with discouragement.

Now: beware a comfort that leaves your brothers to carry the battle alone. Christ bore your burden first, and so his people “bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the people of Reuben and the people of Gad had a very great number of livestock. And they saw the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead, and behold, the place was a place for livestock. So the people of Gad and the people of Reuben came and said to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the chiefs of the congregation, "Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon, the land that the LORD struck down before the congregation of Israel, is a land for livestock, and your servants have livestock." And they said, "If we have found favor in your sight, let this land be given to your servants for a possession. Do not take us across the Jordan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The order of the sentences is the whole diagnosis. The possessions come first, then the looking, then the wanting, then the request. Their case to Moses names nine towns and adds your servants have livestock, without one word about the promise to Abraham, their brothers or the crossing. It is built out of an inventory. Then the words that alarm Moses: Do not take us across the Jordan.

Be fair to them. This land was not forbidden; God had given it to Israel in chapter 21, and Moses will grant the request. Their situation was real: enormous herds and enormous grass. But something has quietly reversed. They had walked forty years toward a promise, and within sight of it asked to stop. The danger to a believer is seldom a decision to abandon God. It is the discovery of somewhere comfortable a few miles short, and the slow conversion of a stopping place into a home.
verseByVerse.note: Gilead lay east of the Jordan; Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh settled there.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben, "Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here? Why will you discourage the heart of the people of Israel from going over into the land that the LORD has given them? Your fathers did this, when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to see the land. For when they went up to the Valley of Eshcol and saw the land, they discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land that the LORD had given them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ question has been quoted in every generation since: Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here? He begins not with their motives but with the other ten tribes, who would cross into fortified cities with the same fighting spread over fewer shoulders.

His real fear is the next verse: what everyone else will conclude when crossing turns out to be optional. Then he names the precedent, Kadesh-barnea. Ten spies did not force anyone to do anything. They described their reluctance out loud, with conviction, and a nation went to pieces, at the cost of forty years and a generation of graves. Nobody in the church makes a purely private decision about how much of God’s call to obey. Somebody is always watching, taking the measure of what is apparently allowed.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD's anger was kindled on that day, and he swore, saying, 'Surely none of the men who came up out of Egypt, from twenty years old and upward, shall see the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, because they have not wholly followed me, none except Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and Joshua the son of Nun, for they have wholly followed the LORD.' And the LORD's anger was kindled against Israel, and he made them wander in the wilderness forty years, until all the generation that had done evil in the sight of the LORD was gone. And behold, you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the LORD against Israel! For if you turn away from following him, he will again abandon them in the wilderness, and you will destroy all this people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses retells the Kadesh story to men who were children when it happened and have lived under its sentence ever since. Look at the reason God gave, quoted twice: they have not wholly followed me, while Caleb and Joshua have wholly followed the LORD. The Hebrew means to fill up after him, to follow all the way. The condemned generation had not renounced God; they followed partially and stopped where it got frightening. Now two tribes propose to follow as far as the river.

Then the sharpest words in the chapter: a brood of sinful men. That is not measured diplomacy. Moses, nearly a hundred and twenty, has buried a generation and cannot bear to watch it begin again. And his charge, you will destroy all this people, holds two tribes responsible for what their choice would do to the other ten. There is no private discipleship in Scripture. If one member suffers, all suffer together (1 Cor. 12:26); none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself (Rom. 14:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Reuben and Gad pledge to arm and go ahead of their brothers, not returning until all Israel has its inheritance. Moses accepts, with the warning: “be sure your sin will find you out.”
verseByVerse.theology: The tribes’ pledge to fight alongside their brothers before enjoying their own rest resolves Moses’ concern: they will not abandon the family of God. Moses’ warning, “be sure your sin will find you out” (v.23), is a timeless truth — a broken vow, a shirked duty, will not stay hidden; God sees, and consequences follow (cf. Gal 6:7, “whatever one sows, that will he also reap”). Solidarity with the brothers and integrity of one’s word are the conditions of the blessing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the two tribes promised to fight for their brothers first and rest afterward, and were warned that a broken promise would surely find them out.

Now: God sees the vow we keep and the one we break; “whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7). The sin that finds us out can also be brought into the light by us, and there it meets mercy (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they came near to him and said, "We will build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones, but we will take up arms, ready to go before the people of Israel, until we have brought them to their place. And our little ones shall live in the fortified cities because of the inhabitants of the land. We will not return to our homes until each of the people of Israel has gained his inheritance. For we will not inherit with them on the other side of the Jordan and beyond, because our inheritance has come to us on this side of the Jordan to the east."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their reply is one of the best moments in the book. They do not argue or defend themselves against a brood of sinful men. They come nearer and improve the request: they will go not merely with their brothers but before them, in the front rank, and not return until every Israelite has his inheritance.

Take the measure of that. They already have their land; nothing on the far bank will ever be theirs. They commit themselves to years of war for the sole purpose of getting other families into fields they will never set foot in. Joshua records the discharge some seven years later: You have not forsaken your brothers these many days, down to this day, but have been careful to keep the charge of the LORD your God (Josh. 22:3).

That is what a Christian is called into: not securing his own standing and watching from the east bank, but crossing over for people whose inheritance will never be his. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others (Phil. 2:4), which Paul grounds at once in the mind of Christ, who did exactly that for us.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses said to them, "If you will do this, if you will take up arms to go before the LORD for the war, and every armed man of you will pass over the Jordan before the LORD, until he has driven out his enemies from before him and the land is subdued before the LORD; then after that you shall return and be free of obligation to the LORD and to Israel, and this land shall be your possession before the LORD. But if you will not do so, behold, you have sinned against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out. Build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep, and do what you have promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses accepts, spelling out the terms with a lawyer’s precision, and then gives the warning that has passed into the language and is usually quoted wrongly: be sure your sin will find you out.

It is often heard as “your secret sins will come to light,” which the Bible says elsewhere (Luke 12:2), but not here. Here the sin is a pursuer. A broken promise will hunt down the man who broke it: not a stain waiting to be discovered but a creditor on the road behind you who knows your name. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal. 6:7). For the Christian there is one place that pursuer is stopped: the cross, where Christ, who kept every word, took the debt of those who had not. A believer outruns his sin not by speed but by turning round and confessing it.

Then a small, easily missed correction. They had said sheepfolds first, then cities for the children. Moses gives them back their own sentence reversed: Build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep. Not a syllable of rebuke, just the words rearranged, and any man who has let his work take precedence over his family knows what has been done to him in that verse.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben said to Moses, "Your servants will do as my lord commands. Our little ones, our wives, our livestock, and all our cattle shall remain there in the cities of Gilead, but your servants will pass over, every man who is armed for war, before the LORD to battle, as my lord orders." So Moses gave command concerning them to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel. And Moses said to them, "If the people of Gad and the people of Reuben, every man who is armed to battle before the LORD, will pass with you over the Jordan and the land shall be subdued before you, then you shall give them the land of Gilead for a possession. However, if they will not pass over with you armed, they shall have possessions among you in the land of Canaan." And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben answered, "What the LORD has said to your servants, we will do. We will pass over armed before the LORD into the land of Canaan, and the possession of our inheritance shall remain with us beyond the Jordan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The agreement is not left as a handshake. Moses commits it to Eleazar, Joshua and the tribal heads, restates the terms before them, and defines the penalty: if they do not cross armed, they forfeit the east bank and take their chances with everyone else in Canaan. It is witnessed, binding, and enforceable after Moses is dead.

That is not cynicism about their sincerity but realism about human memory. Good intentions expressed in a moment of conviction thin out over seven years of war with your family on the other side of a river. Reuben and Gad were helped by having their promise put beyond the reach of their own later feelings, which is why God gives his people vows, covenants and public ceremonies rather than leaving everything to the state of the heart on the day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–42 — The Settlement of the Transjordan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land east of the Jordan is given to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, who build and fortify their cities, still bound to cross over and fight for the rest.
verseByVerse.theology: The settlement (vv.33-42) records the fulfillment of the agreement — land granted, cities built, on the understanding that the pledge will be honored. It shows God accommodating the real circumstances of his people while holding them to their commitments. The Transjordan tribes would later be commended for keeping their word (Josh 22:1-4), a reminder that faithfulness to promises made before God is not optional.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the eastern tribes received and built their inheritance — bound still by their promise to fight for their brothers before enjoying it.

Now: God grants us much, and holds us to our commitments. Received blessing does not release us from promised duty; faithfulness follows us into our rest.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses gave to them, to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben and to the half-tribe of Manasseh the son of Joseph, the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, the land and its cities with their territories, the cities of the land throughout the country. And the people of Gad built Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer, Atroth-shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah, Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran, fortified cities, and folds for sheep. And the people of Reuben built Heshbon, Elealeh, Kiriathaim, Nebo, and Baal-meon (their names were changed), and Sibmah. And they gave other names to the cities that they built.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An easily missed detail: they rebuild Nebo and Baal-meon (their names were changed) and give other names to the cities they built. Most likely the old names were the problem. Nebo was a Babylonian god, and Baal-meon carried Baal’s name. These families had just watched twenty-four thousand die at Baal of Peor, and would not raise their children under that name. God had said, make no mention of the names of other gods, nor let it be heard on your lips (Exod. 23:13), and they took him seriously enough to repaint the signposts.

Taking possession of anything for God involves that kind of renaming. A believer inherits a family, a business, a set of habits, and finds somebody else’s name over the door. Leaving it up because it was there first is how a place quietly stays what it always was.

Why is half of Manasseh here? Machir’s clan had already taken Gilead (vv. 39–42), and Moses gave it to them; the rest of Manasseh settled west of the Jordan (Josh 17).

verseByVerse.quote: And the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead and captured it, and dispossessed the Amorites who were in it. And Moses gave Gilead to Machir the son of Manasseh, and he settled in it. And Jair the son of Manasseh went and captured their villages, and called them Havvoth-jair. And Nobah went and captured Kenath and its villages, and called it Nobah, after his own name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with three men and their conquests, and the tribes east of the Jordan are home.

Was it a mistake? Scripture does not say so, and we should not say more than Scripture. Moses granted it, God permitted it, and Joshua later commended these men in the warmest terms for keeping every word of the bargain (Josh. 22:2–4). But the later history is sober reading. The eastern tribes were outside the river that protected everybody else, first in the path of every invasion from the east, and when the Assyrian came it was Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh who went into exile first (1 Chr. 5:26). Good grass, and no river in front of it. There is nothing here to condemn and a great deal to think about, and the chapter leaves it exactly there.

What it does not leave in doubt is the promise they made and kept. They crossed a river they did not need to cross and stayed until every family in Israel stood on its own ground. That is the shape, in small, of something far greater. An elder Brother who possessed everything left it to fight for brothers whose inheritance he had no need of (Philippians 2:6–8; Hebrews 2:10–11). He has won it, and says what he is doing now: I go to prepare a place for you… I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also (John 14:2–3). He will not count the work finished until every one of his brothers is home.
verseByVerse.note: “Havvoth-jair” means “the villages of Jair” (ESV note).

33.title: The Stages of the Journey: Every Step Known to God
33.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the stages of the people of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt by their companies under the leadership of Moses and Aaron.<sup>2</sup>Moses wrote down their starting places, stage by stage, by command of the LORD, and these are their stages according to their starting places.<sup>3</sup>They set out from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month. On the day after the Passover, the people of Israel went out triumphantly in the sight of all the Egyptians,<sup>4</sup>while the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn, whom the LORD had struck down among them. On their gods also the LORD executed judgments.<sup>5</sup>So the people of Israel set out from Rameses and camped at Succoth.<sup>6</sup>And they set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, which is on the edge of the wilderness.<sup>7</sup>And they set out from Etham and turned back to Pi-hahiroth, which is east of Baal-zephon, and they camped before Migdol.<sup>8</sup>And they set out from before Hahiroth and passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, and they went a three days' journey in the wilderness of Etham and camped at Marah.<sup>9</sup>And they set out from Marah and came to Elim; at Elim there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there.<sup>10</sup>And they set out from Elim and camped by the Red Sea.<sup>11</sup>And they set out from the Red Sea and camped in the wilderness of Sin.<sup>12</sup>And they set out from the wilderness of Sin and camped at Dophkah.<sup>13</sup>And they set out from Dophkah and camped at Alush.<sup>14</sup>And they set out from Alush and camped at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink.<sup>15</sup>And they set out from Rephidim and camped in the wilderness of Sinai.<sup>16</sup>And they set out from the wilderness of Sinai and camped at Kibroth-hattaavah.<sup>17</sup>And they set out from Kibroth-hattaavah and camped at Hazeroth.<sup>18</sup>And they set out from Hazeroth and camped at Rithmah.<sup>19</sup>And they set out from Rithmah and camped at Rimmon-perez.<sup>20</sup>And they set out from Rimmon-perez and camped at Libnah.<sup>21</sup>And they set out from Libnah and camped at Rissah.<sup>22</sup>And they set out from Rissah and camped at Kehelathah.<sup>23</sup>And they set out from Kehelathah and camped at Mount Shepher.<sup>24</sup>And they set out from Mount Shepher and camped at Haradah.<sup>25</sup>And they set out from Haradah and camped at Makheloth.<sup>26</sup>And they set out from Makheloth and camped at Tahath.<sup>27</sup>And they set out from Tahath and camped at Terah.<sup>28</sup>And they set out from Terah and camped at Mithkah.<sup>29</sup>And they set out from Mithkah and camped at Hashmonah.<sup>30</sup>And they set out from Hashmonah and camped at Moseroth.<sup>31</sup>And they set out from Moseroth and camped at Bene-jaakan.<sup>32</sup>And they set out from Bene-jaakan and camped at Hor-haggidgad.<sup>33</sup>And they set out from Hor-haggidgad and camped at Jotbathah.<sup>34</sup>And they set out from Jotbathah and camped at Abronah.<sup>35</sup>And they set out from Abronah and camped at Ezion-geber.<sup>36</sup>And they set out from Ezion-geber and camped in the wilderness of Zin (that is, Kadesh).<sup>37</sup>And they set out from Kadesh and camped at Mount Hor, on the edge of the land of Edom.<sup>38</sup>And Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the command of the LORD and died there, in the fortieth year after the people of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, on the first day of the fifth month.<sup>39</sup>And Aaron was 123 years old when he died on Mount Hor.<sup>40</sup>And the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb in the land of Canaan, heard of the coming of the people of Israel.<sup>41</sup>And they set out from Mount Hor and camped at Zalmonah.<sup>42</sup>And they set out from Zalmonah and camped at Punon.<sup>43</sup>And they set out from Punon and camped at Oboth.<sup>44</sup>And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the territory of Moab.<sup>45</sup>And they set out from Iyim and camped at Dibon-gad.<sup>46</sup>And they set out from Dibon-gad and camped at Almon-diblathaim.<sup>47</sup>And they set out from Almon-diblathaim and camped in the mountains of Abarim, before Nebo.<sup>48</sup>And they set out from the mountains of Abarim and camped in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho;<sup>49</sup>they camped by the Jordan from Beth-jeshimoth as far as Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab.<sup>50</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying,<sup>51</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you pass over the Jordan into the land of Canaan,<sup>52</sup>then you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you and destroy all their figured stones and destroy all their metal images and demolish all their high places.<sup>53</sup>And you shall take possession of the land and settle in it, for I have given the land to you to possess it.<sup>54</sup>You shall inherit the land by lot according to your clans. To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance. Wherever the lot falls for anyone, that shall be his. According to the tribes of your fathers you shall inherit.<sup>55</sup>But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those of them whom you let remain shall be as barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides, and they shall trouble you in the land where you dwell.<sup>56</sup>And I will do to you as I thought to do to them."
33.overview:
Chapter 33 is a travelogue: every place Israel camped from Egypt to the plains of Moab, forty-two stages in all. To the casual reader it is a dry list of unpronounceable names. But God commanded it to be recorded, and in that lies a deep comfort: every stage, every campsite, every weary mile was known to God and noted by him.

Some names recall great deliverances, some bitter failures: Taberah where the fire fell, Kibroth-hattaavah where the cravers were buried, Kadesh where the spies brought their faithless report. The whole forty years are gathered up here, held in his hand.

So the list becomes personal. The journey began with the blood of the Passover lamb, and Christian pilgrims know who that Lamb is (1 Corinthians 5:7). “You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book?” (Psalm 56:8). The God who brought Israel to the edge of Canaan is bringing his people home, and he knows the way they take.
33.theology:
Every stage known to God. God commanded the itinerary recorded, for every campsite of the journey was known and noted by him. Not one mile of the pilgrimage is lost or forgotten.

The redeemed are pilgrims. The rhythm of setting out and camping marks a people always on the move toward the promise, led by God from redemption to inheritance.

Wholehearted obedience. The idols not removed become thorns; sin tolerated becomes a snare. God's people are called to put to death the sins they are tempted to spare.
33.examples:
Then: God commanded Moses to record every stage of Israel's journey, from the deliverance in Egypt to the plains of Moab, every campsite known and noted by the Lord.

Now: Your life is such an itinerary. Every stage of your pilgrimage — the green pastures and the dark valleys, the joys and the failures — is known to God and held in his care. He has collected all your tears, and he is leading you, stage by stage, home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–49 — The Stages of the Journey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses writes down the whole itinerary, camp by camp, from Rameses to the plains of Moab. It is a record of every step God led his people, kept because not one stage was forgotten by him or outside his leading.
verseByVerse.theology: The recorded itinerary (vv.1-49) is a memorial of God’s faithful leading through every stage of the journey, the good camps and the bitter ones alike. That God had Moses write it all down testifies that he remembers the whole pilgrimage of his people — every step, every camp, every hardship (cf. Deut 8:2, “remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you”). None of it was aimless; the God who led by cloud and fire (9:15-23) was writing a purposeful story, stage by stage, all the way home.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: forty years of wandering were recorded camp by camp — every stage of the hard road kept in God’s remembrance.

Now: God remembers every stage of your journey too — the green pastures and the bitter waters alike. Look back and “remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you” (Deut 8:2); none of it was wasted or forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the stages of the people of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt by their companies under the leadership of Moses and Aaron. Moses wrote down their starting places, stage by stage, by command of the LORD, and these are their stages according to their starting places. They set out from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month. On the day after the Passover, the people of Israel went out triumphantly in the sight of all the Egyptians, while the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn, whom the LORD had struck down among them. On their gods also the LORD executed judgments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a single place-name, the chapter says who commissioned the list: by command of the LORD. This is not a diary Moses kept for himself. An old man on the plains of Moab sat with a record of every place his people had pitched a tent, including the places named after failures and the stretches where nothing happened for years, and God said: put it all in. Nothing was too tedious or too shameful to keep.

And the record starts not in the wilderness but at a funeral in Egypt: Israel went out triumphantly while the Egyptians buried their firstborn. The first line of the itinerary is redemption by the blood of a lamb, with an empire in mourning behind them and its gods judged. Every stage that follows is the journey of a people who were bought out. So is every stage of yours; whatever else is on the list, the first entry is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people of Israel set out from Rameses and camped at Succoth. And they set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, which is on the edge of the wilderness. And they set out from Etham and turned back to Pi-hahiroth, which is east of Baal-zephon, and they camped before Migdol. And they set out from before Hahiroth and passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, and they went a three days' journey in the wilderness of Etham and camped at Marah. And they set out from Marah and came to Elim; at Elim there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there. And they set out from Elim and camped by the Red Sea. And they set out from the Red Sea and camped in the wilderness of Sin. And they set out from the wilderness of Sin and camped at Dophkah. And they set out from Dophkah and camped at Alush. And they set out from Alush and camped at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. And they set out from Rephidim and camped in the wilderness of Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The early stages come fast, and one of the greatest miracles of the Old Testament, passing through the midst of the sea, is entered between two campsites in the same tone as everything else.

Then Marah, where the water was bitter; then Elim, with twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, one of the very few descriptive details in the chapter, and a green one. Forty years later a man writing an itinerary still remembered the shade at Elim.

Read the two together, because they came one after the other and always do. God does not run his people through Marah because he has nothing better, nor park them at Elim because the journey is over. The line under each entry is identical: and they set out. Nobody stays at Elim. Nobody stays at Marah either.

verseByVerse.quote: And they set out from the wilderness of Sinai and camped at Kibroth-hattaavah. And they set out from Kibroth-hattaavah and camped at Hazeroth. And they set out from Hazeroth and camped at Rithmah. And they set out from Rithmah and camped at Rimmon-perez. And they set out from Rimmon-perez and camped at Libnah. And they set out from Libnah and camped at Rissah. And they set out from Rissah and camped at Kehelathah. And they set out from Kehelathah and camped at Mount Shepher. And they set out from Mount Shepher and camped at Haradah. And they set out from Haradah and camped at Makheloth. And they set out from Makheloth and camped at Tahath. And they set out from Tahath and camped at Terah. And they set out from Terah and camped at Mithkah. And they set out from Mithkah and camped at Hashmonah. And they set out from Hashmonah and camped at Moseroth. And they set out from Moseroth and camped at Bene-jaakan. And they set out from Bene-jaakan and camped at Hor-haggidgad. And they set out from Hor-haggidgad and camped at Jotbathah. And they set out from Jotbathah and camped at Abronah. And they set out from Abronah and camped at Ezion-geber. And they set out from Ezion-geber and camped in the wilderness of Zin (that is, Kadesh). And they set out from Kadesh and camped at Mount Hor, on the edge of the land of Edom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-two verses pass in which almost nothing is said: name after name, most mentioned nowhere else in the Bible and located on no map we possess. This is what the wilderness years actually consisted of.

A few names still carry their stories. Kibroth-hattaavah means “graves of craving,” where the people demanded meat and were buried in it (11:34). Hazeroth is where Miriam and Aaron turned on Moses (12:1). Verse 36 reaches Kadesh, where the whole thing went wrong.

But most of the list is unremarkable, and that is its value.
