Between the disasters and deliverances lay years of ordinary marching that produced no story, and God had every camp written into his book. The stretches of a life in which nothing happens are not gaps in the record. They are the record. He was there at Rithmah too.

verseByVerse.quote: And Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the command of the LORD and died there, in the fortieth year after the people of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, on the first day of the fifth month. And Aaron was 123 years old when he died on Mount Hor. And the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb in the land of Canaan, heard of the coming of the people of Israel. And they set out from Mount Hor and camped at Zalmonah. And they set out from Zalmonah and camped at Punon. And they set out from Punon and camped at Oboth. And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the territory of Moab. And they set out from Iyim and camped at Dibon-gad. And they set out from Dibon-gad and camped at Almon-diblathaim. And they set out from Almon-diblathaim and camped in the mountains of Abarim, before Nebo. And they set out from the mountains of Abarim and camped in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho; they camped by the Jordan from Beth-jeshimoth as far as Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only here does the list stop for a death, dating Aaron’s to the year, month and day, with his age. An itinerary of a whole nation halts for one man. God counts the stages, and he also counts the men who do not finish them.

From Mount Hor the road turns toward the river, and the list ends exactly where the reader is standing, on the plains of Moab. It ends on the wrong side of the water: forty years, and the final camp within sight of the land and not in it, where Numbers closes and Moses will die.

Hebrews reads the Old Testament this way: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Heb. 11:13). Every believer’s list ends at a riverbank of some sort, and no believer stands there alone: Jesus has gone ahead as forerunner (Hebrews 6:20), through death and out the other side. The question is not whether you get all the way in during this life, but whether God’s record of your stages is that of somebody who went out from Egypt and kept setting out.

His age fits Exodus 7:7, which makes him eighty-three when he first stood before Pharaoh. Deuteronomy 10:6 says Aaron died at Moserah. Moseroth was a camp nearby (33:30), and Mount Hor rose in that region; Deuteronomy names the area, Numbers the mountain.
verseByVerse.note: Aaron died aged 123, in the fortieth year.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands Israel to drive out the inhabitants of Canaan, destroy their idols, and divide the land by lot. Those they spare will become “barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides.”
verseByVerse.theology: The command to dispossess the Canaanites and destroy their idols (vv.51-53) guards Israel from the idolatry that would later ruin them. The warning that spared enemies become “barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides” (v.55) proved tragically true in Judges. It teaches the abiding principle that tolerated sin does not stay contained but festers and wounds — a lesson the New Testament applies to the sin we must put to death in ourselves (Col 3:5; Rom 8:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel was warned that the idolatry they tolerated would become thorns in their sides, and in Judges it happened exactly so.

Now: the sin we spare in ourselves does not stay quiet. But the call to “put to death… what is earthly in you” (Colossians 3:5) comes to people already raised with Christ, and it is “by the Spirit” that they do it (Romans 8:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you pass over the Jordan into the land of Canaan, then you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you and destroy all their figured stones and destroy all their metal images and demolish all their high places. And you shall take possession of the land and settle in it, for I have given the land to you to possess it. You shall inherit the land by lot according to your clans. To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance. Wherever the lot falls for anyone, that shall be his. According to the tribes of your fathers you shall inherit. But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those of them whom you let remain shall be as barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides, and they shall trouble you in the land where you dwell. And I will do to you as I thought to do to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter turns from history to command, and the command is total. Not tolerate, not regulate, not co-exist with: destroy. Israel had just watched twenty-four thousand of her own die because they were invited to the sacrificial feasts of Moab’s gods (25:2). God will not leave the shrines standing.

Then the warning Israel’s whole later history illustrates, in two images chosen with care. A barb in the eye: small, permanently painful, ruining your sight. A thorn in the side: out of reach, catching every time you move. Neither is fatal; both are unbearable, and neither goes away on its own. That is what a tolerated sin does to a believer. Judges 1 and 2 record Israel doing exactly what she was warned of, and Judges 2:3 quotes this verse back at her.

The last line is the most sobering: I will do to you as I thought to do to them. Israel had no immunity; if she took up the Canaanites’ sins, she would be judged for them, and the exile proved it. Being inside the covenant was never a licence; it was a calling. So Paul writes to Christians, Put to death therefore what is earthly in you (Col. 3:5): not manage it, put it to death. But he says it to people whose life is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3:3), who do it by the Spirit (Rom. 8:13). And Israel’s failure to finish the job, repeated in every believer, is the reason the gospel is good news: Christ fought sin to the end and never once made terms with it, and his obedience is counted to those who confess they have spared what they should have slain.

Was it just? This was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Gen 15:16; Deut 9:4–5), including child sacrifice (Deut 12:31), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Lev 18:24–28). It was a unique command, carried out through Israel at one moment in redemptive history. It is no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36), and the church’s weapons are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4).

The land was divided by lot so that no one could accuse Moses or Joshua of favouritism; God decided (Prov 16:33). The apostles’ use of the lot (Acts 1:26) came before the Spirit was given, and Christians now seek God’s will through Scripture, prayer and wise counsel.

34.title: The Boundaries of Canaan: The Specificity of God's Promise
34.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel, and say to them, When you enter the land of Canaan (this is the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance, the land of Canaan as defined by its borders),<sup>3</sup>your south side shall be from the wilderness of Zin alongside Edom, and your southern border shall run from the end of the Salt Sea on the east.<sup>4</sup>And your border shall turn south of the ascent of Akrabbim, and cross to Zin, and its limit shall be south of Kadesh-barnea. Then it shall go on to Hazar-addar, and pass along to Azmon.<sup>5</sup>And the border shall turn from Azmon to the Brook of Egypt, and its limit shall be at the sea.<sup>6</sup>"For the western border, you shall have the Great Sea and its coast. This shall be your western border.<sup>7</sup>"This shall be your northern border: from the Great Sea you shall draw a line to Mount Hor.<sup>8</sup>From Mount Hor you shall draw a line to Lebo-hamath, and the limit of the border shall be at Zedad.<sup>9</sup>Then the border shall extend to Ziphron, and its limit shall be at Hazar-enan. This shall be your northern border.<sup>10</sup>"You shall draw a line for your eastern border from Hazar-enan to Shepham.<sup>11</sup>And the border shall go down from Shepham to Riblah on the east side of Ain. And the border shall go down and reach to the shoulder of the Sea of Chinnereth on the east.<sup>12</sup>And the border shall go down to the Jordan, and its limit shall be at the Salt Sea. This shall be your land as defined by its borders all around."<sup>13</sup>Moses commanded the people of Israel, saying, "This is the land that you shall inherit by lot, which the LORD has commanded to give to the nine tribes and to the half-tribe.<sup>14</sup>For the tribe of the people of Reuben by fathers' houses and the tribe of the people of Gad by their fathers' houses have received their inheritance, and also the half-tribe of Manasseh.<sup>15</sup>The two tribes and the half-tribe have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, toward the sunrise."<sup>16</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>17</sup>"These are the names of the men who shall divide the land to you for inheritance: Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun.<sup>18</sup>You shall take one chief from every tribe to divide the land for inheritance.<sup>19</sup>These are the names of the men: Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh.<sup>20</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Simeon, Shemuel the son of Ammihud.<sup>21</sup>Of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad the son of Chislon.<sup>22</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Dan a chief, Bukki the son of Jogli.<sup>23</sup>Of the people of Joseph: of the tribe of the people of Manasseh a chief, Hanniel the son of Ephod.<sup>24</sup>And of the tribe of the people of Ephraim a chief, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan.<sup>25</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Zebulun a chief, Elizaphan the son of Parnach.<sup>26</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Issachar a chief, Paltiel the son of Azzan.<sup>27</sup>And of the tribe of the people of Asher a chief, Ahihud the son of Shelomi.<sup>28</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Naphtali a chief, Pedahel the son of Ammihud."<sup>29</sup>These are the men whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance for the people of Israel in the land of Canaan.
34.overview:
Before Israel has set foot in the land, God draws its borders, south, west, north and east, and names the leaders who will divide the inheritance among the tribes. God does not promise a vague, indefinite blessing; he defines the inheritance border by border, as a man marks out the deed to a property he is about to give.

The specificity is the point. This is not a hazy ideal but a surveyed, deeded inheritance, spoken of as already settled. The borders are drawn in advance because the gift is sure.

That comforts God's people in every age. The inheritance Christ has secured is as concrete as a surveyed land. Peter speaks of “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4), and Jesus himself has gone to prepare the place (John 14:2). The promise has edges, drawn by his own faithful hand.
34.theology:
The specificity of God's promise. God draws the borders before Israel enters. His promises are not vague but definite, with edges and dimensions, as sure as a surveyed and deeded inheritance.

A reserved inheritance. The defined land prefigures the inheritance imperishable and undefiled, kept in heaven for God's people (1 Pet 1:4). Christ goes to prepare a real and definite place.

Divine apportioning. The land is divided by lot and by appointed leaders. God sovereignly assigns each his portion, ordering the inheritance by his own faithful hand.
34.examples:
Then: Before Israel entered, God drew the borders of Canaan and appointed leaders to divide the inheritance, defining the promised land with precision.

Now: Your inheritance in Christ is not a vague hope but a definite reality. He has gone to prepare a real place for you, an inheritance kept in heaven, certain and secure.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Boundaries of the Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God traces the borders of the inheritance on every side. It is no vague promise but a real, bounded gift, mapped before Israel has set foot in it.
verseByVerse.theology: God defines the land’s boundaries in detail (vv.1-12) — the inheritance is concrete and certain, “the land... that shall fall to you for an inheritance” (v.2). What God promises he specifies; his gifts are not vague sentiments but definite realities. The earthly inheritance, carefully bounded, points to the sure and “imperishable” inheritance God has mapped out for his people in Christ (1 Pet 1:4; John 14:2, “I go to prepare a place for you”).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: before Israel crossed over, God had already drawn the borders of their home — a definite, promised place waiting for them.

Now: our inheritance is just as certain and just as prepared: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2). God’s promises have addresses, not just sentiments.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel, and say to them, When you enter the land of Canaan (this is the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance, the land of Canaan as defined by its borders), your south side shall be from the wilderness of Zin alongside Edom, and your southern border shall run from the end of the Salt Sea on the east. And your border shall turn south of the ascent of Akrabbim, and cross to Zin, and its limit shall be south of Kadesh-barnea. Then it shall go on to Hazar-addar, and pass along to Azmon. And the border shall turn from Azmon to the Brook of Egypt, and its limit shall be at the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things are remarkable here, and neither is the geography. The first is the tense. Israel does not own a square foot of this; there is a river in front of them and walled cities beyond it. Yet God speaks of it as settled, the land that shall fall to you, and does what a man does when a property is already his: he walks the boundary and names the corners.

The second is the precision. God gives not a land but a surveyed one, with a southern border defined to the wadi and named turning points. Vagueness is the mark of promises nobody intends to keep. A man who is actually going to hand over a field tells you where the fence runs.

The borders here are smaller than the river-to-river promise of Genesis 15:18, which David and Solomon’s rule reached (1 Kgs 4:21). Israel never fully occupied even these (Judg 1), through its own failure, not God’s.

Does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people and modern Israel? Dispensationalists hold that it does: God’s promise to Abraham’s physical descendants remains literal, with its borders, and awaits fulfilment. But Joshua says that Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed (Josh 21:45), and the New Testament widens the promise: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Rom 4:13), and the patriarchs looked for a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Heb 11:16). The land is fulfilled in Christ and the new creation his people will inherit (Matt 5:5). Faithful Christians differ on this. This commentary reads the land promise as widened in Christ because the New Testament itself widens it, while honouring brothers who hold the land promise still stands, and gladly agreeing with the many, Reformed believers among them, who expect a great future turning of the Jewish people to their Messiah (Romans 11:25–26).

verseByVerse.quote: "For the western border, you shall have the Great Sea and its coast. This shall be your western border. "This shall be your northern border: from the Great Sea you shall draw a line to Mount Hor. From Mount Hor you shall draw a line to Lebo-hamath, and the limit of the border shall be at Zedad. Then the border shall extend to Ziphron, and its limit shall be at Hazar-enan. This shall be your northern border. "You shall draw a line for your eastern border from Hazar-enan to Shepham. And the border shall go down from Shepham to Riblah on the east side of Ain. And the border shall go down and reach to the shoulder of the Sea of Chinnereth on the east. And the border shall go down to the Jordan, and its limit shall be at the Salt Sea. This shall be your land as defined by its borders all around."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Most of these places cannot now be located with confidence, and that does not matter for the point. They could be located then. This is a legal description of real estate, drawn before possession, and closed all around: there is no open side.

That is the certainty the New Testament gives a Christian’s inheritance. Peter, writing to people who owned little and were about to lose that, calls it an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Pet. 1:4). Kept: already under guard. Heaven is as definite as a surveyed coastline, and God speaks of it the way a man speaks of a deed he has already signed.
verseByVerse.note: The Great Sea is the Mediterranean; the Sea of Chinnereth is the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses commanded the people of Israel, saying, "This is the land that you shall inherit by lot, which the LORD has commanded to give to the nine tribes and to the half-tribe. For the tribe of the people of Reuben by fathers' houses and the tribe of the people of Gad by their fathers' houses have received their inheritance, and also the half-tribe of Manasseh. The two tribes and the half-tribe have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, toward the sunrise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes are not written out of Israel; their portion is recorded as already settled, and the map is drawn for everyone else. Two chapters ago they made a bargain, and here it is in the title deeds. God keeps the arrangements his people make before him.

Yet there is a wistful note. The land surveyed here is the land of Canaan, the promise proper, and the eastern portion is described only by where it lies in relation to somewhere else: beyond the Jordan, toward the sunrise. Their inheritance is real, granted by God. It is simply not inside these borders. Scripture does not moralise about it, and neither should we.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–29 — The Leaders Who Will Divide the Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names the men who will divide the land: Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and a chief from each tribe, so that the inheritance is shared out rightly by appointed, accountable leaders.
verseByVerse.theology: God appoints named, accountable leaders — a priest, a commander, and a representative from each tribe — to divide the inheritance (vv.17-29). The orderly distribution under appointed authority reflects God’s character as a God “of peace” and order (1 Cor 14:33), not confusion. Even the good work of sharing out the promise is done through God-ordained structures, that all may be done “decently and in order” (1 Cor 14:40).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the land was divided not by a free-for-all but by appointed leaders, so that every tribe received its due fairly.

Now: God still works through appointed, accountable leadership, and loves order over chaos. His good gifts are distributed rightly, “decently and in order” (1 Cor 14:40).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "These are the names of the men who shall divide the land to you for inheritance: Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun. You shall take one chief from every tribe to divide the land for inheritance. These are the names of the men: Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh. Of the tribe of the people of Simeon, Shemuel the son of Ammihud. Of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad the son of Chislon. Of the tribe of the people of Dan a chief, Bukki the son of Jogli. Of the people of Joseph: of the tribe of the people of Manasseh a chief, Hanniel the son of Ephod. And of the tribe of the people of Ephraim a chief, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan. Of the tribe of the people of Zebulun a chief, Elizaphan the son of Parnach. Of the tribe of the people of Issachar a chief, Paltiel the son of Azzan. And of the tribe of the people of Asher a chief, Ahihud the son of Shelomi. Of the tribe of the people of Naphtali a chief, Pedahel the son of Ammihud." These are the men whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance for the people of Israel in the land of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will not have the inheritance divided by an anonymous committee. Every man who will hold a measuring line over somebody else’s future is named, with the tribe he answers to. None of them could take a bribe or favour his clan without the whole nation knowing who did it. Accountability in God’s work is not a modern administrative virtue; it is written into the arrangements from the start.

And look at one name: Caleb the son of Jephunneh. Nearly forty years earlier he walked into this land as a spy and told a terrified nation let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it (13:30), and they picked up stones to kill him. He watched every man who disagreed with him die in the desert, one funeral at a time. Now, nearly eighty, he sits on the commission that will hand out the fields.

God had promised him this land when nobody else believed a word of it (14:24), and here the promise begins to be paid, in a list of surveyors. He is faithful to nations and to maps and to old men who were right and had to wait four decades to be shown it.

35.title: Cities of Refuge: A Place to Flee, a Death That Frees
35.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel to give to the Levites some of the inheritance of their possession as cities for them to dwell in. And you shall give to the Levites pasturelands around the cities.<sup>3</sup>The cities shall be theirs to dwell in, and their pasturelands shall be for their cattle and for their livestock and for all their beasts.<sup>4</sup>The pasturelands of the cities, which you shall give to the Levites, shall reach from the wall of the city outward a thousand cubits all around.<sup>5</sup>And you shall measure, outside the city, on the east side two thousand cubits, and on the south side two thousand cubits, and on the west side two thousand cubits, and on the north side two thousand cubits, the city being in the middle. This shall belong to them as pastureland for their cities.<sup>6</sup>"The cities that you give to the Levites shall be the six cities of refuge, where you shall permit the manslayer to flee, and in addition to them you shall give forty-two cities.<sup>7</sup>All the cities that you give to the Levites shall be forty-eight, with their pasturelands.<sup>8</sup>And as for the cities that you shall give from the possession of the people of Israel, from the larger tribes you shall take many, and from the smaller tribes you shall take few; each, in proportion to the inheritance that it inherits, shall give of its cities to the Levites."<sup>9</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan,<sup>11</sup>then you shall select cities to be cities of refuge for you, that the manslayer who kills any person without intent may flee there.<sup>12</sup>The cities shall be for you a refuge from the avenger, that the manslayer may not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment.<sup>13</sup>And the cities that you give shall be your six cities of refuge.<sup>14</sup>You shall give three cities beyond the Jordan, and three cities in the land of Canaan, to be cities of refuge.<sup>15</sup>These six cities shall be for refuge for the people of Israel, and for the stranger and for the sojourner among them, that anyone who kills any person without intent may flee there.<sup>16</sup>"But if he struck him down with an iron object, so that he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death.<sup>17</sup>And if he struck him down with a stone tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death.<sup>18</sup>Or if he struck him down with a wooden tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death.<sup>19</sup>The avenger of blood shall himself put the murderer to death; when he meets him, he shall put him to death.<sup>20</sup>And if he pushed him out of hatred or hurled something at him, lying in wait, so that he died,<sup>21</sup>or in enmity struck him down with his hand, so that he died, then he who struck the blow shall be put to death. He is a murderer. The avenger of blood shall put the murderer to death when he meets him.<sup>22</sup>"But if he pushed him suddenly without enmity, or hurled anything on him without lying in wait<sup>23</sup>or used a stone that could cause death, and without seeing him dropped it on him, so that he died, though he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm,<sup>24</sup>then the congregation shall judge between the manslayer and the avenger of blood, in accordance with these rules.<sup>25</sup>And the congregation shall rescue the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to his city of refuge to which he had fled, and he shall live in it until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil.<sup>26</sup>But if the manslayer shall at any time go beyond the boundaries of his city of refuge to which he fled,<sup>27</sup>and the avenger of blood finds him outside the boundaries of his city of refuge, and the avenger of blood kills the manslayer, he shall not be guilty of blood.<sup>28</sup>For he must remain in his city of refuge until the death of the high priest, but after the death of the high priest the manslayer may return to the land of his possession.<sup>29</sup>And these things shall be for a statute and rule for you throughout your generations in all your dwelling places.<sup>30</sup>"If anyone kills a person, the murderer shall be put to death on the evidence of witnesses. But no person shall be put to death on the testimony of one witness.<sup>31</sup>Moreover, you shall accept no ransom for the life of a murderer, who is guilty of death, but he shall be put to death.<sup>32</sup>And you shall accept no ransom for him who has fled to his city of refuge, that he may return to dwell in the land before the death of the high priest.<sup>33</sup>You shall not pollute the land in which you live, for blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it.<sup>34</sup>You shall not defile the land in which you live, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel."
35.overview:
Chapter 35 establishes the Levitical cities, and within them six cities of refuge, a provision rich with gospel meaning. In a society without police or prisons, where a slain man's blood was avenged by his nearest kinsman, the cities sheltered the one who had killed unintentionally until his case was judged. Here mercy and justice meet.

The balance is exact. The deliberate murderer found no refuge. But the one who killed by accident could flee and live. Deuteronomy 19:3 commands that the roads be prepared, and later Jewish tradition says they were kept clear and signposted, so the fleeing man might reach safety in time. God does not let murder go unpunished, and he provides shelter for the one overtaken by tragedy.

The deepest wonder is in verse 25: the manslayer must remain in the city “until the death of the high priest.” His freedom was secured by a death. Hebrews gives the language: those “who have fled for refuge” to “hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18). Christ is both the refuge and the High Priest. We have fled to him, and because he has died, we are free.
35.theology:
Justice and mercy meet. The cities of refuge shelter the unintentional manslayer without sparing the murderer. God is both righteous and gracious, providing safety without denying justice.

Christ our refuge. We have fled for refuge to hold fast to the hope set before us (Heb 6:18). Christ is the city to whom the guilt-stricken flee from the avenging justice of the law.

Freed by the high priest's death. The refugee's release came through the death of the high priest. Christ is both our refuge and our High Priest, whose own death secures our everlasting freedom.
35.examples:
Then: God appointed cities of refuge where the unintentional manslayer could flee from the avenger of blood and remain safe until the death of the high priest released him.

Now: Flee to Christ, your city of refuge, from the avenging justice of the law. He is both your refuge and your great High Priest, and because he has died, you are set free forever. You have run to him, and the door of mercy stands open.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites have no territory, for the LORD is their inheritance, so the other tribes give them forty-eight cities with pastureland, scattered throughout the land, so that the knowledge of God is never far from anyone in Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: The Levites, having no land-inheritance because “the LORD is their portion” (18:20), are given forty-eight cities distributed among all the tribes (vv.7-8). The scattering was strategic: those set apart for God’s service lived within reach of every Israelite, so that instruction in God’s law and the ministry of worship permeated the whole nation. It pictures how God means the knowledge of himself to saturate the life of his people, never confined to one corner (cf. Mal 2:7, the priest’s lips guarding knowledge).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the tribe devoted to God was spread through all the others, so no Israelite lived far from the ministry of the Word.

Now: God still means the knowledge of himself to permeate all of life, not stay walled off in one place. His servants are scattered as salt and light throughout the world (Matt 5:13-14).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying, "Command the people of Israel to give to the Levites some of the inheritance of their possession as cities for them to dwell in. And you shall give to the Levites pasturelands around the cities. The cities shall be theirs to dwell in, and their pasturelands shall be for their cattle and for their livestock and for all their beasts. The pasturelands of the cities, which you shall give to the Levites, shall reach from the wall of the city outward a thousand cubits all around. And you shall measure, outside the city, on the east side two thousand cubits, and on the south side two thousand cubits, and on the west side two thousand cubits, and on the north side two thousand cubits, the city being in the middle. This shall belong to them as pastureland for their cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites get no territory, and God will not therefore leave them homeless: they receive towns inside everyone else’s region, with pastureland measured round each.

A reader who checks the figures will find an apparent conflict: verse 4 gives a thousand cubits and verse 5 two thousand on each side. The usual explanation is simple: verse 4 measures outward from the wall, and verse 5 gives the length of each side of the resulting square. It is a surveyor’s description, though the exact layout is uncertain.

Look at what the arrangement does. Levi is not settled in a block but distributed, so that families throughout the nation lived within reach of someone whose life was the law of God. Jacob had said on his deathbed what sounded like a curse: I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel (Gen. 49:7). The scattering came, and in God’s hands the punishment became the means by which a nation was taught. He does not always remove what he has pronounced. Sometimes he turns it round and uses it for good.

verseByVerse.quote: "The cities that you give to the Levites shall be the six cities of refuge, where you shall permit the manslayer to flee, and in addition to them you shall give forty-two cities. All the cities that you give to the Levites shall be forty-eight, with their pasturelands. And as for the cities that you shall give from the possession of the people of Israel, from the larger tribes you shall take many, and from the smaller tribes you shall take few; each, in proportion to the inheritance that it inherits, shall give of its cities to the Levites."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six of the forty-eight are cities of refuge, named first. The cities where a man could run for his life were priests’ towns. The fugitive arrived not at a garrison but among men whose business was the mercy and holiness of God. Sanctuary and instruction were put in the same place on purpose: a man running for his life would end up living among those best equipped to tell him why he was still alive.

The cost is spread by a rule that runs through Scripture: many cities from the larger tribes, few from the smaller, in proportion. Nobody gives the same; everybody gives proportionally. The New Testament applies it to Christian giving unaltered: if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have (2 Cor. 8:12).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six Levite cities become cities of refuge, where one who killed accidentally is safe from the avenger of blood until judged, and then until the high priest’s death sets him free. Through it all runs a solemn truth: bloodshed pollutes the land, and life is sacred to God.
verseByVerse.theology: The cities of refuge picture the gospel: a God-appointed place to flee where the guilty-yet-not-condemned are safe from the avenger — “we who have fled for refuge” (Heb 6:18). Most strikingly, the manslayer is freed to return home only at “the death of the high priest” (vv.25, 28): the high priest’s death releases him. So the death of our great High Priest sets us free (Heb 9:15). And the insistence that innocent blood “pollutes the land” which can be cleansed only by the blood of the one who shed it (vv.33-34) upholds the sanctity of life and the justice of God — justice fully satisfied at the cross, where the High Priest was himself the sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the manslayer lived safe inside the city of refuge, and was set free to go home only when the high priest died.

Now: we have fled for refuge to Christ, and the death of our High Priest is the very thing that sets us free (Heb 9:15). Run to him, and no accuser can reach you.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan, then you shall select cities to be cities of refuge for you, that the manslayer who kills any person without intent may flee there. The cities shall be for you a refuge from the avenger, that the manslayer may not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The institution needs its background. In a society with no police and no public prosecutor, pursuing a killer fell to the dead man’s nearest relative, the avenger of blood (goel haddam). That was not lawlessness; it was the only enforcement the ancient world had, and without it a man could be killed and nothing would happen.

But it had a terrible weakness. A grieving brother riding out on the day of the funeral is in no condition to distinguish murder from accident. Between the death and the vengeance there was nothing: no hearing, no evidence, no delay.

So God puts something in the gap: that the manslayer may not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment. More than three thousand years ago, God legislated a right to a hearing before execution. The whole purpose is to slow a killing down long enough for the facts to be established. That is God’s justice written into statute: not indifference to blood (the next paragraphs are ferocious about blood) but an absolute refusal to let a man die before anybody has found out what he did.
verseByVerse.note: Six cities of refuge sheltered someone who had killed accidentally, until trial.

verseByVerse.quote: And the cities that you give shall be your six cities of refuge. You shall give three cities beyond the Jordan, and three cities in the land of Canaan, to be cities of refuge. These six cities shall be for refuge for the people of Israel, and for the stranger and for the sojourner among them, that anyone who kills any person without intent may flee there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three cities each side of the Jordan, spread so that a man could reach one in time: God arranged the map around the speed of a frightened human being.

Then a clause this book keeps repeating: the cities are for Israel and for the stranger and for the sojourner among them. The foreigner gets the same protection on the same terms. The water of cleansing was for the stranger who sojourns among them (19:10); the offerings were one statute for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you (15:15); now the refuge. Long before any Gentile had heard of him, the God of Israel had written the outsider into the emergency provisions of his law. When Paul writes that Christ has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility (Eph. 2:14), it is not a change of mind but the finishing of something begun here.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if he struck him down with an iron object, so that he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death. And if he struck him down with a stone tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death. Or if he struck him down with a wooden tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death. The avenger of blood shall himself put the murderer to death; when he meets him, he shall put him to death. And if he pushed him out of hatred or hurled something at him, lying in wait, so that he died, or in enmity struck him down with his hand, so that he died, then he who struck the blow shall be put to death. He is a murderer. The avenger of blood shall put the murderer to death when he meets him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before mercy is extended, murder is defined with care, on two tracks. The first is the instrument: iron, stone or wood that could cause death. A man who swings an iron bar at somebody’s head has told you what he intended, whatever he says afterwards.

The second is the heart, stated three ways in two verses: hatred, lying in wait, enmity. God’s law is not content to establish that a death occurred; it goes after what the man wanted and how long he had wanted it.

The distinction between murder and manslaughter, on which Western law still turns, is not an obvious idea, and few ancient codes drew it so carefully. It is here because the God who gave the law reads motives. And he takes it further, into a place no court can reach: everyone who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). The law of Moses could reach only the hand. Jesus went for the enmity that puts the weapon in it, and then bore on the cross the guilt of every heart he exposed.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if he pushed him suddenly without enmity, or hurled anything on him without lying in wait or used a stone that could cause death, and without seeing him dropped it on him, so that he died, though he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm, then the congregation shall judge between the manslayer and the avenger of blood, in accordance with these rules.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The other case is written with unusual tenderness. Three tests, each looking inside the man rather than at the corpse: no enmity, no lying in wait, no desire for his harm. And the picture in the middle is utterly ordinary: a man with a stone in his hands, somebody below he never saw. It took a second, and a man is dead.

This is the passage for anyone who has caused a death: the driver at the junction, the doctor who missed it, the parent who looked away for the length of a phone call. People carry these for decades under the same accusation: “you are a killer.” God’s law had a different category for them. It did not pretend nothing had happened: a life was gone, and the man went into exile for years. But it said: this is not murder, you are not a murderer, and there is a place for you where the accuser cannot reach you.

And who decides? The congregation shall judge: not the frightened man, who would always plead accident, nor the grieving man, who would always call it murder, but God’s assembly, hearing both, at a distance from the grave. Mercy in Scripture is never a failure to look at the facts. It is what the facts turn out to allow, once somebody has heard them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the congregation shall rescue the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to his city of refuge to which he had fled, and he shall live in it until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil. But if the manslayer shall at any time go beyond the boundaries of his city of refuge to which he fled, and the avenger of blood finds him outside the boundaries of his city of refuge, and the avenger of blood kills the manslayer, he shall not be guilty of blood. For he must remain in his city of refuge until the death of the high priest, but after the death of the high priest the manslayer may return to the land of his possession.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence is like nothing else in the law. No fine, no fixed term, no labour: he lives in the city until the death of the high priest. His freedom hangs on one man’s life ending, next week or in forty years, and nothing he does affects it. The reason is not arbitrary. The high priest stood for the whole nation before God, bearing the tribal names over his heart and making atonement for the people. When he died an era closed, and, as the law itself implies, the outstanding blood-guilt died with him. It took a death to release the man: not his own, not the victim’s, but the priest’s.

Christians have long seen Christ here, with good reason. We who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us (Heb. 6:18) is written in the language of this chapter by a man whose whole letter is about a High Priest. Ours has died, and every soul who has run to him is free, not by serving out a term or by improving, but because the sentence went into the ground with him. And here the picture breaks toward glory: the manslayer’s release came by an accident of timing, from a priest who never knew his name. Ours died on purpose, knowing exactly who we were and what we had done, and calling it love. And unlike every priest of Aaron’s line, he did not stay dead: he holds his priesthood permanently and always lives to intercede for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:24–25), so the release can never be undone.

The warning attached is severe: a manslayer who goes beyond the city’s boundaries may be killed, and the avenger shall not be guilty of blood. Inside the wall, untouchable; one step outside, unprotected. That is the gospel’s comfort and seriousness together. There is complete safety in Christ and none anywhere else, and the man who wanders out to see whether the old country is still there has left the only place where he cannot be reached. Abide in me, and I in you (John 15:4).
verseByVerse.note: The manslayer went free at the high priest’s death.

verseByVerse.quote: And these things shall be for a statute and rule for you throughout your generations in all your dwelling places. "If anyone kills a person, the murderer shall be put to death on the evidence of witnesses. But no person shall be put to death on the testimony of one witness. Moreover, you shall accept no ransom for the life of a murderer, who is guilty of death, but he shall be put to death. And you shall accept no ransom for him who has fled to his city of refuge, that he may return to dwell in the land before the death of the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two prohibitions close the legal section, both about money. First, no ransom for a murderer. In much of the ancient world a killing could be settled by payment, and a rich man could afford a death. Israel forbade it, because of what a human being is: Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image (Gen. 9:6). The law will not put a price on the image of God at any figure.

Second, no ransom for the manslayer to go home early. The system cannot be bought at either end.

Hold those two verses and then read this: The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). God had declared in his own law that for a life like ours no ransom would be accepted. Then the only ransom he would ever take, he provided himself, at the price of his own Son. You were ransomed… not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet. 1:18–19). It was never going to be money.

Does the death penalty for murder still apply? The civil law of Israel ended with its theocracy, but the command to punish murder came earlier, to all mankind (Gen 9:6), and Paul says the ruler does not bear the sword in vain (Rom 13:4). Some Christians hold that the death penalty has no place in a modern state, and faithful believers differ here. The better reading is that the state retains the right to take the life of a murderer, used with due process and certain guilt; whether it does so is for just rulers. And no one may be condemned on one witness (v. 30): the two-witness rule protects against false accusation, and the New Testament applies it to church discipline (2 Cor 13:1; 1 Tim 5:19).

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not pollute the land in which you live, for blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it. You shall not defile the land in which you live, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends by saying why all this mattered. Blood soaks into ground and stays: not a legal fiction but a stain that ceremony, payment and time cannot wash out. So it has been since the first murder: the voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground (Gen. 4:10).

And the reason the land must be kept clean is the reason for everything in the book: I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel. Not visits; dwells. The camp arranged around a tent, the Levites ringing it, the cleansing of the death-defiled, the refuge cities, the boundaries, all exist for that clause. A God who lives among people has views about the ground they live on.

So the book that opened by arranging a camp around God’s dwelling closes its law with blood crying out of the ground. There is one place in Scripture where that voice is answered. The church has come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Heb. 12:24). Abel’s blood cried for justice and could not be quieted. Christ’s blood was poured out on the same cursed ground, and what it says is not “avenge” but “forgive.” The Priest has died. The refuge is open, and its door is a Person.

36.title: The Inheritance Preserved: God's Faithfulness to the Last Detail
36.text: <sup>1</sup>The heads of the fathers' houses of the clan of the people of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of the people of Joseph, came near and spoke before Moses and before the chiefs, the heads of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>They said, "The LORD commanded my lord to give the land for inheritance by lot to the people of Israel, and my lord was commanded by the LORD to give the inheritance of Zelophehad our brother to his daughters.<sup>3</sup>But if they are married to any of the sons of the other tribes of the people of Israel, then their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of our fathers and added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry. So it will be taken away from the lot of our inheritance.<sup>4</sup>And when the jubilee of the people of Israel comes, then their inheritance will be added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry, and their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of the tribe of our fathers."<sup>5</sup>And Moses commanded the people of Israel according to the word of the LORD, saying, "The tribe of the people of Joseph is right.<sup>6</sup>This is what the LORD commands concerning the daughters of Zelophehad: 'Let them marry whom they think best, only they shall marry within the clan of the tribe of their father.<sup>7</sup>The inheritance of the people of Israel shall not be transferred from one tribe to another, for every one of the people of Israel shall hold on to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers.<sup>8</sup>And every daughter who possesses an inheritance in any tribe of the people of Israel shall be wife to one of the clan of the tribe of her father, so that every one of the people of Israel may possess the inheritance of his fathers.<sup>9</sup>So no inheritance shall be transferred from one tribe to another, for each of the tribes of the people of Israel shall hold on to its own inheritance.'"<sup>10</sup>The daughters of Zelophehad did as the LORD commanded Moses,<sup>11</sup>for Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married to sons of their father's brothers.<sup>12</sup>They were married into the clans of the people of Manasseh the son of Joseph, and their inheritance remained in the tribe of their father's clan.<sup>13</sup>These are the commandments and the rules that the LORD commanded through Moses to the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.
36.overview:
Numbers ends not with a thunderclap but with a quiet matter of inheritance law, and that quietness is a kind of glory. In chapter 27 the daughters of Zelophehad won the right to inherit their father's land. Now, if they marry into another tribe, the land will pass with them and the allotment will be disturbed. So God provides that they marry within their own tribe.

It seems a small thing on which to end a great book. But the God who split the sea and spoke from Sinai is also the God who cares about the preservation of a single family's portion. The book that began with the ordering of the people ends with the securing of their inheritance down to the last allotment.

And it has a voice in the Gospels: Jesus says it is his Father’s will that of all he has been given he should lose nothing, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39). The book that journeyed through grumbling, rebellion and judgment ends on God's unwavering faithfulness: the inheritance is preserved, and the God who keeps his word will bring his pilgrim people home, not losing one of them.
36.theology:
God's faithfulness in the smallest detail. The God who split the sea attends to the preservation of a single family's portion. No detail of his promise is too small for his meticulous care.

The inheritance preserved. God secures the allotment so that not one portion is lost, prefiguring the inheritance kept in heaven for those guarded by his power through faith (1 Pet 1:4–5).

Faithful obedience. The daughters obey God's word, and the book ends on trust and submission to the Lord's commandments, the people ordering their lives by his word.
36.examples:
Then: God secured the inheritance of Zelophehad's daughters within their own tribe, and the book ended with their faithful obedience on the plains of Moab.

Now: The God who ensured no tribe lost its portion guards your inheritance in Christ, down to the last detail. Not one of his promises will fail, and he will bring his pilgrim people home, losing none.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Keeping the Inheritance in the Tribe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A concern is raised: if Zelophehad’s daughters marry into another tribe, their father’s land will pass with them. God’s answer honours both the daughters’ rights and the tribes’ integrity, and the book closes with the land guarded, ready to be received.
verseByVerse.theology: The final chapter guards the inheritance so that “no inheritance shall be transferred from one tribe to another” (v.9) — God’s gifts are to be kept, not squandered or lost. That Numbers, a book of wandering and failure, ends fixed on the secure inheritance testifies to God’s unwavering faithfulness: despite forty years of rebellion, the promise stands, mapped, apportioned, and protected, waiting for the new generation. It points to the inheritance “kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet 1:4) that can never be lost, because God himself guards it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the book of wandering ends not in the desert but with the inheritance secured — every tribe’s portion guarded, the promise intact.

Now: our inheritance is guarded by God himself, “kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet 1:4). Despite all our wandering, the promise stands, and the land is ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: The heads of the fathers' houses of the clan of the people of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of the people of Joseph, came near and spoke before Moses and before the chiefs, the heads of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel. They said, "The LORD commanded my lord to give the land for inheritance by lot to the people of Israel, and my lord was commanded by the LORD to give the inheritance of Zelophehad our brother to his daughters. But if they are married to any of the sons of the other tribes of the people of Israel, then their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of our fathers and added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry. So it will be taken away from the lot of our inheritance. And when the jubilee of the people of Israel comes, then their inheritance will be added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry, and their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of the tribe of our fathers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book closes with a legal query, raised with scrupulous care. The heads of Gilead come openly before Moses and the chiefs, and they begin by reciting the earlier ruling, correctly, as the word of the LORD.

Their difficulty is real. If the daughters marry outside the tribe, the land goes with them permanently, because at the jubilee, when every field reverted to its original family, it would revert to the wrong family. The jubilee, designed to keep land in the clan for ever, would here lock the loss in.

They bring it to the leadership rather than to the women, and they do not object that the daughters got too much; they ask only how to keep the ruling from unravelling something else. That is what honest disagreement among God’s people looks like: a question asked openly, to the right people, about the consequences of a decision rather than the decision itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses commanded the people of Israel according to the word of the LORD, saying, "The tribe of the people of Joseph is right. This is what the LORD commands concerning the daughters of Zelophehad: 'Let them marry whom they think best, only they shall marry within the clan of the tribe of their father. The inheritance of the people of Israel shall not be transferred from one tribe to another, for every one of the people of Israel shall hold on to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers. And every daughter who possesses an inheritance in any tribe of the people of Israel shall be wife to one of the clan of the tribe of her father, so that every one of the people of Israel may possess the inheritance of his fathers. So no inheritance shall be transferred from one tribe to another, for each of the tribes of the people of Israel shall hold on to its own inheritance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are almost the words God used nine chapters earlier of the daughters themselves: The daughters of Zelophehad are right (27:7). The same verdict, to the other side. God had not made a mistake in chapter 27; he had made a ruling that raised a second question, and now answers that too.

And the answer costs neither party anything. The freedom comes first and the limit second: whom they think best, more choice than most women in the ancient world had, and then one boundary around it. The daughters keep the land and the choice; Manasseh keeps its allotment.

God is not obliged to settle every dispute by finding one party at fault. Sometimes two legitimate claims collide, and the answer is not a compromise in which everyone loses a little but a provision neither side had thought of. He can uphold the rights of five orphaned women and the integrity of a tribe at the same time, without shaving anything off either.

verseByVerse.quote: The daughters of Zelophehad did as the LORD commanded Moses, for Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married to sons of their father's brothers. They were married into the clans of the people of Manasseh the son of Joseph, and their inheritance remained in the tribe of their father's clan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last thing this book records about Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah and Noah is obedience. The women who walked to the front of a national assembly and pressed a claim nobody had ever granted now accept a restriction on whom they may marry, without a word of protest.

Both halves belong to the same character. It takes courage to tell Moses and the chiefs that the law as it stands is not right, and something as rare to hear God narrow your options afterward and comply. Faith that contends for what God has promised and then bows to how God orders it is a whole thing. A person who can only do the first is not brave, only wilful; one who can only do the second is not humble, only passive.

And they did not get less than they asked: their inheritance remained. Because five women asked, a man who had died in the wilderness still had a place among the people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the commandments and the rules that the LORD commanded through Moses to the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last verse of Numbers has no fanfare: no summary, no oration, no crossing. Just a map reference: by the Jordan at Jericho. On the wrong bank, in sight of the walls.

Consider how the book began: a census at Sinai, a nation drawn up in order around the tent of God, about to march eleven days to the promise. Then the quail and the graves of craving, ten spies and a night of weeping, forty years, Korah, the rock struck twice, Miriam buried, Aaron stripped on a mountain, the serpents, Peor, Moses told he may look and not enter. Numbers records a generation that could not be got into a land eleven days away.

Yet look at what stands on that riverbank. A nation as large as the one that left Sinai. A high priest in office and a commissioned leader with the Spirit in him. A calendar of worship, a law of refuge, a map with borders drawn, and five women whose title deeds are in order. Everything Israel deserved was a wilderness. Everything Israel has is a gift.

The book with the most human failure in the Pentateuch ends with not one promise of God cancelled by that failure. If we are faithless, he remains faithful—for he cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13). The reader is left on the near bank with the land in view, where every believer stands. He did not bring them through the wilderness to leave them at the water. Behind them the graves; in front of them the Jordan; over them the same pillar of cloud that had never once failed to move on ahead.
